added: 0 Skip to Content About Abby Issues Candidate Comparison Endorsements Volunteer Contribute Open Menu Close Menu About Abby Issues Candidate Comparison Endorsements Volunteer Contribute Open Menu Close Menu About Abby Issues Candidate Comparison Endorsements Volunteer Contribute At-A-Glance Download the comparison Need more reasons to say “NO” to Jahnelle Garcia this November?
Jahnelle has listed three different properties as her home, but only one is located in House District 27: a home on Walnut Creek.
The current resident of the Walnut Creek property says Jahnelle doesn’t live there.
He has lived at the property for over a year and continues to receive her mail, despite Jahnelle listing the address as her primary residence as recently as July.
Online property records show that Jahnelle’s real home is in Los Lunas, over 40 miles away from House District 27, where one of her private businesses operates.
Her third property is located on Albuquerque’s Westside in House District 68.
And Democrats and independents aren’t the only ones asking questions.
Even Republicans have called Jahnelle evasive and are considering filing their own complaint against her .
Jahnelle owes nearly $1 MILLION in federal tax liens Jahnelle Garcia has twice told the Albuquerque Journal that she has never been the subject of a tax lien, most recently on October 3rd, 2026 .
But records obtained from the Valencia County Clerk tell a different story.
Recently obtained documents reveal five tax assessments dating back to 2022, totaling nearly $1 million.

Date of Assessment Unpaid Balance of Assessment 11/21/2022 $29,080.51 11/24/2025 $467,640.77 12/08/2025 $199,508.99 12/08/2025 $145,519.35 05/04/2026 $154,807.70 Total: $996,557.32 And the IRS isn’t the only place Jahnelle owes money.
She’s also taken out almost $200,000 in loans to fund her campaign for House District 27.
If we can’t trust Jahnelle to manage her own money, how can we trust her with taxpayers’ money?
Jahnelle Garcia blatantly lied to the press and the public when she claimed she had never been subject to a tax lien.
And that’s in addition to the many lies she’s told about Abby Foster.
Jahnelle has accepted contributions from numerous groups tied to MAGA Republicans and insurance companies.

She frequently touts doctors as supporters of her campaign but doctors who have contributed to her, and the groups associated with them, have been linked to controversies involving botched medical procedures.
Many are Republicans who don’t live in House District 27 and New Mexico.
And her healthcare-industry donors raise even more questions.
Jahnelle’s campaign has accepted tens-of-thousands from healthcare corporations and PACs.
One of which, the New Mexico Hospital Association PAC , has opposed legislation establishing minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios and stronger oversight of hospital mergers and acquisitions.
Lifepoint Health PAC, operates a Memorial Medical Center in Las Cruces.
The hospital became the subject of a state investigation following allegations that cancer patients were denied treatment or required to pay upfront before receiving care.
These are the healthcare interests helping fund Jahnelle Garcia’s campaign.
Jahnelle has also accepted contributions from groups tied to attacks on universal childcare .

At a time when New Mexicans are struggling to pay their bills, Jahnelle has chosen to put herself in the pocket of interest that oppose policies intended to help middle and working-class families care for their children and loved ones.
Jahnelle also accepted money from a principal Albuquerque real estate company who faced allegations of workplace sexual harassment .
MAGA Jahnelle and her MAGA donors.
Jahnelle Garcia doesn’t think our laws apply to her.
A House District 27 voter recently filed an ethics complaint against Jahnelle Garcia for failing to include legally required disclaimers on her campaign signs.
Then, Friends of Abby Foster filed another ethics complaint with the Secretary of State, alleging Jahnelle used campaign funds to pay for advertisements promoting her private practice and business.
These campaign-funded online advertisements promoted her business, which sells facial contouring services and liquid IVs, and reached more than one million people.

She treats camping finance laws as mere suggestions and apparently believes she can use the money from her donors and her campaign loans to advertise her own business, attract new clients, and sell her so-called “healthcare” products.

“Albuquerque homeowner says Republican candidate doesn't live at contested address” Source NM Albuquerque, NM - September 28, 2026 Media contact: Deb Michel, Friends of Abby Foster Deputy Campaign Manager friendsofabbyfoster@gmail.com | 505-492-9004 VOTER FILES CAMPAIGN FINANCE COMPLAINT AGAINST JAHNELLE GARCIA Albuquerque, NM - Today, an HD27 voter filed a complaint with the State Ethics Commission alleging Republican nominee for HD27, Jahnelle Garcia, violated New Mexico campaign finance law by placing signs throughout the district without the legally required disclaimer identifying who authorized and paid for them.
New Mexico campaign finance law requires qualifying campaign advertising to disclose who authorized and paid for it.
According to the complaint, Garcia's campaign signs failed to include that basic disclosure.

She wants to manufacture controversy around donors that I have publicly, legally disclosed, while she doesn't follow fundamental election law." Foster said, "If she wants to make this race about transparency, she should start with her own campaign.
This is incredibly disappointing, but unfortunately it is a pattern," Foster added.
The complaint comes just weeks after controversy over Garcia's candidate filing address.

Garcia repeatedly listed an HD27 home as her residence in various campaign finance documents, even though the home's current owner told Source New Mexico's Patrick Lohmann that he had lived there for more than a year.
This is corroborated by property records listing Garcia's home in Los Lunas.
"Transparency isn't optional when you're asking the public to trust you." Foster continued, "Voters shouldn't have to investigate where a candidate actually lives.
They shouldn't have to wonder who paid for campaign ads.

And they shouldn't have to repeatedly ask whether a candidate followed basic election laws.' Foster said the recurring issues are particularly concerning because Garcia is seeking to be the next HD27 State Representative, where her job would be to understand and write state law.
"I've worked for the legislature and know firsthand that you must understand the law and be accountable to the people you want to represent.

Jahnelle keeps giving voters reasons to question her ability to do so." Foster continued, "At this point, I genuinely don't know which is worse: that Jahnelle doesn't understand basic laws or that she may understand them, but doesn't think they apply to her." #### Albuquerque, NM - October 5, 2026 Media contact: Deb Michel, Friends of Abby Foster Deputy Campaign Manager friendsofabbyfoster@gmail.com | 505-492-9004 GOP CANDIDATE FOR HD27 USED CAMPAIGN FUNDS TO ADVERTISE HER COMPANIES Albuquerque, NM - Jahnelle Garcia, the Republican nominee for State House Representative in District 27, faces yet another State Ethics Commission complaint, this time alleging that she used campaign funds to pay for social media advertisements promoting her own businesses.
The ad, paid for by the "Committee to Elect Jahnelle," contains no substantive policy content.
Its only written text lists Garcia as an entrepreneur and nurse practitioner and spotlights two of her businesses.
The complaint notes that Meta listed a potential audience of over one million people, which vastly exceeds the 23,000-person electorate of House District 27.
"The rules for campaign money are strict, and every treasurer is expected to follow them," said Julie Rochman, treasurer for Friends of Abby Foster.
"Jahnelle doesn't get a different set of rules.
Her campaign paid to promote her private companies to a massive audience.

At the very least, she must take accountability so that the voters and the donors who've supported her can see how she's using their funds." The New Mexico Campaign Reporting Act and Administrative Code limit how campaign contributions may be spent and prohibit the personal use of campaign funds.

The complaint points out that Garcia's businesses make up a substantial part of the advertisement, are not tied to any identifiable campaign proposal, and provide a commercial benefit to the companies associated with Garcia.
"People donate to a campaign to help a candidate share their ideas and earn votes," continued Rochman.
"Jahnelle used that money to show a million people ads for her businesses, which sell IV drips and weight loss treatments.
This is yet another illegal act by Jahnelle that violates New Mexico law." Garcia's campaign has drawn repeated questions about its compliance with election law.
Last week, a voter filed a separate complaint alleging that Garcia's campaign signs lacked the legally required disclaimer identifying who paid for them.

Garcia also came under scrutiny for listing an HD27 home as her residence on campaign finance documents, even though the home's current owner told Source New Mexico he had lived there for more than a year.
"These rules are not optional," Abby Foster, Garcia's opponent, stated.
"Jahnelle seems to think basic laws and requirements apply to everyone but her.

Our district deserves someone focused on serving our community, not using a political campaign to promote a business in Los Lunas." #### Feel free to review our sources: 1. https://login.cfis.sos.state.nm.us/#/exploreDetails/9PxfzNZJeW4oa4yE-7W5ZP4048PFnxLXRUfdOLcQk01/14/33/125/2026 2. https://sourcenm.com/2026/08/27/albuquerque-homeowner-says-republican-candidate-doesnt-live-at-contested-address/ 3. https://www.vitalitynm.com/service/facial-contouring 4. https://ivoterguide.com/candidate/91631/race/32712/election/1474 5. https://www.facebook.com/retinaconsultantsofnm/posts/hear-from-real-new-mexican-doctors/1420493356910898/ Contribute Volunteer Showing Up Fostering Change Volunteer Contribute Contact About Abby Issues Paid for and authorized by Friends of Abby Foster

Abdul El-Sayed Calls Out Red Wings Billionaire Owners… And Mike Rogers Can’t Spell October 14, 2026 MICHIGAN – In a recent edition of Octopus Thrower , Dr.
Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers were asked about the Red Wings’ contract standoff with young phenom Simon Edvinsson and the current state of the team.
Abdul spoke about his personal connection to the franchise and the billionaire owners’ consistently shameful and cheap conduct.
Florida man and likely Panthers fan Mike Rogers, on the other hand, failed to address the team’s hold out with Edvinsson, and couldn’t even be bothered to proofread his own statement… Dr.
Abdul El-Sayed: I was at the game when Darren McCarty took on Claude Lemieux.
The ‘97 and ‘98 Stanley Cup championships are still highlights of my childhood.
The teams the last few years have been a far cry from the Wings I came to love as a kid.
They’re stacking losing season on losing season, yet the Ilitch family’s wealth has done nothing but grow.
Michiganders are sick of sky-high ticket and concession prices buying them nothing but disappointment.
The team holding out on Simon Edvinsson is just the latest example in a long series of ownership prioritizing their bottom line over the team and the fans.
Our teams aren’t just assets for billionaires, they’re part of our culture and heritage.
Mike Rogers: Hockeytown, USA will always be a coveted destination for the world’s top players.
The Detroit Red Wings boast one of the league’s most storied and respected histories, dating back to their days as one of the Original Six franchises.
Few professional organizations can match the tradition, legacy and rpestige that define this iconic franchise.

Mike Rogers can pretend to watch as many Wings games at empty bars as he wants, but when he can’t call out the team’s poor performance in their 10 year playoff drought, Michiganders can see him for the fake fan that he is.

top of page Home Platform Meet Ace Endorsements Voices of WV Voices of WV In the News Ace’s Blog Get Involved Events Volunteer Join Our Mailing List Events Volunteer Join Our Mailing List Donate Menu Close Ace’s Blog Mountaineers can’t be free with ongoing collusion between Big Tech and government Ace Parsi Mar 14 3 min read Montani semper liberi: Mountaineers are always free.
That’s our state motto, and we’re rightly suspicious of a government that grows too powerful and has so much information about you that it can control your life, your choices, and your thoughts.
George Orwell’s “1984,” a high school literature standard, is a book that describes a society with such control.
This year is the 250 th anniversary of the U.S.
Declaration of Independence, and West Virginians should chafe at that type of government, whether it involves what people can own guns or what we decide about our healthcare.
The crazy thing is that over the last 25 years, we’ve given that control to Big Tech, which then linked arms with the federal government.
Now both know what you do and where you do it, what you purchase and from whom, what information you access, and how the people around you react.

They use and sell that information to push addictions—anything that takes your attention, time, or money—not caring what that does to your kids’ mental health, your friendships, your relationships, or your savings.
Big Tech is cooperating with big government, providing Americans’ personal information to strengthen its surveillance system.
They bend the knee to help identify immigrants and critics of our current presidential administration, and they suppress content the government doesn’t want you to see.
As an American, an immigrant, and a dad, this centralized power and cooperation scares the shit out of me, and it should scare the shit out of you as well.
Four years before I was born, there was a revolution in Iran.
When the Islamic fundamentalists had overthrown the Shah of Iran, they came after pro-democracy students, one of whom was my uncle.
They used the power of the state and cooperated with industry to find and arrest those students.
It was a reminder that once a government creates a precedent to use power one way, it can use that power in all different sorts of ways in the future.
In other words, today, it’s immigrants.
Tomorrow, whether under this political regime or another, it’s you.
So, what are we going to do about this?

If elected to represent you in West Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, I will check every level of unchecked data-related power in the same way our founders checked different levels of government some #ago—by having clear bills of rights: A Government Data Bill of Rights : No government under any presidential administration or political party, Democrat or Republican, should have unfettered access to your data.
This is especially important as artificial intelligence makes access to that data easier and more dangerous.
There should be clear checks and balances on executive authority—whether that’s a president, a governor, or a mayor—when it comes to how your data is accessed and used.
America was founded on freedom from excessive government control.
Let’s not give it away so easily.
A Big Tech Bill of Rights : Government is not the only entity aiming to control you.
Right now, the default with any big tech-supported system is that there are no walls between what they can do with your data and how they can manipulate you with their algorithms.
Big Tech benefits from long, complex systems of fine print that their lawyers can maneuver.
You benefit from clear, transparent standards and protections.
I’ll work for you, not Big Tech.

I’ll fight to make sure Big Tech cannot sell your data to the government or any other entity, and I’ll ensure that requests to share your information are made in clear language—not endless pages of fine print—and required to be re-asked periodically.
Stop the Collusion: There should be very strict lines of separation between government and Big Tech, whether that’s under a Democrat or Republican party.
Let’s make strong walls between what tech and government can do together with the data they have on you.
Back in 1838, Abraham Lincoln noted that the greatest threat to our democracy wasn’t a foreign power: “At what point then is the approach of danger to be expected?
I answer, if it ever reach us, it must spring up amongst us.
If destruction be our lot, we must ourselves be its author and finisher.
As a nation of freemen, we must live through all time, or die by suicide.” Let’s create a system that allows us to live free for all time, regardless of who is in power.

Amy Acton on The 11th Hour: “I’ve worked with people on both sides of the aisle to try to improve the lives of Ohioans” FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: October 14, 2026 CONTACT: [email protected] Dr.
Amy Acton on The 11th Hour: “I’ve worked with people on both sides of the aisle to try to improve the lives of Ohioans” COLUMBUS, OH– Yesterday, Dr.
Amy Acton appeared on MS NOW’s the 11th Hour with Ali Velshi, where she discussed the state of her campaign to become Ohio’s next governor.

Acton reiterated that she is “laser-focused on the needs of everyday Ohioans” and called out self-funding billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy for having the most “out-of-touch” and “reckless plans possible for Ohio.” WATCH: Dr.
Amy Acton on MS NOW’s The 11th Hour with Ali Velshi “95% of what I hear about no one disagrees on.

It is the cost of everyday living, from child care to health care costs, trying to rent, let alone buy a house, property taxes going up, electric bills going up.” “People are longing for someone and for public servants who actually solve problems instead of making problems.” “[Vivek Ramaswamy] has some of the most… reckless plans possible for Ohio.” “I’m an Ohio girl through-and-through.
I grew up in Youngstown, Ohio, the stuff of Bruce Springsteen songs, and I experienced a lot of neglect and abuse.
I know what it’s like to feel this way.” “People delivering [babies] roadside in Ohio, the seventh largest state… [with] some of the largest health institutions.

And yet with these Medicaid changes coming, you know, we’re having rural hospitals collapse, urban.” “[Vivek Ramaswamy said] Medicaid and Medicare are mistakes, he wants to dismantle them.” “And recently he has said that Social Security needs work requirements.

Well, I can tell you, to seniors on fixed incomes who are trying to get by with property taxes rising, electric bills rising, you know his policies are actually not just out-of-touch and out for himself, which he is. — They’re dangerous to my state.” “I’ve been at this a long time, and I’ve worked with people on both sides of the aisle to try to improve the lives of Ohioans.” “I will work with anyone who actually wants to solve problems instead of make them.” ### SHARE Donate to Stand with Amy for Ohio $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# Other Amount Other Amount If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately.

added: 7–0 Votación del Concejo Municipal de Provo que rechazó el centro de datos de East Bay en marzo de 2026.
50 MW El límite efectivo para cualquier nuevo centro de datos en Provo, según las reglas que aprobó el concejo en abril de 2026.
7K–12K gal/día La propia estimación de agua de East Bay para su primera fase, antes de cualquier expansión.
Un ejemplo local Lo que pasó en East Bay En febrero de 2026, un desarrollador le pidió a Provo cambiar la zonificación de parte del antiguo campus de Novell, en 1507 S.
180 E., para construir un centro de datos.
Según sus propias estimaciones, podría usar de 5 a 50 megavatios de energía y de 7,000 a 12,000 galones de agua al día en su primera fase.
La comisión de planificación recomendó aprobarlo.
Entonces los vecinos alzaron la voz.
Preguntaron por qué lo pondrían junto a una escuela y dos hoteles, si su plan de agua realmente funcionaría y qué tan poco aportaría a la economía local una vez construido.
Los concejales también se preocuparon por las tarifas de luz y las emisiones.
El 10 de marzo, el Concejo Municipal votó 7–0 para rechazarlo.
Dijeron que querían terminar el plan económico de la ciudad antes de tomar una decisión a largo plazo.
En abril, el concejo fue más allá.
Votó 5–1 para impedir que los centros de datos construyan sus propias plantas de energía, lo que limita cualquier centro nuevo a 50 megavatios o menos.
También exigió sistemas de enfriamiento que no evaporen agua.
Los líderes de Provo escucharon porque los residentes se presentaron.
No todas las comunidades tienen esa oportunidad.
Utah County está escribiendo ahora mismo reglas para centros de datos en zonas rurales, y la gente allí merece la misma oportunidad de opinar.
Lo que impulsaré a nivel estatal 01 Publicar la demanda esperada de electricidad y agua en términos comprensibles para los ciudadanos.

01 Ciudad de Provo Solicitudes actuales del Distrito Central y estado de proyectos ↗ 02 Comisión de Planificación de Provo Paquete informativo de febrero de 2026 y proyecciones del solicitante ↗ 03 Comisión de Planificación de Provo Acta de la reunión del 11 de febrero de 2026 y condiciones ↗ 04 Concejo Municipal de Provo Acta del 10 de marzo de 2026 y rechazo 7–0 a la zonificación especial ↗ 05 Daily Herald El Concejo de Provo rechaza la rezonificación de East Bay (marzo de 2026, en inglés) ↗ 06 Daily Herald Votación 5–1 del concejo para restringir grandes centros de datos (abril de 2026, en inglés) ↗ 07 Citizen Portal Borrador de reglas de Utah County para centros de datos en zonas rurales (septiembre de 2026, en inglés) ↗ 08 Deseret News Stratos: aprobaciones estatales y del condado, superficie y apelación del referéndum (junio de 2026, en inglés) ↗ 09 Daily Herald Retiran la solicitud de agua de Stratos tras unas 3,900 protestas (mayo de 2026, en inglés) ↗ Nota de fuente: Las cifras de energía y agua de East Bay son estimaciones del desarrollador de febrero de 2026, no mediciones de una instalación en funcionamiento.
La estimación de agua combina enfriamiento y uso doméstico.
El límite de 50 MW viene del cambio de reglas de abril de 2026: la agencia de energía de Provo exige que los centros de datos de más de 50 MW generen su propia energía, y la ciudad ya no lo permite.
removed: 5–50 MW La estimación del solicitante en febrero de 2026, con expansión según la capacidad disponible de Provo Power.
7K–12K gal/día Estimación de la primera fase del solicitante en febrero de 2026 para enfriamiento y uso doméstico.
Febrero de 2026 Estas cifras describen la propuesta en ese momento, no el estado actual de permisos ni el uso de recursos medido.
Un ejemplo local La propuesta de East Bay En febrero de 2026, documentos de planificación describieron una propuesta de centro de datos de 66,000 pies cuadrados en 1507 S.
180 E. en Provo.
El solicitante proyectó una demanda eléctrica de 5 a 50 megavatios, con expansión sujeta a la capacidad disponible de Provo Power.
Su estimación de agua para la primera fase fue de 7,000 a 12,000 galones diarios para refrigeración y uso doméstico.
Estas eran estimaciones de la propuesta en ese momento.

added: 7–0 Provo City Council vote turning down the East Bay data center in March 2026.
50 MW The effective limit for any new Provo data center, under rules the council passed in April 2026.
7K–12K gal/day East Bay's own first-phase water estimate, before any expansion.
A local example What happened at East Bay In February 2026, a developer asked Provo to rezone part of the old Novell campus at 1507 S.
Its own estimates said it could use 5 to 50 megawatts of power, and 7,000 to 12,000 gallons of water a day in its first phase.
They asked why it would go next to a school and two hotels, whether its water plan would really work, and how little it would add to the local economy once it was built.
Council members also worried about power rates and emissions.
On March 10, the City Council voted 7–0 to turn it down.
They said they wanted to finish the city's economic plan before making a long-term decision.
In April, the council went further.
It voted 5–1 to stop data centers from building their own power plants, which keeps any new one at 50 megawatts or less.
It also required cooling systems that don't evaporate water.
Provo's leaders listened because residents showed up.
Not every community gets that chance.
Utah County is writing rules right now for data centers in rural areas, and people there deserve the same chance to weigh in.

added: top of page HOME MEET ALINA 8-POINT PLAN EVENTS NEWS CONTACT MERCH FOLLOW US GET INVOLVED DONATE Platform THE 8-POINT PLAN My 8 Point Plan focuses on safer communities, lower taxes, affordable housing, reliable energy, a fair justice system, and a government that is transparent, accountable, and works for every New Yorker.
BAIL REFORM The 2019 bail reforms addressed a real injustice by ensuring low-income individuals do not sit in jail for minor charges simply because they cannot afford bail.
However, by nearly eliminating judicial discretion, the legislature went too far, leaving judges unable to consider public safety or protect communities from repeat violent offenders.
What I'll do Carnegie Hill Restore judicial discretion to consider public-safety risks when setting bail for repeat violent offenders.
Carnegie Hill Preserve all existing protections that prevent the detention of low-income defendants charged with non-violent offenses.
Carnegie Hill Require risk assessment tools that are transparent, auditable, and bias-tested before they can be used in bail decisions.
Carnegie Hill Close the loophole that permits individuals with multiple violent arrests to cycle through the system without meaningful judicial review.
SAFE SHELTERS The shelter placement system should prioritize child and neighborhood safety while protecting the dignity of residents honestly working to rebuild their lives.

Instead, the framework operates without transparency or geographic limits, routinely placing individuals with violent histories near schools and daycares without community notice, and zero identity verification therby no thorough safety background checks are possible, and the outside community absorbs the danger.

What I'll do Carnegie Hill Establish strict geographic restrictions and mandatory buffer zones to completely ban the placement of violent offenders and registered sex offenders in facilities adjacent to schools, daycares, and playgrounds.
Carnegie Hill Mandate a proactive, early-stage community notification infrastructure that requires the state to inform residents before any new shelter is proposed near residential homes.
Carnegie Hill Require government-issued identification or verified legal documentation for shelter enrollment to eliminate identity fraud and systemic exploitation.
Carnegie Hill Require government-issued identification or verified legal documentation for shelter enrollment to eliminate identity fraud and systemic exploitation.

Carnegie Hill Reestablish dedicated state psychiatric institutions for the severely mentally ill who pose a clear, ongoing danger to themselves or society, moving them out of community shelters and into secure clinical care.
FAMILY COURT REFORM Family Court should deliver timely decisions, enforce its own orders, and protect the rights of parents and children through due process.
Too often, cases drag on for years while parent-child relationships deteriorate, families experience unnecessary trauma, and financial and emotional costs continue to mount.
What I'll do Carnegie Hill Raise evidentiary standards for temporary orders of protection and require prompt hearings so allegations can be reviewed without unnecessary delay.
Carnegie Hill ​Enforce custody and parenting time orders with meaningful consequences for repeated violations.

Carnegie Hill Establish firm case timelines and vacate actions that remain stagnant due to repeated adjournments, failure to prosecute, or manipulation of the court process designed to delay resolution, increase penalties, or prolong family separation.

Carnegie Hill Reform child support enforcement policies to prevent their use as coercive tactics and ensure support calculations are based on actual financial circumstances, including net income and reasonable cost-of-living expenses for all parties.
Carnegie Hill Increase oversight and accountability for court-appointed attorneys, evaluators, therapists, and other Family Court professionals.
HATE CRIME Religiously motivated violence and bias-related crimes have reached historic highs across New York, targeting Jewish New Yorkers.
While the state possesses a powerful tool in Article 485 to increase penalties for these offenses, prosecutors face high evidentiary hurdles, causing clear bias attacks to go unenhanced.
An attack on a house of worship or an individual based on identity is an attack on our collective safety and demands a full, uncompromised legal response.
What I'll do Carnegie Hill Push for full and consistent prosecution under Article 485 in all cases with clear bias motivation.
Carnegie Hill Work to clarify evidence requirements so that proof of bias or motive in trials is easier to establish.
Carnegie Hill Establish a dedicated hate crimes unit in the Manhattan and outer borough DAs' offices with specialized prosecutors.
TAX & TOLL RELIEF New York’s tax policy should foster economic growth and allow working families, young professionals, and seniors to affordably build and keep their lives here.
New York's congestion toll system should target true peak gridlock without penalizing working commuters or turning local neighborhoods into revenue traps.

Instead, Albany inflicts crushing tax burdens at every stage of life, driving ambitious young workers to low-tax states, straining single parents, and forcing lifelong seniors into out-of-state retirement.
What I'll do Carnegie Hill Introduce a NO State Income tax exemption for young adults under 30 who are working to help build an early financial footing here rather than leaving.
Carnegie Hill Expand childcare cost deductions for single parents and working parents to reflect the actual cost of care in New York City.
Carnegie Hill New York's congestion toll system should target true peak gridlock without penalizing working commuters or turning local neighborhoods into revenue traps.

HOUSING Over 60,000 vacant residential units across New York City sit empty because broken state laws prevent them from exiting rent stabilization, leaving landlords unable to fund heavy capital repairs.
Oppose COPA and protect property owners’ right to sell.
Reform unfair rental laws to bring vacant apartments back to market, and ease building restrictions under housing incentive programs to encourage more construction.

What I'll do Carnegie Hill Carnegie Hill Provide targeted property tax credits to building owners who completely fund and execute essential structural, safety, and infrastructure repairs on vacant apartments.
Remove long-term vacant units from rent stabilization constraints if they require extensive capital rehabilitation to meet legal human-occupancy standards.
HEALTHCARE Health insurance has become increasingly unaffordable for working New Yorkers and the businesses that employ them.
The average employer-sponsored health plan now costs $9,325 a year for individual coverage and nearly $27,000 for family coverage.
New York adds extensive state coverage requirements to health plans, limiting insurers’ ability to offer consumers more affordable options.
While many of these benefits are valuable, not every individual or family needs the same level of coverage.
A one-size-fits-all system can force people to pay for benefits they may not need while making basic health insurance increasingly difficult to afford.

What I'll do Carnegie Hill Introduce Stage Choice Give individuals and employers an alternative to the current one-size-fits-all state benefit requirements, allowing insurers to offer plans with lower premiums.

Carnegie Hill Reduce Unnecessary Mandates Allow consumers to choose plans that do not automatically include every state-mandated service they may not need, reducing the cost built into their premiums.
ENERGY INDEPENDENCE New York needs a cleaner, more reliable, and more affordable energy system capable of supporting residents, businesses,s and the growing digital economy.
Solar and wind are important parts of that system, and battery storage can extend their availability.
However, weather-dependent generation and current storage capacity cannot alone guarantee dependable power around the clock.
New York needs a balanced portfolio that combines renewables, storage, transmission improvements, nuclear energy, and other reliable resources.
The closure of Indian Point removed approximately 2,000 megawatts of dependable, low-carbon generating capacity before an equivalent replacement was available.
New York must restore that lost reliability without compromising public safety.

The State Senate’s recent $200 million infrastructure allocation for solar energy is an inefficient waste of taxpayer money that deepens the dependency on imported natural gas rather than investing in nuclear energy—the zero-emission global gold standard.
What I'll do Carnegie Hill Support cost-effective solar, wind and energy-storage projects with measurable standards for performance, reliability and value to ratepayers.

Carnegie Hill Reevaluate New York’s blanket fracking ban only for appropriate locations and under strict safeguards for drinking water, methane emissions, setbacks, continuous monitoring and public accountability.
Carnegie Hill Require an independent engineering, environmental, economic and federal safety review to determine whether any Indian Point capacity can be safely and responsibly restored.
If reopening is not feasible, pursue modern nuclear generation at appropriately selected locations.

Carnegie Hill Develop sufficient generating and transmission capacity to support data centers and other emerging industries while requiring large energy users to contribute fairly toward the infrastructure they require, rather than shifting those costs to residential ratepayers.
Carnegie Hill Invest in advanced nuclear technology as a source of dependable electricity that produces no direct carbon emissions during operation.

added: THE SHELTER SAFETY AND ACCOUNTABILITY ACT A Proposed Amendment to New York State Law Proposed by Alina Bonsell Candidate for New York State Senate, District 28 Prepared by the Alina for NY Policy Team Under the direction of Alina Bonsell September 2026 www.alinabonsell.com This document is a candidate policy proposal and draft legislative language.
It has not been introduced in the New York State Legislature and does not represent enacted law.

S. (insert senator) 2025-2026 Regular Sessions IN SENATE Introduced by Sen. (xyz) — read once and referred to the Committee on Social Services AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to establishing geographic safeguards, community notification requirements, identity verification standards, and identity document assistance for homeless shelters The People of the State of New York, represented in Senate and Assembly, do enact as follows: Section 1.
This act shall be known and may be cited as the “Shelter Safety and Accountability Act.” § 2.
The legislature hereby finds and declares that: 1.
Every New Yorker, whether housed or unhoused, is entitled to safety, dignity, and honest government.

The current shelter placement system permits individuals with violent or predatory criminal histories to be placed in facilities adjacent to schools, daycare centers, and playgrounds without adequate geographic safeguards, and without timely notice to the families and neighbors who live nearby.

The absence of meaningful identity verification at intake undermines the integrity of the shelter system, exposes residents and staff to preventable danger, and makes the system vulnerable to exploitation and misrepresentation.

Community notification of proposed shelter siting is inconsistent across the state, leaving residents without a meaningful opportunity to raise legitimate safety concerns before placement decisions are finalized.

Many individuals experiencing homelessness lack the government-issued identification and vital records necessary to access housing, employment, healthcare, and public benefits, and lack of identification should not be used as a pretext to deny emergency shelter to those who need it most.
The current system lacks sufficient mechanisms to prevent waste, fraud, and abuse, resulting in inefficient use of public funds and weakening public confidence in the shelter system.

Stronger identity verification, community oversight, transparent reporting, and meaningful enforcement will improve shelter safety, reduce opportunities for corruption, waste, and fraud, and ensure that public resources are used efficiently and for their intended purpose.

The purpose of this act is to establish statewide minimum standards that protect the safety of children and communities, ensure the integrity of the shelter intake process, guarantee timely and verifiable community notification, reduce waste and fraud, establish meaningful community oversight, and expand access to identification and vital records for shelter residents, while preserving safe and humane access to emergency shelter for all in need, including victims of domestic violence, human trafficking, and other emergencies. § 3.
Article 2-A of the Social Services Law is amended by adding a Title 5, consisting of sections 53 through 59, to read as follows: § 53.
FOR PURPOSES OF THIS ARTICLE, THE FOLLOWING TERMS SHALL HAVE THE FOLLOWING MEANINGS: 1.

“SHELTER” OR “HOMELESS SHELTER” MEANS ANY FACILITY, OPERATED DIRECTLY OR UNDER CONTRACT BY A SOCIAL SERVICES DISTRICT, PUBLIC AGENCY, NONPROFIT ORGANIZATION, OR OTHER CONTRACTOR, THAT PROVIDES TEMPORARY HOUSING TO INDIVIDUALS OR FAMILIES LACKING A FIXED, REGULAR, AND ADEQUATE NIGHTTIME RESIDENCE, INCLUDING TRANSITIONAL HOUSING AND CONGREGATE EMERGENCY SHELTERS, BUT EXCLUDING RESIDENTIAL PROGRAMS FOR VICTIMS OF DOMESTIC VIOLENCE DESCRIBED IN ARTICLE SIX-A OF THIS CHAPTER.
“OPERATOR” MEANS ANY ENTITY THAT OWNS, MANAGES, CONTRACTS TO OPERATE, OR CONTROLS A HOMELESS SHELTER.
“SENSITIVE LOCATION” MEANS ANY PUBLIC OR PRIVATE ELEMENTARY OR SECONDARY SCHOOL, LICENSED DAYCARE CENTER, OR PUBLIC PLAYGROUND.

“RESTRICTED REGISTRANT” MEANS (A) ANY INDIVIDUAL REQUIRED TO REGISTER AS A LEVEL TWO OR LEVEL THREE SEX OFFENDER PURSUANT TO ARTICLE SIX-C OF THE CORRECTION LAW, OR DESIGNATED AS A SEXUAL PREDATOR, SEXUALLY VIOLENT OFFENDER, OR PREDICATE SEX OFFENDER THEREUNDER; OR (B) ANY INDIVIDUAL WITH A CURRENT CONVICTION FOR A VIOLENT FELONY OFFENSE AS DEFINED IN SECTION 70.02 OF THE PENAL LAW COMMITTED AGAINST A PERSON UNDER EIGHTEEN YEARS OF AGE, WITHIN TEN YEARS OF THE PROPOSED PLACEMENT DATE.

“BUFFER ZONE” MEANS A DISTANCE OF TWENTY-SIX HUNDRED AND FORTY FEET, OR ROUGHLY TEN STANDARD MUNICIPAL BLOCKS, MEASURED FROM THE NEAREST PROPERTY LINE OF THE SHELTER TO THE NEAREST PROPERTY LINE OF THE SENSITIVE LOCATION, UNLESS A DIFFERENT DISTANCE IS ESTABLISHED BY REGULATION CONSISTENT WITH SECTION 54 OF THIS ARTICLE.

“VERIFIED IDENTITY DOCUMENTATION” MEANS A GOVERNMENTISSUED PHOTO IDENTIFICATION DOCUMENT, OR, WHERE UNAVAILABLE, AN ALTERNATIVE FORM OF IDENTITY VERIFICATION AUTHORIZED BY THE OFFICE BY REGULATION, INCLUDING VERIFICATION THROUGH GOVERNMENTAL RECORDS, A SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER, MEDICAL RECORDS, IDENTITY-RELATED RECORDS MAINTAINED BY A GOVERNMENTAL AGENCY, VERIFIED RESPONSES TO PERSONALIDENTIFICATION QUESTIONS, FACIAL-RECOGNITION TECHNOLOGY WHERE AUTHORIZED BY LAW, OR OTHER RELIABLE IDENTIFYING INFORMATION.
“OFFICE” MEANS THE OFFICE OF TEMPORARY AND DISABILITY ASSISTANCE.
“COMMUNITY MEETING” MEANS A PUBLICLY NOTICED MEETING HELD FOR RESIDENTS OF THE DISTRICT IN WHICH A PROPOSED SHELTER IS LOCATED FOR THE PURPOSE OF CONSIDERING AND VOTING UPON THE PROPOSED SHELTER.

“COMMUNITY NOTIFICATION EVIDENCE” MEANS DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE SUFFICIENT TO ESTABLISH THAT THE NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS OF SECTION FIFTY-FIVE OF THIS ARTICLE WERE SATISFIED, INCLUDING AT LEAST TWO SEPARATE EVIDENTIARY PIECES ORIGINATING FROM AT LEAST TWO SEPARATE INDIVIDUALS, AT LEAST ONE OF WHOM IS AN ELECTED OFFICIAL OR MEMBER OF THE STAFF OF AN ELECTED OFFICIAL REPRESENTING THE DISTRICT. § 54.
(A) NO SOCIAL SERVICES DISTRICT, OPERATOR, OR AGENCY THEREOF SHALL KNOWINGLY PLACE, REFER, OR ADMIT A RESTRICTED REGISTRANT TO A SHELTER LOCATED WITHIN A BUFFER ZONE OF A SENSITIVE LOCATION.

(B) PRIOR TO PLACEMENT OF ANY INDIVIDUAL IN A SHELTER, THE PLACING AGENCY SHALL QUERY THE REGISTRY ESTABLISHED UNDER ARTICLE SIX-C OF THE CORRECTION LAW TO DETERMINE WHETHER THE INDIVIDUAL IS A RESTRICTED REGISTRANT.

NOTHING IN THIS SECTION SHALL BE CONSTRUED TO REQUIRE DISCLOSURE OF AN INDIVIDUAL'S REGISTRATION STATUS TO SHELTER STAFF OR OTHER RESIDENTS BEYOND WHAT IS NECESSARY TO COMPLY WITH SUBDIVISION (A) OF THIS SECTION.

(C) WHERE A RESTRICTED REGISTRANT CANNOT BE PLACED IN A SHELTER DUE TO THE BUFFER ZONE REQUIREMENT OF THIS SECTION, THE OFFICE SHALL MAINTAIN, OR CONTRACT FOR, A SUFFICIENT NUMBER OF SHELTER BEDS LOCATED OUTSIDE BUFFER ZONES TO ENSURE THAT NO RESTRICTED REGISTRANT IS DENIED EMERGENCY SHELTER SOLELY ON ACCOUNT OF THIS SECTION.

(D) THIS SECTION SHALL NOT APPLY TO PLACEMENTS MADE ON AN EMERGENCY BASIS DURING A DECLARED LOCAL, STATE, OR FEDERAL EMERGENCY, INCLUDING CODE BLUE OR CODE RED WEATHER EMERGENCIES, PROVIDED THAT ANY RESTRICTED REGISTRANT SO PLACED SHALL BE TRANSFERRED TO A SHELTER OUTSIDE A BUFFER ZONE AS SOON AS PRACTICABLE AND IN NO EVENT LATER THAN SEVENTY-TWO HOURS AFTER THE EMERGENCY PLACEMENT, ABSENT GOOD CAUSE DOCUMENTED BY THE PLACING AGENCY. § 55.

(A) NO SOCIAL SERVICES DISTRICT OR OPERATOR SHALL EXECUTE A LEASE, CONTRACT, OR AGREEMENT TO OPEN A NEW SHELTER, OR TO EXPAND THE CAPACITY OF AN EXISTING SHELTER BY MORE THAN TWENTY-FIVE BEDS, UNLESS IT HAS FIRST PROVIDED WRITTEN NOTICE AS REQUIRED BY THIS SECTION AND OBTAINED COMMUNITY APPROVAL AS PROVIDED IN SUBDIVISION (E) OF THIS SECTION.

(B) WRITTEN NOTICE SHALL BE PROVIDED, NOT LESS THAN FORTY-FIVE DAYS PRIOR TO EXECUTION OF THE LEASE, CONTRACT, OR AGREEMENT, TO: (I) THE COMMUNITY BOARD OR, IN A CITY WITHOUT COMMUNITY BOARDS, THE EQUIVALENT LOCAL GOVERNING BODY, WITH JURISDICTION OVER THE PROPOSED LOCATION; (II) THE MEMBER OF THE CITY COUNCIL, TOWN BOARD, OR VILLAGE BOARD REPRESENTING THE DISTRICT IN WHICH THE PROPOSED LOCATION IS SITUATED; (III) THE STATE SENATOR AND ASSEMBLY MEMBER REPRESENTING THE PROPOSED LOCATION; AND (IV) THE CHIEF EXECUTIVE OF THE COUNTY OR CITY, AS APPLICABLE.

(C) THE NOTICE REQUIRED BY SUBDIVISION (B) OF THIS SECTION SHALL INCLUDE THE PROPOSED ADDRESS, CAPACITY, POPULATION TO BE SERVED, SERVICES TO BE PROVIDED, EXPECTED LENGTH OF STAY, SECURITY AND SAFETY PROCEDURES, AND ANY OTHER INFORMATION REQUIRED BY THE OFFICE.

(D) THIS SECTION SHALL NOT APPLY TO: (I) EMERGENCY PLACEMENTS MADE PURSUANT TO SUBDIVISION (D) OF SECTION 54 OF THIS ARTICLE; (II) RESIDENTIAL PROGRAMS FOR VICTIMS OF DOMESTIC VIOLENCE DESCRIBED IN ARTICLE SIX-A OF THIS CHAPTER, FOR WHICH DISCLOSURE OF LOCATION WOULD COMPROMISE RESIDENT SAFETY; OR (III) RENEWAL OF AN EXISTING LEASE, CONTRACT, OR AGREEMENT AT THE SAME LOCATION AND SAME OR LESSER CAPACITY.
(E) PRIOR TO EXECUTION OF THE LEASE, CONTRACT, OR AGREEMENT, THE SOCIAL SERVICES DISTRICT OR OPERATOR SHALL CONDUCT AT LEAST ONE PUBLIC COMMUNITY MEETING.

THE CHAIR OF THE COMMUNITY BOARD, OR EQUIVALENT LOCAL GOVERNING BODY, AND A MEMBER OF THE STAFF OF AT LEAST ONE ELECTED OFFICIAL REPRESENTING THE DISTRICT SHALL EACH SIGN A WRITTEN CONFIRMATION THAT THE COMMUNITY NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS WERE SATISFIED.

SUCH CONFIRMATION SHALL INCLUDE AT LEAST TWO SEPARATE EVIDENTIARY PIECES FROM AT LEAST TWO DIFFERENT INDIVIDUALS ESTABLISHING THAT THE COMMUNITY WAS NOTIFIED, AT LEAST ONE OF WHOM SHALL BE AN ELECTED OFFICIAL OR A MEMBER OF THE STAFF OF AN ELECTED OFFICIAL REPRESENTING THE DISTRICT.
(F) A PROPOSED SHELTER SHALL NOT BE APPROVED UNLESS THE PROPOSAL RECEIVES THE APPROVAL OF AT LEAST FIFTY-ONE PERCENT OF THE ELIGIBLE RESIDENTS PRESENT AND VOTING AT THE COMMUNITY MEETING.
PRIOR TO VOTING, THE COMMUNITY BOARD OR EQUIVALENT LOCAL GOVERNING BODY SHALL ESTABLISH A PROCEDURE TO VERIFY THAT EACH PERSON PARTICIPATING IN THE VOTE ACTUALLY RESIDES WITHIN THE DISTRICT.
SUCH VERIFICATION MAY INCLUDE GOVERNMENTISSUED IDENTIFICATION, VOTER REGISTRATION RECORDS, PROPERTY OR TENANCY RECORDS, OR OTHER RELIABLE PROOF OF RESIDENCY.
NO PERSON SHALL CAST MORE THAN ONE VOTE.

(G) NOTHING IN THIS SECTION SHALL APPLY TO EMERGENCY PLACEMENTS MADE PURSUANT TO SUBDIVISION (D) OF SECTION 54 OF THIS ARTICLE OR TO RESIDENTIAL PROGRAMS FOR VICTIMS OF DOMESTIC VIOLENCE DESCRIBED IN ARTICLE SIX-A OF THIS CHAPTER, FOR WHICH DISCLOSURE OF LOCATION WOULD COMPROMISE RESIDENT SAFETY. § 56.
(A) EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN SUBDIVISION (C) OF THIS SECTION, NO OPERATOR SHALL ENROLL AN INDIVIDUAL IN A SHELTER WITHOUT FIRST COLLECTING VERIFIED IDENTITY DOCUMENTATION FROM THAT INDIVIDUAL.
AN OPERATOR THAT KNOWINGLY ADMITS OR RETAINS AN INDIVIDUAL IN VIOLATION OF THIS SUBDIVISION SHALL BE SUBJECT TO THE PENALTIES ESTABLISHED UNDER SECTION 58 OF THIS ARTICLE.

(B) WHERE AN INDIVIDUAL PRESENTS FOR SHELTER WITHOUT VERIFIED IDENTITY DOCUMENTATION, THE OPERATOR SHALL PROVISIONALLY ADMIT THE INDIVIDUAL AND SHALL BEGIN AN IDENTITY-VERIFICATION PROCESS WITHIN TWENTY-FOUR HOURS.

THE OPERATOR SHALL EXHAUST REASONABLE METHODS OF VERIFYING IDENTITY, WHICH MAY INCLUDE REVIEW OF A SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER, GOVERNMENTAL RECORDS, MEDICAL RECORDS, VITAL RECORDS, PRIOR SHELTER RECORDS, VERIFIED RESPONSES TO PERSONAL-IDENTIFICATION QUESTIONS, CONTACT WITH APPROPRIATE GOVERNMENT AGENCIES, AND FACIAL-RECOGNITION TECHNOLOGY WHERE AUTHORIZED BY LAW.
THE OPERATOR SHALL BE RESPONSIBLE FOR THE COST OF SUCH VERIFICATION.

(C) THE IDENTITY VERIFICATION REQUIREMENT OF SUBDIVISION (A) OF THIS SECTION SHALL NOT APPLY TO: (I) AN INDIVIDUAL SEEKING SHELTER AS A VICTIM OF DOMESTIC VIOLENCE, HUMAN TRAFFICKING, OR SEXUAL ASSAULT, WHO SHALL BE ADMITTED WITHOUT REGARD TO IDENTITY DOCUMENTATION AND WHOSE INTAKE SHALL BE GOVERNED BY THE CONFIDENTIALITY PROTECTIONS OF TITLE SIX OF ARTICLE SIX-A OF THIS CHAPTER; (II) AN INDIVIDUAL SEEKING SHELTER DURING A DECLARED EMERGENCY DESCRIBED IN SUBDIVISION (D) OF SECTION 54 OF THIS ARTICLE; (III) AN UNACCOMPANIED MINOR; OR (IV) ANY INDIVIDUAL FOR WHOM THE OFFICE DETERMINES BY REGULATION THAT REQUIRING IDENTITY DOCUMENTATION WOULD CREATE AN UNREASONABLE BARRIER TO ACCESSING EMERGENCY SHELTER.

(D) AN OPERATOR SHALL NOT ADMIT OR RETAIN AN INDIVIDUAL IN A SHELTER WHO IS DETERMINED THROUGH THE REQUIRED IDENTITY AND BACKGROUND VERIFICATION PROCESS TO BE A PERSON WHOSE CURRENT FELONY STATUS PROHIBITS PLACEMENT UNDER THIS ARTICLE OR OTHER APPLICABLE LAW.
ANY SUCH DETERMINATION SHALL BE DOCUMENTED AND REPORTED TO THE OFFICE.

(E) IDENTITY INFORMATION COLLECTED PURSUANT TO THIS SECTION MAY BE SHARED, SUBJECT TO APPLICABLE PRIVACY AND CONFIDENTIALITY LAWS, WITH THE OFFICE, SOCIAL SERVICES DISTRICTS, RELEVANT STATE AGENCIES, COMMUNITY BOARDS, AND OTHER STAKEHOLDERS RESPONSIBLE FOR SHELTER OVERSIGHT.
SUCH INFORMATION SHALL NOT BE PROVIDED DIRECTLY TO A FEDERAL IMMIGRATION AUTHORITY EXCEPT PURSUANT TO A JUDICIAL WARRANT OR AS OTHERWISE REQUIRED BY FEDERAL LAW. § 57.

(A) THE OFFICE, IN COORDINATION WITH THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH, THE DEPARTMENT OF MOTOR VEHICLES, AND SOCIAL SERVICES DISTRICTS, SHALL ESTABLISH AND ADMINISTER A STATEWIDE IDENTITY DOCUMENT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM TO HELP INDIVIDUALS EXPERIENCING HOMELESSNESS OBTAIN BIRTH CERTIFICATES, NON-DRIVER PHOTO IDENTIFICATION CARDS, AND OTHER IDENTITY DOCUMENTS NECESSARY TO ACCESS HOUSING, EMPLOYMENT, HEALTHCARE, AND PUBLIC BENEFITS.

(B) THE PROGRAM SHALL, AT A MINIMUM: (I) PROVIDE THAT INDIVIDUALS VERIFIED AS EXPERIENCING HOMELESSNESS SHALL NOT BE REQUIRED TO PAY STATE FEES FOR OBTAINING A BIRTH CERTIFICATE OR NON-DRIVER IDENTIFICATION CARD; (II) REQUIRE THE OPERATOR OF THE SHELTER TO PAY THE APPLICABLE ADMINISTRATIVE AND PROCESSING COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH OBTAINING SUCH DOCUMENTS; (III) REQUIRE THE DEPARTMENT OF MOTOR VEHICLES TO PRIORITIZE APPLICATIONS FOR IDENTIFICATION DOCUMENTS SUBMITTED THROUGH THE PROGRAM; (IV) FUND CASEWORKER POSITIONS, EITHER DIRECTLY OR THROUGH CONTRACTS WITH OPERATORS, DEDICATED TO ASSISTING SHELTER RESIDENTS IN OBTAINING IDENTITY DOCUMENTATION; AND (V) ESTABLISH A SINGLE POINT OF APPLICATION, TO THE EXTENT PRACTICABLE, ALLOWING AN INDIVIDUAL TO APPLY FOR MULTIPLE IDENTITY DOCUMENTS THROUGH ONE INTAKE PROCESS.
(C) EVERY OPERATOR SHALL INFORM EACH INDIVIDUAL ADMITTED TO A SHELTER OF THE AVAILABILITY OF THE PROGRAM ESTABLISHED UNDER THIS SECTION AND SHALL PROVIDE A REFERRAL TO THE PROGRAM AT INTAKE.

(D) THE OFFICE SHALL REPORT QUARTERLY TO THE GOVERNOR, THE LEGISLATURE, COMMUNITY BOARDS, AND THE PUBLIC ON THE NUMBER OF INDIVIDUALS SERVED BY THE PROGRAM, THE NUMBER AND TYPE OF DOCUMENTS ISSUED, THE AVERAGE TIME BETWEEN REFERRAL AND ISSUANCE, THE NUMBER OF IDENTITY VERIFICATION CASES COMPLETED, AND THE COSTS PAID BY EACH OPERATOR. § 58.

(A) AN OPERATOR WHO VIOLATES SECTION 56 OR 57 OF THIS ARTICLE SHALL BE LIABLE FOR A CIVIL PENALTY BEGINNING AT ONE THOUSAND DOLLARS AND INCREASING TO FIVE THOUSAND DOLLARS FOR EACH OCCURRENCE PER PERSON, AS PROVIDED BY REGULATION.
EACH DAY A VIOLATION CONTINUES SHALL CONSTITUTE A SEPARATE OCCURRENCE.

(B) PRIOR TO ASSESSMENT OF ANY CIVIL PENALTY UNDER THIS SECTION, THE OFFICE SHALL PROVIDE THE OPERATOR WITH WRITTEN NOTICE OF THE VIOLATION AND AN OPPORTUNITY TO SUBMIT A CORRECTIVE ACTION PLAN WITHIN FIFTEEN DAYS.

(C) WHERE AN OPERATOR ACCUMULATES FIFTY THOUSAND DOLLARS OR MORE IN CIVIL PENALTIES UNDER THIS ARTICLE, THE OFFICE SHALL SUSPEND THE OPERATOR'S AUTHORIZATION TO OPERATE THE SHELTER AND SHALL PROHIBIT NEW ADMISSIONS UNTIL THE OFFICE CERTIFIES THAT THE OPERATOR HAS COME INTO COMPLIANCE.

(D) CIVIL PENALTIES COLLECTED UNDER THIS SECTION SHALL BE DEPOSITED IN A DEDICATED SHELTER OVERSIGHT ACCOUNT AND USED TO FUND ENFORCEMENT ACTIVITIES UNDER THIS TITLE AND THE IDENTITY DOCUMENT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM ESTABLISHED UNDER SECTION 57 OF THIS ARTICLE.

(E) THE OFFICE SHALL ESTABLISH A HOMELESS SHELTER OVERSIGHT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW COMPLIANCE WITH THIS ARTICLE, INCLUDING QUARTERLY REPORTS, IDENTITY VERIFICATION, BACKGROUND CHECKS, COMMUNITY NOTIFICATION, COMMUNITY APPROVAL, SHELTER EXPENDITURES, AND ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS.
THE COMMITTEE SHALL INCLUDE REPRESENTATIVES OF THE OFFICE, RELEVANT STATE AGENCIES, SOCIAL SERVICES DISTRICTS, COMMUNITY BOARDS, AND OTHER STAKEHOLDERS DESIGNATED BY THE OFFICE.
(F) FINAL DETERMINATIONS OF THE OFFICE UNDER THIS SECTION ARE SUBJECT TO JUDICIAL REVIEW UNDER ARTICLE SEVENTYEIGHT OF THE CIVIL PRACTICE LAW AND RULES. § 59.
(A) THE OFFICE SHALL, WITHIN THE NEXT QUARTER OF THE EFFECTIVE DATE OF THIS ARTICLE, PROMULGATE REGULATIONS NECESSARY TO IMPLEMENT SECTIONS 53 THROUGH 58 OF THIS ARTICLE.

(B) THE FIRST REPORT ISSUED PURSUANT TO THIS ARTICLE SHALL INCLUDE, TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED BY LAW AND SUBJECT TO NECESSARY PRIVACY PROTECTIONS: (I) THE NUMBER OF SHELTER RESIDENTS WHO WERE SCREENED AGAINST THE SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY; (II) THE NUMBER OF MATCHES OR POTENTIAL MATCHES IDENTIFIED THROUGH SUCH SCREENING; (III) THE NUMBER OF INDIVIDUALS WHO RECEIVED IDENTITY VERIFICATION AND THE METHODS USED; (IV) THE NUMBER OF REQUIRED MENTAL HEALTH OR MENTAL-FUNCTION EVALUATIONS, WHERE APPLICABLE AND LAWFUL; (V) THE NUMBER AND TYPE OF IDENTITY DOCUMENTS OBTAINED; (VI) THE NUMBER OF INDIVIDUALS ADMITTED, DENIED, TRANSFERRED, OR REMOVED PURSUANT TO THIS ARTICLE; (VII) THE TOTAL AMOUNT OF PUBLIC MONEY RECEIVED AND SPENT BY EACH SHELTER OPERATOR; (VIII) COPIES OR ACCESSIBLE RECORDS OF IDENTITY DOCUMENTATION MAINTAINED BY OPERATORS FOR AUTHORIZED OVERSIGHT PURPOSES; (IX) ALL ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS, CIVIL PENALTIES, CORRECTIVE ACTION PLANS, AND COMPLIANCE DEADLINES; AND (X) ANY OTHER INFORMATION NECESSARY TO EVALUATE SHELTER SAFETY, COMPLIANCE, AND USE OF PUBLIC FUNDS.
(C) THE OFFICE SHALL MAKE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC A BROAD, AGGREGATED OVERVIEW OF SHELTER OPERATIONS THAT DOES NOT DISCLOSE PROTECTED PERSONAL INFORMATION.

SUCH OVERVIEW SHALL INCLUDE, AT A MINIMUM: (I) AVERAGE AND MEDIAN LENGTH OF STAY; (II) SHELTER CAPACITY AND OCCUPANCY; (III) NUMBER OF ADMISSIONS AND TRANSFERS; (IV) AGGREGATE IDENTITY VERIFICATION RESULTS; (V) AGGREGATE INFORMATION REGARDING CRIMINAL-RECORD SCREENING; (VI) AGGREGATE INFORMATION REGARDING MENTAL-FUNCTION OR OTHER REQUIRED EVALUATIONS, WHERE LAWFUL; (VII) AMOUNTS OF PUBLIC MONEY RECEIVED AND SPENT; (VIII) NUMBER AND TYPES OF SAFETY INCIDENTS; (IX) NUMBER OF COMPLAINTS AND ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS; AND (X) THE SHELTER'S COMPLIANCE GRADE OR OTHER STANDARDIZED OVERSIGHT RATING ESTABLISHED BY THE OFFICE.
(D) THE OFFICE SHALL ESTABLISH PROCEDURES TO ENSURE THAT ALL RECORDS REQUIRED UNDER THIS ARTICLE ARE ACCURATE, AUDITABLE, AND AVAILABLE TO AUTHORIZED OVERSIGHT ENTITIES. § 4.

If any provision of this act, or the application thereof to any person or circumstance, is held invalid, the invalidity shall not affect other provisions or applications of this act which can be given effect without the invalid provision or application, and to that end, the provisions of this act are severable. § 5.

This act shall take effect on the first day of the twelfth month after it shall have become a law; provided, however, that shelters operating on such effective date shall have 60 days from such date to come into compliance with sections 56 and 57 of the social services law, as added by section three of this act, and may operate provisionally during that period subject to interim standards established by the office of temporary and disability assistance.

title.after: MEET ALINA BONSELL | Candidate for New York State Senate District 28

added: top of page HOME MEET ALINA 8-POINT PLAN EVENTS NEWS CONTACT MERCH FOLLOW US GET INVOLVED DONATE WHY I'M RUNNING I’m tired of the excuses coming out of Albany while our neighborhood pays the price.
I’m tired of career politicians with no term limits falling in line with a far-left, DSA-driven agenda and endorsing someone for mayor whom nearly two-thirds of their own constituents rejected.

They look the other way as antisemitism rises, our streets and subways become less safe, homeless encampments become more prevalent, and more shelters open in our neighborhoods without addressing mental illness or the underlying problems they are supposed to solve. ​ I’m tired of unfair taxes, struggling small businesses, and a broken family court system where cases drag on for years, hurting parents and children.
This campaign is personal because neglect has been personal for me and for so many people across District 28.
After 24 years of neglect under the same state senator, it’s time for a change.
My Story ALINA BONSELL My family came to America as Jewish refugees from Soviet Ukraine and settled in Brooklyn with almost nothing.
I later lived in Staten Island and Long Island before making Manhattan’s East Side my home more than #ago.

I graduated from Hofstra University, built a career in healthcare and pharmaceuticals, started my own business, and completed an entrepreneurship program at Wharton. ​ I married young, raised two sons, and learned that life rarely goes according to plan.
Like so many New Yorkers, I’ve gone through divorce, fought for my children in a broken family court system, faced housing struggles, and dealt with the rising cost of living in this city.
Neglect isn’t an abstract issue to me.

I know what it feels like to fight for your family in a courtroom, struggle to afford the place you call home, and face systems that make people feel powerless while expecting them to accept less. ​ Today, I live in Yorkville and am a businesswoman, entrepreneur, and mother of two.
I don’t come from political connections or inherited privilege.

I believe government should make people’s lives easier, not harder, by providing accountability, opportunity, public safety, support for strong families, and fewer bureaucratic barriers standing in the way.
MY 8-POINT PLAN Watch VIDEOS NOT MAGA I'm not running for a party.
I believe in JUSTICE Court system that is fair and accounable.
WOMEN'S RIGHT The freedom to choose.
PRO ISRAEL ​ ISRAEL Israel has the right to exist.
EDUCATION Support charter school expansion & civics education.
EQUAL RIGHTS Equal opportunity for all.
NO OVERREACH Protect individual freedom and choice.
IMMIGRATION Secure borders and a fair legal process.

Professional Experience BACKGROUND With 20 years of experience across the pharmaceutical and private sectors, my career has been dedicated to leadership, execution, and managing complex systems with accountability and measurable outcomes.
Having worked within the regulatory frameworks that influence businesses, families, and communities, I possess a deep understanding of how policy decisions impact them.

My approach is practical, disciplined, and rooted in real-world rather than political theory, which is the perspective I will bring to the New York State Senate: a commitment to clarity, fairness, and results-driven leadership in Albany.
HOFSTRA UNIVERSITY NEW YORK Frank G.

[image: Every day I wake up to another story of someone being stabbed, shoved, or shot in our neighborhoods in Manhattan. Too many New Yorkers feel like they have to walk around constantly on high alert. The first step toward restoring public safety in New York is fixing our broken bail reform laws. As a candidate for State Senate, I fully support this mission, and as a state legislator, I will fight to make these long-overdue changes. @sarithaforny , candidate for Attorney General, and I share the same commitment to public safety. This election gives New Yorkers an opportunity to replace longtime incumbents like Liz Krueger and Letitia James with leaders who will put the safety of innocent people first. According to the NYPD, the number of individuals arrested three or more times for felony assault has increased by 205.6% since 2018. In May, 76-year-old retired teacher Ross Falzone died after being pushed down subway stairs. The man charged with his murder had four prior arrests that year and had been released from psychiatric evaluation just hours earlier. This is just one of numerous tragedies raising serious concerns about repeat violent offenders. Not every victim dies. Many survive brutal assaults, stabbings and other violent crimes, carrying physical and emotional trauma for the rest of their lives. How many more innocent New Yorkers must suffer before we change the dangerous laws that have failed to protect them? In my latest interview with Patch, I answer these questions candidly, including where I agree and disagree with my own party, my views on immigration and healthcare, and why I believe good policy should never be dictated by party loyalty. I also share what sets me apart from career politicians. I’ve been an immigrant, a renter, a homeowner, a mother, an employee, an entrepreneur, insured and uninsured. I’ve experienced government assistance and navigated government systems that have failed me. I’ve lived many of the challenges that politicians spend their careers debating. I never intended to enter politics. But I believe those experiences give me a perspective that is often missing in Albany. My goal isn’t a political career. It’s to turn real-life experience into meaningful legislative change. Thank you to Patch for the opportunity to share my story, my independence, and the policies I intend to pursue. But over time, I watched the neighborhood I love become harder to live in and harder to recognize.

Democrat Amanda Marie Green is facing Republican Austin Rogers in the race to replace retiring U.S.
Neal Dunn (R), who was first elected in 2016.

Since pulling out a narrow victory in a crowded and contentious Primary for Florida’s 2nd Congressional District, Democratic nominee Amanda Marie Green has wasted no time consolidating support within her party.

title.after: Chehalis Lake Country Park – Andy Zahn

added: Skip to content Andy Zahn Platform About Chehalis Lake Country Park Back in 2021, the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife sought to acquire the former Transalta coal mine near Chehalis/Centralia to turn it into a nearly 9800 acre wildlife area.
Unfortunately, political interests interfered and got the project paused, seemingly indefinitely.
This represents a tragic and frustrating setback for outdoor access to a surprisingly beautiful landscape which many people don’t even know exists.
The mine has been reclaimed, and is now a vibrant tapestry of prairie, forest, and numerous sparkling lakes.
In short, the community here has one of the most beautiful landscapes in the region on its doorstep, yet is unable to set foot there.
Transalta was going to actually donate the land to WDFW.
It is in essence a free 10,000 acre park full of immense potential for outdoor access, just waiting to be unlocked.
I would propose to expand the area from what was originally proposed, in order to create a more cohesive visitor experience, but even just as originally outlined, the concept was amazing.
I suggest that we call this place the Chehalis Lake Country, and that it be managed primarily for wildlife habitat as was originally intended.
However, there is also the opportunity here to establish extensive low impact recreation opportunities.
It is not an exaggeration to state that a hiking trail system here could rival any other in the state for scenic quality and for a variety of terrain.
It is also at an elevation where the trail system would be accessible year-round.
This is important given the need to extend the economic benefit of tourism and outdoor recreation into the winter months.

This area would be particularly attractive during the spring flower season, potentially drawing in folks who might otherwise choose the Columbia Gorge or Eastern Washington as their destination for spring adventures.
Many such areas are becoming badly overcrowded in this season, and Chehalis Lake Country could act as a much-needed pressure valve for those regions.
Additionally, strategic planting of native deciduous species of plants and shrubs such as aspen, paper birch, big leaf maple, and vine maple would turn the area into an autumn destination as well.
As I’m writing this article, Mt.
Rainier National Park, North Cascades Highway, and other areas of the Cascade Mountains are being mobbed by hordes of leaf-peepers and larch-lookers.
There is clearly a growing interest in shoulder-season outdoor attractions, and the Chehalis Lake Country could offer such experiences in a location that’s just a few miles off I-5.
To get an idea of just how enormous the opportunity is here, let’s go over what a potential trail network might look like.
The Northern edge of the park would be located near the town of Bucoda.
In fact, I would suggest having the border be contiguous with Bucoda Volunteer Park.
This would enable residents and visitors to access the new park directly from town, which is precisely what is needed to boost the economy of small towns such as this.
Across the ridge from Bucoda lies the long vanished town of Tono, which was entirely demolished as the Transalta mine expanded.
Today the site is the home of several lakes, including one of considerable size.
The landscape resembles rolling moorland, with wide prairie and groves of trees, inset by deep blue lakes.
It is easy to imagine a looping lakeshore trail here, connecting with other loop trails rambling off into the meadows of the hills.
Southward of the closed coal fired power plant are even more vast areas of meadows and lakes which have been established in place of the former mine.
These stretch far to the East past another former town, Kopiah, and terminate against forested hills North of Onalaska.
A Southern trailhead could even potentially be established to provide easy access to residents of Eastern Lewis County.

There is enough space here even to support overnight backpacking, with high ridgelines offering expansive views, and multiple access points would make the region attractive for multi-day visits and be conducive to repeat visitors.
It’s the dream scenario for tourism and outdoor recreation in rural Washington State.
Protected as a park, it will only become more wild and beautiful with time.

added: top of page Home Meet Anne News Contact Photos Get Involved All Posts Search Debate Recap by CT Examiner #ago 5 min read SALEM — In a civil, policy-focused debate at Gardner Lake Firehouse Wednesday night, nearly 100 local residents and politicos from across the region watched and sometimes cheered loudly as State Rep.
Nick Menapace and his challenger Anne Santoro took questions on electric rates, state budgets, Flock cameras and immigration.
The debate was moderated by CT Examiner Editor-in-Chief Gregory Stroud.
The biggest surprise of the debate may have been what wasn’t said or mentioned by either candidate – President Donald Trump.

Nick Menapace, a progressive Democrat and schoolteacher who defeated Republican Holly Cheeseman by just 99 votes in 2024, is facing a challenge from Anne Santoro, an attorney who previously served on East Lyme’s Deputy First Selectman.
Santoro is running as the Republican and Independent Party candidate.
Menapace offered a variety of policy solutions, including publicly owned utilities, and loosening the state’s fiscal guardrails to allow increased spending on towns and schools.
Santoro argued for reining in spending and rolling back some of the “1,400 unfunded mandates” on the state’s cities and towns.

Asked why residents pay some of the highest electricity rates in the country – and what if anything they would do about it – Menapace pitched what he called a “true public option” to partially undo what he blamed on the failures of deregulation.“It has resulted in all of us paying much, much higher premiums for energy rates,” Menapace said.

“The only other option we have is to create more competition, but you know, frankly, that’s something we can’t do … Eversource doesn’t want to see their monopoly broken up.” Santoro agreed on deregulation, but took aim at the public benefits charge added to customer electricity bills.
“This is definitely an issue, and definitely one way that we can reduce our energy costs.
So this is something I would like to see done by the legislature, examine these programs, figure out if they should stay or go,” Santoro said.
Asked whether the state had struck a fair balance between state income taxes and local property taxes, Santoro emphasized the need for fiscal discipline.

“We need to work towards reduction in our state income tax, and changing categories … this is something that should be a goal, and I think there’s many ways of getting at that if we start budgeting more appropriately,” Santoro said.Menapace argued that the biggest problem driving higher local property taxes was the lack of aid to towns and cities through the state’s outdated Education Cost Sharing formula.

“It is the biggest problem that we are going to be addressing next year, because everyone seems to agree that this is a huge problem … just 14 years is a long time to try to fix this issue,” Menapace said.

“We have every single town doing its own thing and paying for every single thing and when it comes to education, that drives up our costs exponentially.”In her rebuttal, Santoro argued that Menapace was ignoring the many times that Republican lawmakers had already proposed permanent methods of funding ECS.“This is all happening, but it should have happened a lot of years ago, and it should have happened on Mr.

Menapace’s watch as far as I’m concerned,” Santoro said.The candidates also disagreed on the state’s fiscal guardrails, adopted in 2017 as part of a bipartisan deal to limit the use of higher state revenues for public spending.
Menapace argued that loosening those curbs was actually prudent.
“We’ve paid down so much of the debt that it is now being told by all the analysts that it is better for us to start spending that money on our people or reducing taxes.

And we can’t do that unless we adjust the fiscal barriers,” Menapace said.Santoro stood by the current budget constraint and a conservative approach to the state’s sometimes boom-and-bust revenues.“That was so important for stabilizing our economy and providing fiscal discipline.
There’s too much dependence on volatile income in our state,” Santoro said.

On housing, both candidates agreed on the need for more, but had differing solutions to meet the need.Menapace embraced last year’s far-reaching housing bill, passed in a November special session of the state legislature, which eases the conversion of commercial properties into housing and takes a regional approach to apportioning development.

Santoro argued that the state’s efforts dating back to the passage of 8-30g, the state’s affordable housing statute, in 1989 and last year’s housing bill had actually slowed the construction of housing by imposing burdensome and time-consuming demands on developers and towns.
She argued instead for more local control.

Asked how they would ensure that the 37th House District – East Lyme, Salem and Montville – would benefit from the estimated $23 billion of spending and investment over 12 years at Electric Boat in nearby Groton, Menapace emphasized the need for more housing, and investments in Shore Line East.
“If we are not building housing in the area, people are going to be coming from far and farther away to be able to come and work here,” he said.
Santoro also focused on investments in transit.“We need to deal with both buses and trains.
Buses can be very advantageous to take the congestion off of our roads,” she said.

Both candidates shared concerns about Flock cameras, but the next question on immigration enforcement drew by far the sharpest contrast between the candidates – and the strongest response from the audience.
Asked whether they supported the state’s current approach to federal immigration enforcement, both candidates offered strong and by turns emotional responses.
There were equal parts cheers and boos echoing in the hall after each answer.
“I don’t think that there is anything that is appropriate … with no identification going in and grabbing people.
It is not the way to conduct immigration at all,” said Menapace.
Santoro argued that the state’s lack of cooperation with federal immigration had actually exacerbated the problem.
“We have an issue in Connecticut and in other states where there is lack of cooperation.
My solution is, please let’s cooperate.
And where ICE has cooperated in other jurisdictions in other states, you don’t see this conflict,” Santoro said.“When we have criminals who are illegally here — it’s a double whammy.
I think that we need to let ICE do its job,” she said.
Asked to highlight one disagreement with their party’s nominee for governor, Menapace said he wished Gov.
Ned Lamont would be “more forward thinking” on public transit.Santoro offered a nuts-and-bolts critique of State Sen.
Ryan Fazio’s idea of capping property taxes at the rate of inflation .
“I understand the desire to do that, but again, it looks, feels, and sounds like another state mandate to me,” she said.
Both candidates spoke with CT Examiner after the debate, while a crowd stayed and talked among themselves into the evening.
“We disagree with each other, and that’s how we move things forward.
We have to keep pushing that, and I always want everyone to be able to push me on these things.
And I’m really glad that we’re able to do that,” said Menapace.
“I’ve run two other elections for first selectmen, and my opponent never wanted to debate,” Santoro said.

“So for me, this was important, sort of a rite of passage, if you will.” Luke Feeney A 2024 graduate of the University of Connecticut, Luke Feeney covered the Gilgo Beach murders, the 2025 Ryder Cup, as well as local and statewide politics on Long Island prior to joining CT Examiner in 2026.

removed: top of page Home Meet Anne News Contact Photos Get Involved All Posts Search Letter to the Day-Don MacKenzie #ago 2 min read Anne Santoro is running for state Representative in the 37th District representing East Lyme, Montville and Salem.
Anne is a graduate of Stanford University and UConn School of Law.

She is an attorney that has practiced municipal and business law along with an exemplary public service record serving East Lyme as our Deputy First Selectman, the Board of Finance, Chairperson of the ARPA Subcommittee and more.
She and her husband Fred (local pediatrician) have been residents in East Lyme for over 35 years.
Before moving to East Lyme, Anne served as legal counsel for the towns of Milford and Greenwich.
That should cover the smart and hard-working part.
Today a Democratic Governor, House and Senate are governing Connecticut.
I do not hate Democrats, but a strong government must have some semblance of balance and ideas coupled with healthy dialogue.

Based on standings amongst other states, our “one-party rule” obviously is not a recipe that is working for our state as Connecticut continually ranks among the most expensive states in the country to live in as more people are still moving out than moving in.
There is only one reason for that, the cost of living.
Groceries, gasoline and utilities, especially electricity rates, are a heavy financial burden for our residents.
Our state is also well-known for its tax structure.

Beyond the state’s income taxes, residents face exceptionally high property taxes, vehicle taxes and estate taxes, therefore being forced to move to tax-friendlier states which represent financial relief for them.
When they leave, they also take their spending and tax dollars elsewhere.
They would prefer to stay in Connecticut, but their fixed income is just that, fixed income.
Now to Anne Santoro and playing well with others.
Let’s face it, her opponent has had a rough term regarding “playing well with others,” not only with the opposing party but his own party as well.
I cannot recall a time when the Speaker of the House has called out one of his own in public.
This has been well-documented in the media as well.
Send Anne Santoro to Hartford and let us try something different.
It is time for a change as she is indeed smart, hard-working and plays well with others.

Don MacKenzie Niantic Editor's note: The writer is Chairman of the East Lyme Republican Town Committee Stay Connected, Hear from Anne on the Campaign Trail Email * Yes, subscribe me to your newsletter.
