title.after: DATA CENTERS #2

added: Purpose and Intent D R A FT Data centers are unique developments associated with technology, information systems, data infrastructure, data hosting and management, data processing, data storage, and related services.

Due to their operational characteristics, data centers may generate substantially less traffic than traditional industrial uses while requiring significant electrical and utility infrastructure that may not be readily available in existing industrially zoned areas.

The purpose of this Section is to establish standards and procedures for permitting data centers in appropriate locations while protecting surrounding properties, residents, environmental resources, public health, safety, and welfare, and the character of the County.

Definition Data Center: A physical building or facilities associated with technology, information systems, data infrastructure, data hosting and management activities, and similar information-age uses, including data processing, data storage, and related services.
Structures and land may also be used for uses customarily incidental and accessory to the primary data center use.

Closed-Loop Cooling System: A sealed cooling system in which water or another cooling fluid is continuously recirculated within the cooling system and is not routinely discharged, consumed, evaporated, or replaced through normal cooling operations.

I (Industrial) District A data center may be permitted within an I (Industrial) zoning district, subject to the applicable use procedures, site plan review requirements, and all other development regulations and standards.
Minimum Parcel Area.​ A data center shall be located on a parcel or assemblage of contiguous parcels containing a minimum of ten (10) acres.

Conditional Use Versus Rezoning.​ Because a data center may be permitted as a Conditional Use rather than through rezoning to the I, Industrial District, the applicant shall demonstrate that the proposed location is appropriate for a data center and that the property is better suited for a Conditional Use than rezoning to the I District.

Utility, Water, Electric, and Gas As part of the Concept Plan submittal, the applicant shall provide a utility inventory identifying existing and proposed utility infrastructure necessary to serve the development.

The inventory shall include, as applicable, electrical transmission and distribution lines, utility corridors, easements, water and wastewater infrastructure, natural gas facilities, and other significant utility infrastructure.

D R A FT The utility inventory shall demonstrate the availability and suitability of the proposed utility infrastructure to support the development and shall identify any significant utility improvements, extensions, or easements necessary to serve the proposed data center.
Letters of approval or capacity confirmation from all applicable utility providers shall be submitted with the Concept Plan.

Each letter shall confirm that the utility provider has the capacity and ability to accommodate the development's projected maximum peak demand and all required utility infrastructure, including any necessary improvements, extensions, or upgrades.

Review Criteria.​ In reviewing a Conditional Use application for a data center, the County shall consider the potential impacts of the proposed development on surrounding properties and the community, including, but not limited to: 9/ 24 1.​ Traffic and transportation impacts; 2.​ Noise; 3.​ Exterior lighting; 4.​ Visual impacts; 5.​ Electrical and other utility infrastructure; 6.​ Groundwater and other environmental resources; 7.​ Stormwater and drainage; 8.​ Compatibility with adjacent land uses; and 9.​ Other impacts reasonably related to the proposed development.
The County may impose additional conditions reasonably necessary to mitigate impacts associated with the proposed data center.

Such conditions may include, but are not limited to, increased setbacks, enhanced landscaping or screening, additional buffers, noise limitations, lighting restrictions, traffic-control measures, limitations on hours of construction, utility-related requirements, stormwater controls, environmental protections, and other appropriate development standards.

General Development Standards All data centers shall comply with the following minimum development standards, in addition to all other applicable requirements of this Ordinance and the County's development regulations.
Building Height D R A FT Principal buildings shall not exceed fifty (50) feet in height, measured from the structure pad level.

This height limitation shall not apply to accessory or incidental structures and equipment such as water towers, conveyor systems, smokestacks, and other similar uninhabited structures or components customarily associated with the operation of a data center.
Setbacks A minimum setback of one hundred (100) feet shall be maintained from all exterior property lines when the property is zoned I (Industrial).
When an Industrial-zoned property is adjacent to or abuts property zoned Residential, a minimum setback of four hundred (400) feet shall be maintained from the adjoining residential property line.
See Section 4(G) for additional applicable requirements.
Minimum Lot Frontage 9/ 24 The development shall have a minimum of one hundred (100) feet of frontage adjoining a public street.
Minimum Lot Width The minimum lot width at the building line shall be one hundred (100) feet.
Minimum Lot Area The minimum lot area shall be ten (10) acres.
Green Space 1.​ All data centers shall maintain a minimum of fifteen percent (15%) of the total parcel area as green space.
DRAFT D R A FT 2.​ Green space shall consist primarily of natural vegetation and may include trees, shrubs, flowers, native grasses, and other appropriate plant materials.
3.​ Required green space shall be maintained in a healthy, orderly, and aesthetically pleasing condition and shall be regularly groomed and maintained.
4.​ Required green space shall not be used for the placement of buildings, equipment, parking areas, driveways, storage, or other impervious surfaces, except as specifically permitted by the County.
5.​ The property owner or data center operator shall be responsible for the ongoing maintenance, replacement, and care of all required vegetation and landscaped areas.

Buffer and Screening Requirements 1.​ In addition to required setbacks, a minimum four-hundred-foot (400) buffer shall be maintained along property boundaries adjoining residentially used or residentially zoned property, unless a greater buffer is required as a condition of Conditional Use approval.
2.​ The required buffer shall remain undisturbed to the maximum extent practicable.

3.​ Where the Zoning Administrator determines that an undisturbed buffer will not provide adequate visual screening, the Zoning Administrator may require supplemental landscaping, berms, fencing, walls, or other improvements necessary to provide adequate screening for adjoining properties.
4.​ The required buffer shall be maintained in perpetuity for the life of the data center use, subject to approved modifications or replacement plantings.

Air-Conditioning, HVAC, and Mechanical Equipment 1.​ Air-conditioning units, HVAC systems, generators, mechanical equipment, and similar exterior equipment shall be thoroughly screened from view from public rights-of-way and adjacent properties through the use of walls, fencing, architectural elements, roof elements, landscaping, or a combination thereof.
2.​ The screening requirement shall not apply where the equipment is located more than four hundred (400) feet from an adjacent property line, unless otherwise required as a condition of approval.
Front Building Facade 1.​ The front building facade of each principal building shall be oriented toward the street frontage or an adjacent arterial street frontage.

DRAFT 2.​ This requirement shall not apply when the front of the building is located more than four hundred (400) feet from the public right-of-way or when the building is not visible from the public right-of-way.

Security Fencing and Walls D R A FT 1.​ Security fencing and walls shall not be located within a required buffer unless such fencing or wall complies with the general fencing regulations of this Ordinance and has been approved as part of the development plan.

2.​ Fences and walls located outside required setbacks and buffers shall not be subject to otherwise applicable height limitations when necessary for site security, provided that they comply with applicable safety and visibility requirements.
Accessory Structures 1.​ Accessory structures shall comply with the standards of the applicable zoning district and all other applicable County regulations.

2.​ Notwithstanding other provisions of this Ordinance, guardhouses, security buildings, and secured-entry features shall be permitted at public road entrances when customarily associated with the operation of the data center.
Internal Development Roads 9/ 24 Internal development roads may be public or private and shall comply with applicable County engineering standards and development regulations.
Exterior Lighting Exterior illumination shall be designed to minimize impacts on surrounding properties and preserve existing nighttime darkness to the greatest extent practicable.
Lighting shall be shielded and directed downward to prevent glare and light trespass onto adjacent properties.
The following minimum standards shall apply: A.
All exterior lighting fixtures shall be full-cutoff fixtures.
Light poles shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height.
All light poles shall be set back a minimum of fifty (50) feet from any exterior property line.
Illumination at any exterior property line shall not exceed a maximum of 0.5 foot-candles.

The Zoning Administrator may require a photometric lighting plan demonstrating compliance with these requirements as part of the Concept Plan, site plan, building permit, or other applicable development review.
Noise Data center operations shall be designed and operated to minimize noise impacts on surrounding properties.

Daytime Noise Standard Data center operations shall not produce continuous sound exceeding an average of 65 decibels (dBA) over any thirty (30)-minute period between 8:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., measured at any adjacent property boundary between the data center site and a residential property.

Nighttime Noise Standard Data center operations shall not produce continuous sound exceeding an average of 55 decibels (dBA) over any thirty (30)-minute period between 6:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., measured at any adjacent property boundary between the data center site and a residential property.

Sound Testing 9/ 24 Following issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy for each data center building, the County may conduct or require the data center owner or operator to provide a professional sound study to verify compliance with the applicable noise standards.

Notice of Violation and Corrective Action If a data center is determined to be in violation of the applicable noise standards, the County may issue a notice of violation requiring the owner or operator to take appropriate corrective action.
The Zoning Administrator may require the owner or operator to submit a corrective-action plan identifying the proposed solution and a reasonable period for implementation.
If the corrective-action plan is approved by the Zoning Administrator, the owner or operator shall implement the approved corrective measures within the time period established by the County.

Penalties Failure to successfully implement an approved corrective-action plan within the established time period may constitute a violation of this Ordinance and may be subject to applicable enforcement remedies, including a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars ($1,000) per day for each day the violation continues, to the extent authorized by applicable law.

Cost of Testing D R A FT The data center owner or operator shall bear the reasonable costs of any sound test or professional sound study required by the County to determine compliance with this Section.
Water Conservation and Cooling Systems A.

Cooling System Requirement. ​ Every new data center subject to this Ordinance shall utilize a Closed-Loop Cooling System or another cooling technology demonstrated to the satisfaction of the County to provide equivalent or greater protection against consumptive water use.

Cooling Technology Documentation. ​ The applicant shall identify the proposed cooling technology and provide sufficient documentation for the County to determine compliance with this requirement as part of the development application.
Monitoring Wells and Groundwater Protection A.

Identification of Wells.​ Any data center proposed or located on a parcel of land that contains an existing private well, public well, or monitoring well, or that is adjacent to property containing such wells, shall identify, locate, and document all known wells within and adjacent to the property.

Monitoring Program.​ The data center owner or operator shall establish and maintain a monitoring program for applicable wells to monitor groundwater conditions and identify any potential impacts associated with the construction or operation of the data center.
Monitoring Records.​ All monitoring data and records shall be maintained in a current, accurate, and legible manner.
Records shall include, at a minimum: DRAFT 1.​ The location of each monitored well; 2.​ Dates of monitoring; 3.​ Measurements and test results; and 4.​ Any other information required by the County.
Reporting.​ Monitoring records shall be submitted to the County at intervals established by the County and shall be made available for inspection upon request.
D R A FT All submissions shall be complete, legible, current, and maintained in a format acceptable to the County.

Additional Monitoring.​ The County may require additional monitoring, testing, reporting, or documentation when necessary to protect groundwater resources or determine whether the construction or operation of a data center is adversely affecting existing wells or groundwater conditions.

Applicability.​ This Section shall apply to any new data center, expansion of an existing data center, or substantial modification of an existing data center that includes one or more stationary diesel-fueled electric generating units intended to provide emergency, standby, backup, or supplemental electrical power.

Tier 4 Requirement.​ 9/ 24 All new stationary diesel-fueled electric generating units installed at a data center subject to this Section shall be certified by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) as meeting applicable Tier 4 Final emission standards and shall comply with all applicable federal, State of Georgia, and local air-quality requirements.

No diesel-fueled electric generating unit that is not Tier 4 Final-certified shall be installed, permitted, or operated as part of a data center subject to this Section, except as expressly provided in subsection (f).

Certification and Documentation.​ Prior to the issuance of any building permit, installation permit, or certificate of occupancy, as applicable, the owner or operator of a data center subject to this Section shall provide documentation reasonably satisfactory to the County demonstrating that each applicable diesel-fueled electric generating unit: DRAFT 1.​ Is certified by the EPA as meeting applicable Tier 4 Final emission standards; 2.​ Meets all applicable requirements of the federal Clean Air Act and implementing regulations; 3.​ Meets all applicable requirements of the Georgia Environmental Protection Division (“EPD”) and any applicable air-quality permit; 4.​ Is installed, configured, maintained, and operated in accordance with the manufacturer's certified configuration and applicable emissions-control requirements; and 5.​ Includes and maintains all emissions-control equipment necessary to preserve the unit's Tier 4 Final certification during operation.
D R A FT The County may require additional documentation reasonably necessary to verify compliance with this Section.

Replacement and Expansion.​ Any replacement stationary diesel-fueled electric generating unit installed at a data center after the effective date of this Section shall comply with the Tier 4 Final requirement established by this Section, regardless of the emissions classification of the generating unit being replaced.
Any additional stationary diesel-fueled electric generating unit installed as part of an expansion or substantial modification of an existing data center shall likewise comply with this Section.

Prohibition on Circumvention.​ No person shall install, operate, replace, modify, maintain, or configure a stationary diesel-fueled electric generating unit subject to this Section in a manner that causes the unit to lose its EPA Tier 4 Final certification or that defeats, bypasses, disables, removes, or materially reduces the effectiveness of any emissions-control equipment required for such certification.

9/ 24 This subsection shall not prohibit actions expressly authorized by applicable federal or State law or actions reasonably necessary to address an immediate emergency involving life safety, property protection, or emergency response, provided that such actions are otherwise lawful.

Limited Exemption.​ Upon written application by the owner or operator, the Board of Commissioners of Walker County may approve a limited exemption from the Tier 4 Final requirement only upon making written findings that one or more of the following circumstances exists: 1.​ A Tier 4 Final-compliant generating unit is not commercially available for the specific application; 2.​ Compliance would create a demonstrated and unreasonable threat to electric-system reliability, life safety, or emergency response capability; or 3.​ An alternative generating technology provides equivalent or greater emissions performance.

DRAFT Any exemption granted under this subsection shall: 1.​ Be limited to the minimum scope necessary to address the demonstrated circumstance; 2.​ Be limited to the minimum duration reasonably necessary to address such circumstance; 3.​ Identify the specific generating unit or units covered by the exemption; 4.​ Be documented in writing and maintained as part of the County's records; and 5.​ Not relieve the owner or operator from compliance with any applicable federal or State emissions requirement, air-quality permit, or other legally applicable requirement.

More Stringent Requirements.​ D R A FT Compliance with this Section shall not relieve any person from compliance with any more stringent requirement imposed by federal or State law, regulation, air-quality permit, or other applicable governmental authority.

Compliance With Other Regulations Approval of a data center as a Conditional Use shall not exempt the development from compliance with any other applicable provision of the County Code, zoning ordinance, subdivision regulations, development regulations, building codes, fire codes, stormwater requirements, environmental regulations, utility requirements, or other applicable federal, state, or local laws.
Where the standards of this Section conflict with a more restrictive applicable regulation, the more restrictive requirement shall apply unless otherwise expressly provided by this Ordinance.

Additional Conditions of Approval 9/ 24 The Board or other approval authority may impose reasonable and site-specific conditions on a Conditional Use approval when necessary to protect surrounding properties, public health, safety, and welfare, or to mitigate identified impacts of the proposed data center.
Such conditions may include, but are not limited to: A.
Limitations on construction activities; DRAFT G.
Other reasonable measures supported by the record of the application.
D R A FT No condition shall be imposed in a manner inconsistent with applicable federal or state law.

Enforcement A violation of any applicable provision of this Section, any approved Conditional Use, or any condition imposed as part of Conditional Use approval shall be subject to the enforcement remedies provided by this Ordinance and applicable law.
Nothing in this Section shall be construed to limit any other enforcement authority or remedy available to the County under applicable law.
Fire, Life Safety, and Emergency Response A.

Compliance with Applicable Codes 9/ 24 All data centers shall comply with all applicable Georgia State Minimum Standard Codes, fire codes, building codes, electrical codes, life-safety requirements, and other applicable federal, state, and local requirements.
Fire-protection and life-safety systems shall be designed, installed, inspected, tested, and maintained in accordance with applicable law and adopted codes.
Nothing in this section shall be construed to supersede or conflict with the authority of the State Fire Marshal, the applicable fire authority, or other governmental agency having jurisdiction.

Emergency Response Plan Prior to issuance of a certificate of occupancy, the owner or operator of a data center shall submit a site-specific Emergency Response Plan ("ERP") to the County and the appropriate emergency-response agencies.

The ERP shall be maintained in current form and updated whenever a material change to the facility affects emergency response, fire protection, hazardous materials, emergency access, electrical systems, backup power, or battery-energy-storage systems.

Emergency Contacts D R A FT The owner or operator shall maintain current emergency contact information for: 1.​ The facility owner or operator; 2.​ An on-site facility representative; 3.​ A 24-hour emergency contact authorized to make operational decisions; 4.​ The facility security contact; and 5.​ Other contacts reasonably necessary to support emergency response, including utility, generator, fuel, fire-protection, or battery-system personnel when applicable.
Emergency contact information shall be provided to the County and appropriate emergency-response agencies and updated promptly following any change.

Site-Specific Safety Measures Where the applicable fire or emergency-response authority identifies a site-specific hazard requiring additional measures, the County may require reasonable mitigation through the development-review process to the extent authorized by applicable law.
Any such requirement shall be based upon applicable code, law, recognized fire or safety standards, or documented site-specific conditions.
Decommissioning Plan 9/ 24 Prior to the permanent closure of a data center, the owner or operator shall submit a Decommissioning Plan to the Walker County Planning Office for review and approval.

The Decommissioning Plan shall describe the proposed procedures and schedule for the orderly cessation of operations, removal, reuse, recycling, or disposal of equipment and infrastructure, management of hazardous or regulated materials, disconnection of utilities, site security, and restoration of the property.
The Decommissioning Plan shall identify, as applicable: 1.​ Anticipated Closure Date.
The anticipated date on which data center operations will permanently cease.

An inventory of equipment and infrastructure proposed for removal, reuse, recycling, or disposal, including, as applicable, servers, racks, generators, cooling systems, transformers, electrical equipment, fuel systems, batteries, telecommunications equipment, and other associated infrastructure.

Procedures for the identification, handling, removal, transportation, recycling, treatment, and disposal of batteries, generators, fuel, refrigerants, chemicals, electronic equipment, and other hazardous or regulated materials in accordance with applicable federal, state, and local laws.
Procedures for the safe disconnection and termination, as applicable, of electrical, telecommunications, natural gas, water, wastewater, cooling, fuel, and other utility services.
DRAFT D R A FT 5.​ Demolition and Removal.

A description of proposed demolition, dismantling, removal, or abandonment of buildings, structures, foundations, equipment, tanks, generators, cooling systems, electrical infrastructure, and other site improvements.

Measures to prevent unauthorized access to the property during and following decommissioning, including securing buildings, structures, equipment, hazardous materials, and other potential safety hazards.

Proposed measures for restoring the property following decommissioning, including removal of debris and abandoned equipment, repair of disturbed areas, stabilization of exposed areas, removal or securing of subsurface infrastructure, and restoration of the site to a safe and orderly condition.
The anticipated schedule for commencement and completion of decommissioning activities, including significant milestones.

The identity, qualifications, and applicable licenses or certifications of contractors responsible for major decommissioning, demolition, environmental remediation, hazardous-material handling, or site-restoration activities.
Any other information reasonably required by the Walker County Planning Office to demonstrate compliance with this Ordinance and applicable federal, state, and local laws.

The owner or operator shall complete all decommissioning activities in accordance with the approved Decommissioning Plan and within the timeframe established therein, unless an extension is approved in writing by the Walker County Planning Office.

Performance Bond 9/ 24 The Board of Commissioners (BOC) may, in its discretion, require the applicant or owner of a proposed data center to provide a performance bond or other financial assurance to ensure the proper decommissioning of the data center and associated facilities upon cessation of operations.

The amount, form, duration, and conditions of any required performance bond or other financial assurance shall be established by the BOC and approved prior to the issuance of any permit for the data center.

Such financial assurance shall be maintained for the duration specified by the BOC and shall be sufficient to address the anticipated costs of decommissioning, removal of facilities, and restoration of the site.

Steven Doan Is Working to Clean Up Frankfort!

Experienced Leadership Served on Judiciary, Education, and Local Government standing committees Successf ull y repr esented law enforcement in Federal Court General Counsel for the Governor’s Office of Agricultural Policy Former Erlanger City Councilman Set policy at a statewide level Fiscally responsible leadership Passed legislation to expand freedom Steven's legislative record speaks for itself.
“As a father with two children under the age of three, I am deeply concerned by the state of our economy, educational system, and the erosion of the American dream.
Too often our leaders make promises and never uphold them.
I can proudly say that when I tell you I am “fighting for the future of Kentucky,” you can see it in my actions.

I am fighting not only for the future of my children, but for the futures of children all over the Commonwealth.." As State Representative, Steven will continue to advocate for policies that better the lives of hard working Kentuckians throughout the district and Kentucky.
Steven is running for re-election because it's time that the legislature aggressively advance conservative public policy.

Steven’s Policy Stances Steven is committed to defending the unborn and will advocate for the life at conception act. ​ Steven will support your right to self defense and will advocate for your Second Amendment rights.
Steven promises to guard your financial interests and will fight back against special interests seeking to raise taxes.
Steven is steadfast in his intent to clean out corruption from Frankfort while making it easier for you to live your life without government interference.
Steven’s Background Steven Doan, a lifelong resident of Erlanger, resides there with his family.
He is an alumnus of Lloyd High School (2005) and Northern Kentucky University (2009), where he obtained his degree.
His academic journey continued as he earned a Juris Doctorate from the esteemed Salmon P.
Chase College of Law in 2012. ​ Embarking on his legal career, Steven initially specialized in representing police officers in civil rights matters.
Later, in 2016, he assumed the pivotal role of General Counsel for the Governor’s Office of Agricultural Policy.

In this capacity, he managed substantial funds, including a multimillion-dollar grant fund and an $80 million-plus revolving loan fund. ​ Following his tenure with the Governor’s Office of Agricultural Policy, Steven has actively served clients across Northern Kentucky.

Simultaneously, he has dedicated himself to community betterment, contributing significantly through non-profit advocacy and his role on Erlanger's city council. ​ Elected to the general assembly in 2022, Steven has been unwavering in advocating for conservative public policies.
Throughout the 2022 session, he notably served on pivotal committees such as education, judiciary, and local government.
He takes pride in his consistent voting record, which includes advocating for tax reduction, safeguarding the welfare of children, and championing support for small businesses.

A recent Gallup poll says only 10% of Americans approve of Congress.
That’s only 1% above the all-time low of 9% (in November of 2013).
Gallup has measured approval since 1974, when approval was at 30%.

So you might say that normally people think Congress stinks, but nowadays?
There’s no getting around it; it sucks.

title.after: Rebuilding Pride in America: Why I’m Running for Colorado House of Representatives

added: top of page Home Events Blog Notifications Volunteer DONATE All Posts Rebuilding Pride in America: Why I’m Running for Colorado House of Representatives Douglas Jones Jun 17 4 min read A recent NBC News poll reveals a sharp decline in the number of Americans who feel extremely proud to be American.
The share dropped from the high 60s and low 70s in the years following 9/11 to just 33% today.
Alongside this, negative and ambivalent feelings about the country are growing.
This shift reflects deeper issues that affect our national spirit, especially here in Colorado, where Democrats control the state government while Republicans hold sway in Washington, DC.
This divide has left many feeling disconnected from the ideals that once made America a beacon of hope and opportunity.
Unlike other countries, America’s pride comes not from grand government programs but from the freedoms we enjoy.

These freedoms include the ability to start a business and prosper, the right to live without fear of discrimination based on skin color, religion, or heritage, and the freedom from government interference in personal medical and life decisions.

I am running for the Colorado House of Representatives because I believe in restoring these freedoms and rebuilding the pride that comes from living in a place that respects our right to pursue happiness.
I am a Libertarian because I believe government should focus on doing a few things well and do them efficiently, not overreaching into every aspect of our lives.

Colorado State Capitol Building, symbol of state governance The Decline of American Pride and What It Means for Colorado The drop in national pride is not just a number; it reflects real frustration and disillusionment.
Many Americans feel that government policies have drifted away from protecting individual freedoms and instead focus on expanding control.
This shift has created a sense of helplessness and division.
In Colorado, this is especially visible.
The state government, controlled by Democrats, sees your income as their boodle, pushing policies that limit personal choice and economic freedom.
Meanwhile, the federal government, controlled by Republicans, seeks wars of aggression, vanity construction projects for the President, and intimidation of minorities and immigrants.
This political tug-of-war leaves citizens caught in the middle, unsure who truly represents their interests.
The result is a loss of trust and pride in the institutions meant to serve us.
Why Freedom Defines American Pride America’s pride has always been rooted in freedom.

This freedom is not abstract; it is practical and personal: Freedom to start and grow a business Entrepreneurs in Colorado have built thriving companies because they can operate with fewer restrictions and more opportunity.
This freedom fuels innovation and creates jobs.
Freedom from discrimination Living without fear that your skin color, religion, or family background will make you a target is fundamental.
Colorado’s diverse communities deserve respect and equal treatment under the law.
Freedom from government overreach People want to make their own medical and personal decisions without government mandates dictating their choices.
This respect for individual autonomy is essential for a free society.
When these freedoms are protected, people feel proud to be part of a community and a country that values their rights and dignity.
What Government Should Do Government’s role should be clear and limited.
It should focus on a few key responsibilities and perform them well: Protecting individual rights Ensuring laws protect freedom of speech, religion, and equal treatment.
Maintaining public safety Providing effective law enforcement and emergency services.
Supporting infrastructure Building and maintaining roads, bridges, and essential services efficiently.
Ensuring fair and transparent governance Making government accountable and accessible to citizens.
When government tries to do too much, it often fails to do anything well.
Overregulation and excessive programs can stifle freedom and innovation.
Why I Am Running as a Libertarian I chose the Libertarian path because it aligns with the belief that government should be limited and focused.
Libertarian principles emphasize: Individual liberty People should have the freedom to live their lives as they choose, as long as they do not harm others.
Personal responsibility Citizens should be empowered to make decisions and accept the consequences.
Free markets Economic freedom leads to prosperity and opportunity for all.
Non-intervention Government should avoid unnecessary interference in personal and business affairs.
By running for the Colorado House of Representatives, I want to bring these values into state government.
I want to help rebuild the trust and pride that come from living in a state that respects freedom and opportunity.
How We Can Rebuild Citizen Pride in Colorado Rebuilding pride requires action and commitment.
Here are some practical steps: Promote policies that protect freedom Support laws that reduce unnecessary regulations and protect individual rights.
Encourage entrepreneurship Create an environment where small businesses can thrive without burdensome taxes or red tape.
Foster community respect and inclusion Work to ensure all Coloradans feel valued and safe, regardless of background.
Increase government transparency and efficiency Make government operations clear and accountable to citizens.
Engage citizens in decision-making Encourage public participation and listen to diverse voices.
These steps can restore faith in government and rebuild the pride that comes from living in a free and fair society.
The Hope for Colorado and America Despite the challenges, I have hope.
Colorado has a history of innovation, resilience, and community spirit.
By focusing on freedom and responsibility, we can turn the tide and restore pride in our state and country.
This campaign is about more than winning a seat.
It is about standing up for the values that make America unique and helping every Coloradan feel proud to call this place home.
If you believe in freedom, opportunity, and responsible government, I invite you to join me in this effort.
Together, we can rebuild pride in Colorado and set an example for the nation.
Let’s work to create a government that does a few things well, respects our rights, and supports the pursuit of happiness for all.

title.after: Why do people think government sucks?

added: top of page Home Events Blog Notifications Volunteer DONATE All Posts Why do people think government sucks?
Douglas Jones Apr 28 2 min read A recent Gallup poll says only 10% of Americans approve of Congress.
That’s only 1% above the all-time low of 9% (in November of 2013).
Gallup has measured approval since 1974, when approval was at 30%.
That is staggering, even if you consider the average approval over the years is only 28% and disapproval is 65%.
So you might say that normally people think Congress stinks, but nowadays?
There’s no getting around it; it sucks.
Republicans’ perception of Congress has fallen the furthest, with approval at 63% in March of last year and now sitting at 20%.
Democrats were unhappy already in 2025, with only 23% approving, but now that approval rating is resting in the toilet at 3%.
Pew research has recent polling on trust in government going back to 1958.
I was four years old then, and trust in government was at 73%.
It has declined quite steadily since then and now sits at a 17% level of trust in government.
Republicans and Republican-leaning independents trust the government at the rate of 25%.
Democrats trust the government at the rate of 9%, the lowest level of trust for them ever.
Why don’t we love our government?
Here are some reasons I can think of… 1.
Government doesn’t do what it is supposed to do.
For instance, the TSA is famously unpopular, adding time and hassle to your travel plans.
But with the DHS shutdown, waiting lines at the TSA are simply horrible.
Yes, we hate the TSA but we sure wish it would do its job efficiently and not make our lives worse than it already did.
With ICE’s record of denying people their basic rights and trampling on due process, many wonder why we need the department at all.
Government was supposed to defend rights and ensure constitutional restrictions on itself, wasn’t it?
Both parties controlling government want to expand it.
If it’s not for war, then it’s for control of the individual.
Regulatory burden on businesses never lets up and it only gets worse.
And it doesn’t matter which party is in power.
There is a clear correlation between the size and scope of government and people’s trust in it.
Government simply has no incentive to do better.
As they say, “When a private business does a bad job, it suffers.
But when government does a bad job, you suffer.” My takeaway is this: As long as the two big government parties control government, we are going to get more of the same.
More wars, more inflation, more control over the individual, more bureaucracy.
And our satisfaction with the job government does will continue to decline.
But it doesn’t have to be this way.
You don't have to vote for one of the old "business as usual" parties.
The Libertarian Party has been working since 1972 to fight the all-powerful government.
Fighting for more freedom to pursue happiness.
Fighting for your right to keep the fruits of those pursuits.
It’s time to give individuals like you and me a chance, and the Libertarian option is worth your vote.
And if we reduce the size, the intrusiveness, and the expense of government, we’ll be happier with the result.

Endorsements Endorsed by Children’s Campaign Fund!
As the chief budget writer for House Republicans in Olympia and the father of two young boys, I’m especially honored to be endorsed by Children’s Campaign Fund .

CCF “provides a non-partisan, collective voice and means for the people of Washington state to elect leaders who will put kids first, and to hold them accountable for supporting the whole child.” Here’s what Children’s Campaign Fund has to say about their mission and vision: We are dedicated to electing state leaders who will champion the health, well-being, safety and education of the children and youth of Washington state, especially those who are underserved and have been historically marginalized.
We provide a non-partisan, collective voice for the people of Washington to elect state leaders who will put children and their families first, and to hold these leaders accountable.
Washington state invests in a thriving present and future for every child and their family.
All state leaders recognize that providing for the health, well-being, safety and education of our children is not optional — it is vital.
I’m so thankful that this organization has chosen to endorse me as the best choice for the 31st District!

In the News Rep.-elect Stokesbary named to House committees I’m very excited to share that I received my committee assignments for the Legislature.
Session begins in less than two weeks!

From the Auburn Reporter : Drew Stokesbary , elected in November as state Representative from the 31st Legislative District, has received his committee assignments for the upcoming legislative session.
Stokesbary (R-Auburn) will serve on the Appropriations, Finance and Judiciary Committees.
The House Appropriations Committee considers the state operating budget, while the Finance Committee considers issues relating to tax policy.
The House Judiciary Committee considers a wide variety of subjects involving civil and criminal law.
“I am humbled to be selected for these legislative committees, and excited to get to work on behalf of the 31st District,” Stokesbary said.

“I campaigned on the idea of funding education first, and serving on the Appropriations Committee will allow me to work collaboratively with other legislators to ensure that our schools are funded adequately and fairly.” Stokesbary is an attorney and graduate of Duke University and Notre Dame Law School.
He lives in south Auburn with his wife, Ashley, and their 7-month-old son, Jackson.
The 31st Legislative District includes the communities of Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Carbonado, Edgewood, Enumclaw, Lake Tapps, South Prairie, Sumner and Wilkeson.

Endorsements The Seattle Times recommends Drew Stokesbary Washington’s largest newspaper, The Seattle Times , has endorsed my re-election campaign!
The Times wrote: To get things done in Washington’s divided Legislature, lawmakers must be able to work across party lines.
That’s an attribute of Drew Stokesbary , an Auburn attorney and Republican seeking a second term representing the 31st Legislative District, which straddles Highway 410 from Sumner to Mount Rainier.
Voters should re-elect Stokesbary to the House.
He has been a particularly effective representative during his first term.
A thoughtful, pro-education policy wonk, he can also help the entire state by advancing education-funding reforms.
Read the full editorial at SeattleTimes.com .

Mike Katz praises University of Delaware student leaders, slams Senator Chris Coons and Campaign Manager Matt Schoonmaker for allegedly scolding a Democrat student, shutting down a bipartisan student-led debate proposal; calls out press blackout.
Announces a town hall at the University of Delaware.
For Immediate Release Press Contact: Hunter@drmikekatz.com NEWARK, DE — Dr.
Mike Katz, Republican nominee for U.S.
Senate, criticized Senator Chris Coons and his campaign following their reported rejection of a debate jointly proposed by the University of Delaware College Democrats and College Republicans.

Following the cancellation, without a public announcement, of the University's traditional Delaware Debates, student leaders from both organizations came together to offer voters an opportunity to hear directly from the candidates and compare their positions.
Katz accepted the invitation and offered to debate Coons in any format, at any time, and in any setting on campus.
According to the student organizations, the Coons campaign declined.

"When the UD College Democrats and College Republicans put aside their political differences to promote open debate, elected leaders should applaud their leadership — not shut them down." The Katz campaign highlighted deeply concerning allegations regarding Coons campaign manager Matt Schoonmaker, who allegedly scolded a Democrat student leader for taking the initiative to organize a transparent public forum.
"Students should never be discouraged or reprimanded for asking elected officials to participate in the democratic process.

Senator Coons and his campaign should encourage these young leaders, not dismiss their efforts." The Coons campaign also previously declined a televised debate opportunity offered through WDEL and CoastTV.
"Senator Coons has served in Washington for 16 years.
Delaware voters deserve to compare our records, our positions, and our plans for the future before voting begins.

Why will Senator Coons not do the same?" Katz also raised concerns about the declining scrutiny of political leadership by Delaware's major news organizations, particularly The News Journal/Delaware Online and Spotlight Delaware.
"Delaware already has a limited number of major news outlets.
That makes independent, investigative journalism more important than ever.

When significant political developments receive little scrutiny, voters lose an essential source of information needed to hold their elected officials accountable." "When College Democrats and College Republicans unite to organize a debate and the incumbent Senator declines, that is news." When traditional debates are canceled without a public announcement and additional debate opportunities are rejected, that deserves serious journalistic investigation.
"Delaware has been under one-party Democratic control for years.
The concentration of political power makes a free and independent press more essential, not less.

Journalism must serve as a check on those in power — not allow political decisions to escape public scrutiny." "The News Journal, Delaware Online, and Spotlight Delaware present themselves as important sources of news and accountability for Delaware.

With that responsibility comes an obligation to ask difficult questions, investigate significant decisions, and report the facts regardless of political party." Katz Praises Student Leaders and Confirms October 19 Town Hall Katz recognized College Democrats President Sophie Douglas, College Republicans President Tim Schugsta, and their respective leadership boards for demonstrating bipartisan cooperation and civic engagement.

They demonstrated that people with different political views can come together to promote open dialogue and civic engagement." Katz confirmed his participation in the upcoming University of Delaware campus town hall.

Mike Katz at the University of Delaware Date: Monday, October 19, 2026 Time: 7:00–8:30 PM Location: Trabant University Center, Multipurpose Rooms — University of Delaware, Newark Open to: All UD students Press are welcome to attend but must be approved by the campaign in advance.
Contact Hunter Dworsky, Campaign Manager, at Hunter@drmikekatz.com .

"I look forward to meeting with students — Democrats, Republicans, and Independents alike — listening to their concerns, answering difficult questions, and discussing Delaware's future." "Students from both political parties have demonstrated their willingness to bring people together and ask difficult questions.
Senator Coons, will you agree to debate before early voting begins?" About Dr.
Mike Katz is the Republican nominee for the United States Senate in Delaware.
A pediatric critical care anesthesiologist, business executive, former Delaware State Senator, and nationally recognized healthcare leader, Dr.
Katz has dedicated more than three decades to serving Delaware families through medicine, business leadership, and public service.
He and his wife, Trish, have called Delaware home for thirty years, where they raised their family.

His campaign is focused on restoring accountability, strengthening Delaware's economy, supporting law enforcement and veterans, defending agriculture, securing America's borders, protecting constitutional freedoms, making America healthy again, and always putting Delaware first.
Media Contact Hunter Dworsky, Campaign Manager Dr.

Coming to YOUR County!
My campaign is not about Nashville or big-city politics—it is about the heart of Tennessee, and the heart of Tennessee beats in all 95 counties .

This is a low-budget, grassroots campaign relying on the spirit and hospitality of Tennesseans.

Past events OCT 13 TUE Happy Hour Tuesday, October 13, 5:30 PM 2894 On Main , 2894 Main St, East Troy Why I Am Running I was nine when my parents came to America with few resources to begin a new life.
Nine was a wonderful age to learn and grow into American citizenship.
With hard work I earned a bachelor's and master's in engineering as well as a law degree.
I have been shaped by those who have guided me while learning American values and the many opportunities offered by our great nation.
Now, I wish to give back!
I call myself a Servant Leader and I am committed to serve all communities across the 11th District.
PAST EXPERIENCE Volunteer, New Orleans post-Katrina cleanup Volunteer, Rutgers University, Cambiando Vidas Patent Examiner, U.S.
Patent & Trademark Office, Alexandria, VA Editor, Polish Global Village, Washington, D.C.
Metro Area Law Clerk, Sughrue Mion, PLLC, Washington, D.C.
As your Senate candidate for the 11th District, I am committed to help everyone realize a prosperous future, one that offers opportunities for all.

DISTRICT 11 CHALLENGES High state income taxes Unallocated surplus funds for schools and farmers Escalating fuel, energy, and food costs Division and mistrust between citizens and government Wisconsin's GOP majority has failed to manage the State's massive surpluses needed to support economic growth.
As a result, taxpayers, including those in the 11th District, face continuing school and municipal referendums, while surpluses sit idle.
As inflation continues to devalue the State's surplus, business owners and homeowners, as well as our farmers, are required to pay additional real estate taxes.
It is disingenuous to boast about surpluses when, in fact, local schools, taxpayers, businesses, and municipalities require referendums to fund basic needs.
Increasing property taxes is avoidable when surpluses are utilized as shared revenue.
As a Servant Leader, I value your insight for ideas that will support future growth across the 11th District.
Please know, I am uninterested in political infighting that turns neighbor against neighbor.
By working together, we can build and achieve a sound economic future.
I would be honored to represent you and your families in the 11th District and I respectfully ask for your support in the November 3, 2026 General Election .
Endorsements SHARE Steve Doelder SHARE Sen.

I would be honored to represent you and your families in the 11th District and I respectfully ask for your support in the November 3, 2026 General Election .

DONATE Rekindling the True Spirit of Christmas: Why Remembering the Reason Matters Blair Eddins Dec 21, 2023 2 min read Isaiah 9:6-7a “For a child will be born to us, a son will be given to us; And the government will rest on His shoulders; And His name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Eternal Father, Prince of Peace.
There will be no end to the increase of His government.” Merry Christmas!
This is the time of year when we celebrate the birth of Jesus.
When we say Merry Christmas, what we say is more than a phrase we traditionally express to others this time of year.
Whether people recognize this or not, the celebration of Christmas is part of our nation’s founding on Judeo-Christian principles.
Our country has a long history of celebrating the birth of Jesus Christ.
However, the Left attacks Christmas and seeks to replace it with its multicultural agenda, which aims to destroy the American identity.
The reason why the Left hates Christmas is because Christmas recognizes Jesus as Lord.
Christ, not man or government, is King.
Just as Isaiah points out, Christmas points to King Jesus as ruler over kings, presidents, prime ministers, parliaments, and Congress.
Also, “there will be no end to the increase of His government.” The rule and authority of Jesus have threatened the influence of governments throughout history.
From the Roman Empire to the Soviet Union, faithful Christians were threats to their governments because they believed that Christ, not Ceaser, was the Lord.
Christ’s rule and authority supersedes that of government.
True Christians will obey the authority of Christ and Scripture over that of government when that government exceeds and abuses its God-given authority.
Christ is the ruler of kings, and it is by faith in Him alone that man can be saved.
Salvation does not come from our government.
So, no matter how much the Left tries to attack Christmas, we will continue to say Merry Christmas in our towns.
We are not going to cave to the multicultural agenda and allow them to erase or replace Christmas.
In our district and our state, we say Merry Christmas.
That said, my family and I want to wish you and your family a Merry Christmas.
We look forward to what God has in store for us in 2024, but more than that, we eagerly await the second coming of His Son.
He rules the world with truth and grace, and makes the nations prove the glories of His righteousness and wonders of His love, and wonders of His love, and wonders, wonders of His love.

added: VOTE - November 3rd 2026 Early Voting Begins October 22, 2026 Home About Ayanna Volunteer Blog More Home About Ayanna Volunteer Blog Home About Ayanna Volunteer Blog My Blog All Posts Regarding Comments from School Board Member Elena Brenner October 14, 2026 | News, Official Statement Throughout my years of working with community organizations and supporting minority and underserved populations, I have witnessed firsthand the damage that discriminatory rhetoric can cause to families and entire communities.
The recent statement from School Board member Elena Brenner is atrocious, deeply offensive, and raises serious concerns about the responsibility that comes with educational leadership.
Brenner asked, “Why would I want that ideology here?” My response is simple: EVERYONE IS WELCOMED!
Over the past several days, several community organizations asked me to help shape their public responses.
They came to me because I have spent years working with minority communities on the receiving end of exactly this kind of generalization.
I work with business owners and families who know what it means to be judged as a group before they are seen as individuals.
I have watched parents stop raising concerns because they expect to be dismissed, and I have watched children learn to make themselves smaller.
That is the harm a post like this does, and it outlasts the post itself.
Muslim families are a valued part of this district.
They are parents, students, teachers, coaches and neighbors.
This is not up for debate.

I am calling for a formal public apology, entered into the school board’s official meeting record, and a review of appropriate disciplinary measures, including probationary status if permitted under applicable law and policy.
Freedom of speech does not eliminate public accountability.
All children deserve leadership that reflects the principles of fairness, dignity, and inclusion.
EVERYONE IS WELCOMED HERE Diversity is not the threat.

added: #YourIndependentVoice brad@electbarnhill.net 702-613-2576 Nevada Secretary of State close menu close menu Home About Independent Endorsements News Announcements Commentary Policy Events Contact Donate Volunteer no I’ll Hold My Office to the Same Standard I Held Theirs electbarnhill Oct 14, 2026 0 Comments For most of this campaign, I’ve asked the Secretary of State’s office a simple question: show me the rule you’re following, and show me you followed it.
When the office closed my complaint about 9,607 Nevadans with duplicate active voter registrations without disputing the data, I took that question to federal court .
Now I’m asking you to hire me for that office.
That means the question turns around.
If I’m elected, I’ll be the official who has to show the rule and prove I followed it.
Here is the standard I’m asking you to hold me to, in writing, before a single vote is cast.
A shield and a sword I think about public power this way.
Statutes are the sword: they give an official the authority to act, to maintain voter rolls, enforce deadlines, and certify results.
The Constitution is the shield: it protects citizens from how that authority gets used.
You don’t get to swing the sword and ignore the shield, and you don’t get to hide behind the shield to avoid doing the job the statute requires.
Twenty years as a systems analyst and twenty as a Nevada litigation paralegal taught me the same lesson from two directions.
A process is only as good as its rules, and the rules only matter if they apply to the people running the process.
The rules I’ll follow even when they slow me down Barnhill v.
Aguilar is about duties the National Voter Registration Act places on election officials.
If I win, those duties become mine, including the parts that limit me.
The NVRA requires list maintenance to be uniform and nondiscriminatory.
It sets notice and waiting periods before a voter who may have moved can be removed.
It bars systematic removal programs in the 90 days before a federal election.
I’ll follow every one of those rules, including on days when I’d rather move faster.
That’s why my approach to the voter rolls has always been flag and investigate, never remove first and ask questions later.
Clean rolls and lawful voters’ rights aren’t opposites.
The law voters choose, not the law I’d choose The same goes for Question 7.
Whatever Nevada voters decide on November 3, and whatever the courts say afterward, the Secretary of State’s job is to administer the result faithfully, clearly, and the same way in all 17 counties .
I’ve published my plan for implementing Voter ID so every lawful voter can comply.
If the outcome goes another way, I’ll carry that out with the same care.
An official who only enforces the laws he likes isn’t enforcing the law.

My same-standard commitments Here’s what voters can check me on, starting my first day: Follow the NVRA’s timelines and notice rules , and report list-maintenance activity in the quarterly public reports I’ve already committed to.
Answer public records requests within the five business days Nevada law requires , and publish how many requests came in and how quickly they were answered.
Explain every closed complaint in writing.
When a citizen brings evidence to my office, they’ll get a written answer saying what was checked, what was found, and whether the office disputes their data.
No more closing a file without an explanation.
Comply with court rulings promptly , without stalling or asking to put cases on hold indefinitely .
Check citizen-reported errors and report back.
If you find a problem in the state’s data, my office will investigate it and tell you what it found.
That last one matters to me most.
You shouldn’t have to file a federal lawsuit to get an answer from your Secretary of State.
Accountability that doesn’t depend on a party I’m the Independent American Party’s candidate, and I’m not controlled by either major party.
That independence is only worth something if it cuts both ways: I won’t go easy on an official because of their party, and I don’t expect anyone to go easy on me because of mine.
Measure me the way I’ve measured the office, and the way I think every candidate for this office owes voters : by the rules, by the record, and by results.
The foundations of this approach are in Public Trust Starts With Elections Done Right and Election Transparency in Nevada Means Showing the Work .
You can follow my case, and every filing in it, here .
I’ve put my plans in writing and taken the fight for clean voter rolls to federal court.
Is your candidate for Nevada Secretary of State fighting this hard to protect your vote?
If not, it’s time to take a closer look.
Get to know me · Join the campaign · Donate · See all policy positions I’m not asking you to trust a party on any of this.
I’m asking you to hold the office accountable for solving real problems.

DONATE GET INVOLVED All Articles Search Representative Brandy Fluker-Reid Announces Support for Mayor Wu’s Re-Election Campaign And Eager To Partner to Deliver Results For Constituents Team Brandy Sep 8, 2025 3 min read BOSTON – Representative Brandy Fluker-Reid today announced her support for the re-election of Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, citing key initiatives that have advanced economic development, neighborhood improvement, and housing stability in her district.
In announcing her endorsement, she emphasizes the need for deeper partnership to build on areas of alignment and deliver for constituents.

As the Representative of the Blackest district in the City and the Commonwealth, she remains resolute in her expectation that Black and Brown communities will be at the center of this work in the next term and looks forward to partnering with Mayor Wu.

She highlighted the need to prioritize the hub-school model in the City’s budget, ensuring adequate and sustainable funding, and also highlighted the outstanding commitments to Madison Park Technical Vocational High School and called for transparency and delivery of resources to strengthen the institution.

“Mayor Michelle Wu demonstrated deep investments in climate equity, public transportation access, and low-income housing during her first-term, and I look forward to partnering with her in her second term to strengthen BPS, support Blue Hill Ave as a business corridor and continue to improve services for our seniors across all fixed-income levels,” said state representative Brandy Fluker-Reid. “ Mayor Wu has strived to make Boston a place where everyone can thrive.

I am moved to endorse her to build on previous successes, and I hope that Black and Brown communities will be the focal point of her policies next term to strengthen Black-owned businesses, to increase responsiveness in City services, and to support a shared goal that every Boston resident across the Diaspora receives the same investments to thrive and sense belonging in City Hall and throughout our neighborhoods.” Mayor Wu’s administration has advanced initiatives that have meaningfully touched small businesses in the 12th Suffolk district through her Legacy Business Awards initiative.

Fluker-Reid hopes that a second Wu administration will support Blue Hill Avenue as a business corridor by providing the necessary infrastructure for those businesses to thrive while laying a stronger foundation for neighborhood commerce.

Efforts to support economic mobility for Black-owned businesses by fostering commercial property ownership, and expediting the permitting through the Inspectional Services Department are also necessary barriers to be removed in order to foster business growth.
In Mattapan Square, the City has advanced beautification projects and created a locally focused task force to engage community members in shaping the future of the neighborhood.

The Representative looks forward to seeing this work continue and expanded with tree canopies and looks forward to policies that expand housing stability for seniors across a range of income levels, which will support residents seeking to remain rooted in our communities.

To strengthen the City government’s accountability to Black residents, the legislator also recommended the creation of an Office of Black American Affairs, modeled after the City’s Office of Immigrant Advancement, to ensure that Black residents’ concerns and contributions are fully represented within City government.
Finally, she noted the importance of improving constituent responsiveness, both through the 3-1-1 system and in addressing broader service delivery challenges.

By affirming her support of Mayor Wu’s re-election campaign, Representative Fluker-Reid is committed to continuing collaboration with the City to secure long-term investments in education, economic development, and neighborhood stability for Boston’s residents.

As she extends her support, Representative Fluker-Reid is clear in her expectations of a second Wu administration that partners to deepen its focus on these issues and others that remain central to Black and Brown constituents.

added: Skip to main content Fighting for you.
Donate Volunteer Democratic Primary · Sept 1, 2026 Meet Erika Platform Newsletter Donate Meet Erika Platform Newsletter Endorsements Get Involved Donate Newsletter · October 14, 2026 Nine questions.
Why is your ballot so long this year?
Here's how these questions got there, and more importantly, who paid to put them there.
This November, Massachusetts voters will answer NINE statewide ballot questions, more than you’re used to seeing on a single ballot.

The list of questions covers a wide range of issues this year: Public records, unionizing public defenders, primaries voting systems, voter registration, a Reagan-era tax limit, conservation land, minimum lot sizes, marijuana, and gun control.
Every question on the ballot is there because somebody spent time and money to put it there.
Once you understand how a question gets on the ballot, you start to see who has the power to put one there.
That’s what I’ll cover in this newsletter.
For the next five weeks, I'm going to walk you through all nine questions.
I'll share what each one actually does, who is behind it, and how I'm voting and why.
If you know anyone who would be interested in this series, please forward this email or send them to my newsletter sign up here: sign up for my newsletter!
Three roads to your ballot The Massachusetts Constitution gives voters three main ways to put a question on the ballot.
The rules come from Article 48, which was added over #ago.
It’s a tool used when a constituency isn’t happy with the lack of movement in the State House.
Road 1: Propose a new law (an "initiative petition").
This is the most common road.
Questions 1 through 8 this year all got on the ballot this way.
A group writes a law, gets the Attorney General to approve it, collects signatures, and then gives the Legislature a chance to pass it.
If the Legislature does nothing, the group collects more signatures and the question goes to voters.
During this year-long process, the language also needs to survive any legal challenges that anyone can file to remove the question from the ballot.
This road is a much longer process.
A citizen-proposed amendment has to win support from at least 25% of lawmakers in two separate legislative sessions before it reaches the ballot.
That takes years and it is rare, but it can be powerful.
The Fair Share Amendment, our millionaire's tax, is the best recent example.
Voters passed it in 2022, and it now brings in billions of dollars a year for schools and transportation.
Road 3: Repeal a law the Legislature just passed (a "referendum").
Think of this as the "just say no" road.
A group does not need to write any new law.
It just asks voters to throw out a law that was already passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor.
There is no Attorney General review of new language and no court fight over drafting.
Question 9, the gun safety law, takes this approach.
Each road also has different signature thresholds based on percentages of votes cast statewide in the most recent Governor’s election.

Here is a summary of the requirements for each of the 3 roads: Road Signatures needed Other hurdles New law (Q1–Q8) 74,574 in the fall, then 12,429 more the next spring AG must certify it; Legislature gets first crack; courts can strike it Constitutional amendment 74,574 in the fall, no second round 25% of lawmakers must vote yes in two sessions Repeal a new law (Q9) 37,287 to make the ballot; 49,716 to pause the law until the vote Must file within # days of the law passing One more rule for collecting signatures: no more than one quarter of the signatures can come from any single county.
This means you cannot just camp out in population centers in or near Boston.
You need people collecting signatures across the state.
Who can actually afford to play?
On paper, anyone with 10 friends can start a ballot question.
In real life, it takes a massive amount of organizing and/or hefty funding.
There are two ways to collect 75,000+ signatures.
You can build a huge volunteer network, which is what the rent control campaign (that ended up getting thrown off the ballot by a lawsuit) did.
Organizers turned in over 124,000 signatures with volunteers in every corner of the state.
But more commonly, most ballot questions pay for signature collection.
Massachusetts lets campaigns hire paid signature gatherers, and well-funded groups spend anywhere from a few hundred thousand dollars to a few million to qualify.
The AG has to certify that a question follows the Constitution.
For example, all its parts have to be "related" to each other, and some topics are off-limits.
Even after the AG signs off, opponents can sue in the Supreme Judicial Court (SJC).
This is where money really talks.
This year, three certified questions were knocked off the ballot: Rent control.
Corporate landlords sued over a one-line exemption for religious buildings.
In June, the SJC agreed and struck it, even though polls showed about 6 in 10 voters supported capping rent increases.
Slashing the income tax from 5% to 4%.
Labor unions sued, arguing the AG's summary was misleading because it left out that the question would also cut the tax on capital gains.
This would have limited the extra pay leadership hands out to loyal lawmakers.
The SJC said it dealt with the Legislature's internal rules, which voters cannot change this way.
In 2022, Uber and Lyft spent millions on a question to keep treating drivers as contractors instead of employees.
The SJC threw it out because it hid a second, unrelated policy in vague language at the end.
And in 2018, the court struck the first version of the millionaire's tax.
They went back to the Legislature, got it passed as a constitutional amendment, and voters approved it in 2022.
Step three: the Legislature can take the question up.
Before a new-law question reaches you, lawmakers can pass it, pass their own version, or ignore it.
But sometimes a ballot threat forces a deal.
In 2018, labor groups were headed to the ballot with a $15 minimum wage and paid family and medical leave.
Business groups had a question to cut the sales tax.
The Legislature brokered a "grand bargain": workers got $15 and paid leave, business dropped its sales tax cut, and all three questions went away.
Workers won big, but they also lost time-and-a-half pay on Sundays and public sector workers were cut out of paid family and medical leave in the deal.
That kind of negotiation is rare.
This year, lawmakers did not act on a single question.
The nine questions at a glance Here are all the State Ballot Questions in one table, using the official summaries from the Secretary of State.
I'll go deep on each one in the coming weeks.

1 Public records Open up most records of the Legislature and Governor's office to the public 2 Public defenders Let public defenders and other staff at the state's public defender agency form a union 3 "Top-two" primaries Replace party primaries with one primary where the top two finishers advance, even if they're from the same party 4 Election Day registration Let eligible voters register or update their address at the polls on Election Day 5 State revenue cap Tighten the cap on how much the state can collect, count millionaire's tax money under it, and refund anything over the cap 6 Conservation fund Send sales tax on sporting goods, RVs, and golf to a new land conservation fund 7 Lot sizes Allow single-family homes on lots of 5,000 square feet or more where there's public water and sewer 8 Marijuana Repeal legal retail sales of recreational marijuana 9 Gun safety law Keep the 2024 gun safety law (a NO vote repeals it) A quick tip on Question 9: it is a repeal question, voting YES keeps the current law.
Why I think this process needs reform Ballot questions are supposed to be the people's tool.
When the Legislature won't act, voters can go around it.
That's a real power, and I believe in it.
It's how we won the millionaire's tax, and won the $15 minimum wage in 2018, and paid family medical leave.
But here is the thing: the tool works better for whoever can fund a million dollars, ie. corporate actors, local billionaires and oligarchs.
This is why nearly every 2-4 years, large businesses use ballot questions to threaten cutting taxes and thereby gutting public funding for schools, healthcare, transportation, and infrastructure.
It’s simply blackmail and you can learn more about extreme corporate greed in a video I made before this nasty ballot question got kicked off the ballot.
Check out my MAGA tech bro explainer video → Some states, like California, make it so easy to get on the ballot that corporations can buy their way onto it every cycle.
Our bar is high, and the legal gauntlet is long.
That sounds like it should protect us from big money.
In practice, it cuts both ways.
A grassroots campaign can do everything right, like the rent control campaign did, and still get knocked off by a lawsuit that corporate landlords can easily afford.
Meanwhile, business groups can use the threat of a ballot question, like a massive tax cut, to pressure lawmakers into giveaways.
And a well-funded campaign can simply pay its way through the signature stage.
That’s why some states ban, limit, or regulate paid signature gathering.
I’ll be filing legislation on this because currently Massachusetts has no material restrictions on the ability for corporate interests to get a question on the ballot.
This year we saw over 40 proposals filed.
The ones that survived were mostly the ones with deep pockets or the strongest organizing.
I want a process where a question lives or dies based on what voters think, not on who can afford it.
I'll be writing more about what that reform should look like.
In the meantime, the best defense is an informed voter.
Next week, I’ll dig into the first few questions.
Now that we look toward the general election in less than two months, I need your help to maintain this momentum and keep our campaign moving forward.
Can I count on you to chip in $27 right now?
