JESSICA: My name is Jessica Bradley Rushing and I’m running to be the next state representative for the Sixth Plymouth District, which includes all or parts of Duxbury, Marshfield, Pembroke, Hanson, and Halifax.
I am running to represent this district because I simply believe that we must do more to improve residents’ quality of life and keep this district a thriving community for everyone.
Some of the challenges that I see are that years of unfunded and underfunded mandates have left municipalities with budget constraints that can’t and shouldn’t be addressed with overrides.
All five towns in this district this year had a budget shortfall and were seeking overrides on their ballots in the spring.

Residents deserve high-quality, consistent services, but fixed costs are eating more and more of the budgets, and towns can only raise the tax levy by 2 and a half percent each year, which is good, but not when the costs of health care, gas, and other fixed costs are rising by significantly higher amounts.

When you have these constant underfunded, unfunded mandates and budget shortfalls, and we are relying on taxpayers to fill those gaps, we create a situation where taxpayers simply cannot continue to approve those overrides.
And we saw this in many of the towns in the district this year.
Revenues in Halifax have not kept pace with rising fixed costs.
And in the past year alone, the town has been hit with major unavoidable expense hikes.
This includes health insurance that went up 14.2%, pension assessments which went up 7.1%, liability insurance up nearly 28%, and the regional school assessment up 6%.
Now, when your town can only raise the tax levy by 2 and a half percent and your fixed costs are rising by anywhere from 6 to 28%, you are going to face budget shortfalls.
We simply have to do a better job of bringing state resources back to the district so that towns aren’t continuing to ask to ask taxpayers to sh— to shoulder that burden.
We’ve also seen deferred maintenance in towns, which creates infrastructure needs that can’t continue to be ignored.

But when we’re asking for operational overrides just to balance the budget, we don’t have the ability to also look at projects that need to be done across the district, um, that towns may be willing to pass an override for had they not already been asked to come up with money just to balance the budget.
And when some towns pass overrides and some don’t, we see the level of services offered, and therefore the the quality of life across the district, different from town to town.
As state rep, I think it’s really critical that we do a better job of bringing state resources back to the district, including as earmarks.
You know, there are small projects that can be addressed with earmarks that every state rep can include in the annual budget each year.
These projects can be something small.

When I was on the select board in Pembroke, I worked with our then state rep, Josh Cutler, to bring $30,000 into the district for a project that we used to replace a playground that was at the Madakis ball fields.

It was an old playground, but tons of kids used that space every spring and summer while their siblings were playing on the baseball fields. $30,000 isn’t a lot of money, but it enables the town to complete a project without relying on taxpayer funding.

I think that as your state representative, one of my most critical jobs will be to bring those earmarks back to the district and to bring more state resources back to the district across the board, including money for our public schools, so that we can see that public schools are fully funded, so that every child in every community in the district has the opportunity to get the best education possible.
As your state rep, I would prioritize state resources, which also leads to the question of affordability and supporting working families across the district.
That’s what I see as the biggest challenge, and that’s what I will do as your state rep.
QUESTION: What are the priorities you see in the role of state representative?

JESSICA: As your state representative, my biggest priorities will be to ensure that the quality of life for residents of the Sixth Plymouth District continues to improve so that residents and this community can thrive.
Budget shortfalls lead to overrides, and taxpayers can’t bear that burden.
Earmarks to offset district projects, but we don’t get them if our state rep votes against the budget and doesn’t bring that money back to our district.
My single biggest priority as your state representative will to be to bring more state resources back to the district.
We need to make meaningful progress on fully funding K through 12 education by ensuring that Fair Share Act money is going where it’s intended and where it’s needed the most.
We need to reform Chapter 70 funding formulas so that school districts get the support they need.
And we need to ensure that towns get the earmarked funds submitted for local projects rather than see them stripped out of the annual budget.
We need to lower energy costs with legislation that would eliminate hidden fees and curb price price spikes.
And we need to rein in corporate and shareholder profits within the energy systems and boost renewable energy sources.
I know personally that my own utility bills have gone up sharply over the course of the last few years.
It’s getting harder and harder to afford to be able to keep your home warm in the winter and cool in the summer.

And we need to do more to ensure that residents of the Sixth Plymouth District have the ability to heat, cool, and and have electricity and power in their homes for an affordable— for an affordable amount of money.
We also need to lower health care costs.
We need to cut insurance red tape, cap prescription prices and out-of-pocket expenses, and cut insurance administrative waste.
There’s legislation that has been passed and and additional legislation before the state legislature that would do many of those things, which I would support.
Army veteran, I believe that Massachusetts also has a responsibility to ensure that veterans and their families can access health care and benefits that they have earned through their service.
I would support fully funding veteran services, strengthening our networks of local veteran service officers, and making it easier for veterans to navigate state and federal health care programs.

When I worked in the office of Congressman Bill Keating, one of my primary roles was to serve as a veterans constituent caseworker, and I saw firsthand how difficult it was to navigate these complex systems.

Veteran service officers in each of our towns play a critical role in helping residents access those benefits, and I was proud to work alongside those individuals to ensure that veterans got every bit of assistance and support that they had earned.

I will also advocate for strong support for Massachusetts veterans homes and for the policies that address the unique health care needs of veterans, including behavioral health, disability-related care, and the needs of aging veterans.
And beyond that, I will work to ensure that working families have the support that they need.
We need to build more housing of more diverse types so that young families can afford to live in the district and seniors can afford to retire and stay where they’ve lived for most of their lives.
I know as a parent of four kids that it is a really difficult market right now to try and look at housing in the Sixth Plymouth.
Housing prices are skyrocketing, and my kids look ahead and don’t believe that they will necessarily have the ability to live in the place where they grew up.

I want to make sure that we’re addressing housing, both adequate housing stock and affordable housing, so that when my kids are older, they have the ability to raise their families in the place that they call home.

As your state rep, those will be the biggest priorities that I have, and I’ll work every day to make sure that the families and the communities within the Sixth Plymouth District have everything they need to thrive.
QUESTION: What are the opportunities you see in the role of state representative?
JESSICA: As your state representative, the biggest opportunity I see is to advocate for the residents of the Sixth Plymouth on Beacon Hill for the issues that matter most to you.
I know, and I’ve said, that we need to increase aid and funding from the state.
Massachusetts is a great state to live in.
We have an incredible public education system.
We have an incredible health care system.
But we can always do more and make improvements to make life even better for all of our residents.
We need to fully fund education.

Although Massachusetts has the number one education— public education system in the country, there are certainly ways that we could do more to ensure that all of our students have access to that high-quality education in the ways that matter most to them.
We need to expand vocational opportunities.
We need to ensure that school transportation is funded in a way that towns can manage.

We need to ensure that all the access that we have right now to free community college across the Commonwealth, that that is expanded, and that we’re also looking at ways to more meaningfully use the funds that we’ve raised from things like the Fair Share Act to direct that funding where it’s needed most within the education system.
We also need to address the cost of child care.
As a mom of four, I actually left the workforce for a period because the cost of child care was so expensive for four kids that it made more sense for me to stay home.
That was a difficult decision to make, and I was lucky to have been able to make it.
But child care is one of the biggest drivers of women leaving the workforce that we see nationally, and that’s true here in Massachusetts as well.
We need to expand the number of child care slots.
We need to make it easier to build and renovate existing child care, uh, facilities.
Um, and we need to see partnerships between businesses and child care, uh, systems so that employees have the ability to put their kids in child care that is safe, high-quality, and near their work.
We also need to address aging infrastructure.
All across the district, we’ve seen towns that need overrides in order to build a new public safety building, build a community center like we did in Pembroke.
We see towns looking for funding for libraries and for DPW facilities.

We know that there’s aging infrastructure, and we need to do more to bring state resources into the district to offset the costs so that residents of the towns have the services and the facilities that they need, want, and deserve.
We also need to address the aging infrastructure in our water systems and our bridges, like at Powder Point in Duxbury, and we need to consider climate resilience.
I see this as a major opportunity.
There are two coastal towns in the Sixth Plymouth District, Duxbury and Marshfield, and those coastal towns are going to be hit harder by climate issues than the inland towns will.
And they’ll be hit harder, and they’ll be hit faster.

We have a real opportunity to make meaningful progress on addressing climate resilience and ensuring that the residents who live in those coastal towns are safe when and if major storms hit and when we see the results of climate change.

As your state representative, it would be my privilege and honor to do the work on Beacon Hill to make sure that we are addressing the needs of every single resident in the district, whether that is a young family just building their their lives with young kids or whether that is a retiree who’s been in the district for 40, 50, 60 years.

Um, I see this as an opportunity to really get to know even more of the the nitty-gritty issues that people across the district are concerned about, whether that’s beach access, whether that is battery storage, whether that is transportation.
Um, there’s there’s a variety of issues across the Sixth Plymouth and across the Commonwealth that I think we need to do a better job of making meaningful progress to address.
And as your state representative, I will see the biggest opportunity is bringing your voices to Beacon Hill to advocate for what matters most to you.

CLOSING REMARKS FROM JESSICA: I’m running to represent this district because I believe that we have to do more to improve the quality of life of the residents of the towns and keep this district a thriving community for everyone.
I grew up in Pembroke, and I graduated from Silver Lake, went to Boston University, joined the Army, and spent the last 25 years working in and around government and nonprofit organizations.
I moved back here to Pembroke almost a decade ago because I wanted my four kids to grow up in the place that I call home.
Since moving back, I’ve been deeply involved in the community and in government.
I served on the Pembroke Select Board from 2019 to 2022, including as my— as chair in my final year, and I was only the third woman to ever serve on that board.
I worked for Congressman Bill Keating on veterans and immigration services, where I was heavily involved in the evacuation of Kabul after it fell to the Taliban in August 2021.

State Department created an office to continue Afghan relocation efforts, I went over to State, where I worked as a deputy director for communication, and for two years helped build the operation that enabled almost 200,000 Afghan allies, people who worked alongside the U.S. mission during the course of our longest war, to follow the immigration pathways they’d earned through their service to our government and to come here and build new lives and pursue their American dreams.

When those operations were suspended by this administration and the entire senior leadership team in my office was DOGE’d, I went on to work as the chief of staff at AfghanEvac, a civil— the civil society arm of relocation operations that is still today working to ensure that those pathways are reopened for our Afghan allies, a step which 80% of the American public supports.
And before all of that, I worked as the director of communication at a nonprofit called the Officer Down Memorial Page, the largest law enforcement memorial in the country.

I want to use my experience at the local, state, and federal levels and in nonprofits to serve this district, and I want to bring that expertise to bear to ensure that the towns in the Sixth Plymouth can thrive now and into the future.
I am dedicated to making this district a place where my children can someday also build their lives and raise their families, should they so choose.
But the stark reality is that the cost of living here is increasingly making that harder.
Health care and energy costs continue to surge.
And towns’ budgets are struggling to keep up with rising costs.
As a result, the services that residents need, want, and deserve are being cut, and it just makes it harder and harder for people to get ahead.

I am the oldest daughter of two union members: my mom in the Mass Teachers and Mass Nurses— Mass Nurses Associations, as she worked as the school nurse at Whitman-Hanson High School for more than 20 years, and my dad in the Letter Carriers union.

Both of my parents served as reps in their respective organizations, and I grew up understanding that unions are the means by which families achieve stability, dignity, safe working conditions, and a fair shot.

I know that every opportunity I’ve been given in my life was the result of their strong union jobs, which is why I am such a strong union supporter, and I am so proud to have the endorsement of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO and of former Secretary of Labor Marty Walsh.
I have spent most of my adult life working in public service because I believe it to be a worthwhile calling.
I’m extremely proud to be a member of the inaugural cohort of the American Service Fellows at the Harvard Kennedy School.
This year, I am earning my master’s in public administration and learning even more about how best to serve this country, this Commonwealth, and this district.
I am running for state rep because the rising costs of housing, health care, and child care are outpacing wages.
The affordability crisis is forcing seniors, young families, and working people out of the communities they have long called home.
It is well past time for Beacon Hill to take meaningful action to make Massachusetts more affordable and ensure that every family has an opportunity to build a future here.
The time to act to address these issues is now.
This past cycle, every single one of the towns in this district faced a budget shortfall and sought an override to bridge those budget gaps.
But we cannot keep asking taxpayers to shoulder the burden and foot the bill.
We have to take steps to bring more state resources into the district for schools and for infrastructure and to offset the climbing costs of health care and energy.

We can’t afford to wait, and we can’t afford to have a representative on Beacon Hill who is more interested in taking performative votes against the annual budget than he is in bringing actual money back to these towns.
This election is just a couple of weeks away, on November 3rd.
Early voting is open from October 17th to October 30th.

For the next few weeks, I and my campaign will be laser-focused on talking to as many voters across the district as possible in— in me— in in as many ways as possible, whether that’s knocking doors, making phone calls, sending texts, or sending mail.
We’re talking to people one-on-one about the issues that matter to them.

And I’m really proud to have the support of so many folks, incredible folks across all five towns, and I’m excited to keep building the momentum that we’ve already seen to get us across the finish line on November 3rd so that I can get to work for the residents of this district.
To learn more about me, about my campaign, and about my priorities for the Sixth Plymouth, please go to www.electjbr.com .
You can sign up to volunteer or request a lawn sign.
Follow me on social media and join this momentum.
Join this team to get us across the finish line.
And please vote for me on November 3rd.

And towns’ budgets are struggling to keep up with rising costs.
As a result, the services that residents need, want, and deserve are being cut, and it just makes it harder and harder for people to get ahead.

I am the oldest daughter of two union members: my mom in the Mass Teachers and Mass Nurses— Mass Nurses Associations, as she worked as the school nurse at Whitman-Hanson High School for more than 20 years, and my dad in the Letter Carriers union.

Both of my parents served as reps in their respective organizations, and I grew up understanding that unions are the means by which families achieve stability, dignity, safe working conditions, and a fair shot.

I know that every opportunity I’ve been given in my life was the result of their strong union jobs, which is why I am such a strong union supporter, and I am so proud to have the endorsement of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO and of former Secretary of Labor Marty Walsh.
I have spent most of my adult life working in public service because I believe it to be a worthwhile calling.
I’m extremely proud to be a member of the inaugural cohort of the American Service Fellows at the Harvard Kennedy School.
This year, I am earning my master’s in public administration and learning even more about how best to serve this country, this Commonwealth, and this district.
I am running for state rep because the rising costs of housing, health care, and child care are outpacing wages.
The affordability crisis is forcing seniors, young families, and working people out of the communities they have long called home.
It is well past time for Beacon Hill to take meaningful action to make Massachusetts more affordable and ensure that every family has an opportunity to build a future here.
The time to act to address these issues is now.
This past cycle, every single one of the towns in this district faced a budget shortfall and sought an override to bridge those budget gaps.
But we cannot keep asking taxpayers to shoulder the burden and foot the bill.
We have to take steps to bring more state resources into the district for schools and for infrastructure and to offset the climbing costs of health care and energy.

We can’t afford to wait, and we can’t afford to have a representative on Beacon Hill who is more interested in taking performative votes against the annual budget than he is in bringing actual money back to these towns.
This election is just a couple of weeks away, on November 3rd.
Early voting is open from October 17th to October 30th.

For the next few weeks, I and my campaign will be laser-focused on talking to as many voters across the district as possible in— in me— in in as many ways as possible, whether that’s knocking doors, making phone calls, sending texts, or sending mail.
We’re talking to people one-on-one about the issues that matter to them.

And I’m really proud to have the support of so many folks, incredible folks across all five towns, and I’m excited to keep building the momentum that we’ve already seen to get us across the finish line on November 3rd so that I can get to work for the residents of this district.
To learn more about me, about my campaign, and about my priorities for the Sixth Plymouth, please go to www.electjbr.com .
You can sign up to volunteer or request a lawn sign.
Follow me on social media and join this momentum.
Join this team to get us across the finish line.
And please vote for me on November 3rd.

added: Home MEET JENNIFER PLATFORM ENDORSEMENTS Get Involved Press Releases What Voters Need to Know DONATE Home MEET JENNIFER PLATFORM ENDORSEMENTS DONATE Get Involved Press Releases What Voters Need to Know What Voters Need to Know Independent and non-MAGA Republican voters outside of Johnson County need to see on YouTube that Pat Proctor has said on the record that he wants to take away all early voting, including in-person and mail-in voting.

October 14, 2026 Kansas Secretary of State Candidate Jennifer Day Releases New Ad: “Your Voice” “This ballot is more than just a piece of paper.

It’s the beginning of better schools and healthcare, the first step to lowering costs and pushing back on corruption.” — Jennifer Day First Ad / New Ad This week, Jennifer Day, Democratic candidate for Kansas Secretary of State , released a new campaign ad titled “Your Voice,” highlighting her commitment to ensuring safe and secure elections.

The new ad compliments her campaign ad released last week, “This Ballot,” which centers on protecting voting access and connecting the ballot box to the issues that matter to Kansans, including better schools, accessible healthcare, and lower costs.

Both are part of a nearly half a million dollar statewide ad buy to introduce Day to voters ahead of the November 3 election. ﻿ In the “This Ballot” ad, Day draws on her experience as a small business owner, former legislator, and election worker to explain why she is running for Secretary of State.
She criticizes her opponent, Pat Proctor, for pushing to eliminate in-person early voting and vote by mail, arguing that his position would restrict Kansans’ ability to participate in elections.
“This ballot is more than just a piece of paper,” Day says in "This Ballot.
“It's the beginning of better schools and healthcare.

The first step to lowering costs and pushing back on corruption.” The ad releases come as recent polling shows a close race for Kansas Secretary of State, with Jennifer Day and Pat Proctor just two points apart.

The polling shows Day taking a sizable lead once voters hear her message, highlighting the importance of introducing Kansans to her vision for protecting voting access and restoring Kansas values to the Secretary of State’s office.
Full ad transcript: This Ballot Jennifer Day: “This ballot is more than just a piece of paper.
It's the beginning of better schools and healthcare.
The first step to lowering costs and pushing back on corruption.
In the legislature, Pat Proctor pushed to eliminate early voting altogether in person and by mail.
He wants to take away your vote.
I'm Jennifer Day, a small business owner, former legislator, and a proud Johnson County election worker.

I'm running to be your next Secretary of State because our Kansas values run through the ballot.” Full ad transcript: Your Voice Jennifer Day: “Your vote is your voice and every eligible Kansan deserves to be heard.
Pat Proctor wants to eliminate early voting altogether in person and by mail.
For 8 years, I've served as an election worker, protecting every eligible citizen's right to vote.
I will uphold the law, including ensuring only American citizens are allowed to register and cast a ballot.
I'm Jennifer Day, and I approve this message.

Canons deserve elections they can trust.” ### October 7, 2026 ICYMI: Kansas Republican Secretary of State Candidate Admits to Federal Wage Violations and Owing More Than $93,000 in Back Wages to Employees OVERLAND PARK, KS – In an interview earlier this week, Kansas GOP Secretary of State candidate Pat Proctor admitted to owing over $93,000 in back pay to the employees of his restaurant business.

removed: Please ensure Javascript is enabled for purposes of website accessibility Skip to content Chip in now to stand with Team Ossoff and a Stronger Georgia Donate to Join Team Ossoff If you've saved your information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately. $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# $# Other Amount Other Amount Home About Jon News Shop Volunteer Home About Jon News Shop Volunteer Facebook X-twitter Instagram Youtube Donate Donate Donate Donate BIO Jon Ossoff Born and raised in Atlanta, Jon Ossoff represents Georgia in the United States Senate.
Jon has established a reputation as a legislative workhorse and a relentless investigator exposing corruption and the abuse of power.
Investigating Corruption Before his election to the Senate, Jon was an investigative journalist.
His small business produced award-winning investigations of corruption and war crimes for international news organizations.
Their investigations exposed serious crimes including human trafficking, judicial corruption, bribery, and sexual slavery.

In the Senate, Jon has applied those skills to expose corruption and abuse in government, including the abuse of children in Georgia’s foster care system, mistreatment of military families by private housing contractors, and civil rights abuses in the federal prison system.
Reforming a Broken System Jon is one of few United States Senators whose campaigns refuse to accept campaign contributions from corporate PACs or federal lobbyists.

Jon has introduced legislation to ban corporate PACs altogether and is leading the charge to ban stock trading by Members of Congress, helping pass a Congressional stock trading ban through a major Senate Committee for the first time.

A Legislative Workhorse Senator Ossoff has relentlessly delivered for the state of Georgia – fighting to: Cap insulin prices for seniors at $35/month Lower housing prices Expose abuses in Georgia’s foster care system Crack down on online exploitation of children Strengthen border security Upgrade health care for pregnant women, babies, and children Expose civil rights abuses and corruption in prisons and jails Defend women’s freedom of choice in reproductive health care Ban Members of Congress from trading stocks Help Georgia farmers and growers export more Georgia-grown products Strengthen public safety and tackle the opioid epidemic Deliver record funding for Georgia’s HBCUs Expand mental health care for veterans Expand and help build new health care facilities across the state Expand Medicaid in Georgia Upgrade infrastructure and expand high-speed internet access statewide Hold the U.S.

Postal Service accountable for service delays Expand job training programs Attract thousands of manufacturing jobs to Georgia Protect Social Security and Medicare and strengthen Social Security benefits for public servants Georgia Roots Jon grew up in Metro Atlanta.
He studied diplomacy at Georgetown University and received his Master of Science degree from the London School of Economics.
He lives in Atlanta with his wife, Dr.
Alisha Kramer, and their daughters Eva and Lila.

Mentored by civil rights icon Congressman John Lewis, civil and human rights have been at the core of Jon’s work throughout his career — whether exposing human trafficking and war crimes as an investigative journalist, or exposing the abuse of foster kids as a United States Senator.

added: Skip to content Home Meet Latisha Policies Volunteer D18 Neighborhoods Donate SHOP Home Meet Latisha Policies Volunteer D18 Neighborhoods Donate SHOP WECT Legislative Forum Questions, Candidate Grady’s Answers in Writing / Election Campaign / By Latisha Grady On Monday October 12, 2026, WECT, Port City Daily, WHQR Public Media, and The Seahawk hosted a New Hanover County Legislative Forum on the campus of the University of North Carolina at Wilmington (UNCW).
Policy ideas detailed on my campaign website was the focus of questions directed to me.
After reviewing the transcript, I must clarify a few answers for the record.

V oters Must Know: My policies, are presented from the perspective that legislation starts with ideation from lawmakers or constituents and, from there, is collaboratively constructed with policy advisors and experienced legislators to address feasibility and blind spots.
My website sets a policy direction—not a pretense of having every policy variable solved.
With that in mind, below are the questions from the transcript posed to me and my clarified expanded answers.

Immigration Enforcement and American Workers Replacing Migrants Question: As part of your platform, you’ve talked about immigration reform and suggested tougher penalties for employers hiring illegal immigrants.
What would enforcement of that look like to you?
And what do you think the impact would be on our state’s agricultural and construction industries?
Answer : Enforcement for employers look like increasing the fines–currently in the law–making is more costly for first offenses and repeat violations.
Enforcement for those here illegally would be deportation.
As my website states, those who take accountability for their actions and self-deport may be eligible to apply for legal re-entry.
Question: So you think there is demand for some of those lower-paying agricultural jobs?
Interest in agricultural entrepreneurship and trade careers is growing, especially in the Black community.
Construction, plumbing, HVAC, landscaping, and farming are not low-paying jobs.
American veterans, eligible teens, and formerly incarcerated individuals eligible for work release could fill these jobs.
Migrant hiring has suppressed wages in these fields for decades making them “lower-paying” than they would be otherwise-which is why employers must be held accountable.
Portable Health Insurance Question : One of your proposed policies is decoupling health insurance from employment and making those plans portable.
How would you address federal law, including the Affordable Care Act (ACA) requirement that employers with 50 or more workers offer affordable coverage?
Answer: Decoupling doesn’t eliminate employer plans.
It creates a second way to buy insurance outside of a job and without government subsidies like the (ACA).
Life insurance works this way and is a better comparison than my initial auto example.
You buy a policy through an employer, on your own, or both, and your personal policy follows you if you leave a job.
Many gig workers are priced out of the ACA and go uninsured.
It’s cheaper to pay out of pocket or join a direct primary care network for routine care.
This could be one fix but it would need expert and legislative input to refine.
Military Service & Juvenile Justice Reform Questions: On your campaign blog, you discussed the possibility of exploring mandatory military service in sentencing for certain kinds of repeat offenders.
What would that look like ideally to you?
Most branches of the military do not allow people to accept military service as an alternative to sentencing.
So how would you work around that?
Answer: I don’t know what it would look like, yet.
This blog post documents the conversation I had with four young marines , referenced at the forum .

I clearly state this as an idea (legislative brainstorm) worth exploring as to whether or not a mandatory pathway “could” be created to give juveniles facing significant jail time an alternative with upside.
I am thinking outside the box as I want to mitigate youth crime and poverty cycles in District 18.
If the military won’t allow it, a military-style boot camp could serve the same corrective purpose.
Another example where expert and legislative input is needed to refine.
Funding Education with Tax Caps Questions: You support a number of educational investments, including funding for early literacy, tax relief for teachers, and bringing back master’s pay.
How would you fund those initiatives?” With the state looking to cap the amount that local governments can raise while also lowering its own tax rates, there is going to be a financial squeeze.
So how would you fit your initiatives into the overall budget?
Answer: Based on what I know about the history of Democratic majorities in NC before 2011, I reject the progressive framing of this question.
It presupposes that the progressive characterization of this issue is accurate.
W here were these questions and concerns when state income taxes were at 7.75%, Democrats ran a $5B deficit, and local governments had freedom to raise property taxes without caps?
What majority voted to remove the mandatory 35% lottery allocation for education in 2007?
These tax cap amendments are necessary to protect income tax payers and homeowners from progressive fiscal policies that repeatedly fail.
Look at California, Chicago, NYC, Minneapolis, Los Angeles, Charlotte, Asheville.
Certainly, we can (and should) increase education funding while at the same time ensuring municipal services remain adequately funded.
But only once we ascertain what funding number is “adequate” and realistic baselines are set.
I urge voters to compare past Democratic majority leadership with the GOP’s 15-year record of delivering tangible results at state, city, and county levels.
Transforming the Middle and High School Experience Question: One of your policy platforms is transforming the middle and high school experience to redirect and prevent youth crime.
Can you say more about that?
Answer : My platform on this issue builds on ideas inspired N.C.
Senate Bill 579 and the Chamber of Commerce Career Leadership Development Academy in partnership with the NHC Board of Education.

I advocate expanding these programs into middle school, introducing CTE as early as 4th grade (like Philadelphia’s Mayfair Elementary School ), as well as adding student preparedness in fields like blockchain, cybersecurity, and AI.
Careers in these sectors have high demand for regulatory compliance, ethics, and fraud prevention which all require human judgment making these jobs essential.

I created this policy brief from my ideation session back in the spring when I first became aware that my thinking on this issue was already in alignment an existing bill. ← Previous Post support@electlatishagrady.com P.O.

Absentee ballots available starting Friday, Oct.
2 Early in-person voting begins Monday, Oct.
3 Before you can vote: AM I REGISTERED TO VOTE?
First, make sure you are registered.
If you need to register: Register in person with your town’s Registrars of Voters.
It’s best to register this way if you want to vote in the current election.
You can use Same Day Registration to register on the same day you come in to vote.
Be sure to budget extra time for this step.
Ask your Registrars in advance for more information about Same Day Registration. registrars by town Register online at the Secretary of the State’s website.
16 to do it this way if you want to vote in the current election. register to vote What is on the ballot?
In addition to voting to re-elect Maria in 2026, voters in the Northwest Corner will get to cast their ballots for U.S.

Representative for the 5th Congressional District of CT CT Governor and Lieutenant Governor CT Attorney General CT Secretary of the State CT Treasurer CT Comptroller CT State Representative for the 64th State House District CT State Senator for the 30th State Senate District (some towns are in the 8th and 32nd State Senate Districts) Judge of Probate To Vote Early In Person Oct.
1: Polls will be open from 10 am to 6 pm most days, including weekends .
27 and 29, polling hours will be extended from 8 am to 8 pm.
Check your early polling location before you head out.
In some towns, early voting will be held in a different location than Election Day voting.
Check out the list to the right.
Find more information about early voting at the CT Secretary of the State’s website .
THERE IS NO EARLY VOTING ON MONDAY, NOVEMBER 2.
To Vote In Person on Election Day: If you wish to vote on Election Day, polls will be open from 6 am to 8 pm on Tuesday, November 3.
Anyone in line to vote at 8 pm will be permitted to vote.

Contact your Town Clerk to confirm the polling location in your town. clerks by town To Vote Using An Absentee Ballot: Any Connecticut voter who wishes to vote using an absentee ballot is permitted to do so.
Obtaining an absentee ballot is a multi-step process, however, so you need to plan ahead.
This process is designed to be sure your vote is secure.
Your Town Clerk can explain the details.
APPLY FOR ABSENTEE BALLOT Go to your Town Clerk’s office.
The Clerk has applications and instructions to help you fill it out.
You can also download an absentee ballot application here .
If you apply to your Town Clerk in person, you can receive your absentee ballot and fill it out on the spot.
No need to use the mail if you don’t want to.
Return the application to your Town Clerk.
You can do that by: Giving the application back to the Town Clerk after you have filled it out.
Putting it in the secure Official Ballot Drop Box at your Town Hall.
Be sure to return the application to YOUR Town Hall.
You cannot send your application to a Town Hall different from the town you vote in.
RECEIVE YOUR BALLOT, VOTE, AND RETURN YOUR BALLOT Follow the instructions included with your absentee ballot to vote for the candidates of your choice.
After voting, put the ballot in the optional “privacy sleeve” and insert into the return envelope.
BE SURE TO SIGN THE BACK OF THE OUTSIDE OF THE RETURN ENVELOPE.
Your ballot won’t be counted if you don’t sign the return envelope.
If you’re at Town Hall, you can give your completed ballot, sealed inside the signed return envelope, back to your Town Clerk.
It will be placed in a locked box and counted on Election Day.
You could also place the ballot, sealed inside the signed return envelope, into the secure Official Ballot Drop Box outside of your polling place.
Do not put your ballot in the Drop Box of another town.
If you decide to mail it, please allow extra time for the Post Office to deliver it.
All ballots must be received by the close of the polls at 8 p.m. on Election Day, Nov.
If you have any questions about the voting process call your Town Clerk.

removed: Drew Hansen, 23rd Legislative District Here’s why I’ve endorsed Tarra Simmons: 1.
SHE’S A GOOD LEGISLATOR.
She asks good questions; draws the right distinctions; and genuinely tries to get to the bottom of issues.
I saw this close-up when I chaired the House Civil Rights & Judiciary Committee; Tarra absolutely held her own during some very intense and contentious debates on complex policy bills.
LIVED EXPERIENCE MATTERS.
It changes conversations about prison when you have someone in the caucus who has been in prison; it changes conversations about addiction when you’re serving with someone in long-term recovery.
SHE HAS A STRONG INDEPENDENT STREAK.
You might assume that Tarra just follows the Democratic party line; I can tell you with certainty that this isn’t the case.

Two recent examples: we’re at a town hall focused on public education and someone brings up the subject of a “wealth tax.” This was (and is) a favored cause of many Democrats, but Tarra wasn’t buying it: she comes right out of the gate and says (in essence): “Look, I don’t know that we can be the only state that does this; the billionaires will just move.” Second example: at our Town Hall a few months ago, Tarra says openly that some of the justice reforms that we put in place post-2020 might have gone too far.
There aren’t a lot of Democrats who are saying that publicly right now—especially not ones who share Tarra’s background.
Tarra thinks for herself, draws her own conclusions, and isn’t afraid to say what she thinks.
Those are traits we need more of—not less of—in politics. *** That’s why I endorse Tarra Simmons.
I hope I can serve with her for many more years!

The Upper West Side deserves a leader like him to represent the extraordinary spirit of this community; he will be a lion of reform in the Assembly.” Community Leader & Drag Artist Marti Gould Cummings “﻿We are in living in unprecedented times.
Experience, values, and being of service are tantamount to who we should be electing.
Eli is a principled leader and fighter.
His work for social justice and the fight for New Yorkers is a fight he has done throughout his career.

We need him in Albany to continue the work of making New York one that is for all people.” Midwife & Past President Park West Village Tenants Association Pat Loftman “The Working Class needs someone who is independent of political alliances and who is committed to delivering for every day New Yorkers.

He understands that real estate interests have to get real.
He is on the right side of every important piece of legislation pending in Albany, especially New York For All.

Eli is undoubtedly our guy.” Community Leader Emily Wenzel “Eli is such a strong advocate for all the people of our district.
He will represent us and stand up for us.” Professor & Campus Dissident Michael Thaddeus “Eli is truly our guy.

added: Home Volunteer English Connecticut’s 3rd Senate District East Hartford East Windsor South Windsor Ellington Volunteer Why I Am Running ↓ Campaign Message WHY I AM RUNNING I’m running in the Republican primary for the 3th Senate District in Connecticut because too many families are struggling to keep up.
For years, we have heard Connecticut is becoming too expensive, taxes keep climbing, and our communities need leaders who listen.
I will work for affordability, strong public schools and parental choice, local control, economic opportunity, and accountable limited government.
I believe state government should be transparent, responsive to the people it serves, and focused on practical results.
Decisions made at the Capitol should reflect the real priorities of our towns.
By prioritizing fiscal discipline, protecting taxpayers, and ensuring every parent has a meaningful voice, we can build a stronger, more prosperous future for our families and local businesses.
Explore Priorities ↓ Policy Priorities THOUGHTFUL, DISCIPLINED DECISIONS Policies should reflect the needs, values, and concerns of the people they serve.
The campaign will pursue thoughtful, disciplined decisions centered on the fundamentals of our communities.
01 Make our state more affordable Reduce income and property tax burdens, rein in state spending, and protect household budgets from rising everyday costs.
02 Raise the quality of education and expand parental choice Support strong public schools, empower families with educational options, and uphold parental rights in every classroom.
03 Strengthen communities while respecting local control Respect municipal decision-making, defend local zoning and community leadership, and invest in essential local infrastructure.
04 Reinvigorate our business base and expand opportunity Promote a predictable, pro-growth regulatory environment that sparks private investment, fosters good jobs, and supports small businesses.

05 Demand accountable, limited government Protect personal liberty and privacy, eliminate administrative waste, increase legislative transparency, and ensure government remains strictly accountable to citizens.
About Eliott Meet eliot t Eliott Hughes is a servant leader, problem solver, and advocate for the people of Connecticut—and that's exactly the kind of leadership our state needs today .
Family & Community MEET THE HUGHES FAMILY Strong communities begin with strong families.
Our towns thrive when parents are empowered, children have access to exceptional education, and local neighborhoods remain safe, welcoming places to build a life.
Every child in Connecticut deserves the opportunity to flourish.
By supporting local schools, youth programs, and community-led initiatives, we invest directly in the leaders and innovators of tomorrow.
Active civic engagement and community collaboration form the foundation of resilient towns.
Our campaign believes in bringing neighbors together to solve local challenges through mutual respect and shared purpose.
Preserving our community character means honoring local heritage while creating practical pathways for the next generation to stay, work, and raise their own families right here in Connecticut.
VOLUNTEER Your time, energy, and talents can make a real difference in Connecticut’s 3th Senate District.
removed:  Volunteer  Home Volunteer Eliott Hughes REPUBLICAN for STATE SENATE  East Hartford  East Windsor  Ellington  South Windsor Volunteer Why I Am Running I’m running as the Republican candidate for the 3rd Senatorial District in Connecticut because too many families are struggling just to keep up.
For years, we’ve heard that Connecticut is becoming too expensive.
Today, many people aren’t just worried about rising costs—they’re worried about paying their bills.
Taxes, fees, and everyday expenses continue to rise faster than our paychecks, leaving families feeling squeezed and unheard.
Like many residents, I've watched government decisions impact our communities while citizens' concerns are too often ignored.
Parents deserve a voice in their children's education—and that freedom is increasingly under attack.
Families have long had the ability to choose what is best for their children, whether that means public schools, private schools, or homeschooling.
That choice should always belong to parents, not the government.
Government should serve you—not the other way around.
In a recent legislative session, a majority of the people who signed up to speak were not even permitted to be heard.
Despite overwhelming testimony against the bill, the Senator in my district and many others ignored the voices of the people and pushed it through anyway.
Parents deserve educational freedom.
Taxpayers deserve accountability.
And every resident deserves elected officials who will listen before they legislate.
I'm not running to point fingers or play political games.
I'm running to bring common-sense leadership, transparency, and integrity back to government.

I will fight to make Connecticut more affordable, protect individual freedoms, defend parental rights in education, support local businesses, and ensure that the voices of East Hartford, East Windsor, Ellington, and South Windsor are heard at the Capitol.
If you’re tired of politicians shifting blame instead of solving problems, I invite you to join me on November 3rd, 2026, at the voting polls.
Together, we can restore trust in government and build a stronger future for our communities.
Meet Eliott Eliott Hughes is a servant leader, problem solver, and advocate for the people of Connecticut—and that's exactly the kind of leadership our state needs today .
Meet The Hughes Family For Eliott, Connecticut is more than a place to live—it is home.
He and his wife, Keilani, have been married for nearly 25 years and have built their life together in South Windsor, where they have raised their three children.
As a family, they have invested their time, energy, and hearts into the communities that make Senate District 3 such a special place to call home.
For more than a decade, they have faithfully attended Emmanuel Baptist Church in Newington, where faith, service, and community have remained central to their family's values.
Whether camping under the stars, hiking Connecticut's trails, or enjoying outdoor adventures across the state, the Hughes family embraces the natural beauty and traditions that define our region.
They are active leaders and volunteers in their local American Heritage Girls and Trail Life USA troops, helping young people develop character, leadership, and a spirit of service.

They also cherish the simple joys that make small-town life meaningful—picking strawberries, purchasing fresh eggs, and milk from local dairy farms, supporting neighborhood butchers and local bakeries.

These experiences keep Eliott connected to the people, families, farms, and small businesses that form the backbone of Senate District 3 and inspire his commitment to protecting and strengthening the communities he calls home.

removed:  Voluntario Eliott Hughes REPUBLICANO para senado estatal  East Hartford  East Windsor  Ellington  South Windsor Voluntario Por qué me presento Me presento como candidato republicano por el 3.er Distrito Senatorial de Connecticut porque demasiadas familias están luchando solo para mantenerse al día.
Durante años, hemos oído que Connecticut se está volviendo demasiado caro.
Hoy, mucha gente no solo está preocupada por el aumento de los costes, sino por pagar sus facturas.
Los impuestos, las tasas y los gastos cotidianos siguen subiendo más rápido que nuestros sueldos, dejando a las familias asfixiadas y sin ser escuchadas.
Como muchos residentes, he visto cómo las decisiones del gobierno afectan a nuestras comunidades mientras que, con demasiada frecuencia, se ignoran las preocupaciones de los ciudadanos.
Los padres merecen tener voz en la educación de sus hijos, y esa libertad está cada vez más bajo ataque.
Las familias siempre han tenido la capacidad de elegir lo que es mejor para sus hijos, ya sea la escuela pública, la escuela privada o la educación en casa.
Esa elección debe pertenecer siempre a los padres, no al gobierno.
El gobierno debe servirle a usted, no al revés.
En una reciente sesión legislativa, a la mayoría de las personas que se inscribieron para hablar ni siquiera se les permitió ser escuchadas.
A pesar del abrumador testimonio en contra del proyecto de ley, el senador de mi distrito y muchos otros ignoraron las voces de la gente y lo sacaron adelante de todos modos.
Los padres merecen libertad educativa.
Los contribuyentes merecen rendición de cuentas.
Y cada residente merece representantes electos que escuchen antes de legislar.
No me presento para señalar con el dedo ni para jugar a juegos políticos.
Me presento para devolver al gobierno el liderazgo de sentido común, la transparencia y la integridad.

Lucharé para que Connecticut sea más asequible, proteger las libertades individuales, defender los derechos de los padres en la educación, apoyar a las empresas locales y garantizar que las voces de East Hartford, East Windsor, Ellington y South Windsor sean escuchadas en el Capitolio.
Si está cansado de que los políticos se echen la culpa en lugar de resolver problemas, le invito a unirse a mí el 3 de noviembre de 2026 en las urnas.
Juntos, podemos restaurar la confianza en el gobierno y construir un futuro más sólido para nuestras comunidades.
Conozca a Eliott Eliott Hughes es un líder servidor, un solucionador de problemas y un defensor de la gente de Connecticut, y ese es exactamente el tipo de liderazgo que nuestro estado necesita hoy .

Durante casi 30 años, ha construido una carrera como ingeniero, ejecutivo y líder, ayudando a organizaciones a resolver retos complejos, desarrollar futuros líderes y ofrecer resultados significativos.

A lo largo de su trayectoria profesional en organizaciones como Northrop Grumman, Hartford HealthCare y Aetna/CVS Health, Eliott se ha ganado la reputación de reunir perspectivas diversas, construir equipos sólidos y convertir ideas innovadoras en soluciones prácticas.
Lo que lo distingue no es simplemente su experiencia, sino la forma en que lidera: con un corazón de servidor, un oído empático y el compromiso de comprender las necesidades de los demás.

Ya sea mentorizando a líderes emergentes, mejorando las operaciones empresariales o abordando retos organizativos difíciles, Eliott cree que el liderazgo empieza por escuchar, servir y poner a las personas en primer lugar.

Con integridad, rendición de cuentas y el deseo de dejar cada organización y comunidad más fuerte de lo que la encontró, está comprometido a llevar ese mismo enfoque al servicio de la gente de Connecticut.

Conozca a la familia Hughes Para Eliott, Connecticut es más que un lugar para vivir: es su hogar. Él y su esposa, Keilani, llevan casados casi 25 años y han construido su vida juntos en South Windsor, donde han criado a sus tres hijos.
Como familia, han invertido su tiempo, energía y corazón en las comunidades que hacen del Distrito Senatorial 3 un lugar tan especial al que llamar hogar.
Durante más de una década, han asistido fielmente a la Emmanuel Baptist Church en Newington, donde la fe, el servicio y la comunidad han permanecido en el centro de los valores de su familia.

Ya sea acampando bajo las estrellas, recorriendo los senderos de Connecticut o disfrutando de aventuras al aire libre por todo el estado, la familia Hughes abraza la belleza natural y las tradiciones que definen nuestra región.
Son líderes activos y voluntarios en sus tropas locales de American Heritage Girls y Trail Life USA, ayudando a los jóvenes a desarrollar carácter, liderazgo y espíritu de servicio.

También valoran las alegrías sencillas que dan sentido a la vida en los pueblos pequeños: recoger fresas, comprar huevos frescos y leche en granjas lecheras locales, y apoyar a las carnicerías de barrio y a las panaderías locales.

Estas experiencias mantienen a Eliott conectado con la gente, las familias, las granjas y las pequeñas empresas que forman la columna vertebral del Distrito Senatorial 3 e inspiran su compromiso de proteger y fortalecer las comunidades a las que llama hogar.

Y cada residente merece representantes electos que escuchen antes de legislar.
No me presento para señalar con el dedo ni para jugar a juegos políticos.
Me presento para devolver al gobierno el liderazgo de sentido común, la transparencia y la integridad.

Lucharé para que Connecticut sea más asequible, proteger las libertades individuales, defender los derechos de los padres en la educación, apoyar a las empresas locales y garantizar que las voces de East Hartford, East Windsor, Ellington y South Windsor sean escuchadas en el Capitolio.
Si está cansado de que los políticos se echen la culpa en lugar de resolver problemas, le invito a unirse a mí el 3 de noviembre de 2026 en las urnas.
Juntos, podemos restaurar la confianza en el gobierno y construir un futuro más sólido para nuestras comunidades.
Conozca a Eliott Eliott Hughes es un líder servidor, un solucionador de problemas y un defensor de la gente de Connecticut, y ese es exactamente el tipo de liderazgo que nuestro estado necesita hoy .

Durante casi 30 años, ha construido una carrera como ingeniero, ejecutivo y líder, ayudando a organizaciones a resolver retos complejos, desarrollar futuros líderes y ofrecer resultados significativos.

A lo largo de su trayectoria profesional en organizaciones como Northrop Grumman, Hartford HealthCare y Aetna/CVS Health, Eliott se ha ganado la reputación de reunir perspectivas diversas, construir equipos sólidos y convertir ideas innovadoras en soluciones prácticas.
Lo que lo distingue no es simplemente su experiencia, sino la forma en que lidera: con un corazón de servidor, un oído empático y el compromiso de comprender las necesidades de los demás.

Ya sea mentorizando a líderes emergentes, mejorando las operaciones empresariales o abordando retos organizativos difíciles, Eliott cree que el liderazgo empieza por escuchar, servir y poner a las personas en primer lugar.

Con integridad, rendición de cuentas y el deseo de dejar cada organización y comunidad más fuerte de lo que la encontró, está comprometido a llevar ese mismo enfoque al servicio de la gente de Connecticut.

Conozca a la familia Hughes Para Eliott, Connecticut es más que un lugar para vivir: es su hogar. Él y su esposa, Keilani, llevan casados casi 25 años y han construido su vida juntos en South Windsor, donde han criado a sus tres hijos.
Como familia, han invertido su tiempo, energía y corazón en las comunidades que hacen del Distrito Senatorial 3 un lugar tan especial al que llamar hogar.
Durante más de una década, han asistido fielmente a la Emmanuel Baptist Church en Newington, donde la fe, el servicio y la comunidad han permanecido en el centro de los valores de su familia.

Ya sea acampando bajo las estrellas, recorriendo los senderos de Connecticut o disfrutando de aventuras al aire libre por todo el estado, la familia Hughes abraza la belleza natural y las tradiciones que definen nuestra región.
Son líderes activos y voluntarios en sus tropas locales de American Heritage Girls y Trail Life USA, ayudando a los jóvenes a desarrollar carácter, liderazgo y espíritu de servicio.

También valoran las alegrías sencillas que dan sentido a la vida en los pueblos pequeños: recoger fresas, comprar huevos frescos y leche en granjas lecheras locales, y apoyar a las carnicerías de barrio y a las panaderías locales.

Estas experiencias mantienen a Eliott conectado con la gente, las familias, las granjas y las pequeñas empresas que forman la columna vertebral del Distrito Senatorial 3 e inspiran su compromiso de proteger y fortalecer las comunidades a las que llama hogar.

added:  Volunteer  Home Volunteer Eliott Hughes REPUBLICAN for STATE SENATE  East Hartford  East Windsor  Ellington  South Windsor Volunteer Why I Am Running I’m running as the Republican candidate for the 3rd Senatorial District in Connecticut because too many families are struggling just to keep up.
For years, we’ve heard that Connecticut is becoming too expensive.
Today, many people aren’t just worried about rising costs—they’re worried about paying their bills.
Taxes, fees, and everyday expenses continue to rise faster than our paychecks, leaving families feeling squeezed and unheard.
Like many residents, I've watched government decisions impact our communities while citizens' concerns are too often ignored.
Parents deserve a voice in their children's education—and that freedom is increasingly under attack.
Families have long had the ability to choose what is best for their children, whether that means public schools, private schools, or homeschooling.
That choice should always belong to parents, not the government.
Government should serve you—not the other way around.
In a recent legislative session, a majority of the people who signed up to speak were not even permitted to be heard.
Despite overwhelming testimony against the bill, the Senator in my district and many others ignored the voices of the people and pushed it through anyway.
And every resident deserves elected officials who will listen before they legislate.
I'm not running to point fingers or play political games.
I'm running to bring common-sense leadership, transparency, and integrity back to government.

I will fight to make Connecticut more affordable, protect individual freedoms, defend parental rights in education, support local businesses, and ensure that the voices of East Hartford, East Windsor, Ellington, and South Windsor are heard at the Capitol.
If you’re tired of politicians shifting blame instead of solving problems, I invite you to join me on November 3rd, 2026, at the voting polls.
Together, we can restore trust in government and build a stronger future for our communities.
Meet Eliott Eliott Hughes is a servant leader, problem solver, and advocate for the people of Connecticut—and that's exactly the kind of leadership our state needs today .
For nearly 30 years, he has built a career as an engineer, executive, and leader, helping organizations solve complex challenges, develop future leaders, and deliver meaningful results.

Throughout his professional journey with organizations including Northrop Grumman, Hartford HealthCare, and Aetna/CVS Health, Eliott has earned a reputation for bringing together diverse perspectives, building strong teams, and turning innovative ideas into practical solutions.
What sets him apart is not simply his experience, but the way he leads—with a servant's heart, an empathetic ear, and a commitment to understanding the needs of others.

Whether mentoring emerging leaders, improving business operations, or addressing difficult organizational challenges, Eliott believes leadership begins with listening, serving, and putting people first.

Grounded in integrity, accountability, and a desire to leave every organization and community stronger than he found it, he is committed to bringing that same approach to serving the people of Connecticut.
Meet The Hughes Family For Eliott, Connecticut is more than a place to live—it is home.
He and his wife, Keilani, have been married for nearly 25 years and have built their life together in South Windsor, where they have raised their three children.
As a family, they have invested their time, energy, and hearts into the communities that make Senate District 3 such a special place to call home.
For more than a decade, they have faithfully attended Emmanuel Baptist Church in Newington, where faith, service, and community have remained central to their family's values.
Whether camping under the stars, hiking Connecticut's trails, or enjoying outdoor adventures across the state, the Hughes family embraces the natural beauty and traditions that define our region.
They are active leaders and volunteers in their local American Heritage Girls and Trail Life USA troops, helping young people develop character, leadership, and a spirit of service.

They also cherish the simple joys that make small-town life meaningful—picking strawberries, purchasing fresh eggs, and milk from local dairy farms, supporting neighborhood butchers and local bakeries.

These experiences keep Eliott connected to the people, families, farms, and small businesses that form the backbone of Senate District 3 and inspire his commitment to protecting and strengthening the communities he calls home.

title.after: How We Pay For It — Emily Tseffos

added: Skip navigation menu Meet Emily Priorities How We Pay For It Events Get a Sign!
How are you gonna pay for that?
Government should do the basics well... and we should be honest about how we pay for them.
Here are the funding changes I would pursue to support our schools, roads, and local services while protecting working families.
Meet Emily Priorities How We Pay For It Events Get a Sign!
How are you gonna pay for that?
Government should do the basics well... and we should be honest about how we pay for them.
Here are the funding changes I would pursue to support our schools, roads, and local services while protecting working families.
Let's Start With What Families Actually Pay It's true that Wisconsin has a budget surplus.
It's also true that working folks deserve relief.
But sending you a check while leaving our schools, roads, and emergency services short on funding can leave us all paying more through property taxes, fees, and expenses down the road.
Over the last three years, I’ve sat down with local leaders working hard to keep those basic services running without asking neighbors to pay more.
Those conversations shape my approach: use taxpayer dollars responsibly and look at what families actually pay over time.
I believe government should do the basics well: strong public schools, safe roads, reliable emergency services, and kids with enough to eat.
My opponent and I have a fundamental difference in the role of government.
I believe it should be creative, resourceful, and responsible in finding ways to help as many people as possible.
It should work to lower costs and protect our neighbors from corporate greed.
From where I stand, growth should mean better jobs, stronger communities, and a better life for the people who already live here.
Put the Surplus to Work Responsibly A surplus is money left after the state’s budget commitments.
Some should stay in reserve for emergencies, and some can help pay for overdue repairs and other expenses that happen once.
There's a lot of talk about "returning taxpayer dollars" right now.
But I've been meeting with local leaders and understand that schools, emergency services, and local governments also need reliable funding year after year.
We know a surplus won’t last forever so we should search for lasting ways to pay for those needs.

Here's where I would start. + $792 Million over two years Reform the Manufacturing & Ag Credit + $420 million over two years Reform the Capital Gains Exclusion + $70 Million in first year Legalize and Tax Marijuana Require Accountability for Corporate Subsidies Close Corporate Tax Loopholes Expand BadgerCare Review State Contracts and Spending Clear Numbers and Public Accountability.
These proposals are starting points for the budget process.
Each needs an updated estimate before we commit the money.
Changes to taxes can also affect one another, so individual estimates should not simply be added together.
The figures above come from state analyses of specific proposals in the governor’s proposed 2025–27 budget.
They describe what those proposals were expected to raise, not money already collected or guaranteed future revenue.
You deserve to know where the money comes from, where it goes, and how it makes life better here.
That’s the standard I would bring to Madison.

Donate honestly?
We don’t have to agree on everything.

Politics keeps trying to sort us into teams, but when Emily is out talking with people at their doors, around kitchen tables, on farms, and in small businesses, the same concerns come up again and again.
Meet Emily Priorities Stories Events Get a Sign!
Donate honestly?
We don’t have to agree on everything.

Politics keeps trying to sort us into teams, but when Emily is out talking with people at their doors, around kitchen tables, on farms, and in small businesses, the same concerns come up again and again.
Healthcare costs too much.
Property taxes keep climbing.
Schools and emergency services are stretched thin.
Farmers and small businesses are being squeezed.
Too many decisions are made by people who do not seem to understand what those decisions mean in everyday life.
This project is about making room for a more honest conversation.
You do not have to agree with Emily on every issue.
You do not have to belong to a political party.
You do not even have to be supporting her yet.
We want to hear what is happening in your life, what you want your state senator to understand, and what you believe we should be able to work on together.
WHY WE’RE DOING THIS We have more in common than politics lets us admit.
The loudest political voices often make it seem like every election is a choice between two groups of people who have nothing in common.
That has not been my experience.
At thousands of doors and conversations across this area, I've has met Democrats, Republicans, independents, first-time voters, and people who have kind of given up on voting.
These people don't agree on everything, but so many are asking the same basic questions: Why does everything keep getting more expensive?
Why are we paying more while local services get weaker?
Why is healthcare so difficult to afford and navigate?
Why do farmers, schools, and small towns keep being asked to do more with less?

Why do politicians spend so much time fighting and so little time explaining what they actually did? “ We Don’t Have to Agree on Everything ” is an invitation for all of us to step outside the usual political script.
It is a place to say: I may not agree with Emily on every issue, but I believe she will listen, tell us the truth, and work on the problems affecting our lives.
It is also a place to say: I am not sure who I am voting for yet, but this is what I need my next senator to understand.
Both voices belong in this project. your voice belongs here What do you want your next state senator to understand?
You can send us a short video or write your story using the buttons below.
It does not need to be polished, and you do not need the perfect words.
Talk to us the way you would talk to a neighbor!
You might tell us: What has gotten harder or more expensive for your family?
What is working well in your community that you want protected?
What problem has Madison ignored for too long?
How are healthcare, schools, farming, childcare, housing, or property taxes affecting you?
What would better representation look like to you?
Why are you supporting Emily even if you do not agree with her on everything?
If you are still deciding, what do you need to hear from the candidates?
Ready to be a part of this?
Send it!
This won't work without you - it requires each of us to be a little brave, a little vulnerable, and ready for real change in how we do politics here in Wisconsin.
Send us your video Email us your story Submitting a story does not automatically mean it will be published.
A volunteer from the campaign will contact you before publicly using your name, image, video, or words.
You can also ask us to keep your submission private and use it only to help Emily better understand the district.
Sign up to give a testimonial today!
Join Us People first.
Always.

It is also the most by a non-incumbent for that reporting period.
His campaign raised more than $1.1 million since launching – surpassing the total amount Toney raised over the entirety of his 2022 campaign for attorney general.
“Wisconsinites are tired of Josh Kaul’s broken promises and are ready for change at the Department of Justice.
Voters recognize that a third term for Kaul would be a rubber stamp for the abolish-the-police socialists who are taking over the Democratic Party,” said Eric Toney .
“This level of support for a non-incumbent is proof that voters are fed up and want someone who will put public safety over politics.

We are building the resources and the momentum to win in November and finally bring common-sense leadership back to the DOJ.” Toney’s fundraising haul reflects sustained grassroots and law enforcement support for his campaign, including the bipartisan endorsements from over half the sheriffs across Wisconsin, the Milwaukee Police Association, and other law enforcement groups.
He is in his 14th year as a District Attorney and is the past president of the Wisconsin District Attorneys Association.

He was the 2024 Wisconsin District Attorney of the Year and received an Unsung Hero award from the Wisconsin Law Journal for his bipartisan budget work that delivered significant public safety resources across Wisconsin.

added: Skip to content Meet Eric Get Involved Donate Latest news Donate Eric Toney Releases Plan to Add Crime Fighting Resources for Milwaukee County and Wisconsin October 14, 2026 FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE Wednesday, October 14, 2026 CONTACT: info@erictoney.com Eric Toney Releases Plan to Add Crime Fighting Resources for Milwaukee County and Wisconsin A safer Milwaukee means a safer Wisconsin MILWAUKEE – Fond du Lac County District Attorney and Republican candidate for Attorney General Eric Toney today announced a plan to put state assistant attorney generals on the front lines in Milwaukee and across Wisconsin.
District Attorney Toney was joined by the Milwaukee Police Association, as well as sheriffs and district attorneys from across southeast Wisconsin.
Under the plan, the Wisconsin Department of Justice will seek to have assistant attorneys general (AAG) partner with federal prosecutors by becoming Special Assistant U.S.
Attorneys (SAUSA), allowing them to coordinate with local law enforcement and district attorneys to help prosecute crimes in federal court.
This includes gun crimes, human trafficking, drug crimes, and child exploitation.
“As a prosecutor in a county near Milwaukee, I’ve seen crime spill out into the rest of the state.

Public safety isn’t a partisan issue – I’ll work with anyone to make sure that Milwaukee and all of Wisconsin has the crime fighting resources to crack down on violent crime,” said Eric Toney in a statement .
“I’ve been a prosecutor for over 13 years.
I know what happens when caseloads pile up, court calendars become congested, with repeat offenders remaining on our streets, and victims that wait years for justice.
We know our Wisconsin assistant attorney generals have greater caseload capacity to do more.
I’m going to make sure our Department of Justice does its part to fight violent crime.

As Attorney General, I’ll work with the US Attorneys Office – like we’ve seen in Virginia and Missouri – to have our AAGs federally recognized as SAUSAs to prosecute gun crime, drug crime, human trafficking, and child exploitation from Milwaukee and across Wisconsin in federal court through a coordinated effort with local law enforcement and district attorneys.

We’ll put resources into Milwaukee and across Wisconsin to help carry the load and make sure that the state is doing its part to fight violent crime and get justice for victims.” As Attorney General, Toney will: Seek to have Assistant Attorneys Generals partner with the federal DOJ to serve as Special Assistant U.S.

Attorneys, giving them the ability to help combat crime in Milwaukee County and Wisconsin in federal court while working hand-in-hand with local prosecutors on gun crimes, human trafficking, drug crimes, and child exploitation.
This could help balance caseloads and assist with congestion in state court to make sure that local prosecutors and courts see relief.
Some WI DOJ AAGs currently have less than 15 open criminal cases while local prosecutors in counties around the state often carry caseloads in the hundreds.
Federal courts are primarily in Milwaukee and Madison, which are closer to many state AAGs in the Madison area.
This has made it difficult, costly, and time consuming for rural counties to obtain assistance from our state DOJ.
Publish results, reporting caseloads, charging decisions, and outcomes so Wisconsinites can hold the DOJ accountable.
This is in addition to fixing the forensic testing at our crime labs to get evidence to law enforcement and prosecutors sooner to get criminals off our streets more quickly and justice for victims.
Josh Kaul has called public safety his “top priority,” and Kaul has tried to blame Eric Toney for crime in Fond du Lac.
But under Kaul’s leadership, murders in Milwaukee are up 43.4%, from 99 in 2018 to 142 in 2025, according to FBI data.
Statewide, murders are up 33.5%, and assaults on law enforcement officers have nearly doubled, up 87.9%.
(Sources: 2018 figures: FBI Table 8, Milwaukee ; FBI Table 5, Wisconsin ; FBI LEOKA 2018, Officers Assaulted .

2025 figures: FBI Crime Data Explorer, Documents & Downloads : Table 8 for Milwaukee, CIUS Table 5 for the state, and the LEOKA Assault Map for officer assaults.) As a past president of the Wisconsin District Attorneys Association, Toney worked with a Republican Legislature and a Democratic Governor to secure increased resources for prosecutors and public defenders, more crime lab positions, internet crimes against children resources, and more than 50 new prosecutor positions where the need was greatest, including Milwaukee County.
“I know how to work across the aisle to get things done, and I’ll work with anyone who wants a safer Milwaukee – Republican, Democrat, or Independent,” said Toney .

We need to deliver results for the people of Milwaukee, and the rest of the state will be safer as a result.” District Attorney Toney was joined in support at the announcement by Milwaukee Police Association President Alex Ayala, Ozaukee County Sheriff Christy Knowles, Washington County Sheriff Marty Schulteis, Dodge County District Attorney Andrea Will, Waukesha County District Attorney Lesli Boese, and Washington County District Attorney Barry Braatz.

Privacy Policy Submit “Enough with broken promises.

Let’s return the Department of Justice to its core priorities: protecting Wisconsinites, supporting victims, and keeping our communities safe.” — Eric Toney Meet Eric Eric Toney is dedicated to the safety and security of Wisconsin families.

A tough and proven prosecutor, Eric has successfully prosecuted crimes as varied as human trafficking, homicide, sexual assault, domestic violence, drug trafficking, financial crimes, and racketeering.

Eric served as President of the Wisconsin District Attorneys Association, helping build coalitions across the criminal justice system and both parties to deliver real results for Wisconsin, and was named Wisconsin’s 2024 District Attorney of the Year.
As Wisconsin’s next Attorney General, Eric will restore the Department of Justice’s mission to fight crime, support law enforcement, protect families, and enforce the law.

Learn More about Eric Why I’m Running For more than a decade, I’ve served as Fond du Lac County District Attorney – leading efforts to protect our communities, stand up for victims, and hold violent criminals accountable.
Then, two years ago at age 39, I underwent open-heart surgery.
By the grace of God – and years of running – my heart held on.
That clarity led me here: if I could still make a difference for Wisconsin, I would.

I’m running for Attorney General to put that experience to work for you, because Wisconsin deserves an Attorney General who puts public safety before politics, defends the law without fear or favor , and stands up for every Wisconsinite .
Our Department of Justice has amazing frontline staff, but after nearly eight years of broken promises and political spin from the Attorney General, it’s time for change.
It’s time to restore integrity, accountability, and leadership to an office that has lost its way – and make Wisconsin safer for every family in every community.
Fighting Violent Crime Law and order are on the line.
Violent criminals walk free while families live in fear.
As Attorney General, I’ll back the blue, end the revolving door of justice, and make sure violent offenders are off the streets where they belong.
Read more Confronting the Drug Crisis Fentanyl and meth are flooding into our communities, killing our kids, and fueling crime.
I’ll go after the cartels, traffickers, and dealers who profit from misery—and I won’t back down.
It’s time to take our streets back from the opioid crisis destroying Wisconsin families.
Read more Fixing Our Crime Labs When crime labs fail, justice fails.
I’ll clean up the mess—modernize our labs, end the backlog, and hold leadership accountable.
Victims deserve answers, not excuses, and I’ll make sure our system delivers real results.
