added: Vote for RALPH GROVES, the Libertarian Party candidate in Florida’s 11th Congressional District ​ I'm Ralph Groves, former Chairman of the Libertarian Party of Orange County.
As a husband to an invalid wife and a father to a special-needs daughter, I am very dedicated to both Medicare and Social Security.
In addition, I'm pro-natalist, pro-human rights, and pro-2nd Amendment.

Further, as an Army veteran and Iraq War veteran, I'm very dedicated to issues pertaining to Florida's military personnel (including National Guard), and I favor National Guard troops to be kept at home.
My campaign will give the voters of the 11th Congressional District of Florida a third choice besides the Democrats and Republicans.
A few specifics: First: Medicare fraud.
I will work with Vice President JD Vance, who was appointed by President Trump, to tackle the fraud problem. ​ Second: Uphold the War Powers Act.

I will work with Congress to ensure that Presidents commit U.S. military forces overseas only for defense of the United States, and only for up to 60 days unless Congress authorizes an extended period of time.
Third: Promote a culture that respects life.
As a pragmatic Libertarian, not an ideologue, I am neither "pro-choice" or "pro-life" in a doctrinaire way.
I believe generally that life should be promoted.
Abortions should be available, especially for medical purpose and performed in hospitals, not in outside clinics.

added: RALPH GROVES' LETTERS Letter to President Donald Trump 2015 Donahue Drive Ocoee, Florida 34761 18 March 2026 President Donald J.
Trump The White House 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW Washington, D.C.
20500 Subject: Potential Regime Change in Iran Dear Mr.
Sir, I am Ralph Groves, the 2026 Candidate of the Libertarian Party of Florida for the 11th Congressional District of Florida.

Army Intelligence officer, a former DIA analyst of Iran, and a former resident of Iran during the late Shah's reign, I hereby share with you a summary of my analysis of Iran pertaining to potential regime change.
External pressure on Iran due to the current war will augment the authority of the regime as Iranians are nationalistic and will defend their national sovereignty.

For the proximate future, the regime, composed of the clerical class (the Ulama) – with its thousands of clerics and hundreds of Ayatollahs – along with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), will likely remain embedded in all of Iran’s social and political strata.

Their authority is respected by society at large, and will remain so even if any Supreme Leader, with the rank of Ayatollah, at the apex of national authority, is replaced by another leader from the Ulama.
Broadly, the deeplyentrenched regime will endure.
Eventually, external pressure may prompt leadership change at the apex of national authority but not the kind of change the United States may prefer.
A military officer, probably from the IRGC, with impeccable nationalistic credentials (a Napoleon type figure) coupled with fervent Shi'ite piety, may come to the fore.
His ascendancy to national leadership will have to be approved by the Assembly of Experts.
The historical precedent was the ascendancy of Reza Shah Pahlavi, a former Army officer, who became Shah in 1925, as approved by the Majlis(Parliament) that deposed the former Ahmad Shah Qajar.

(Reza Shah Pahlavi was the father of the late Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who reigned until the 1979 Islamic Revolution when he was overthrown.) A Napoleon type figure would have to be scrupulously deferential to the Ulama as he would recall that the oppositionist Ulama (starting with the efforts by Ayatollah Seyyed Burujerdi in 1959) struggled for 20 years to overthrow the late Shah and could overthrow him, too.
It is unlikely that Iranians will embrace the exiled “Crown Prince” Reza Pahlavi, son of the late Shah, in a leadership role because the erstwhile ruling Pahlavi family was very unpopular.
The Pahlavis' unpopularity was due to the common view that they were not sufficiently nationalistic and that they were irreligious.

The “Crown Prince” is a Westernized figure and has called for a secular Iran, but these factors indicate that he is out of touch with Iranian history and culture – especially that most Iranians are religious and expect leaders to have divine favor to be legitimate.
Therefore, Reza Pahlavi will lack broad popular support just like his overthrown father suffered.
The United States should not play an overt role in Iran’s regime and leadership as it would undermine the regime’s nationalistic credentials.

A precedent exists: Iranians regarded the late Shah as a Western puppet commencing from the 1953 overthrow of his then Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh, which was orchestrated by American and British intelligence services.
This resulted in growing opposition against the Shah and increased anti-Western sentiments.
Likewise, the current war will amplify anti-Western sentiments for many decades .
Army (Ret.), Iraq War Veteran Former DIA Analyst, Pentagon Libertarian Candidate for Congress 11th Congressional District, Florida cc: Vice President J.D.
Vance Secretary of State Marco Rubio Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard Addendum: Ralph Groves knows the Middle East and Southwest Asia.
He visited Israel, lived in Iran, and served in Armenia and Iraq as an Army officer.
Prior to retirement, he served in the Pentagon as an Iran analyst.

His experiences and education support his conformity to the Libertarian principle of a non-interventionist foreign policy. ​ One of Ralph Groves’ books is marketed via The Great British Bookshop and Amazon: Iran’s Shi’ite Clerics’ Opposition to the Shah, 1959-1979 https://www.thegreatbritishbookshop.co.uk/products/iran-s-shi-ite-clerics-opposition-to-the-shah-1959-1979 One of Ralph Groves’ previous books, co-authored with one of his sons, Justin Groves, is likewise marketed via The Great British Bookshop and Amazon: Soviet Raison d’état and Relations with Iran’s Communist Parties, 1920-1979 https://www.thegreatbritishbookshop.co.uk/products/soviet-raison-detat-and-relations-with-irans-communist-parties-1920-1979 His forthcoming book (not yet published): The Demystification of Islamism.

added: RECENT PRESS RELEASES ​ ​ Office of Libertarian Congressional Candidate Ralph Groves For Immediate Release 20 July 2026 Contact: GrovesForCongress@Proton.me ​ Ralph Groves is the official, qualified, 2026 Candidate of the Libertarian Party of Florida for the 11th Congressional District, which includes the communities west of Orlando.
As a Libertarian, Ralph Groves is against committing our military outside the United States in armed conflict except for immediate defense of our country.
Accordingly, Candidate Groves favors the recent House of Representatives resolution that requires President Trump to seek congressional authorization before further military actions in Iran.
Three previous attempts failed to garner enough votes.) Candidate Groves has consistently maintained that the 1973 War Powers Act is a valid Federal Law.
It requires that a president should stop deploying military force after 60 days unless Congress explicitly authorizes further military action.
The war against Iran reached its 60 day limit on 1 May.

Military actions against Iran have been illegal since then (including U.S. air strikes on 26 and 27 June and presently in July, and, earlier, the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports that commenced on 13 April and continued beyond 1 May) because Congress did not authorize such actions.

(Note: a naval blockade is an act of war.) If hostilities against Iran continue, and Iran continues to retaliate against U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, and Jordan -- where U.S. servicemen have been killed -- the Middle East could become further destabilized.
Candidate Groves is concerned that the Florida National Guard might then be mobilized to deploy to the Middle East.
He prefers that the Florida National Guard should stay home.
Candidate Groves lived in Iran, 1977-1979, while working for a multi-national consortium in support of the late Shah, who was pro-American.
As an Army Major, he served in the Iraq War, 2008-2009.
One of his sons is presently a Special Missions Aviator in the U.S.

Candidate Groves sent this press release to Florida Congressmen Daniel Webster (CD 11), Maxwell Frost (CD 10), and Darren Soto (CD 9) to prompt them to hold President Trump accountable to the War Powers Act.
Disclaimer: Candidate Groves exercises his right to protected free speech, which is legal.

He conforms to most Libertarian policies, including avoidance of foreign military interventions, but he is not a spokesman for the Libertarian Party of Florida. ​ ​ For Immediate Release to Media of Communities West of Orlando 17 November 2025 Contact: 407-554-2120 Copy of Letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio Concerning Ukraine-Russia War Candidate Groves, the 2026 Libertarian candidate for U.S.

added: Skip to content Meet Hannah Issues Affordability Education Economic Opportunity Health Care Housing Climate & Energy Accomplishments Endorsements News Volunteer Store Vote Meet Hannah Issues Affordability Education Economic Opportunity Health Care Housing Climate & Energy Accomplishments Endorsements News Volunteer Store Vote Facebook X-twitter Instagram Youtube Tiktok Donate June 30, 2026 A Small Island’s Influence Shaped Hannah Pingree The North Haven native could be the first islander to be elected Maine governor.

By Stephen Betts NORTH HAVEN — Long before becoming the Democratic nominee for Maine governor, Hannah Pingree was raised on this small, close-knit island in Penobscot Bay where community members come together to get things done.
Pingree was born in Belfast and her family moved to North Haven when she was a baby.
The resident population then was 350 and has risen to 417 as of last count.

“I saw my parents involved — they were on the school board, running small businesses, both were EMTs — but that is what everyone else did as well,” Pingree told the Midcoast Villager in an interview after winning the hotly contested June 9 Democratic primary.
She played on sports teams — as nearly all students did, so the tiny school would have enough athletes to field teams.
Pingree ran cross country and was a point guard for the island’s basketball team in high school.
She was named a Courier-Gazette All-Star in her senior year.
Students from the island school attended town meetings each year.
“Even at a young age, I saw people asking, ‘How are we going to keep our school open?
How are we going to build housing for people?’ Obviously, my mom was a big influence for me, running for the state Senate when I was 14 years old,” Pingree said.
Chellie Pingree is now a U.S. congresswoman, though Hannah became speaker of the Maine House before her mother was sworn in to the U.S.
“But the biggest influence was just being in a little town where everyone cared about everybody else,” she said.
“That’s what made me want to become involved in public service at a young age.” When the younger Pingree was 13 or 14, she and her mother went to a Maine Women’s Lobby conference.
Pat Schroeder, a Democrat from Colorado, speak.
That was after Anita Hill gave testimony before Congress for the nomination hearing of Clarence Thomas to the U.S.
Schroeder was instrumental in getting the congressional committee to allow Hill to testify.
At that conference, another woman attendee approached the elder Pingree, said more women need to run for political office, and asked Chellie to run for the state Legislature.

“I saw my parents involved — they were on the school board, running small businesses, both were EMTs —but that is what everyone else did as well.” At that time, Chellie Pingree was on the school board and running a small business, North Island Designs, which produced knitting kits and pattern books.
The Republican candidate was Jack McCormick, a well-known businessman and Rockport town official.
“I knocked on a 1,000 doors for her.
I was very involved in that campaign.
It was an uphill battle but she worked very hard, and she won by a large amount,” the younger Pingree recalled.
Her mother rose over four terms to be Maine Senate majority leader where, among other things, she took on the prescription drug industry, which lost a bid before the U.S.
Supreme Court to overturn the Pingree-sponsored Maine Rx legislation.
“I saw that politics was a way to actually get things done and help people,” Hannah said.
After graduating from the North Haven school, the younger Pingree went to Brown University in Rhode Island and then worked for an internet company in New York.
She returned to Maine in 2001 to help her mother in her campaign to unseat U.S.
Collins won reelection that year to a second six-year term and is on the ballot again this fall for a sixth term.

During that campaign, Maine Democratic party leader Michael Saxl contacted Hannah Pingree and encouraged her to run for the Maine House seat that represented North Haven, Vinalhaven and several Hancock County towns inluding Stonington and Deer Isle, Swans Island, and part of Mount Desert Island.
Pingree said “no” more than once — but Saxl kept calling, citing the lack of young people and women in the Legislature.
“I did exactly what my Mom did — I knocked on thousands of doors,” she said.
Elected at 26, Hannah Pingree said she looked at ways to keep young people in Maine.

Paper mills were shutting down, rural Maine was struggling and many towns were worrying about a vicious spiral where young people moved away to seek better opportunities, weakening the local economy, which would only encourage more people to move.
Pingree got to work on issues that are still relevant today, such as housing, healthcare, and early climate action.

Hannah Pingree served on the important Appropriations Committee in her first two-year term in the Maine Legislature, chaired the Health and Human Services Committee in her second term, was elected Majority Leader in the third term, and in 2008, elected unanimously as Speaker of the Maine House — the youngest person in the country at that time to be speaker of a state legislative body.
Pingree noted she got along with both sides of the political aisle, including with the then-Republican House Leader Joshua Tardy; they are still friends today.
“During that time, we passed bipartisan budgets.
We passed bond packages working with Republicans.
There were definitely issues that we did not agree with, but we kept it civil,” Pingree said.
“I earned respect from Republicans by always listening to people.” She noted that former Republican State Sen.
Chris Rector of Thomaston is now a supporter of her for governor.
When term limits pushed Pingree out of the Legislature in 2010, she returned home to North Haven and she and her husband Jason raised their two children — Oscar and Elsie.
She spent eight years on the island, running the family-owned Nebo Lodge and serving on the school board.
She worked with her father on a housing organization for year-round residents.
In 2008, her mother won election to Congress to represent Maine’s First Congressional District in the U.S.
She is now seeking her 10th term in November.
In 2018, when Democrat Janet Mills was elected governor, Mills tapped Hannah Pingree to be on her transition team.
Mills then asked Pingree to help start and lead the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future which focused on such issues as housing, climate, opioids, and children’s issues.
She served seven years in that post, before stepping down ahead of her run for governor this year.
She kicked off her campaign in Rockland in June 2025 with a speech at the Peasley Park housing project.
“I knew there was still a lot more to get done,” Pingree said about deciding to run for governor.
In a crowded, competitive field of five Democratic candidates, Pingree won the nomination at the conclusion of the ranked choice tabulations.
She will now compete in the November election against Republican nominee Robert Charles of Leeds, and former Republican Party chair and current state Sen.
Rick Bennett of Oxford, who is running as an unenrolled candidate.

Pingree said her goals will be both to be a strong governor to stand up against President Trump to protect reproductive rights and voting rights, but also a governor who will focus on affordability issues such as housing and healthcare.
“If we don’t have housing that people can afford, no young people can stay here, and nothing else works,” the Democratic candidate stated.
Rockland City Councilor and former Rockland Mayor Penelope York has known Pingree since they attended the North Haven school in their elementary years.
Pingree was a couple of grades behind York.
With about 54 students in the entire school, all the students knew each other, York noted.
They participated in Brownies and Girls Scouts together, visiting shut-ins and caroling.
York recalls riding on the back of Pingree’s parents’ float for their farm during Fourth of July parades.
York moved to Rockland as a freshman in high school.
The two women reconnected as adults and have formed a close friendship.
“Hannah has demonstrated the ability to bridge gaps with people.
It’s pretty inherent to how we are as islanders.
You can’t make it through tough times, storms, deaths, anything like this that affects communities unless everybody steps up,” York said.
She said Pingree is a masterful communicator.
She has people who support her who have different perspectives on national politics, but who were eager to support her because she is honest and treats people with respect, York said.
“She really, truly knows you can’t sit down and have a close conversation with someone and be B.S.-ing them at the same time,” York said.
I would do anything to support her,” she said.
“We can cross the political divide and show other states how it can be done.
But we need a leader in the seat of governor.
We want leaders who will speak respectfully to others, even to those who oppose them.” Dr.
Nirav Shah, who finished second in the five-way race, endorsed Pingree after the results were announced.
“I called Hannah Pingree to congratulate her, and I want every Mainer to know that I could not have meant it more.
She ran a campaign of deep conviction and real heart, and our state will be fortunate to have her carrying our banner into November.
She has my whole-hearted support, my sincere admiration, and every ounce of help I am able to give between now and Election Day.
Starting now, I will be working to make her the next governor of Maine,” Shah stated.
Former gubernatorial candidate Shenna Bellows also endorsed Pingree, saying she will make a great governor.
Troy Jackson also offered Pingree his congratulations.

Read it here .
The first time I met Hannah Pingree was at a local parade in Freeport, Maine.
My daughter was working there at the time.
I saw Hannah walking around, casually chatting with folks.
I told her I wasn’t a Maine voter, but I was interested in her ideas for improving housing, which is a real issue for Mainers, as it is for a lot of people across the country.
I was impressed by how substantive her ideas were and the way she talked about them like they were real possibilities—policies she’d pursue if elected, not just talking points.
I’ve paid attention to her ever since.

Hannah, speaking at a recent gathering in Maine Hannah emerged as the winner from a Democratic gubernatorial primary in Maine that was blessed with an abundance of likable, qualified candidates who ran an incredibly collegial race, joking that they’d all work for whoever won at one event.
It was a dose of sanity in the middle of this tense political season, a real respite from the nastiness of Alabama politics.
And a good reminder that people who are in public service for all the right reasons still exist.
We need that right now, especially from America’s governors.
Something we’re seeing is that in the no-guardrails era of would-be king Trump, state leaders have the ability to prevent some of the worst abuses.
Governors have intervened on issues like using the National Guard to police protests and have exerted leadership on a range of issues where national leaders have failed to.
During the final years of Trump’s time in office, it may be governors, along with state attorneys general and secretaries of state, who protect rights like voting and access to medical care.
So I’m especially delighted we have a chance to get to know Hannah better tonight.
We should expect more of our elected officials than the low standards the last decade has left us with.
Talking with Hannah reminds me there is a generation of younger politicians coming along who understand this, and want to deliver.

I love her explanation of what it was like to be the youngest speaker of state in a state legislature anywhere in the country and what she learned from leading the Governor’s Office of the Future in Maine.
“Five Questions” is a Friday feature for paid subscribers, built around the conversations that don’t fit into a news cycle driven by headlines and hot takes.
It’s a chance to spend time with the people shaping the law, politics, and democracy—and to ask the questions that matter most, not just the ones everyone else is asking.
Keeping the daily legal analysis free has always been important to me, and it will stay that way.

These Friday conversations give me a chance to thank paid subscribers for their help ensuring that Civil Discourse remains available to everyone who wants to follow the law beyond the day’s headlines.
Whether you’re a paid subscriber or a free subscriber, I’m grateful you’re here.
Joyce: You’re the youngest woman ever elected to serve as speaker of a state legislature.
Talk with us about that moment, and how it felt to be entrusted with that responsibility?
Hannah: Well, truthfully, I hadn’t planned to run for office at age 25 or to be serving as Majority Leader at age 30 and as Speaker at age 32.
It was an awesome responsibility – and a tremendous honor.
I grew up in a very small island community of just 400 people where you couldn’t wait for someone else to come solve the challenges we faced.
I watched my parents pitch in – on the school board, running businesses, stepping up.
And I saw everyone else in my town doing the same.
It taught me that you have to work with people of all ages, and across the political spectrum, to get things done.
And you can’t give up or wait for someone else to show up.
I also learned that you have to listen and be kind, because even when you have fights or disagreements, the people around you will continue to be your neighbors.
And learning that at a young age gave me a real sense of responsibility, an ability to work with anyone, and a confidence that I could lead other people as well.
So as a very young speaker, I knew I had to be practical, listen, do my homework and work hard, and be willing to collaborate with anyone, Democrat or Republican, who wanted to get something done.
Maine is small enough that you can’t afford to burn bridges.
Like my hometown, you’re going to see those folks at the grocery store or on the sidelines of your kids’ sports games.
I think it’s why I was elected unanimously as Speaker of the House by Democrats, Republicans, and Independents.

I’m proud to have been the youngest woman (sidenote: and the only one in the country to do so while also pregnant) to hold that role, but what I’m proudest of is what we got done together: passed bipartisan budgets, expanded broadband in rural areas, invested in clean energy, lowered health care costs, defended reproductive rights, passed marriage equality, improved housing access, and protected Maine’s working waterfronts.
And even though there were many disagreements, we maintained respect for each other.
Joyce: Under your leadership, Maine became the first state in the country to pass marriage equality.
Barack Obama still wasn’t there, but you were in Maine.
There were legislators who understood the vote might cost them their jobs but still thought it was important to do the right thing.
Can you talk about what gave you all the courage to move ahead in that moment and whether leadership like that still exists?

Hannah: I think about that moment a lot, and I often say that helping lead the fight for marriage equality taught me one of the most important lessons I’ve learned in politics: you have to be brave, especially when the decisions you’re making matter so deeply to people’s lives and families.
When I got married back in 2007 to my husband, two dear friends of mine, David and David, helped marry me.
But, they couldn’t legally get married themselves.
They could celebrate my marriage, but they weren’t entitled to the same rights and protections for their own relationship.
That was personal to me, and it was fundamentally unfair.
And here’s what makes that story especially poignant today.

David and David finally got married just this past year, not because they suddenly decided their relationship mattered more, but because they were worried about what Donald Trump and his administration might do to their rights.
After all these years, they still felt they needed to protect their family from the possibility of losing rights we fought so hard to secure.
Back in 2009, we knew passing marriage equality would be politically difficult.
There were legislators, including Democrats, who were nervous about taking that vote.
Some knew it might cost them their seats.
But they did it anyway.
I’m enormously proud of those colleagues, because they understood that there are moments when doing what’s right matters more than protecting your political future.
That experience shaped me as a leader.
It taught me that courage isn’t about being fearless.
It’s about knowing something matters enough that you’re willing to take a risk for it.
And when you’re talking about people’s families, their dignity, and their fundamental rights, that’s exactly what elected leaders should be willing to do.
Does that kind of leadership still exist?
Absolutely.
I see people in the Maine leadership and communities making difficult decisions and standing up for their neighbors – especially over the course of the last few years.
Whether it is standing up for immigrant neighbors who are being terrorized by ICE or taking politically difficult votes in the Maine legislature.
I also think this moment demands more courage from all of us.
We are watching rights that generations of Americans fought for come under threat, and we can’t afford to let political calculations determine whether we stand up for the people who need us.
I’ve always believed you can be principled and pragmatic at the same time.
You can fight hard for what you believe in and still work with people who disagree with you.
That’s how I approached my work in the Legislature, and it’s how I would approach being governor.
Joyce: You’ve also served on your local school board, a role many people think is one of the most important in government.

How did you get there, and what do you think about the role of local government in making people’s lives better, and how important you think it is to elect committed people to school boards nationwide?
Hannah: I often joke that serving as chair of my local school board was the hardest job I’ve had in politics, but it’s true!
I was elected as I was leaving the Legislature and having my first child, and I went on to serve nine years.
Now, with two teenagers in Maine public schools, I’ve experienced public education as a student, a parent, and a board chair.
And I’ve never seen the challenges facing our schools and school leaders feel more urgent.
I think school boards are one of the most important places where public service happens, because you’re entrusted with something incredibly precious: other people’s children and their futures.
And you’re making decisions that affect your neighbors every single day.
It’s an enormous responsibility.

You’re trying to make sure every child gets a great education, that students who need extra support aren’t left behind, and that teachers and school staff, who are often your friends and neighbors, are treated fairly and paid a wage that allows them to live in the communities they serve.
At the same time, you’re accountable to taxpayers, including seniors and working families who are struggling to afford their property taxes.
Those are real tensions, and there aren’t always easy answers.
And in the last few years, school boards have faced an entirely new set of challenges.

We’ve seen national political fights brought into local classrooms, debates over books and curriculum, attacks on LGBTQ students and educators, and growing pressure on people who are simply trying to do right by their communities.

All while schools are dealing with the very real challenges of student mental health, learning loss, staffing shortages, and preparing kids for a future being transformed by technology and artificial intelligence.
I worry that some of the loudest political battles distract us from what should be our shared responsibility: making sure every child feels safe, supported, and challenged to reach their potential.
You can disagree about education policy, and people certainly do, but we should never lose sight of the kids at the center of those decisions.
That’s also what I love about local government.
It’s personal.
In a small Maine town, the people making decisions are your neighbors.
You see them at the grocery store, at school events, and around town.
You have to listen, explain your decisions, and live with the consequences alongside everyone else.
So yes, I think it’s incredibly important that good people step up to serve on school boards, especially now.

We need people who care deeply about public education, who respect teachers and parents, who are willing to listen to different perspectives, and who won’t let national political divisions get in the way of doing what’s best for children.

Serving on my school board reinforced something I’ve believed throughout my career: government works best when people show up, take responsibility, and care enough about their neighbors to do the hard work.
That’s true in a small-town school board meeting, and it’s just as true in the governor’s office.
Joyce: You’ve told the story of outgoing Maine Governor Janet being so taken with the Kurt Vonnegut quote that “every government ought to have a Department of the Future” that she created one.
And you got to play a role in it.
Explain that to us; tell us what you were involved with and how this shapes your view of the role of government.
Hannah: I was the first director of the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future or GOPIF.
Governor Mills was inspired by that Kurt Vonnegut quote and the previous governor had eliminated the state’s Planning Office, so we were essentially building something new from scratch.
But it truly was an office focused on the future and how we ensure thoughtful planning as well as collaboration, to get to policy solutions for some of the most critical issues facing Maine.
One of the things I’m proudest of is the incredible team we built.
We hired smart, creative, deeply committed people who wanted to tackle some of Maine’s toughest challenges.

And we approached the work with a pretty simple philosophy: bring people together who don’t always agree, listen to the people closest to the problems, use good data and evidence to guide decisions, and be transparent about what we’re trying to accomplish and whether it’s working.
We took on some of the biggest challenges facing Maine, from housing and workforce shortages to climate change, economic development, and the needs of children and older Mainers.
None of these problems could be solved by one agency or one political party.

We brought together local leaders, businesses and workers, advocates, scientists, and people with very different perspectives to develop new approaches and turn them into real policies and investments.
And we delivered results.

We helped make Maine a national leader in heat pump adoption, advanced climate and storm resilience efforts, developed new approaches to housing and workforce challenges, and helped communities and businesses navigate the pandemic and economic recovery.
We weren’t afraid to try innovative ideas, measure what was working, and change course when something wasn’t getting results.
But maybe the biggest lesson I took from that experience is that you can’t give up on the hardest problems.
Housing, climate change, the opioid crisis, the challenges facing working families—these aren’t things you solve with one bill, one budget, or one press conference.
They require sustained attention, honest conversations, collaboration across agencies and political lines, and a willingness to keep pushing even when progress is frustratingly slow.
And it’s how I would lead as governor.
I don’t think Maine people expect the government to solve every problem overnight.
But they have every right to expect us to be creative, accountable, and relentless about making things better.
Leaders shouldn’t just respond to the next crisis.
It should be building the future we want for our kids and our communities.

Joyce: From talking with Mainers, it seems to me that one of the secrets to the high regard you’re held in is that in an era where people tend to think of government as broken, you expect it to be functional and you get things done.
I’ve heard you say that ability makes you hopeful about Maine’s future.
Are you hopeful about the country’s future too?
Hannah: Well, that’s very kind.
I’d say I’ve been lucky to work with a lot of good people who also wanted to get things done.
And yes, I’m hopeful.
I’ll admit it’s not always easy right now.
I think Donald Trump has done enormous damage to our country, to our institutions, and to the basic sense of decency and respect that should guide how we treat one another.

But I also think his presidency has reminded millions of Americans just how precious some of our most fundamental values are: democracy, freedom, the rule of law, and the belief that everyone deserves dignity and opportunity.
These aren’t things we can take for granted, and I see people standing up to defend them every day.
I’ve always believed you can’t lead if you’re not hopeful.
How can you take on the hardest problems and ask people to join you if you don’t believe things can get better?
But hope has to be matched with action.

When you roll up your sleeves and actually solve something, whether it’s a school budget, a housing project, or helping a community recover from a storm, it gives you another reason to believe in what’s possible.
And I see that spirit in Maine all the time.
People show up for each other.
They coach the team, run the community supper, serve on the school board, and help neighbors through tough times, regardless of their politics.
That’s the country I believe in, and I don’t think Donald Trump gets to define who we are as Americans.
So yes, I’m hopeful.
Not because I think things will magically get better, but because I believe there are still far more people who want to build something better than tear it apart.
And I’ve seen what can happen when we bring those people together and get to work.
“People show up for each other.” Isn’t that what this great American experiment is all about?
There is some simple, elegant wisdom in Hannah’s words, and I appreciate that final point she makes, that Donald Trump does not get to define who we are as Americans.
We do.
We’re in this together, Joyce Spread The Word Let's Go!

Democrat Hannah Pingree is the heavy favorite in the Maine governor’s race, a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll found — the first public survey to be conducted since the June primaries.
Pingree, a former speaker of the Maine House of Representatives and an official in Gov.
Janet Mills’ administration, has the support of 50% of likely voters, according to the poll.
Republican Bobby Charles received 36% support, followed by independent Rick Bennett, who received 8%.
The poll, which surveyed 608 likely voters between June 19-26, gives a preview of how the race to November could go and the impact that Bennett’s third-party candidacy will have.
It had a margin of error of +/- 4.8%.
A former Republican who unenrolled from the party when he got in the race a year ago , Bennett has been seen as most likely to draw moderate Republican voters from Charles, a MAGA-style candidate .
According to the polling, most of Bennett’s support comes from voters who identify as independents.
Among those who identified as Democrats, 3% said they were likely to vote for Bennett, compared to 6% of Republicans and 12% of voters who identified as independents.
Pingree performed the best with independent voters.
She pulled 47% of those who identify as independents, while Charles got 31%.
Nine percent said they were not sure whom they would support for governor or didn’t answer the question.

When voters were asked to pick between just Pingree and Charles, or volunteer a different candidate they planned to support, Pingree’s lead over Charles increased, suggesting that Bennett is pulling slightly more from Pingree’s supporters than Charles’.
Fifty-five percent of respondents picked Pingree over Charles in the one-on-one matchup, with Charles drawing 40% support.
Four percent said they didn’t know who they would vote for or didn’t answer the question, while less than 1% volunteered a different name.

Dennis Reeves, a retired pastor from Sanford and an independent voter who participated in the poll, said he is likely to support Pingree “not because I necessarily agree with her on many things, but because I won’t support anyone who supports Trump.” Pingree has made pushing back on President Donald Trump a key issue in her campaign, while Charles has sought to align himself with the president.
Bennett voted for Trump in 2016 , but has not supported him more recently.
He hasn’t made the president a big talking point on the campaign trail.
Reeves, a former Republican who said he changed his registration after Trump was nominated for the presidency in 2016, said he didn’t know much about Bennett.

He noted that he doesn’t agree with Pingree’s support for allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls’ sports — an issue that conservatives are trying to bring to a statewide referendum in November.
Bennett, a state senator from Oxford, voted last year against bills aimed at preventing transgender athletes from competing in girls’ sports.
Charles has expressed support for the referendum seeking to ban trans athletes from participating on teams that don’t match their gender at birth.
“Obviously I’m going to have to vote for somebody I don’t totally agree with,” said Reeves, 78.

“I’m going to make my decision based on character and their willingness to follow the law and follow the Constitution.” Kirsten McQuillan, a real estate broker from Sidney and a registered Democrat, is backing Pingree — though she said she has also voted for Republicans in the past, including U.S.
She said she looks for “the right person and the person who has a good moral compass” in elections.
In the governor’s race, she wants someone who will address key issues such as affordable housing and who will take a humanitarian approach to the job.
“I like her presence,” McQuillan, 50, said of Pingree.
“She has a good commanding presence and is trustworthy.

In this crazy political environment, we need someone who has their head on straight and has commonsense values.” In Aroostook County, Charles supporter Daniel Deveau said high energy costs are a key issue for him, and he feels the Republican candidate will take the right approach to bring them down.
Charles’ energy plans include reforming Maine’s Public Utilities Commission and negotiating completion of key natural gas pipelines.
Deveau, a retiree from Cyr Plantation, is optimistic about Charles’ chances.
He thinks the candidate’s message will resonate particularly in rural Maine, but said it could be a tough race.
“Now you have an independent in there, so who knows what’s going to happen,” he said.
Independents make up about one-third of Maine voters, and the state has a history of supporting them for key offices.
One of four members of Maine’s congressional delegation, U.S.
King also served as an independent governor from 1995 to 2003.
All of Maine’s recent gubernatorial elections dating to 2010 have featured independent candidates, though how much support they’ve received has varied widely.
In the last election for governor, in November 2022 , retired doctor and political outsider Sam Hunkler received about 2% of the vote in a race featuring incumbent Gov.
In 2010, independent Eliot Cutler, a lawyer and lobbyist, finished second to LePage in a five-way race in which he received close to 36% of the vote.
The New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll of Maine voters was funded with support from the Maine Trust for Local News.

added: Skip to content Meet Hannah Issues Affordability Education Economic Opportunity Health Care Housing Climate & Energy Accomplishments Endorsements News Volunteer Store Vote Meet Hannah Issues Affordability Education Economic Opportunity Health Care Housing Climate & Energy Accomplishments Endorsements News Volunteer Store Vote Facebook X-twitter Instagram Youtube Tiktok Donate June 5, 2026 Bangor Daily News: Hannah Pingree leads poll of Maine’s toss-up Democratic gubernatorial primary Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree was in a toss-up race with Nirav Shah for the Democratic nomination for the right to replace outgoing Gov.
Janet Mills in a poll released Thursday, five days before the primary election.
It was the first survey of the race to show Nirav Shah , the former Maine public health chief, in second place.

But he and former Senate President Troy Jackson were bunched tightly together in the poll of nearly 500 Maine Democrats by SurveyUSA in partnership with the Bangor Daily News and the electoral reform group FairVote.
In the survey released Thursday, Pingree wins in a photo finish with Shah with 52% of votes to his 48% after a ranked-choice simulation.
But more than 1 in 10 voters were still undecided in the first round, showing a deeply uncertain race given the ranked-choice voting dynamics.
Pingree and Jackson are in a ranked-choice voting alliance that is vying to overcome Shah.
Shah and Jackson have gone toe-to-toe with both campaigns alleging “shady” tactics in recent days tied to dark-money PAC ads and messaging about each other’s records.
A pair of recent polls have shown Jackson surging late in the election.
This is the first poll showing Pingree separating from Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who is in the alliance with Pingree and Jackson but was in fifth place with just 11% first-choice support.
Former clean energy executive Angus King III was the top choice for 14% of Democrats.
Bellows notched the fewest first-choice votes and dropped first in the poll’s ranked-choice simulation.
When undecided voters are set aside, her votes are reallocated and King drops, the contest narrows further, with Shah at 36% of the vote, Pingree 33% and Jackson 31%.
While a plurality of Jackson voters tap Bellows as their second choice, they prefer Pingree as their third choice over Shah, giving her the overall narrow lead in the final round of the simulation.
However, small shifts in the electorate could swing the race.
For example, her voters look poised to break for Shah rather than Jackson if she is the third candidate eliminated.
The survey shows that the alliance of more progressive candidates boosted U.S.
Senate candidate Graham Platner could hold some power in the final days of the campaign.
The three sealed the alliance last week , urging voters to pick each other second or third.
Shah has been the frontrunner despite much more institutional support for the three longtime officeholders.
He announced his first endorsement from a sitting or former legislator on Thursday.
But he is being backed by $768,000 in ad spending from an offshoot of 314 Action Fund, which works to elect Democrats with science backgrounds.
That group attacked Jackson in an ad released Wednesday that focused on anti-abortion votes from early in his tenure representing the socially conservative St.

A group opposing Shah that is tied to Platner’s allies launched an effort to knock down Shah , who has faced late criticism for a Legionnaires’ disease outbreak he oversaw the response to in Illinois.
The candidates have been releasing final policy plans and touring the state with get-out-the vote events this week.
Jackson will attend a Bar Harbor rally Friday night featuring Platner, U.S.
Ro Khanna, D-California, and state Auditor Matt Dunlap, who’s fighting among three other Democrats to face former Gov.
Paul LePage in a race for the 2nd Congressional District.
Thursday’s poll, which was conducted between May 28 and June 3, suggested Shah had the most support among seniors, a third of whom ranked him first.
He also ran strongest among those who call themselves “somewhat liberal,” at 30% first-choice support.
Jackson performed strongest among “very liberal” voters with 34% ranking him first — at least 15 percentage points higher than anyone else.
Pingree, who is endorsed by Mills , was the top choice of 27% of the early voters who have already cast a ballot, which was 12% of respondents, SurveyUSA said.
Full results and crosstabs from the poll can be viewed here .
It has an error margin of 5.4 percentage points in the Democratic gubernatorial primary.
The survey was paid for by FairVote, a group that supports ranked-choice voting.
The BDN had input on questions.

On Wednesday, members of the group appeared with Pingree in Portland’s Lincoln Park and credited her experience, character, temperament, and ability to govern in a bipartisan manner when she worked for Governor Janet Mills and served in the state House of Representatives, including one term as Speaker.
“The problems facing Maine families are not partisan,” Pingree said, citing the costs of housing, health care, childcare, and energy.
“The Maine that I believe in is not red or blue.
It’s about communities where people show up for each other, and they show up for their neighbors.” “She has always commanded respect, and she has always displayed respect for others.

I watched her work up close for many years,” said Don Marean , a horse farmer and a former Republican state representative from Hollis who served 12 terms in the legislature, including when Pingree was in the House. “ I know the difference between a politician who talks and one who actually gets things done.
She works across the aisle, and that mattered.

It mattered to me.” Tony Payne , a former Maine GOP Executive Director who left the party in 2018, said Pingree is “well versed” in housing, health care, and energy policy and prepared to work with the Republican-led federal government in Washington.
“Making it work for Maine is going to be a very tall order, and Hannah’s experience in working across the aisle is perfectly legendary, so far as the times that we’re serving in,” Payne said.

Ed Crockett , a former Democratic state representative from Portland who left the party last year and ran for governor this year as an independent, falling short of the required signatures to earn a spot on the November ballot, also announced his support for Pingree.
“In my opinion, the biggest challenge facing our next governor will be working with a legislature that has drawn deep partisan lines in the sand,” Crockett said.
“To truly deliver for the people of Maine, the governor and the full legislature have to be on the same page.

It will take a special leader to right that course.” Joann Bautista , an independent who used to be a Democrat and served as a Maine Deputy Secretary of State under Shenna Bellows, is currently an Associate Director with the Bipartisan Policy Center’s Elections Project.
Bautista, a daughter of immigrants to the U.S., alluded to the activities of federal agents for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Pingree has called for ICE agents to leave the state.
“We want ICE not just out of Maine.
We want ICE out of all of our communities,” Pingree said at a protest last month.
“What we’re seeing happening in our ports, in our neighborhoods and to our institutions is not right, and we need a governor who recognizes that,” Bautista said.

“What we’ve seen happening in our state — what is still happening in our state — is very real and very personal to me, so we need a governor who knows how to use every tool available to them to protect the rights of every single person who lives in our state.” Spread The Word Let's Go!

added: Skip to content Meet Hannah Issues Affordability Education Economic Opportunity Health Care Housing Climate & Energy Accomplishments Endorsements News Volunteer Store Vote Meet Hannah Issues Affordability Education Economic Opportunity Health Care Housing Climate & Energy Accomplishments Endorsements News Volunteer Store Vote Facebook X-twitter Instagram Youtube Tiktok Donate October 9, 2026 Wabanaki Tribal Chiefs Endorse Hannah Pingree for Governor Chiefs back Hannah’s plan to restore full Tribal sovereignty and strengthen government-to-government partnership INDIAN ISLAND – Hannah Pingree, former Speaker of the Maine House and Democratic nominee for governor, joined Wabanaki Nation Tribal Chiefs and leaders today to announce their endorsements of her campaign, ahead of Indigenous Peoples’ Day weekend.
During her years in public service, Hannah has partnered with Tribal leaders on economic opportunity, infrastructure, climate resilience, and public health.
As governor, she will build a strong government-to-government relationship to continue taking action on these issues.
More pictures and video available upon request Hannah supports full tribal sovereignty and will work with the Tribal Nations and the Legislature to pass legislation in her first 100 days in office.
She believes the Wabanaki Nations deserve the same rights and opportunities as every other federally recognized tribe.
“Sovereignty is not a favor from the state.
Restoring it means Tribal Nations will have the same rights and autonomy as every other federally recognized Tribe.
It is an issue of fairness.
Getting this done will be a top priority for me,” said Hannah.
Statements of Support from Wabanaki Chiefs Chief Sheila McCormack, Mi’kmaq Nation: “Hannah Pingree has my full support to be the next Governor of Maine.

She has demonstrated a consistent commitment to working together with Tribal governments and has the experience and temperament to deliver on her campaign promise of Tribal Sovereignty within her first 100 days in office.” Chief William Nicholas, Passamaquoddy Tribe at Indian Township: “I’m proud to endorse Hannah Pingree for Governor of Maine.
She is a leader who listens first and works alongside people to get things done.

She has shown that she values real partnership, and I believe she will bring that same collaborative spirit to the governor’s office.” Chief Kirk Francis, Penobscot Nation: “Hannah is a proven leader with deep roots in Maine.
As Speaker of the House and as a community leader, she has a reputation for listening, bringing people together, and honoring her word.
I’m so pleased to support her for Governor.” Chief Clarissa Sabattis, Houlton Band of Maliseets: “Hannah Pingree does not back down when it matters for Maine families.

Hannah also earned strong reviews for her debate performances.
Eight public polls have shown her with a commanding lead as early voting begins and heading into November.

added.text: A double header for Senator Hardy and me as we par [image: A double header for Senator Hardy and me as we participated in TWO great panels on Tuesday night! The first at the Ilsley Library to discuss Early Education. Great questions about preschool access, Act 76, and how family, housing challenges are a huge factor in Vermont kids’ educational success. It was unfortunate that only Democratic candidates showed up for this incredibly important issue, but here we are in our dedication and glory! (@stroupforvt arrived just after the photo was taken) @robinscheu @bykerforvermont @mikeroyforvermont @ari_for_addison3 @jubilee4vt @hescockforvthouse @ruthhardyvt Then on to Addison to discuss hunting and fishing and land use with the Addison County Sportsman’s Club. It was a full house at the Addison Fire Station for a lively meeting. Hunting is a huge and critical part of Vermont culture and, like farmers, our outdoors people are often times the closest to, and have the most reverence for, our natural environment. We appreciate the invitations!]

Fascinating hour at the Middlebury Waste Water tre [image: Fascinating hour at the Middlebury Waste Water treatment facility today. Thank you Dean and crew for showing us the process. You do amazing and essential work. I know you’re excited about the upgrades in the future! Truly a brilliant system of reduce, reuse, recycle ♻️. Nothing is wasted. Keep taking your probiotics Addison County- it helps your system and this system!]

It’s important to follow the money, like Spence sa [image: It’s important to follow the money, like Spence says! The differences could not be more clear. I’m also proud to say that I (and Ruth, too!) have spent nearly every penny of campaign funds with LOCAL businesses. Whether it’s our printed palm cards, website development and design, advertising, lawn signs and mailers it’s all been spent supporting in-district and Vermont businesses. How one runs their campaign tells you a lot about what they value. We value local and we appreciate the support from so many friends and neighbors and are paying it forward. Remember to vote!]

removed.text: A great canvassing crew and a lovely Sunday at the [image: A great canvassing crew and a lovely Sunday at the Shoreham Apple Festival. added: Donate About Issues News Join Donate News FOX NEWS: Tax Man McCann Pocked Energy Lobbyist Cash, Then Voted To Raise Energy Bills $3,000 A Year July 23, 2026 Back to News HOLLAND, MI. – A new report from Fox News reveals Tax Man McCann was busy pocketing lobbyist cash from the energy industry while voting to DOUBLE electricity bills on Michigan families and raise rates nearly $3,000 a year.

In case you missed it… Dem supported ‘Green New Deal’ after receiving nearly $60k from energy groups, now wants Congressional seat Fox News | Leo Briceno | July 23, 2026 FIRST ON FOX: Sean McCann, a Democratic candidate for Congress in Michigan’s 4th Congressional District, has taken at least $57,600 in contributions from energy groups while supporting Green New Deal policies that were projected to increase utility costs, records show.
McCann’s record on energy is resurfacing as he wages an uphill campaign to unseat Rep.
Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., and raises questions about his approach to federal energy policy.
McCann first served as the Kalamazoo city commissioner from 1999 to 2008.
He would then go on to serve in the Michigan House from 2011 to 2015 and in the Michigan Senate from 2019 to 2023.
During his time in the Senate, he served as chair of the Senate Energy and Environment Committee.
Since 2011, records show that McCann has accepted at least $57,600 from the DTE Energy PAC, a Michigan-based energy group, and CMS Energy Corporation Employees for Better Government.

He also accepted at least $560 in food and beverages from energy lobbyists since 2021. … McCann has also supported policies projected to increase utility costs, such as SB 271 of 2023 — Michigan’s “Green New Deal,” as Republican critics called it.
The bill, which ultimately passed and was signed into law by Gov.
Gretchen Whitmer in 2023, set clean energy requirements in order to reach a 100% clean energy standard by 2040.

Among its many provisions, it required utility companies to implement at least a 50% renewable energy portfolio by 2030, a change some experts project will spike energy costs for consumers.” That plan would cost Michiganders $386 billion by 2050, which amounts to an average annual cost increase of $2,746 per customer, or an additional $228.83 on monthly utility rates,” the center said in a report on the plan.” It would expose Michigan residents to a greater risk of blackouts.
The most prolonged blackout based on the model would last 61 continuous hours during winter when Michigan residents need reliable energy the most,” the report added.
The Mackinac Center is a policy nonprofit that champions the principles of free markets and limited government.
DTE did not respond to requests for comment on whether the company had taken a position on the plan or whether it stood to benefit from its implementation.
McCann praised the bill’s passage as a key environmental piece of legislation.
“These policies will safeguard public health and better protect our environment now and for future generations,” McCann said in a statement following its passage.

During that same time, McCann voted against an amendment for a separate bill, SB 502, that would have prevented utility companies from raising electric rates on residential Michigan customers until 2040.

The new site will serve as a one-stop shop for voters to learn the growing number of ways Sean McCann has voted to make life more expensive while lining his own pockets.

added: Donate About Issues News Join Donate News Tax Man McCann Doubles Down on Making Energy More Expensive for Michigan Families July 24, 2026 Back to News HOLLAND, MI — In an interview with Fox News yesterday , “Tax Man McCann” doubled down on his support for radical energy mandates that will jack up household utility bills on Michigan families by nearly $3,000 a year.

When pressed on his vote for Michigan’s “Green New Deal” – a plan projected to spike average utility bills by $2,746 annually – McCann defended the crushing price hikes saying, “These policies will safeguard public health and better protect our environment now and for future generations.” In other words: no regrets for making families pay through the roof for energy, as long he can keep pocketing that sweet, sweet cash.

“Tax Man McCann voted to double energy bills, voted to allow energy companies to jack up your rates, and now has the nerve to tell Michigan families that paying nearly $3,000 more a year is doing them a favor,” said Calvin Moore, spokesperson for the Huizenga campaign.

“Southwest Michigan doesn’t need an out-of-touch career politician like Tax Man McCann who has raises rates, fees and taxes every chance he gets.” Share: PAID FOR BY HUIZENGA FOR CONGRESS PRIVACY POLICY · TERMS AND CONDITIONS About Issues News Join

Huge shout out to Congresswoman Kim Schrier and her team for joining us in Sultan this afternoon to knock doors!
And thank you to our incredible volunteers, both this afternoon and this morning in Marysville.
Remember, Ballots are in the mail!
Please vote early and get your ballots to the ... ballot boxes.

But I want to say clearly where I stand.
I've spent my career in child welfare, juvenile justice, courts, government budgeting, and nonprofits, and I know how these systems connect (or don't).
When we cut ... community supports, the cost doesn't disappear.
It shifts to ERs, first responders, and the housing and homelessness crisis.
Families lose stability, and kids lose the consistency, routines, and medications they depend on.
When children and family systems lose that support, they are no longer low risk.
They can escalate into higher cost systems like foster care, intensive residential services, and institutional care.
We have a culture where we are trained to respond to crisis instead of investing in prevention, and prevention costs less than crisis response.
In the end, taxpayers, hospitals, first responders, social workers, and behavioral health providers pay the price of these cuts.
2,655 neighbors is not a line item.
I'll be fighting for them in Olympia.

But I want to say clearly where I stand.
I've spent my career in child welfare, juvenile justice, courts, government budgeting, and nonprofits, and I know how these systems connect (or don't).
When we cut ... community supports, the cost doesn't disappear.
It shifts to ERs, first responders, and the housing and homelessness crisis.
Families lose stability, and kids lose the consistency, routines, and medications they depend on.
When children and family systems lose that support, they are no longer low risk.
They can escalate into higher cost systems like foster care, intensive residential services, and institutional care.
We have a culture where we are trained to respond to crisis instead of investing in prevention, and prevention costs less than crisis response.
In the end, taxpayers, hospitals, first responders, social workers, and behavioral health providers pay the price of these cuts.
2,655 neighbors is not a line item.
I'll be fighting for them in Olympia.

Those years taught me that successful government-to-government work begins with understanding sovereignty and respecting history, culture, and treaty rights. It grows through consistent communication and a deep regard for the longstanding ties between our communities. I am grateful for the trust placed in me. In Olympia, I will work to strengthen the government-to-government relationship between the state and Tribal nations.

What is happening in Gaza is a GENOCIDE.
I call for an immediate ceasefire, unrestricted humanitarian aid, and demand Palestinian rights, self-determination and statehood.
There can be no lasting peace without justice and accountability.
I demand Netanyahu’s immediate arrest and prosecution for war crimes.
I oppose unconditional U.S. aid to Israel, support an arms embargo to Israel, and oppose investing state or federal taxpayer dollars in Israeli bonds.
I support requiring AIPAC to register as a foreign entity and banning its political funding in any form.

added: Get Campaign Updates Join EVERETT JACKSON FOR CONGRESS Home About Issues News Get Involved DONATE Meet Everett Jackson A proven community leader ready to bring real change to Washington.
A Fighter for Our Community Everett Jackson's story is the American story.

Growing up in a working-class family in Dallas, he witnessed firsthand the challenges that everyday Texans face—rising costs, limited opportunities, and a government that seemed to work for everyone except them.
Instead of accepting the status quo, Everett dedicated his life to serving the people in his community and leading by example as a Small Business Owner and Community Organizer.
Now, he's running for Congress because TX-30 deserves a representative who serves our district, shares our values, and places YOU above their unquenchable need for fame.
Our Values The principles that guide everything we do.

Integrity Always putting people before politics and staying true to our values Community First Building solutions from the ground up with input from those affected Results-Driven Focused on delivering real, measurable change for our district Accountability Transparent leadership that answers to the people, not special interests Ready to Make a Difference?
Join us today to help bring real conservative leadership to TX-30.

Janelle Bynum Champions Oregon Business and Sets Sights on Strengthening Key Industries PRESS RELEASE Bynum Reports Massive Quarter 1, Raising over $750K PRESS RELEASE Bynum Decisively Wins Primary, Ready for General Election Fight PRESS RELEASE Bynum to Debate PRESS RELEASE Bynum Releases First TV Ad, “Rip It Up” PRESS RELEASE BYNUM ANNOUNCES COSPONSORSHIP OF MEDICARE FOR ALL PRESS RELEASE BYNUM STANDS OUT AS CLEAR CHOICE FOR OREGON IN FORUM PRESS RELEASE BYNUM AND JAYAPAL TOUT MEDICARE FOR ALL AT PORTLAND TOWN HALL Oct 13 2026 PRESS RELEASE BYNUM AND JAYAPAL TOUT MEDICARE FOR ALL AT PORTLAND TOWN HALL Clackamas, OR – Today, Congresswoman Janelle Bynum and Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal held a joint town hall in Portland to talk about Medicare for All.
They discussed the rising cost of health insurance, recent cuts to federal healthcare spending, and their work to make sure every American can access high-quality care.
Jayapal leads the Medicare for All Act in the House, and Rep.
Bynum is a cosponsor of the legislation.
“The system does not make sense to me,” Rep.
“As a mother of four who’s had to take their kids to the hospital and like so many Oregonians, I’m tired of the lip service we get from Washington on healthcare.
We have to turn the whole system on its head.
There’s something fundamentally wrong with a system where the institutions who control access to healthcare can thrive while the people who actually need the healthcare are scared to use it.
That is why I’m proud to cosponsor Medicare for All.
We’ve had enough.” "It is criminal that in the richest country in the world, people are sick and dying because they cannot afford the care they need,” said Rep.

“At a moment when Trump and Republicans have slashed healthcare funding, and one in four people in this country face a medical debt of over $1,000, it is clear we cannot continue to tinker around the edges of the sick care system we currently have.

That is why I'm proud to lead the Medicare for All Act, to reimagine a system where every single person has coverage from the day they're born 'til the day they die, and I am thrilled today to welcome Congresswoman Bynum as a cosponsor." Background Republicans slashed $1 billion in federal healthcare spending under their “One Big Beautiful Bill” which Congresswoman Bynum strongly opposed.
Because of these spending cuts, roughly 7.5 million Americans will lose health insurance coverage, including nearly 200,000 Oregonians .
Under this bill, 28,000 people in Oregon’s Fifth Congressional District will experience skyrocketing healthcare costs due to the Republicans' decision to end Affordable Care tax credits.
The Medicare for All Act ensures every American can access high quality healthcare and restores access from these harmful cuts.

added: The records show a clear pipeline : billionaire donors invest in candidates, and in return, those candidates deliver specific votes.
In 2024, the "price of admission" for the most powerful endorsements in the party was a vote for private school vouchers.

From Jeff Yass, the Pennsylvania billionaire who gambled on vouchers with Donald Trump's assistance to rout and replace the Raney Republicans, to Elon Musk and Texans for Lawsuit Reform, District 14 is being treated as a billionaire's acquisition.

While millions flow into the coffers of the "Team," the local cost is borne by us: higher prices, eroded public services, and a representative who answers to "the Team" in Austin rather than the families in Bryan and College Station.
SB 1362 — Extreme risk protective orders "The Record is Clear" It is difficult to determine what Paul Dyson actually stands for.
His public presence is inconsistent—his website remains stuck in 2024 and is riddled with errors .
But while his digital presence is neglected, his campaign mailers are polished, telling you he is 'tough on traffickers.

Click here to dive deeper with "The Live Oak Paradox: Vouchers, Traffickers, and "The Team" in District 14 In reality, the "Team" protects its own The record is indeed clear , but not in the way he wants you to believe: In our backyard: While he campaigns on "toughness," the most infamous child-trafficking facilitator in modern history, Ghislaine Maxwell, was moved into a low-security camp on the very land that served as the genesis of the private school Dyson chairs.
In the AG's office: This is the "Team" mentality in action.
While Dyson touts trafficking laws, the Attorney General's office attempted to broker a "sweetheart deal" for a predator who abused a young boy—seeking a sentence of just one single day in prison.
When the "toughness" is only for the cameras, and the protection is only for the connected, the record isn't clear—it's a performance.
Academic Freedom at Texas A&M Texas A&M has helped shape this community, and many of us have built our lives here because of it.

added: How to fold a zine → Press Coverage Can Amanda Janoo Pull Off an Upset in the Race for Governor? [Each town hall] also introduces a core tenet of Janoo’s political philosophy: Policy makers should build upon the strengths, resources and ideas that already exist within communities rather than focusing on what they lack.
Or, as Janoo often says, “Together, we have everything we need.” It’s an oversimplified statement, as any campaign tagline is.
But Janoo’s message is clearly resonating with voters.
Since she announced her candidacy for governor in March, the 39-year-old economist has traversed the state to share her vision for Vermont with citizens of all stripes.

Thousands have shown up — at coffee shops and senior centers, barns and auditoriums — to hear her ideas about universal primary care, bottom-up decision-making, and why the state needs to fight back against corporate and private-equity ownership of Vermont’s housing stock, which disadvantages everyday people.

added: Skip to main content Skip to footer Opens in a new tab Join the team to re-elect JB Meet JB Accomplishments Meet Christian News & Updates Meet JB Accomplishments Meet Christian News & Updates Sign Up Make a Plan to Vote Meet JB Accomplishments Meet Christian News & Updates Sign Up Make a Plan to Vote Governor JB Pritzker, Christian Mitchell Receive Endorsement from Major Healthcare Organizations at Healthcare Workers for JB Event CHICAGO, IL — Today, Governor JB Pritzker and lieutenant gubernatorial candidate Christian Mitchell received the endorsements of the Illinois State Medical Society and Mental Health PAC.
Members of Planned Parenthood Illinois Action and the Illinois Pharmacists Association were also in attendance to support Gov.
To watch the livestream of the event, click here .
“Illinois is home to some of the most extraordinary health professionals in the nation,” said Governor JB Pritzker .
“Their dedication to their patients and communities is second to none.
Not only are they world-class providers, they’ve also been indispensable partners in our fight to strengthen healthcare access and affordability across Illinois.

I’m so grateful for all they do and look forward to many more years of collaboration.” “Illinois healthcare workers dedicate their lives to caring for others, driven by the belief that every person deserves the dignity of quality care, no matter their background or their bank account,” said lieutenant gubernatorial candidate Christian Mitchell .
“It’s a belief I learned from my mom, who was a NICU nurse for nearly 40 years.
JB shares that belief, and it’s one of the reasons I’m so proud to be running alongside him.

For nearly eight years, he’s invested in our providers, the places they work, and the patients they serve, and together we’ll keep fighting for them.” “Governor Pritzker has been a staunch ally for Illinois physicians and the patients we serve, and he has been a champion for both public health and access to care,” said the Illinois State Medical Society .

“We look forward to partnering with him for another term.” “Governor Pritzker has been a powerhouse for mental health — moving the dial on every front, from health insurance to school mental health to protecting kids online,” said Kathleen Daughety, Director, Mental Health PAC .
“He took on the insurance industry with one of the nation’s strongest reform laws, ending the delays and denials that keep people from care.
Soon every public school student will get an annual mental health screening, and Illinoisans are protected from AI chatbots posing as therapists.

Progress on mental health takes a champion, and Governor Pritzker has proven he’s the champion Illinois needs.” “In Rochelle, our families, friends, and neighbors depend on our pharmacy for medications and trusted care close to home,” said Rupesh Manek, owner of Rochelle Pharmacy in Rochelle, IL .

We were having our credit rating go down, down, down, 24 times over the prior 15 years.
And over the last eight years, I have balanced the budget eight times and gotten 12 credit upgrades.
We have a whole lot more work to do.
But making sure that we’re being fiscally responsible is hugely important.” On delivering for working families: “So, I want to tell people who I am.
I’m somebody who fights for expansion of healthcare.
I think everybody should have a doctor.
I think we need universal preschool.
I’ve been fighting for that my entire time in office… and I’ve been making sure that we lifted wages for people across the state.
I voted and signed a bill that I pushed for to raise the minimum wage.
He wants to lower your wages.
I want to raise your wages, and I want to cut costs.” On Darren Bailey’s constant lies: “Lie after lie after lie.
That’s what you’re hearing from Darren Bailey.

And let me be clear also that Darren Bailey voted against balanced budgets every single year and he attacks my character… It’s another lie, let me tell you the truth.” On Darren Bailey raising property taxes: “Darren Bailey also mentioned property taxes, and let me be clear: property taxes are set at the local level.
And when Darren Bailey had the opportunity, he raised property taxes 13 times… 81% is how much property taxes went up, when he had the opportunity.
I’ve never voted in favor of raising property taxes.” On Darren Bailey supporting Trump’s failing economic policies: “Darren likes to talk about the amount of money that people are owed for tariffs.

They haven’t been getting that money back from the government, and Donald Trump lost at the Supreme Court. $2,200 was owed to every working family in the state of Illinois; they have not received a dime of it.
Now, by the way, families are out about $3,300 per family.
And I want to say, Darren Bailey’s never spoken up at all against Donald Trump’s policies.

So, while he’s hurting farmers, Darren Bailey’s just letting it happen.” On protecting public safety in Illinois: “Let me be clear about some of the things that we’re doing in fighting for public safety.
It is a vital part of what it is to live in the state of Illinois, to make sure that we have more police, and I’ve invested in state police.
To make sure we have community violence interruption programs, which Darren Bailey once again voted against, and the prior Republican governor decimated.

And a ban on assault weapons because I don’t think that something that can fire, as happened in Highland Park, and shoot 48 people within 60 seconds, that’s not a weapon that I think should be on the streets.

He has no answer to public safety except he thinks more guns on the streets is the answer.” ### CONTACT: press@jbpritzkercampaign.com Join #TeamJB Sign up to join the team today and receive updates from the campaign, learn about volunteer opportunities, and more.

title.after: Mayor William Cogswell: Why I Support Jenny Honeycutt

added: Home About Platform News Support DONATE DONATE Home About Platform News Support DONATE Friday, October 2, 2026 Opinion Editorial: Why I'm Supporting Jenny Costa Honeycutt for Congress Charleston Mayor William Cogswell (Published in Charleston Mercury) Charleston's biggest challenges don't stop at the city limits.
Flooding, traffic and the cost of housing are local problems, but solving them takes a partner in Washington who understands how the work actually gets done on the ground.
That is why I am supporting Jenny Costa Honeycutt for Congress.
Since I took office, I have worked across the table from Jenny on Charleston County Council.
I'll be honest: we haven't always agreed.
She has pushed the city to justify what we ask for and made sure county taxpayers were treated fairly.
That is exactly what you want from someone responsible for public money.
But she also gets to yes.
When it came to allocating funding to the Battery Extension, she made the case that flood protection downtown is about whether an ambulance can reach the hospital when the streets are underwater.
When talks over county land for affordable housing on Morrison Drive stalled, she kept working toward a solution when it would have been easier to walk away.
And she has been a steady voice for fixing the roads and infrastructure our growth has left behind.
Much of that work will depend on federal partners, from the Army Corps of Engineers to transportation funding.
Our next representative needs to understand these issues firsthand, not learn them on the job.
Jenny has spent years in the details of local government, and she knows the Lowcountry because she was raised here and has served here.
The Lowcountry needs someone in Congress who will show up, do the homework and deliver.
Jenny Costa Honeycutt will do that, and I'm proud to support her.
### William Cogswell is the Mayor of Charleston, South Carolina, and a former member of the South Carolina House of Representatives.

added: WHEN YOU SERVE OUR COUNTRY, JENNY HAS YOUR SIX As the daughter and granddaughter of veterans, Jenny has tremendous respect for those who serve our nation and their families.
Jenny believes veterans shouldn't have to fight a second battle against bureacracy to receive the healthcare, benefits, and opportunities they've earned.

That is why Jenny has created "I've Got Your 6," a six-point commitment to improve veterans’ healthcare, benefits, employment opportunities, housing, and transition to civilian life while cutting bureaucratic red tape and demanding greater accountability for serving Lowcountry veterans and their families.

RSVP Time & Location Oct 19, 2026, 3:30 PM – 5:30 PM Firestone/Frederick About the event Statewide Democratic candidates John Hickenlooper, Phil Weiser, Jena Griswold, Amanda Gonzalez, and Jeff Bridges are touring the state to meet voters and help turn out the vote for candidates like Jillaire McMillan and Manny Rutinel.
Come by the Monday afternoon stop in HD19 and CD8 to meet the candidates.
Volunteers will be entered in a drawing to get paired up with one of the statewide candidates or another elected official to knock some doors nearby and help flip two seats blue!
RSVP to get the precise location.
There will also be a simple non-canvassing activity to help get out the vote.
Spread the word and let's get people excited to vote for these candidates!

For months, we've seen Flock cameras across the country be used to stalk Americans, aid ICE thugs in illegal raids, and trample our Fourth Amendment rights.
