What Is on Your Ballot: The Official 2026 Constitutional Amendments When voters step up to the ballot-marking device (BMD), they encounter legal text on three statewide constitutional amendments.
Questions from readers and local residents have highlighted the need for a plain-English explanation of these measures before heading to the polls.

Below is what each official 2026 amendment proposes, along with the core policy arguments on both sides: Amendment 1: Increasing the Agricultural & Timber Conservation Property Tax Cap (HR 32) Official Ballot Text: “Shall the Constitution of Georgia be amended so as to increase the maximum acreage of bona fide agricultural and timber property that may be classified as conservation use property from 2,000 acres to 4,000 acres?” What It Does: Georgia’s Conservation Use Value Assessment (CUVA) program allows qualifying farmland and timberland to be assessed based on its current agricultural or timber use rather than market development value, in exchange for a binding 10-year conservation covenant.
Current law caps enrollment at 2,000 acres per owner or entity.
Amendment 1 increases that cap to 4,000 acres.
Why Supporters Favor It: Farm and forestry advocates argue that rising rural land values make contiguous tracts expensive to maintain under market valuation.

Proponents maintain that doubling the cap provides tax relief for growing family farms and working timber operations, encouraging them to keep land in agricultural production rather than subdividing for development.

What Skeptics Note: Opponents and local budget observers caution that expanding property tax exemptions reduces the taxable digest that rural county governments and public schools rely on to fund local services.
Critics also note that owners of larger acreage tracts stand to benefit most, which could place pressure on local millage rates.

Amendment 2: Requiring Nonpartisan Elections for Probate Court Judges (HR 251) Official Ballot Text: “Shall the Constitution of Georgia be amended so as to require that all probate court judges in the state be elected on a nonpartisan basis?” What It Does: Georgia Superior Court and appellate judges are elected on nonpartisan ballots.

Amendment 2 establishes a uniform statewide constitutional requirement that all 159 county probate court judges be elected on a nonpartisan basis, eliminating partisan party primaries where they currently exist.
Why Supporters Favor It: Supporters contend that party affiliation has no legitimate role in probating a will, appointing a guardian, or administering an estate.
Proponents argue that nonpartisan elections protect judicial impartiality and keep courthouse administration free from partisan primary politics.

What Skeptics Note: Opponents point out that political party designations give voters a familiar baseline philosophical cue when researching down-ballot courthouse races with minimal campaign advertising.
Critics also suggest that removing party labels can increase the electoral advantage of well-known incumbents.

Amendment 3: Dedicated Next Generation 9-1-1 Emergency Trust Fund (HR 1243) Official Ballot Text: “Shall the Constitution of Georgia be amended so as to authorize the General Assembly to dedicate revenues derived from fees assessed on emergency telephone communications services to a nonlapsing trust fund to be used exclusively for the expansion, maintenance, and operation of 9-1-1 systems in this state?” What It Does: Amendment 3 authorizes the General Assembly to establish a dedicated, nonlapsing “Georgia Next Generation 9-1-1 Fund.” Under this amendment, state revenues derived from existing emergency telephone service fees would be constitutionally restricted to funding 911 communications infrastructure and dispatch upgrades.

Why Supporters Favor It: First responders and public safety officials argue that fees collected from monthly telephone bills for 911 services should be locked into emergency communications rather than subject to being redirected into the state general fund during budget cycles.
Proponents emphasize that reliable dedicated funding is critical for rural dispatch centers upgrading to digital mapping and text-to-911 capabilities.

What Skeptics Note: Fiscal traditionalists generally oppose constitutionally dedicating state revenue streams, arguing that earmarking fees reduces the legislature’s budgetary flexibility to reallocate funds during economic downturns or unforeseen state emergencies.
For an extensive, neutral breakdown of the legal mechanics and financial implications, read our full Georgia 2026 Ballot Measures Explainer .

Pocket Checklist: Practical Rules for the Voting Booth Before you head to the polls this Saturday, keep these operational rules in mind: Acceptable Photo ID: Georgia law requires government-issued photo identification to vote in person.

Acceptable forms include a Georgia driver’s license (even if expired, pursuant to state election rules), a free state voter ID card, a U.S. passport, military photo ID, tribal photo ID, or a government employee photo ID.

Surrendering a Mail Ballot: If you received an absentee ballot by mail but choose to vote in person on Saturday, bring your unvoted paper ballot with you to the check-in desk to surrender it to poll workers.
If you lost it, never received it, or do not have it with you, poll workers will provide a standard cancellation affidavit to sign before an in-person ballot is issued.

Cell Phone Restrictions & Personal Notes: Under Georgia law ( O.C.G.A. § 21-2-413(e) ), the use of cellular phones or other recording devices is prohibited in the voting room while voting is underway.
Voters commonly bring handwritten notes or a printed sample ballot into the voting booth to reference their choices privately.
Ensure any notes are kept private for personal use and not displayed to other electors, and consult poll workers if you have questions about local polling room policies.

Preferential Treatment During Advance Voting: Under O.C.G.A. § 21-2-385.1 , electors who are 75 years of age or older, electors with physical disabilities, or electors accompanied by children aged two or younger are entitled upon request to vote without waiting in line during advance voting.
Why Showing Up Matters Representative government works best when voters have direct access to their elected officials.

Our communities face urgent issues: retaining healthcare staff at local critical-access facilities, defending local control over land use, supporting multi-generational timber and farming operations, and preparing young people for skilled trade careers through our technical colleges.
We invite you to cast your ballot this Saturday during advance voting, and then join us at 6:00 PM at South Tattnall Middle School Gym in Glennville .
Bring your questions, bring your neighbors, and let us discuss the future of our home together.

The NFIB’s endorsement of Michele Tafoya highlights the confidence small business owners have in her to champion policies that help small businesses thrive.

Mike McKay Volunteer Meet Mike Georges Creek Flood Response Sponsored Legislation Voting Record Senate Scholarship Program Office Contact News & Updates Events Volunteer Donate September 18th, 2026 AFL-CIO Endorses Senator Mike McKay CUMBERLAND – September 18, 2026 Senator Mike McKay earned the endorsement of the AFL-CIO in his bid for re-election to the Maryland Senate — an endorsement that does not often […] September 18th, 2026 AFL-CIO Endorses Senator Mike McKay CUMBERLAND – September 18, 2026 Senator Mike McKay earned the endorsement of the AFL-CIO in his bid for re-election to the Maryland Senate — an endorsement that does not often […] CUMBERLAND – September 18, 2026 Senator Mike McKay earned the endorsement of the AFL-CIO in his bid for re-election to the Maryland Senate — an endorsement that does not often go to a Republican.
McKay represents a district built by union labor.

Allegany, Garrett, and Washington Counties are coal country, rail country, and building-trades country, where a third-generation miner and a third-generation Democrat are frequently the same person, and where the question at the kitchen table is whether the work is still going to be here in ten years.
“I do not ask a man who he voted for before I go to work on his job,” McKay said.
“Out here the paycheck is not a partisan issue.

Either the work stays in Western Maryland or it does not, and I am judged on which one happens.” McKay sponsored Senate Bill 26 this session to create a new energy framework allowing independent power providers to serve new commercial and industrial customers without raising costs for households already on the grid.
He argued the bill in committee as a jobs measure: a way for Maryland to compete for industrial investment without sending the bill to families who are already struggling to pay for electricity.

He has also fought the steady climb of state fees that come straight out of a working paycheck, pushing amendments this year to roll back vehicle registration increases and to create a dedicated Roads and Bridges Account so transportation money actually reaches roads and bridges.
“Western Marylanders are feeling these costs everywhere, at the MVA, at the pump, in the utility bill,” McKay said.

“I went to Annapolis to fight for relief, not to watch the majority keep nickel-and-diming the people I represent.” ### Stay up to date on Senator McKay’s fight for Western Maryland — sign up for his District Newsletter at MikeMcKayMD.com/#newsletter .

NFIB, the leading small-business association in […] October 14th, 2026 NFIB Endorses Senator Mike McKay for Re-Election CUMBERLAND – October 14, 2026 The NFIB Maryland PAC has endorsed Senator Mike McKay for re-election to the Maryland State Senate on November 3rd.
NFIB, the leading small-business association in […] CUMBERLAND – October 14, 2026 The NFIB Maryland PAC has endorsed Senator Mike McKay for re-election to the Maryland State Senate on November 3rd.

NFIB, the leading small-business association in the nation with thousands of members across Maryland, said in its endorsement that it believes McKay will be committed to “the needs of thousands of Main Street small businesses and their employees in Maryland.” McKay, a Republican who represents Allegany, Garrett, and Washington Counties, built and ran a small business in Western Maryland before he was elected, employing local workers.
“I ran a small business in Western Maryland before I ever ran for office,” McKay said.
“I know what it is to make payroll, and I know what it is to open a letter from Annapolis with a new fee in it.
The people who sign the front of the paycheck deserve somebody in the Senate who has done it.” In Western Maryland, Main Street is the economy.
The hardware store, the diner, the contractor with four trucks, and the family shop that has been open for three generations are where most people here work.
McKay sponsored Senate Bill 26 this session to let independent power providers serve new commercial and industrial customers without raising costs for households already on the grid.

He also pushed budget amendments to roll back vehicle registration fee increases and to create a dedicated Roads and Bridges Account, so money collected for transportation is spent on roads and bridges.
“A small business out here does not have a lobbyist or a lawyer on retainer,” McKay said.
“It has an owner who is already working sixty hours a week.
Every fee and every mandate lands on that one person, and I am going to keep saying so in Annapolis.” ### Stay up to date on Senator McKay’s fight for Western Maryland.
Sign up for his District Newsletter at MikeMcKayMD.com/#newsletter .

description.after: My name is Bernice Mireku-North and I serve as Delegate for District 14, Montgomery County, which includes various neighborhoods of Silver Spring (Colesville, Fairland, Briggs Chaney), Burtonsville, Brookville, Spencerville, Laytonsville, Olney and parts of Damacus and Clarksburg.

Contribute Build with Bernice Leadership you can count on for healthier, safer, stronger communities.

Meet Delegate Bernice Get Ready to Vote about Meet Bernice IMG_0003k-1 PHOTO-2025-12-30-14-29-57 IMG_2861_edited IMG_0003k-1 1/10 I am a Democrat and member of the House of Delegates, representing District 14.
For the past four years, I've fought for better schools, affordable housing, and economic opportunity for every family in our community.
Now, I'm asking for your support to continue this work.
Together, we're building a stronger Maryland.

Learn more about me Watch My Welcome Message See My Priorities Maryland District 14 MD Distict 14 District 14 includes vibrant communities across Montgomery County, spanning parts of Brookeville, Olney, Ashton, Sandy Spring, Damascus, Laytonsville, and parts of Silver Spring and Burtonsville.

I'm proud to represent the diverse families, small businesses, and community organizations that make our district strong. ​ District 14 Communities Include: Olney Brookeville Damascus Laytonsville Ashton Sandy Spring Silver Spring (partial) Burtonsville Fairland Briggs Chaney Calverton (partial) ​ ZIP Codes Served: 20833, 20832, 20853, 20860, 20861, 20862, 20866, 20904, 20905 ​ Not sure if you're in District 14?

Use the map above to see our district boundaries, or check your voter registration at elections.maryland.gov See What I've Delivered Laws I've passed and funding I've secured for District 14 Child Care & Families Education & Young People Workers & Economic Security Community & Civic Life Accomplishments for Child Care & Families Child Care Scholarships: Keeping Families Enrolled During Freezes When the state's Child Care Scholarship Program runs low on funding, it sometimes freezes new enrollments, which can cut off exactly the families who need help most.

This law makes sure families on public assistance, siblings of children already enrolled, and kids experiencing homelessness can never be turned away because of an administrative pause. ​ Securing $3.7 Million for Therapeutic Child Care Programs Families of young children with developmental, physical, or behavioral disabilities often can't find child care equipped to meet their child's needs.

This law secures $3.7 million from FY2027–2029 for specialized programs serving children from birth to age 6, so these kids get the care they need and their parents can stay in the workforce. ​ Better Pay Pathways for Early Childhood Educators Maryland's Career Ladder program was designed to reward early childhood educators with better pay and professional development.
But arbitrary enrollment deadlines were blocking qualified educators from advancing.
I replaced those deadlines with flexible, progression-based timelines, so qualified educators can move up, and earn more, without bureaucratic delay.

Accomplishments for Education & Young People Expanding College Tuition Waiver for More Foster Youth Maryland waives college tuition at state schools for young people who grew up in the foster care system, but children adopted before their 13th birthday were shut out of this support.

I lowered that qualifying age to 8, opening the door to higher education for more foster youth. ​ Tackling the School Psychologist Shortage Maryland schools are facing a serious shortage of mental health professionals.

This law joins Maryland to a national compact that lets licensed school psychologists from other member states work here without restarting the licensing process, making it faster and easier to put qualified professionals in front of students who need support.
Student Loan Relief for School Nurses As the daughter of a nurse, this one is personal.

This law extends Maryland's existing loan assistance program to include school nurses, helping address the nursing shortage in our schools while relieving the debt burden on the people who care for our kids every day.
Accomplishments for Workers & Economic Security ​Waiving Business Start-Up Fees for Displaced Federal Workers Thousands of Marylanders lost federal jobs this year through no fault of their own.

I secured $150,000 in the budget to waive state business licensing fees for former federal employees who are ready to start something new in Maryland. ​ Protecting Tenants in Mental Health Crises When someone is in a serious mental health crisis, they shouldn't be trapped in a home they can no longer safely stay in or owe months of back rent for leaving.

This law lets tenants with a documented condition break their lease early, capped at two months' liability. ​ Independent Appeals Rights for WSSC Workers Workers at the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission had no path to independent review when they faced disciplinary action.
This law gives those employees the right to appeal suspensions to the Office of Administrative Hearings, an independent state body, so disputes are resolved fairly.
Accomplishments for Community & Civic Life Language Access at the Polls If you can't read the ballot or communicate with poll workers, your right to vote is incomplete.

This law requires eligible counties to translate online voting materials, provide real-time interpretation at polling places, and actively recruit bilingual election judges, so every eligible voter in our diverse district can actually exercise their vote. ​ Honoring District 14 History at Freedman's State Park This law renames two state parks to better reflect their varied amenities and history.

Right here in District 14, Freedman's State Park honors Enoch George Howard, a man born enslaved in 1814 who purchased his own freedom, bought back the land he was once enslaved on, and built schools and a church for his community.
The site is believed to have been a stop on the Underground Railroad.
The law also updates the name of Port Deposit State Park.

Contribute Build with Bernice Legislative Wins During my time in office, I've fought for the priorities that matter most to our community.
From the classroom to the State House floor, here's what we've accomplished together.
Explore by topic below to see highlights from my work in the Maryland General Assembly.
Watch the Legislative Recap videos from the past few years below.

Child Care & Families Education & Young People Workers & Economic Security Community & Civic Life Accomplishments for Child Care & Families Child Care Scholarships: Keeping Families Enrolled During Freezes When the state's Child Care Scholarship Program runs low on funding, it sometimes freezes new enrollments, which can cut off exactly the families who need help most.

This law makes sure families on public assistance, siblings of children already enrolled, and kids experiencing homelessness can never be turned away because of an administrative pause. ​ Securing $3.7 Million for Therapeutic Child Care Programs Families of young children with developmental, physical, or behavioral disabilities often can't find child care equipped to meet their child's needs.

This law secures $3.7 million from FY2027–2029 for specialized programs serving children from birth to age 6, so these kids get the care they need and their parents can stay in the workforce. ​ Better Pay Pathways for Early Childhood Educators Maryland's Career Ladder program was designed to reward early childhood educators with better pay and professional development.
But arbitrary enrollment deadlines were blocking qualified educators from advancing.
I replaced those deadlines with flexible, progression-based timelines, so qualified educators can move up, and earn more, without bureaucratic delay.

Accomplishments for Education & Young People Expanding College Tuition Waiver for More Foster Youth Maryland waives college tuition at state schools for young people who grew up in the foster care system, but children adopted before their 13th birthday were shut out of this support.

I lowered that qualifying age to 8, opening the door to higher education for more foster youth. ​ Tackling the School Psychologist Shortage Maryland schools are facing a serious shortage of mental health professionals.

This law joins Maryland to a national compact that lets licensed school psychologists from other member states work here without restarting the licensing process, making it faster and easier to put qualified professionals in front of students who need support.
Student Loan Relief for School Nurses As the daughter of a nurse, this one is personal.

This law extends Maryland's existing loan assistance program to include school nurses, helping address the nursing shortage in our schools while relieving the debt burden on the people who care for our kids every day.
Accomplishments for Workers & Economic Security ​Waiving Business Start-Up Fees for Displaced Federal Workers Thousands of Marylanders lost federal jobs this year through no fault of their own.

I secured $150,000 in the budget to waive state business licensing fees for former federal employees who are ready to start something new in Maryland. ​ Protecting Tenants in Mental Health Crises When someone is in a serious mental health crisis, they shouldn't be trapped in a home they can no longer safely stay in or owe months of back rent for leaving.

This law lets tenants with a documented condition break their lease early, capped at two months' liability. ​ Independent Appeals Rights for WSSC Workers Workers at the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission had no path to independent review when they faced disciplinary action.
This law gives those employees the right to appeal suspensions to the Office of Administrative Hearings, an independent state body, so disputes are resolved fairly.
Accomplishments for Community & Civic Life Language Access at the Polls If you can't read the ballot or communicate with poll workers, your right to vote is incomplete.

This law requires eligible counties to translate online voting materials, provide real-time interpretation at polling places, and actively recruit bilingual election judges, so every eligible voter in our diverse district can actually exercise their vote. ​ Honoring District 14 History at Freedman's State Park This law renames two state parks to better reflect their varied amenities and history.

Right here in District 14, Freedman's State Park honors Enoch George Howard, a man born enslaved in 1814 who purchased his own freedom, bought back the land he was once enslaved on, and built schools and a church for his community.
The site is believed to have been a stop on the Underground Railroad.
The law also updates the name of Port Deposit State Park.

Contribute Build with Bernice Hello, My name is Bernice Mireku-North.
I am a Democrat and member of the House of Delegates, representing District 14.

Welcome Message from Bernice My Story Personal and Academic Background I'm a daughter of Ghanaian immigrants, wife, mom, sister, auntie, and cousin to family members from Ghana, across the U.S. and Mexico and Europe.
I am a product of Montgomery County Public Schools.
After graduating from Montgomery Blair High School's Communication Arts Program, I enrolled and graduated from the University of Maryland, College Park.
I earned my Juris Doctorate at Howard University School of Law.
I currently reside in the Fairland area of Silver Spring with my husband Terrill and daughter Adjoa.
Professional Background After two trial judicial clerkships, I served as Assistant State's Attorney for six years before going into private practice.
I am currently Managing Attorney of The North Law Group, LLC and have been active in various bar associations.
Since 2023, I serve as Delegate for District 14 to ensure we have laws that promote safer, stronger, and healthier communities for all.
In Annapolis, I serve on the Ways and Means Committee, Local Revenues Subcommittee, and Early Childhood Subcommittee.
I am also a member of the Legislative Black Caucus, Legislative Latino Caucus, Transit Caucus, and the Women Legislators of Maryland.

When I am not in session, I am serving individuals in my capacity as a lawyer in criminal defense, family law, wills and trusts and business litigation. ​ ​ Community Background I have served my community for over 15 years, with leadership roles that included being Chair of the Silver Spring Citizens Advisory Board, Co-Chair of the Reimagining Public Safety Task Force.
I am currently a member of the Eta Theta Sigma Alumnae Chapter of Sigma Gamma Rho Sorority, Inc., and a Board member of Silver Spring Village and WeAchieve.​ #BuildwithBernice Join the movement.

Contribute Build with Bernice Privacy Policy & Terms of Service Privacy Policy Friends of Bernice Mireku-North Effective Date: June 2026 By Authority: Friends of Bernice Mireku-North, Matthew Enokwe, Treasurer 1.
Overview Friends of Bernice Mireku-North ("Campaign," "we," "us," or "our") is committed to protecting the privacy of supporters, volunteers, and constituents who engage with our campaign.
This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, and protect your personal information — including mobile phone numbers — in connection with our SMS communications program and campaign activities.

Information We Collect We collect the following information when you complete our volunteer sign-up form or otherwise engage with the Campaign: Full name Email address Mobile phone number Volunteer interests and activity preferences SMS consent status and date of consent We do not collect financial account information, medical information, or any other sensitive personal data through our volunteer sign-up form or SMS program.
How We Collect Your Mobile Number We collect mobile phone numbers through our online volunteer sign-up form hosted on the Campaign website.

At the point of collection, an unchecked SMS consent checkbox presents the following disclosures before any message is sent: The identity of the sender (Friends of Bernice Mireku-North) The types of messages to be sent (campaign updates, election reminders, volunteer coordination, and get-out-the-vote notifications) That message frequency varies That message and data rates may apply How to opt out (reply STOP) How to request help (reply HELP) Links to this Privacy Policy and our Terms of Service No SMS message is sent until the supporter affirmatively checks the consent box and submits the form.
Consent is not a condition of participation in any Campaign activity.

Legislative Scholarship When to apply - The application for the 2026-2027 school year is now open .
The deadline to apply for this year's scholarship is April 30th, 2026. ​ Who May Apply - Current high school seniors and full-time or part-time, degree-seeking undergraduate and graduate students.
Undocumented students eligible for in-state tuition and s tudents attending a private career school may also apply.
You must also be a resident of District 14 - click here to check, if you are unsure. ​ How to apply - Click here to fill out the application. ​ ​ Eligible majors - All majors are eligible.
You may use this scholarship at an out-of-state school if your major is not available at a Maryland school and if your delegate agrees.
The Office of Student Financial Aid (OSFA) must verify that your major is unique.

Contact OSFA for further information on the unique major status. ​ Eligibility Requirements: You must enroll at a two-year or four-year Maryland college or university as a full-time or part-time, degree-seeking undergraduate or graduate student, or attend certain private career schools.
Full-time undergraduate students must maintain 12 credits or more per semester, while part-time undergraduate students must maintain 6-11 credits.
Full-time graduate students must maintain 9 or more credits per semester, while part-time graduate students must maintain 6-8 credits per semester.
You must be a Maryland resident.

If you are currently living outside of the 14th Legislative District because you are attending college, use your home address from within the 14th Legislative District to apply. ​ Changes in Enrollment Status: If your enrollment status changes after being offered the scholarship, your award amount may also change.
For example, if a student offered a full-time award drops to part-time (6-11 credits), their award may be reduced.
If a student offered a part-time award enrolls full-time, their award may increase.
Students who enroll for less than 6 credits will see their scholarship cancelled. ​ Award Amount: The minimum annual award is $200.
You may hold the Delegate Scholarship with all State awards.
The total dollar amount of all State awards may not exceed your cost of attendance as determined by your school’s financial aid office or $12,617, whichever is less.
Funds may not be available to award all eligible students. ​ Renewing an Award: Awards are not automatically renewed.
You must re-apply each year to your delegate(s).
If you have applied in previous years, you must write a new essay in order to be considered.

alt://scontent-den2-1.cdninstagram.com/v/t51.82787-15/811102719_18125217631856774_5474713764406420584_n.jpg|Great news… TXDOT approved $12,962,750 in funding for pavement improvements at the Maverick County Airport!! alt://scontent-den2-1.cdninstagram.com/v/t51.82787-15/825269613_18125310928856774_1654457435001601724_n.jpg|As Chairman of the MALC Special Committee on Border Security, today our bipartisan committee sent a letter to Governor Abbott advocating that the federal government’s $7.5 billion reimbursement for border security operations should be reinvested in our border communities. This reimbursement is the perfect opportunity to revitalize our border communities and make a generational impact for our communities from Brownsville to El Paso. Think fixing our roads, improving our water systems, supporting local law enforcement, expanding access to healthcare, strengthening our public schools, and so much more. This bipartisan committee is committed to working on legislation to ensure these dollars are invested in the communities that were on the front lines of Texas’ border security efforts.

alt://scontent-den2-1.cdninstagram.com/v/t51.82787-15/825269723_18125621371856774_4056921205086721184_n.jpg|Great to join local leaders and TXDOT Commissioner Alex Meade for the groundbreaking ceremony of Juno Loop (SL 480) here in Eagle Pass! After years of advocating for this funding in Austin, it’s now becoming a reality! Now is the time for our region to prepare for future growth and our infrastructure lays that foundation. As your State Representative, I remain committed to securing projects like SL 480 across HD74!

removed: top of page for State Representative Fighting for District 23 — Every Day, For Every Family Vote in the Primary on September 9, 2026 Home About Meet the Candidate Legislative Homepage Accessibility Statement Meet the Candidate Legislative Homepage Accessibility Statement Events Community Calendar Campaign Photo Gallery Community Calendar Campaign Photo Gallery News & Press In the News Press Releases Endorsements Social Media In the News Press Releases Endorsements Social Media Get Involved Volunteer Form Contact Us Volunteer Form Contact Us Voter Information Menu Close Contribute Accessibility Statement This statement was last updated on May 23, 2026.
Site developers at AuroraIQAdvisory are working to make our site https://mutoforwarwick.com , accessible to people with disabilities.
What Web Accessibility Is An accessible site allows visitors with disabilities to browse the site with the same or a similar level of ease and enjoyment as other visitors.
This can be achieved with the capabilities of the system on which the site is operating, and through assistive technologies.
Accessibility Adjustments on This Site We have adapted this site in accordance with WCAG 2.2 guidelines, and have made the site accessible to the level of AAA.
This site's contents have been adapted to work with assistive technologies, such as screen readers and keyboard use.

As part of this effort, we have also: Used the Accessibility Wizard to find and fix potential accessibility issues Set the language of the site Set the content order of the site’s pages Defined clear heading structures on all of the site’s pages Added alternative text to images Implemented color combinations that meet the required color contrast Reduced the use of motion on the site Ensured all videos, audio, and files on the site are accessible Declaration of partial compliance with the standard due to third-party content ​The accessibility of certain pages on the site depend on contents that do not belong to the organization, and instead belong to Google.
The following pages are affected by this: https://www.mutoforwarwick.com/accessibility-statement.
We therefore declare partial compliance with the standard for these pages.
Accessibility Arrangements in the Organization Bill Muto for State Representative does not have a physical location, and maintains an online presence only.

Requests, Issues, and Suggestions If you find an accessibility issue on the site, or if you require further assistance, you are welcome to contact us through the organization's accessibility coordinator: AuroraIQAdvisory; bjt@bjtcivicsolutions​.com Contribute Report a Website Issue: Click Here © # Bill Muto for State Representative .

removed: top of page for State Representative Fighting for District 23 — Every Day, For Every Family Vote in the Primary on September 9, 2026 Home About Meet the Candidate Legislative Homepage Accessibility Statement Meet the Candidate Legislative Homepage Accessibility Statement Events Community Calendar Campaign Photo Gallery Community Calendar Campaign Photo Gallery News & Press In the News Press Releases Endorsements Social Media In the News Press Releases Endorsements Social Media Get Involved Volunteer Form Contact Us Volunteer Form Contact Us Voter Information Menu Close Contribute All Posts Endorsements Warwick Councilman Bill Muto announces run for State Representative, District 23 William Muto May 26 3 min read Lifelong Warwick resident will continue serving Ward 6 while seeking the open seat WARWICK, R.I. — Warwick City Councilman William (Bill) Muto announced today that he is running as a Democrat for State Representative in District 23.
He plans to keep his Ward 6 seat while he campaigns, bringing to the General Assembly the same approach he has taken at City Hall: show up, do the work, and be straight with people.
“Representing Ward 6 has been one of the greatest honors of my life,” Muto said.
“I have worked every day to lead with integrity and a commonsense approach to city government.
I’m running for State Representative because the challenges facing our neighborhoods demand steady leadership and real collaboration.

District 23 deserves a representative who understands this community, stands with it, and works hard for it.” Why He Is Running Now For Muto, this campaign is a continuation of his Council work, not a break from it.
Sitting on the budget side of city government gave him a direct view of how state decisions land on Warwick.
Unfunded mandates show up in tax bills and in cuts to services families count on.
“When you sit on the budget side of city government, you see clearly how state mandates—especially unfunded ones—show up in our tax bills and in the services families rely on,” Muto said.

“I’ve seen where those pressures come from, and I believe I can keep making a difference for Warwick by serving at the state level while continuing to show up for Ward 6.” A Warwick Native Muto grew up in a family of eight in the Buttonwoods section of Warwick and went to the city’s public schools.
He still lives in the home his parents built more than #ago.
He and his wife Joanne—an English teacher at Pilgrim High School—raised their two children, Michaela and Alexander, there, and cared for their parents as they got older.
“Warwick is not just where I live.
It’s who I am,” Muto said.
“My parents raised six of us here and taught us to work hard, keep our word, and give back.

I know our neighborhoods and our schools because I’ve lived them.” His Record on the Council On the Council, Muto has focused on the basics: showing up, following through, and helping residents cut through city bureaucracy.
He has worked on street safety, government transparency, and building relationships with labor, small businesses, school officials, and city departments.
His background in business intelligence—more than 30 years helping organizations turn data into decisions—shapes how he approaches problems.
“The issues in front of us—workforce development, affordability, education, infrastructure, public safety, economic competitiveness—are not solved with speeches,” Muto said.
“They require steady, collaborative leadership.
I want to be a partner who understands the issues, respects the process, and works with people to build practical solutions.” Where He Stands Warwick roots.
Lifelong resident with board service at Boys Town New England and Bridgemark.
Accountable spending .
Muto backs Council motions that include built-in outcome measurements and public reporting—he wants the public to see where the money goes and whether it worked.
Plain-language policy.
Committed to making state legislation readable: plain summaries, infographics, and regular feedback channels so residents actually know what their government is doing.
Constituent engagement.
Open-office hours in neighborhood parks and libraries, combined with paper surveys and digital polling, so every resident has a way to be heard.
The Road Ahead “Rhode Island succeeds when its leaders work together,” Muto said.
“Times are tough for a lot of families, and there are no easy answers.
Warwick has always met its challenges by working hard and being straight with one another.
I’m asking my neighbors for their support and their ideas, and I’m ready to get to work.” Learn more, volunteer, or donate at www.mutoforwarwick.com.
About Bill Muto: William (Bill) Muto is a lifelong Warwick resident, business consultant, and Ward 6 City Councilman.
He serves on the boards of Boys Town New England and Bridgemark.

added: Skip to content Facebook X-twitter Instagram Menu Contribute Press Release New Poll: Democrat Nathan Johnson Pulls Ahead In Texas Attorney General Race October 14, 2026 Johnson takes 48% to his opponent’s 47% among likely voters in nonpartisan Texas Politics Project poll (Dallas, Texas) — Nathan Johnson has taken the lead in the race for Texas Attorney General, according to the new University of Texas / Texas Politics Project survey, which puts him at 48% to his Republican opponent’s 47% among likely voters.
In August, the same pollsters had Johnson down five with one in five voters still undecided.
Those voters have now made up their minds, and they broke toward Johnson by better than two to one.
52% of voters say Texas has gone off on the wrong track, and corruption, a key issue for Johnson, is ranked as the second most important problem facing the state.
“People are tired of the Attorney General‘s office being run as a political show.
Middleton pledges to continue the show, with the same tired tricks, the same tired rhetoric.
I pledge to restore the office to its constitutional purposes,” said Nathan Johnson, Democratic candidate for Attorney General.

Johnson’s anti-corruption plan, That’s My Lawyer, would increase scrutiny of state contracting, employ conflict-of-interest review across agencies, and restore the office’s focus on consumer protection.

added: “That’s My Lawyer” Rebuilding the Attorney General’s Office to Reverse the Tide of Corruption Nathan Johnson's plan to end the corruption at the Attorney General's office The Attorney General is the one statewide official who can use the rule of law to stop the corrupt use of power.

Whether it’s corporations rigging markets and preying on consumers or government officers bending and breaking the law to favor themselves and their allies, the Office of Attorney General (“OAG”) is there to put an end to it.
For more than a decade, a corrupted Texas OAG has done precisely the opposite.

Ken Paxton has used the office, and Republican AG nominee Mayes Middleton has pledged to continue using the office, to promote the political agenda of a hostile faction along with the ever-increasing consolidation of corporate power, all at the expense of everyone else.
This failure is itself corruption in the American historical sense of the word: where the rot and deformation of political institutions allows public power to be used to promote private interests.
Nathan Johnson's anti-corruption plan reverses that.

Nathan Johnson would run the attorney general's office as it was intended: not as a political operation, but as the check and balance envisioned by the framers of the Texas constitution, who trusted consolidated power in the hands of no one.
Johnson would: ●​ Ensure honest public contracting.

Consider that Elon Musk’s company, Starlink, received 99% of the state awards in what was supposed to be a competitive bidding process for the provision of Low Earth Orbit satellite broadband service.

Without drawing conclusions for the moment, the whole process may have involved coordinated corruption among the Trump administration, the illegally empowered DOGE czar Musk, private entities (Starlink), the governor’s office and the broadband development office.

The OAG, acting in concert with the Office of the State Comptroller, must ensure that public contracting is administered honestly and legally. ●​ Investigate and prosecute public corruption regardless of who participates.
The test for OAG action is not party registration or rank on a donor list, but whether someone, public or private, Republican or Democrat, broke laws that protect people.

The current AG not only failed to investigate and prosecute friends and allies, like the felon Nate Paul, but instead used the power of the office to facilitate their corruption and shield them from investigation.

This was the subject of the Paxton impeachment trial in the Texas Senate, wherein, despite the evidence, Mayes Middleton, the Republican nominee for Attorney General, voted to acquit Paxton of abuse of office.
(Johnson voted to convict.) ●​ Protect whistleblowers instead of punishing them.
The people who report 1 ●​ ●​ ●​ ●​ ●​ ●​ ●​ ●​ wrongdoing inside the government should be respected and protected, not fired.

Johnson would restore that protection to an office that made a national example of destroying it — full compliance with the Texas Whistleblower Act, a private internal reporting channel that runs outside the AG's front office.
Never bill taxpayers for legal defense of illegal actions.
The OAG’s resources belong to the 32 million Texans it serves, not to the officeholder.
Johnson would put it in writing: no staff time or agency funds will be spent on defending actions that fall outside the scope of the office.
Consumer protection and fair market enforcement.

Restore staffing and case volume in consumer protection and antitrust, two areas that have withered while the OAG devoted investigative and legal resources to fighting culture wars and waging disinformation campaigns.
Work with agencies to ensure honest industry oversight and to avoid regulatory capture by corporate interests.
Anti-corruption can take the form of establishing routine communication with agencies to steer them away from bad decisions.
Hire people who want to serve the public, not an agenda.
Paxton’s corruption drove many good public servants out of civil service.
Johnson will recruit and hire dedicated individuals who take pride in public service, not in the pursuit of political agendas.
Coordinate law enforcement with federal agencies, like the DOJ and FTC and CFPB, in investigations and prosecutions – to the extent the Trump administration will allow it.
Johnson has a record of working on a bipartisan basis on essential matters of public interest.

Where the federal government abdicates its responsibilities to the public, Johnson will work independently of federal agencies that fail to fulfill responsibilities to protect consumers and enforce fair competition laws, as many attorneys general recently did in the Live Nation litigation.
Meet the legal challenges created by rapidly changing technology in a rapidly changing marketplace.
Emerging technologies and marketing innovations create opportunities for consumer abuse by the private sector.

In areas like FinTech, AI-generated persuasion, consumer surveillance by data brokers and others, “personalized pricing”, price-gouging and price-fixing, “dark patterns” (often used in subscriptions), hidden junk fees, leveraging market dominance to dominate parallel markets: these are all places where corrupted government allows abuse of commercial power, where a responsible OAG can protect people and promote free and fair competitive markets.
Advance laws that respond to technology-based marketing changes that enable companies to evade existing law.
Texas has a solid body of consumer protection and fair competition laws, but innovative corporations find innovative ways to circumvent those laws.

As an attorney general serving the public interest, Johnson will not only apply existing law, but, where necessary, will also work closely and collaboratively with the Legislature to update the law to protect the public interest in previously unanticipated scenarios.
Routine review of agency regulation for conflicts of interest.
The OAG must be aware of actual and potential conflicts of interest within agencies, in order to ensure that the public trust is not violated.

An AG who upholds the rule of law through these and other measures, who stays out of Texans' personal lives, who keeps the branches of government in their lanes, and reserves the power of the office for the people it belongs to, reverses what has been a corrupt course, in 2 fulfillment of the responsibilities of the OAG.
Corruption is firing the people who try to stop corruption.
In 2020, eight of Ken Paxton's most senior deputies reported his corruption to the FBI.
They were hard ideological conservatives who worked closely with Paxton, who shared his ideological views.
They concluded that he was abusing the office to help a single man: Austin real estate developer and campaign donor, Nate Paul.
Every one of the eight quit or was fired.
Four sued Paxton and won; a Texas court found they had been improperly fired and awarded them $6.6 million.
Paxton's response reveals how he saw the office.
Rather than pay the judgment himself, Paxton formally requested the Legislature to pay $3.3 million in taxpayer money to settle it.
That led the Texas House to investigate, and then to impeach him – only the third impeachment in Texas history.
The Republican-controlled Senate acquitted Paxton despite the clear evidence.
But eventually the whistleblowers were vindicated in federal court.
Nate Paul pleaded guilty to a federal felony in January 2025.

It is relevant to the race to succeed Ken Paxton as Texas Attorney General that Republican AG nominee Mayes Middleton voted to acquit Paxton, despite the clear evidence presented at trial; Middleton voted to condone abuse of the office he now seeks.

Concentrated commercial power does two things at once: it places market control in the hands of a few individuals who can raise prices and manipulate markets almost at will, while it captures the government offices whose job it is to regulate market behavior.
Concentrated political power, fueled by money from concentrated commercial interests, saps the power of democracy.
Politicians and corporations eventually talk only to each other, with the public shut out of the conversation.
Prices rise, quality falls, choices dwindle, innovation retreats, employees lose options.
And, as democracy erodes, consumers lose their last line of defense.
Concentrated power sows corruption, which concentrates power further.
It is a cycle, and Texans pay for it in lost money and civic faith.
This is where the OAG matters most.
The AG is the chief consumer-protection and antitrust enforcer in the state.
If the OAG is run as a political shop, price gougers and fraudsters and market manipulators operate with near impunity.
Run honestly and true to its purpose, the OAG can break the cycle of political and commercial consolidation of power that corrupts the rule of law at the expense of the public interest.
The AG’s power to uphold the rule of law to combat corruption has never mattered more.
Federal enforcement of consumer protection and antitrust law has largely ceased under Donald Trump.
And relying on the courts and agencies won’t meet the need anymore.

On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that the President may fire commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission at will, overturning the 91-year precedent that kept the nation's top antitrust and consumer-protection enforcers insulated from politics.
The decision reaches well past the FTC, to roughly two dozen independent agencies that police unsafe products, workplace discrimination, and corporate abuse.

The federal regulators on whom Texans have relied to keep big companies honest now serve at the pleasure of a president who is manifestly 3 not interested in either consumer protection or free and fair markets.

When federal regulators can be fired for enforcing the law, Texans need someone who only they hire and fire to protect their interests, someone who will uphold the rule of law to reverse the tide of corruption.
The Texas Attorney General is now the most durable check Texans have left against monopolistic power and undue influence over policy and enforcement.
The choice of who holds the office of Attorney General is now a question of whether the check will work at all.
The path ahead: two visions for the Attorney General.
Mayes Middleton has pledged to continue the Paxton model.
His political support comes from the same fringe faction that produced the status quo, and in the Paxton impeachment trial, Middleton voted to protect it.
Nathan Johnson offers the alternative on the merits.

A commercial litigator and Dallas state senator since 2019, Johnson has put 135 bills into law across four sessions – strengthening the electricity grid, regulating data brokers, blocking AI fraudsters, and even passing laws to make the OAG itself more effective and efficient, while opposing myriad unconstitutional laws on legal grounds.
It is telling that in the Republican primary, not a single one of the major Texas metro dailies endorsed Mayes Middleton.
In the Democratic primary, every one of them endorsed Nathan Johnson.
The contrast is competence and independence and concern for the public interest, versus grift and disinformation and fealty to DC puppet masters.
One candidate would restore the AG's office to public service.
The other would maintain it as a political tool and corruption facilitator.
That is the choice, and that is why the Attorney General’s race will determine whether the government in Texas can be made to work for the 32 million people it is supposed to serve.

added: Skip to content Nathan Ballentine People, not Politics About Issues Nathan’s News Get Involved Contact Donate July 1, 2007 COMMUNITY UPDATE: July 2007 Here’s this month’s regular update to keep you informed of what’s going on in the State House and in our community.
Feel free to forward to your friends and neighbors!
I’m sorry for the delay in not sending this out sooner (I usually try to email the first few days of the month).
Between family vacation and the new requests to be added to the distribution list, it took a little longer than I had planned for the July update.
Remember, when you send me email, please place the word CONSTITUENT in the subject line so that I can reply to your email before the others I receive daily.
Even when we’re out of session in Columbia, the email volume is tremendous.
STATE HOUSE Just two weeks ago, we FINALLY finished the 1st session of the 117th General Assembly.
You may have read all the flurry of events in the final days and oftentimes work from earlier in the session gets overlooked.
In this brief space, I will recap some of the major legislation enacted in 2007.
(I’ll cover the approved budget in the next section).
In the upcoming weeks and months, I will report in more detail the specifics of these laws in my New Irmo News columns.
Elimination of Grocery Tax: EFFECTIVE November 1, 2007.

Department of Transportation Reform (includes): qualifications and screening for DOT Commissioners, a Secretary of Transportation appointed by the Governor, mandatory ethics training for employees, a chief internal auditor, compliance and performance audits, and the prioritization of projects using objective criteria.

Prevention of Underage Drinking and Access to Alcohol Act of 2007 requires registration of kegs, equalizes the penalties for the purchase or possession of beer, wine and liquor by minors, requires certain repeat DUI offenders to pay for and have ignition interlock devices installed on any vehicle the repeat offender operates.
South Carolina Critical Need Nursing Initiative Act addresses the need for more nurses as our state is facing a nursing shortage.

Provides incentives to retain nurse faculty scholars, attract new nurse faculty, provide loans, grants, and scholarships to IN-STATE resident nursing students, establishes a research office to predict health care workforce needs.

Workers’ Compensation Reform (includes): enhanced penalties for making fraudulent claims, provides for new means of discouraging and investigating fraud, limits and ultimate eliminates the Second Injury Fund, and establishes new requirements for proving medically complex workers’ compensation claims.
Ryan’s Law: requires health insurers to provide coverage for the treatment of autism and other pervasive developmental disorders.
Joint Resolution creating a committee to study the feasibility of offshore natural gas exploration.
Energy Freedom and Rural Development Act establishes tax credits, rebates, and incentive programs to encourage biomass fuel development and utilization.
To learn more about legislation that passed this year (or the status of pending bills), please visit www.scstatehouse.net and explore the site.
If you have a specific question and need my assistance, please call or write and I’ll look into the matter for you.

YOUR MONEY Obviously in a $7 BILLION budget, I can’t mention everything that is included, but I’ll try to touch on some “highlights” for fiscal year 2007-2008: $221 million in tax relief; a 3% pay raise for state employees and a cost of living adjustment for retirees using $62.7 million; $38.5 million to cover the increased cost of health insurance for state employees; an increase of $94 million to fully fund the Education Finance Act base student cost ; $21 million for Education and Economic Development Act initiatives; $28 million to provide for a nurse in every elementary school in the state; $30.5 million for school buses and $29.5 million for bus fuel and parts; an additional $20 million in recurring and $10 million in non-recurring funds for Medicaid; $22 million in recurring funds to expand coverage of the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIPs) for children of low-income families so that it includes 200% of poverty level; $5.2 million in recurring funds to provide for 100 new highway patrol troopers; $167 million in non-recurring funds for the port access road; $30 million for advertising South Carolina as a tourist destination.
COMMUNITY Friarsgate Park will receive $25,000 for the construction of much needed sidewalks.
As you may know, the Irmo Little League plays their ball games at the park and have expanded to include a Challenger Series (league for handicapped children).
Obviously the sidewalks will be a huge benefit for the children and our community!
Local politics: Irmo Town Councilman, Barry Walker, has announced his intentions to run for the Mayor of Irmo.
For details, please visit: http://www.thestate.com/154/story/110238.html Iceland Skating Rink: A deal is in the works for the purchase of Iceland Irmo.
Department of Agriculture rural development office in Columbia said the ice rink is under contract, but he would not disclose the people involved in the deal.
The deal should be finalized by the end of the month, Light said.
The buyer is expected to keep the facility as an ice rink.
Iceland closed in May, marking the second failed attempt at owning and managing the large ice rink.
The company that owned the business, Roustan Columbia, a subsidiary of Roustan United of Johnstown, Pa., reported it had lost $700,000 on the rink since taking over in 2003.
The USDA must approve any sale of the rink because it guaranteed the loan when Iceland was built in 2001.
If you haven’t been on board the Southern Patriot for a Purple Martin Cruise, you haven’t experience the lake like only our area can!

Today, Lezlie Patterson (also a member of the community) wrote a great story about Jay Downs and I encourage you to check it out at http://www.thestate.com/154/story/114349.html Richland County Council has approved funding for the operation of the “Ballentine Library”.
As you already know, the facility will be located where the present Bookmobile is parked (outside the Ballentine Food Lion) until a permanent location can be found.
SCHOOLS Last month, the Board of Trustees voted on proposed changes to the 2007-08 and 2008-09 calendars that would provide student and staff holidays on both Veterans Day and Memorial Day.
The board voted unanimously to leave the 2007-08 calendar as previously approved.
Therefore, Memorial Day and Veterans Day will not be holidays.
The first day of school for teachers will be Thursday, August 16, 2007 and the first day of school for students will be Thursday, August 23, 2007.
The last day of school for students will be Thursday, June 5, 2008.
The board also voted unanimously to observe the Memorial Day holiday in the 2008-09 school year.
Therefore, staff will begin on Wednesday, August 13, 2008 and the first day for students will be Wednesday, August 20, 2008.
Over the past few months, several committees have been at work on various projects for Lexington/Richland School District Five.

To learn more about these projects, please visit: http://www.lex5.k12.sc.us/super/schoolfacinfo.html THANK YOU I want to thank you for the honor you give me representing you in the South Carolina House of Representatives.
Please contact my office, 734-2969, or email me at BallentineN@scstatehouse.net anytime I can be of service to you or your family.
Nathan Ballentine House of Representatives, District 71 Richland-Lexington Counties 320A Blatt Building Columbia, SC 29221 Post navigation COMMUNITY UPDATE: August 2007 Comments are closed.

added: Skip to content Nathan Ballentine People, not Politics About Issues Nathan’s News Get Involved Contact Donate August 1, 2007 COMMUNITY UPDATE: August 2007 Here’s this month’s regular update to keep you informed of what’s going on in the State House and in our community.
Feel free to forward to your friends and neighbors!
Remember, when you send me email, please place the word CONSTITUENT in the subject line so that I can reply to your email before the others I receive daily.
Even when we’re out of session in Columbia, the email volume is tremendous.
Each month new addresses or added the distribution list.

If you talk with someone and find out they are not receiving these or if you have friends and neighbors you think would appreciate staying informed, feel free to have them email me and ask to be included.
I’ll add them before next month’s update!
STATE HOUSE You may have noticed that the General Assembly will return this Friday to elect a new State Treasurer to complete the remaining balance of this unexpired term.
You may have also noticed my name has been mentioned for this position in local and statewide media the last few weeks.
While I was certainly flattered and understood why I was approached, last week I announced I would not pursue the office.

My statement read as follows: “No longer a candidate for the office of State Treasurer, I will still continue to be a good steward of our taxpayer’s dollars as an active member of the South Carolina House of Representatives.
It is my hope that the Treasurer we elect next week will share my fiscal conservative philosophy and vision towards government reform.

The support from my House colleagues and Senators has been tremendous but my desire to serve the Irmo, Chapin, Dutch Fork community is where my heart and passion lie.” It is my belief that the new Treasurer may be Converse Chellis, a C.P.A. and current House Member from the Lowcountry.
If he is elected Friday, he will be present at the Community Cookout I am hosting August 14th at the Rusty Anchor (see COMMUNITY below for more details).
I can introduce him to our area at that time.
YOUR MONEY Hopefully you are aware that this weekend is a “Tax Free Holiday”.
As we prepare to send our children off to schools, this is a good time to save some extra money.

Not all items are exempt though, be sure to click here for more information: http://www.sctax.org/Tax+Information/Sales+and+Use+Tax/salesTaxHolidayInfo.htm A few weeks ago, the Government Efficiency Accountability Review (GEAR) Report was released and, to no surprise, it appears there are several ways our state can save taxpayer dollars.

I am still reviewing the rather lengthy report (you can read for yourself if you’d like by clicking http://www.statehousereport.com/pdfs/070713_gearreport.pdf) and I am unsure what changes we may be able to implement next year.

As you know, change is slow among 170 elected officials but I do know everyday we get closer and closer to improving our state and I will continue to push as a public servant and not lifelong, entrenched politician.
COMMUNITY I wanted to make you aware of a Community Cookout I am hosting on August 14th at The Rusty Anchor from 6:00 – 7:30 pm.

When I ran for office in 2004, I stated that elected officials who stay in touch with their community are better able to listen, understand, and consider all points of view when representing their constituents.

Too many times, you only see or hear from politicians at election time and I wanted all our local (and a few state) elected officials to come to a casual event at the lake so that you and your neighbors can talk and share your ideas in this setting.
You may have seen an invite in your mailbox but if not, check the Irmo News this Friday and next for more details.
Please RSVP to the telephone number or email on the invitation if you plan to attend.
There will be no “political speeches” but instead a chance for people to talk openly and meet other neighbors.
Obviously I am very proud of our community and our many individuals who do so much everyday!
Unfortunately I was on vacation and not able to join in the presentation of the state’s highest honor to one of our own two weeks ago.
Sheriff Leon Lott is obviously a great member of our local community – and state – and was very deserving of this honor.
I joined Senator Lourie in making the request for the honor and was glad to see Sheriff Lott recognized for his achievements and service to our state.

Sheriff Lott is just one of the officials who plans to be there at the Cookout. http://www.rcsd.net/media/july07/7-18-orderofpalmetto.html SCHOOLS Last week, the Chairman of our School Board had the following letter appear in The State newspaper.

I think everyone should take time to educate themselves on this important issue our community will consider in the coming months. http://www.thestate.com/editorial-columns/story/131198.html Another article also appeared last week with more information. http://www.thestate.com/education/story/126917.html You may certainly also visit the School District’s webpage for more information as well as informational meeting dates that have been and will continue to be held. http://www.lex5.k12.sc.us/ THANK YOU I want to thank you for the honor you give me representing you in the South Carolina House of Representatives.
Please contact my office, 734-2969, or email me at BallentineN@scstatehouse.net anytime I can be of service to you or your family.
During the summer and winter months, it may take a little extra time to have your email returned – but please know that I read everyone I receive!

Discussions focused on fraud, affordability, oversight of state programs, taxes, public safety, and community development.
Smith on Fraud “I combat fraud for a living,” Smith said.

“We can expand protections for whistleblowers, close policy loopholes that fraudsters exploit, and have stronger and more effective penalties when fraud does occur.” Smith also noted he worked as a citizen to draft fraud prevention legislation in 2025.
Smith on Affordability During the forum Smith highlighted affordability issues like housing, health care and childcare costs.

He discussed increasing housing supply by reducing “red tape,” supporting first-time buyers with grants or tax credits, lowering prescription drug costs and revisiting insurance prior-authorization rules to reduce premiums.
He also wants to consider targeted tax relief.
“There are real things we can do,” Smith said.

“Support first-time homeowners, lower prescription drug costs, take on what people are feeling at the grocery store and the gas pump, and reduce childcare costs.” Watch the forum here : https://www.youtube.com/live/mrZu9aQdLJ0 Read the Stillwater Gazette article here: https://www.hometownsource.com/stillwater_gazette/community/fraud-and-affordability-dominate-first-stillwater-gazette-candidate-forums/article_69b6b827-9a75-4d30-bad5-a3a356f3cb0a.html Nat Smith Next Next Nat Smith Pledges to Continue Fighting Fraud and lower costs in First Digital Ad Contact the Campaign Email us Follow us PREPARED AND PAID FOR BY NAT SMITH FOR MN STATE SENATE COMMITTEE PO Box 116, Stillwater, MN 55082 Photo Gallery | Privacy Policy

Neva Parker Apr 9 2 min read This is in response to this article in Abridged.org .
For over 20 years I sat through more than my fair share of floor debates for bills to fund transportation that over and over assured members that the money wouldn't be diverted elsewhere.
And year after year, the roads I used to get to the capitol to sit through those debates got decidedly worse and worse, despite those bills passing.
Anyone driving Watt Avenue from Roseville through North Highlands and Sacramento will tell you that.
Or Business 80 from Sac through Arden.
I can't fix a road on my own.
I pay taxes so that the government, which exists to do for me what I can't do for myself, can.
I don't want that money to go to bailing out a company that made billions last year and gave a part of those earnings to political campaigns.
I grew up in Hercules, which is right next to Rodeo where the refinery talked about in the article is.
I haven't been to Rodeo in a few years, but it's a small town, with one main road running from the freeway through the town and through the hills to the refinery itself.
I'd bet good money that road needs fixed.
And if it doesn't need fixed now, it definitely needs constant maintenance.
Just like a personal budget - don't go spending money on "can't miss opportunities" when the toilet keeps overflowing and the roof leaks.

And to clarify, I support efforts to improve clean energy, but not taking care of roads leads to less efficient gas usage, contributing poorly to the environment and costing drivers more money on gas and car maintenance.

Peep's endorsement reflects a shared belief that the best solutions come when local leaders, residents, and state representatives work together.

I am incredibly honored to have the endorsement of former Senator Larry Hart.

I'm ready to get to work for Orange County. nicholasdilorenzo8 Jun 24 1 min read Community Bingo Challenge: "Explore Local" What makes Bradford, Fairlee, and West Fairlee special isn't just our beautiful scenery, historic buildings, or local businesses?

title.after: Building Bridges and Shaping Tomorrow’s Leaders

added: top of page Menu Close Home News & Events Get Involved Donate All Posts Building Bridges and Shaping Tomorrow’s Leaders nicholasdilorenzo8 Jun 1 2 min read In a time when communities are searching for ways to strengthen trust, civic engagement, and youth development, the collaboration seen here provides a powerful example of education extending beyond the classroom.
For generations, we have focused on developing character, leadership, citizenship, and service.
Building Trust Through Relationships One of the greatest benefits of collaboration is the opportunity to build relationships before a crisis occurs.
Young people interact with officers as mentors, educators, and community partners rather than only during emergencies or enforcement situations.
These positive interactions help break down misconceptions and foster mutual understanding.
When youth and law enforcement work side-by-side on service projects, leadership exercises, and educational programs, they develop respect and trust that strengthens the entire community.
Developing Future Community Leaders This youth leadership model encourages children to lead, plan, communicate, and take responsibility for their actions.
Through mentorship from law enforcement professionals and other community leaders, participants learn skills that will serve them throughout their lives, regardless of their chosen career path.

Whether a young person becomes a police officer, teacher, business owner, firefighter, elected official, or volunteer, the lessons learned help create engaged citizens who understand the value of service and civic responsibility.
Investing in the Future and What Does It Mean to Serve My Community?
Communities are strongest when they invest in their youth.
Serving the community means choosing to make a positive difference in the lives of others and contributing to the well-being of the place you call home.
It is not defined by a title, uniform, or position.
Service is found in the everyday actions that help build a stronger, safer, and more connected community.
Ultimately, serving your community means recognizing that we are all connected.
When we invest our time, talents, and energy into helping others, we strengthen the bonds that make our towns, schools, and neighborhoods thrive.
Service is not measured by recognition or rewards—it is measured by the positive impact we leave behind and the lives we help improve along the way.

This challenge is about more than completing a bingo card.
It's about strengthening community connections, supporting local businesses, encouraging outdoor activity, and building pride in the places we call home.
Every stop represents a piece of our shared community story.
Together, we can create stronger connections, support one another, and celebrate the best of Bradford, Fairlee, and West Fairlee.
We invite everyone to participate, share their photos, and help make this a community-wide celebration.

added: top of page Menu Close Home News & Events Get Involved Donate All Posts Leadership Is Being There When It Matters nicholasdilorenzo8 Aug 17 2 min read Before Nicholas became my child’s caseworker, I felt completely overwhelmed, unheard, and alone.
I was constantly fighting to make people understand the seriousness of my child’s disabilities and developmental delays.
Too often, I felt like his needs were being minimized and that I was the only person in the room willing to fight for him.
Then Nicholas became part of our lives, and everything changed.
From the very beginning, Nicholas treated my son like a person whose future mattered.
At every IEP meeting, he spoke up, asked the difficult questions, challenged decisions when necessary, and pushed for the services my son desperately needed.
For the first time, I did not feel like I was standing alone against an entire system.
I finally had someone beside me who was willing to advocate for my child with the same determination and passion that I had.
Because of Nicholas’s advocacy, my son was able to receive additional professional services through his IEP that made a real difference.
He started gaining skills, understanding more, and receiving an education that actually addressed his individual needs.
Nicholas did not simply help my son access services—he helped give him a stronger chance at succeeding.
What makes Nicholas different is that his dedication did not end when the meeting was over.
He genuinely cared about my son and our entire family.
He helped empower my child, encouraged us when we felt defeated, and reminded us that my son deserved every opportunity to grow, learn, and thrive.
Nicholas also went far beyond educational advocacy.
During some of the most difficult moments for our family, he helped us navigate financial hardships and connected us with resources we did not even know were available.
He looked at the needs of our whole family, not just one piece of paperwork or one diagnosis.
His compassion, persistence, and willingness to go above and beyond gave our family something we desperately needed: hope.
Nicholas changed the way our family experienced the system.
He made sure our voices were heard.
He made sure my son was seen.
And most importantly, he made sure my child was never treated as though his disabilities meant he deserved anything less.
There are people who simply do their jobs, and then there are people who make a lasting difference in the lives of the families they serve.
Nicholas is one of those people.
Our family is stronger because he was willing to stand beside us, fight with us, and believe in my son.
I will never forget the difference he made in our lives. -Samantha L.

added: top of page Menu Close Home News & Events Get Involved Donate All Posts Wear R.E.D. on Fridays nicholasdilorenzo8 Mar 12 1 min read RED Friday: Remember Everyone Deployed RED Friday stands for Remember Everyone Deployed , a tradition that encourages civilians and military families to wear red on Fridays to show support for U.S. service members serving overseas.
The movement became popular in the early 2000s during conflicts such as the Iraq War and the War in Afghanistan (2001–2021).
By wearing red, people help raise awareness and remind others to keep deployed troops in their thoughts.
RED Friday is simple to participate in—anyone can wear a red shirt, hat, or ribbon.
Though it’s a small gesture, it symbolizes appreciation, unity, and support for those serving far from home.
Let's all show our support to our troops who are deployed in theater and stateside.
Let our communities stand together for freedom.

title.after: Ready to Work - Ready to Win!

added: top of page Menu Close Home News & Events Get Involved Donate All Posts Ready to Work - Ready to Win! nicholasdilorenzo8 May 15 1 min read I’m honored and excited to officially be on the ballot to serve the people of Vermont!
This campaign has never been about politics as usual.
It’s about hard work, common sense, and making sure rural communities and working families still have a strong voice.
Vermont is where we raise our families, support our neighbors, and build our future.
But too many people feel ignored, overtaxed, and left behind.
I’m running because I believe Vermonters deserve leadership that listens , shows up , and fights for the people who keep this state moving every single day.
Over the coming months, I’ll be working hard — knocking on doors, listening to concerns, and earning every vote.
I want to hear directly from the people of this state about what matters most to them and what kind of future they want for their families.
This campaign is about bringing practical solutions, accountability, and a renewed sense of pride back to Vermont.
I’m grateful for the support so far, and I’m ready to keep working hard every day to earn the trust of the voters.
Thank you, and let’s move Vermont forward together.

title.after: Triumphs in Advocacy

added: top of page Menu Close Home News & Events Get Involved Donate All Posts Triumphs in Advocacy nicholasdilorenzo8 May 6 2 min read To whom it may concern, I am writing this letter of recommendation for Nicholas Dilorenzo.
Nick is a very special man who worked at my mother's assisted living community.
He was always looking out for her best interest, always communicating with me about her health, if she was having a bad day, he would always let me know.
He would even take the time to have conversations and learn about her life.
My mom truly loved Nick, she would always tell me, “Nick is the best!
He never rushes me and listens to me, other people could learn a lot from him”.
She was right we were so lucky to have him in our lives.
He was someone I could go to with anything, and he would help if he could or direct me where to go.
His day didn’t always end at the end of his shift.
I know for me he was always there for our family when we needed him.
He would recommend things to me that would make my mom's life/ days easier.
He even came to the hospital when my mom was passing.
He gave me a big hug and then he went to my mom to make sure she was comfortable (he knew how she liked to be when resting) also brought her favorite stuffed animal friends.
I also want to add my son came to the assisted living center to move my mom's stuff out as she was passing.
Nick was the only one that offered to help him, get him something for lunch and say he was sorry for what he was going through.
He’s there for everyone that needs him in any circumstance.
So, I believe Nicholas Dilorenzo would be the best pick for Vermont state Representative.
Nick is all about being there for people and helping where he can.
Respectfully, Menta Peavey Recent Posts See All Endorsed by Rep.
