title.after: Rebecca Bennett, Congresswoman Gabby Giffords Host Gun Safety Roundtable with Local Law Enforcement and Advocates - Rebecca Bennett for Congress

added: Skip to content Rebecca Bennett for Congress Meet Rebecca News Priorities Endorsements Events Store Volunteer Vote Meet Rebecca News Priorities Endorsements Events Store Volunteer Vote Meet Rebecca News Priorities Endorsements Events Store Volunteer Vote Meet Rebecca News Priorities Endorsements Events Store Volunteer Vote Facebook X-twitter Threads Instagram Youtube Home Meet Rebecca Priorities Endorsements News Store Upcoming Events Volunteer Donate – ActBlue Donate – Numero Home Meet Rebecca Priorities Endorsements News Store Upcoming Events Volunteer Donate – ActBlue Donate – Numero Donate with ActBlue Donate with Numero Rebecca Bennett, Congresswoman Gabby Giffords Host Gun Safety Roundtable with Local Law Enforcement and Advocates SOMERVILLE, NJ — Today, Congresswoman Gabby Giffords and Rebecca Bennett hosted a roundtable with advocate Kim Banks, Assemblyman Vinnie Kearney, Union County Sheriff Peter Corvelli, and Commissioner Palmieri-Mouded about the need for gun violence prevention and leadership in Washington willing to stand up to the powerful gun lobby.

“I am grateful to Congresswoman Giffords, Kim, Assemblyman Kearney, Sheriff Corvelli, and Commissioner Palmieri-Mouded for coming today to share their stories and ideas of how we can end gun violence in this country.
In Congress, I am committed to fighting to pass commonsense legislation to keep our kids safe and get weapons of war off of our streets,” said Rebecca Bennett .
“As a US Navy helicopter pilot, Air National Guard officer and healthcare leader, Rebecca Bennett has dedicated her career to keeping our country and communities safe, and solving tough problems.

As your next Congresswoman, Rebecca will always put public safety over politics and remain focused on advancing solutions to reduce gun violence and making communities safer,” said former Congresswoman Gabby Giffords.
Kean has shown he won’t show up for New Jersey families, but will side with the gun lobby and take orders from President Trump.

The stakes of this race couldn’t be higher and Rebecca Bennett is the champion the Garden State needs in Washington to build a safer future.” “I lost my middle son, Samaad, to gun violence on December 31, 2019, in Somerset, New Jersey.
To honor him and continue his legacy, I started a nonprofit, One Family One Fight, to be a support system in my community and give young people opportunities to thrive.
I believe we need elected leaders who will help us accomplish this mission.

I’m proud to support Rebecca Bennett because as a mom, I know she’s committed to protecting all of our kids from senseless gun violence,” said Kim Banks, Advocate and Founder of One Family One Fight, Inc .
Navy and understands how to use weapons of war — and as a mom, she understands the impact that gun violence is having on all of our kids.
She’s the type of leader that law enforcement and state legislators are going to be able to rely on to do the right thing in Washington.
Her leadership will help us protect first responders in the line of duty while making sure that our kids can grow up without living in fear,” said Assemblyman Vinnie Kearney .
“I have been serving for 35 years, and know that gun violence prevention is a community effort.
As the Union County Sheriff, I have seen firsthand how when we work together on the local, county, state, and federal level, we can keep our communities safe.
I am supporting Rebecca because she will work with law enforcement and community leaders to make sure that we have the tools to keep our communities safe,” said Union County Sheriff Peter Corvelli .
“Here in Union County, we see firsthand that public safety is about more than responding after violence occurs.
It is also about prevention, mental-health resources, strong partnerships with law enforcement, and making sure communities have the tools to intervene before a crisis becomes a tragedy.
As federal support for these efforts is reduced, the need does not go away.

We need leaders in Washington who understand the impact those decisions have at the local level and who will work with counties and communities to keep illegal guns off our streets and strengthen the resources that help prevent gun violence in the first place.
I was glad to join Rebecca today to have this important conversation about how we can continue working toward safer communities for New Jersey families,” said Commissioner Kimberly Palmieri-Mouded .

The path to flipping the House runs right through NJ-07 and every grassroots dollar raised will help us leave no stone unturned and fire Tom Kean Jr. in November, ” said Rebecca Bennett .
Bennett’s campaign is powered by over 44,000 individual donors , with more than #% of all donations $# or less .

All Posts Press Releases Community Updates Grants & Other Resources Achievements Newsletters Events Wellness Wednesday Search MALDEN DELEGATION SUPPORTS HOUSE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT BILL TO DRIVE GROWTH ACROSS THE COMMONWEALTH Steven Ultrino Jul 14 3 min read BOSTON – Tuesday, July 14, 2026 – Last Wednesday, State Representatives Paul Donato, Kate Lipper-Garabedian, and Steven Ultrino joined their colleagues in the Massachusetts House of Representatives in passing H.5562 , An Act relative to economic development in the Commonwealth, a $561 million economic development bond bill that creates strategic investments to strengthen the state's economy, support innovation, expand housing opportunities, and help communities and businesses thrive.

The legislation includes hundreds of thousands of dollars for local economic development projects in Malden, subject to future bond authorization, while making targeted updates to key economic development programs, promoting job creation, reducing barriers to growth, and positioning Massachusetts to remain competitive in the industries of the future.
"I want to thank Speaker Mariano, House leadership, and my colleagues for their work in advancing this important legislation,” said State Representative Steven Ultrino (D-Malden) .

“This bill reflects a shared commitment to strengthening our economy and supporting communities across the Commonwealth, and I look forward to continuing to work with the Malden delegation to secure key investments for local priorities and programs that will help our community grow." “This comprehensive economic development bill makes critical investments in key sectors of the Commonwealth’s economy, while supporting small businesses, encouraging housing production and strengthening fair housing protections, and investing in our cities and towns through efforts like downtown revitalization,” said State Representative Kate Lipper-Garabedian (D-Melrose) .

“As Co-Chair of the Emerging Technology Caucus, I am glad to see investments in robotics, AI, and cybersecurity that position the Commonwealth as a leader on innovation, while balancing responsible use of these advancements.

Thank you to Speaker Mariano, Chair Michlewitz, Chair Fiola, and Chair Finn for prioritizing this legislation.” “I am very proud of the hard work of the Malden Delegation, as well as House Leadership, to pass this critical bill for the Massachusetts economy,” said State Representative Paul Donato (D-Medford) .

“This will without a doubt catapult much needed changes in Malden and communities across the entire Commonwealth.” Among its most significant provisions, the legislation: Expands housing opportunities by creating new tools for municipalities to encourage housing production and the adaptive reuse of underutilized commercial properties.

The bill streamlines local approvals for commercial-to-residential conversions, establishes a framework for multifamily housing on qualifying religious properties with affordability requirements, and improves local planning and permitting through standardized site plan review procedures and training for local land use boards.

Strengthens tenant protections and fair housing by authorizing municipalities to adopt a local option tenant right of first refusal for certain multifamily property sales while enhancing oversight of the real estate profession.

Improves the Commonwealth's fiscal resilience by creating new resources to respond to federal funding uncertainty, support hospitals and community health centers, invest in critical infrastructure, and provide bridge funding for colleges and universities facing disruptions to federal research funding.

Supports entrepreneurs and small businesses by reducing the filing fee to establish a new limited liability company (LLC) from $500 to $100, making it easier and more affordable to start a business in Massachusetts.

Establishes Massachusetts' first comprehensive micromobility framework by creating statewide safety standards and operational guidelines for electric bicycles and other powered personal transportation devices.
Strengthens the innovation economy by expanding incentives for the film industry and creating a new tax credit to support digital game development in Massachusetts.

The bill includes $561 million in capital authorizations, such as: $100 million for the SHIELD Initiative to strengthen Massachusetts' leadership in defense innovation and national security technologies. $75 million to support artificial intelligence infrastructure, emerging technologies, and innovation. $50 million to help municipalities convert underutilized commercial properties into housing. $50 million for remediation of former state-owned properties. $25 million to expand business development programs supporting commercial, industrial, and manufacturing projects. $25 million to advance robotics research and commercialization through MassTech. $25 million for downtown revitalization projects that strengthen local business districts and public spaces. $25 million to support arts, culture, and creative economy investments. $20 million to attract international businesses and investment to Massachusetts. $20 million for veterans supportive housing initiatives. $10 million to strengthen food science, sustainable agriculture, and agricultural technology.
Having passed the House of Representatives 148-2, the bill now goes to the Senate for consideration.

Most business interactions and transactions happen online and VPN INSIDE TEXAS POLITICS (2/25/18) Posted by: WFAA | Jason Whitely NEWSMAKER The race for an open seat in the Texas House of Representatives is where Inside Texas Politics began today.
Cindy Burkett walked away from her seat in District 113 to run for state Senate.
The 113th is a sliver of eastern Dallas County including some of Rowlett, Garland, Mesquite, Sunnyvale, Balch Springs, part of Dallas, and Seagoville.
Republicans have owned this seat for eight years but Democrats see opportunity.
Two candidates are running for the nomination; Rhetta Andrews Bowers, a part-time educator and Billy Ingram, a 34-year veteran of Dallas Fire-Rescue.
They staked out positions on guns, tolling part of I-635 on the eastern side of Dallas, and overcoming double-digit Republican wins of this seat in the past.
About Rhetta Representative Bowers was elected to serve House District 113 in the Texas House of Representatives on November 8, 2018.
She made history elected as the first African American to represent this district.
House District 113 includes all or parts of Rowlett, Garland, Mesquite, Sunnyvale, Seagoville, Combine, Balch Springs, and Dallas.

added: DONATE COMPARE CANDIDATES MEET NAOMI IN THE NEWS EVENTS ENDORSEMENTS VOLUNTEER CONTACT MEDIA KIT THE RECORD Know the votes.
Campaign ads can show anything, even a cape.
Here are 10 that shape what it costs to work, live and get care in Southwest Colorado.
See the votes Meet Naomi A note from Naomi Southwest Colorado is a place people choose.
We pick up extra shifts, start businesses, raise families, care for aging parents and plan to retire near these mountains.
Most of us aren't asking the state to shield us from every risk.
We're asking it not to make the climb steeper.
A legislator's votes show whether they see it that way.
Below are 10 votes Katie Stewart cast in 2025 and 2026, in plain language and linked to the official record.
Next to each is how I'd approach it.
My opponent and I see the role of state government differently, and you deserve to see that difference clearly.
Read the record, check the sources and decide for yourself.
Naomi Riess The votes Work should pay, and you should keep the money you have earned.
Extra hours, a second job, a growing business: that's how families here get ahead.

Your extra hours, still taxed HB25-1296 · 2025 Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = Higher Taxes Starting with 2026 taxes, Colorado adds qualifying overtime back into state taxable income, even though it is now deductible on federal returns.
Colorado passed this before the federal deduction became law.
Naomi's approach When people work extra hours, they should keep more of that paycheck.
Qualifying overtime should be deductible on state taxes too.
Source: HB25-1296 The tools of work cost more, resulting in more taken from your paychecks HB26-1223 · 2026 Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = Higher Taxes From Jan.
1, 2027, Colorado charges state sales tax on most software: downloads, apps and cloud subscriptions.
Naomi's approach Small businesses, remote workers and students all run on software.
Keep it out of the sales tax and lower costs for everyone.

Source: HB26-1223 fiscal note Local restaurants pay more SB25-285 · 2025 Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = Higher Taxes Raised annual inspection fees for restaurants and other retail food businesses, making the cost of a meal more and everyday life less affordable..
Naomi's approach People deserve to eat out once in awhile.
Food safety matters, and so do the margins of family-run places on Main Street.
Fund inspections efficiently without new costs on the businesses many local jobs depend on.
Source: SB25-285 Care close to home In a district this size, getting to care often means a long drive.

Medical rides: payment cut by two-thirds HB26-1410 · 2026-27 budget Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = Less Healthcare The 2026-27 state budget's Medicaid rate and service cuts totaled $270 million, according to House Democrats, including a medical-ride pickup payment that fell from $36.40 to $12.15.
At least one Western Slope provider says the cuts are forcing it to scale back.
Naomi's approach A missed ride becomes a missed appointment, and a missed appointment can become an ER visit.
Root out fraud and mismanagement of funds in the program without cutting the rides rural patients rely on.

Sources: House vote $270M figure Provider HB26-1328 Fewer choices for expecting families HB26-1092 · 2026 Katie Voted No Katie's Vote = Less Healthcare Voted no in the House Health & Human Services Committee.
It would have barred public hospitals from denying full staff privileges to certified nurse-midwives and certified midwives based on their license alone.
Naomi's approach Families should be able to choose a qualified midwife and still deliver at their local hospital.
Hospitals' concerns deserve a hearing; so do expecting families with few nearby options.

Source: HB26-1092 Higher Insurance Premiums SB26-178 · 2026 Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = Less Affordability Lowered the state reinsurance program's average premium-reduction target from 20% to 18% for people who buy their own coverage.
Naomi's approach Self-employed workers, ranchers and early retirees buy their own insurance.
Every point of relief counts for them.

Source: SB26-178 One more way to see a doctor HB26-1096 · 2026 Katie Voted No Katie's Vote = Fewer Patient Choices Voted no twice on letting Medicaid patients pay a direct primary care practice and keep their Medicaid coverage.
Naomi's approach Patients on Medicaid should be able to choose the primary care that works for them, especially where clinics are few and far between.
Source: HB26-1096 Local communities know best Each town in this district knows its own needs best.

Less local say on housing HB26-1001 · 2026 Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = More Expensive Housing Requires covered communities to approve qualifying housing from certain public and nonprofit owners through an administrative process.
Naomi's approach Southwest Colorado needs more attainably priced housing and a diversity of housing types, built the way each community chooses.
Local officials answer to local voters.

Source: HB26-1001 State restrictions on local zoning HB25-1093 · 2025 Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = More Expensive Housing Limits certain local decisions that make housing more affordable and accessible.
Naomi's approach Growth decisions belong with the people who live with the results.
Regulations cause unintended consequences and impact on adjacent owners.
Source: HB25-1093 Even the governor said no Two of these votes went further than Colorado's Democratic governor would go.

A worker vote, removed HB26-1005 · 2026 Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = More Union Power Would have removed the second election workers hold before a union can negotiate a contract requiring every employee to pay fees.
Polis vetoed it, as he vetoed the same policy in 2025.
Naomi's approach Workers deserve a direct say before fees come out of every paycheck.
Any change should come from a real agreement between workers and employers.
Source: Veto coverage A new fee on game purchases HB26-1418 · 2026 Katie Voted Yes Katie's Vote = Higher Taxes Would have added a 5% fee on qualifying in-game purchases to fund youth services.
Polis vetoed it, so the fee never took effect.
Naomi's approach Fund youth services through the budget, not a new fee on what families buy.
Source: HB26-1418 Where the money comes from Campaign money is public record.
Every contribution to both campaigns is on file with the Colorado Secretary of State's TRACER system, searchable by anyone.
Katie Stewart's campaign ≈#% Denver area Solid majority of my opponent's dollars raised this cycle came from the Denver area, much of it from political committees and lobbyists.
Naomi Riess's campaign ≈#% SW Colorado The vast majority of funds raised for my campaign came from individual donors in Southwest Colorado ... the people I'm asking to represent.
The opponent says she looks out for Southwest Colorado.
Does she really look out for us, or does she follow the money?
Where Naomi stands Five priorities for HD59 Strong Rural Economy & Local Control Local voices, local businesses, and local solutions are the foundation of Southwest Colorado's future.
Sensible Affordability & Opportunity Lower costs and more opportunities help families stay, work, and build a future here.
Safe Communities & Public Accountability Public safety starts with accountability, responsibility, and respect for our communities.
Secure Energy, Water & Resources Reliable energy, protected water, and responsible stewardship keep Southwest Colorado strong.
Strong Families & Healthy Communities When families succeed, our communities succeed.
Care and jobs should be close to home.
Communities should make their own choices.
That's the difference on your ballot.
Ballots go out by mail in mid-October.
Return yours by 7 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov.
Meet Naomi Volunteer Donate About this page These are selected votes from the 2025 and 2026 legislative sessions, not a complete record.
Each summary comes from official bill text, fiscal notes and roll calls at leg.colorado.gov, linked on every card.
Where a vote has another side, we've said so.
Contact the campaign and we'll correct it.

DONATE Feature Event : Trivia Night Fundraiser 2nd Lieutenant Robertson Tribute to a Hero: WWII Veteran Philip H.
Robertson A Tribute from a Son to a Father, Veteran and Hero.
By: David Robertson My dad, Philip Hermann Robertson, was born in Aberdeen, South Dakota on November 29th, 1924.
He had just turned 17 when Pearl Harbor was bombed.
My Dad volunteered for the U.S.
Army Air Corp, hoping to become a pilot or navigator.
He went through basic training in Texas, and then navigational school at Jefferson Barracks in St.
My Dad was 49 when I was born – most people my age would have grandfathers who served in World War II, while I had a father who did.
My Dad was assigned as a navigator for a B-24 Liberator bomber.
Twice he saved the lives of his crew: once by employing a rarely-used navigational technique to locate the Azores Islands on their flight from St.

John’s, Newfoundland, and a second time when he located a dry river bed in Northern Italy where the B-24 could crash land after one of the plane’s engines had been disabled by German flak on a bombing run over Munich.
My Dad was based in Foggia, Italy.
He was told during his training to look to the left and the right – the statistics were that one of you will not make it through the tour of bombing missions.
After my Dad’s B-24 crash landed, the crew was taken prisoner by the Germans.
My Dad was sent to Stalag Luft Eins, a German prison camp for Allied air prisoners of war on the Baltic Coast of Germany.
My Dad spent eight months in that camp and almost starved to death (he normally weighed 200 lbs but was 120 pounds as the end of the war).
One day in the winter of 1945 the German guards were gone, and two weeks later the Russian Red Army liberated the camp.
My Dad was a World War II veteran and hero who risked his life to fight for liberty, not only for the citizens of the United States, but for all mankind.
My Dad went on to attend Michigan Law School and became a well-respected trial attorney.
I am honored to have him as my father.

added: Skip to main Become a Sustaining Donor Donate now Volunteer Donate Return to all news Rob Sand Makes Winning Case for a New Direction for Iowa in Second Gubernatorial Debate For Immediate Release Contact: press@robsand.com Rob Sand for Iowa 10/14/2026 SIOUX CITY, IA – Tonight, State Auditor and nominee for governor Rob Sand once again showed Iowans why he is the right choice to serve as Iowa’s next governor.
While Zach Lahn dodged questions about his running mate’s criminal charges, Rob stayed laser-focused on the issues that matter to Iowans.
He laid out his plans to lower costs for hardworking families, strengthen public education, balance our budget, and restore accountability to state government.
Deputy Campaign Manager Emma O’Brien released the following statement: “Tonight on the debate stage, Rob Sand showed Iowans that he’s ready to be our next governor on day one.
Rob laid out a clear vision to lower costs, strengthen public education, and make Iowa’s state government accountable to the people it serves.
Iowans deserve better than a paid political operative who treats Iowa like a flyover state as their next governor with a scandal-ridden running mate.

With less than three weeks until Election Day, the contrast couldn’t be clearer: Rob is ready to move Iowa forward, while Lahn offers more excuses than answers for Iowans.” Iowans know and trust Rob Sand after his seven years as Iowa’s Chief Public Corruption prosecutor and two terms as State Auditor.
They also know him because he shows up in their communities every year.
Rob just wrapped up his 2026 100 Town Hall Tour and has held 900 public town halls in all 99 Iowa counties throughout his career.
Rob Sand has spent years listening directly to Iowans in their communities and understanding the challenges they face.
He has turned those conversations into seven comprehensive policy plans that lay out a clear vision to move Iowa forward and demonstrate that he is ready to lead on day one.
Rob Sand is a public servant, not a politician, and after years of showing up, listening, and delivering for Iowans, they know exactly who he is and what he stands for.

title.after: Rob Sand Meets With Iowans Across the State on “Iowa for All” Tour

added: Skip to main Become a Sustaining Donor Donate now Volunteer Donate Return to all news Rob Sand Meets With Iowans Across the State on “Iowa for All” Tour For Immediate Release Contact: press@robsand.com Rob Sand for Iowa 10/14/2026 DES MOINES, IA – Nominee for governor Rob Sand continued his “Iowa for All” tour across the state the past several days, crisscrossing eastern and central Iowa to meet voters where they are and make the case for a new direction for Iowa.
On Friday, Rob started in Marshalltown with a tour of the JBS Plant, then met with small business owners and local government leaders for a roundtable discussion.
He then stopped by the Iowa Veterans Home to meet with residents and answer their questions, and ended the day in Waukee for a rally with supporters.
Rob spent Saturday meeting with voters in Newton and St.
Ansgar to hear firsthand about the issues that matter most to their communities before joining Iowans at Mason City’s Oktoberfest.
On Sunday, he spent time with festivalgoers and walked in the Madison County Covered Bridges Festival in Winterset.

Rob kept his foot on the gas Monday, starting with a roundtable with small business owners and community leaders in Dubuque before visiting local businesses in Waterloo, and sitting down with college students at the University of Northern Iowa and Coe College to hear about their hopes for Iowa’s future.

He closed out the day with a rally in Cedar Rapids, continuing to make the case for bringing people together, putting Iowans ahead of politics, and making our state not redder or bluer, but better and truer.

See more about Rob’s “Iowa for All” tour below: On Friday, October 9, Rob toured the JBS Plant in Marshalltown to learn more about the jobs they provide and share how his “Opportunities for All” plan will help rebuild Iowa’s struggling economy and bring down costs.
Rob stopped at the Iowa Veterans Home in Marshalltown to host a town hall for residents.
During the town hall, Rob discussed his “Accountability for All” plan, which will restore the power of the State Auditor’s office and bring accountability back to state government.
On Saturday, October 10, Rob hosted a meet-and-greet with voters in St.
Angsar to share his plans to end the two-choice political system and get back to public service, not politics.
Later on Saturday, Rob walked around Mason City’s annual Oktoberfest and spoke with voters.
On Sunday, October 11th, Rob walked in the Madison County Covered Bridges Parade, handing out candy alongside Pow.
On Monday, October 12, Rob toured small businesses in Waterloo, including Spellers True Value Hardware.
During the tour, Rob shared how his “Opportunities for All” will support small businesses, cut red tape, and ensure they have the tools they need to thrive.

Later on Monday, October 12, Rob spoke with students at the University of Northern Iowa and Coe College about the importance of voting in this year’s election and his plan to end the two-choice political system that pits friends and neighbors against each other.

WATCH: KGAN: Rob Sand makes campaign stops in Cedar Falls, Cedar Rapids Democratic candidate for governor Rob Sand made stops in Cedar Falls and Cedar Rapids on Monday as Iowa’s open gubernatorial race enters its final weeks.
Sand met with people at the University of Northern Iowa in Cedar Falls before holding an evening rally in Cedar Rapids.

READ: The Gazette: Rob Sand: We must convince Iowans political balance is good Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for Iowa governor, told a campaign rally crowd Friday that he is aware of the hurdles the party’s statewide candidates have faced in the state for better than a decade.

“We know that the state still hasn’t elected anyone but a Republican being governor in 20 years, so we’re going to have to do some work to make sure that people feel comfortable and know that we can have balance in the state of Iowa again,” Sand said.

“That we remind them of our history as a state that hasn’t been about being focused on being Democrats or Republicans, but one that’s focused on the Iowans.” That message has resonated with many disaffected Republicans across the state.
Among them: Doug Mindrup, of Waukee, who attended Friday’s campaign event.
“I believe in the ideals of the Republican Party (like) less government.
I’ve always been supportive of that,” Doug Mindrup said after Friday’s event.
“But my choice has to be based upon character, and it has to believe in the man or woman doing the job, and I just can’t do that right now with the Republican Party that I’m supporting.
“So my choice is to find somebody with integrity, somebody I can trust, and Rob seems to be that person.” “The Republicans in Iowa have abandoned their constituents,” Mindrup said.

“Rob feels like he’s not there to back a party or an agenda, but to take care of Iowans, which I believe is a good thing.” Dubuque Telegraph-Herald: Sand talks economic policy with Dubuque small-business owners Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand on Monday morning made an appearance in Dubuque, speaking with about 15 small-business owners and other community leaders on economic policy and downtown revitalization.
“From my first year to my second, we had about a 170% growth in sales,” said Noah Riley, owner of the live music venue The Goose, which is located on upper Main Street.
“But even through that, I’m seeing my property tax go up 38%.

I’m up all this money, but I’m still eating every dollar.” Sand said that what Main Street businesses are seeing mimics a similar theme to what’s going on throughout the state of Iowa: a decreasing population resulting in decreasing investment in small businesses.
“What I see in Rob is somebody who is there to begin to heal the divisions that we have,” [Mayor] Cavanagh said.

“This partisanship that we have at the state level and the federal level, we have got to draw that back … (to) where the pendulum doesn’t just keep swinging like a wrecking ball over and over again, every political cycle.” Times-Republican: Gather ‘round the table Slightly more than 10 small business owners and Marshalltown city officials met with Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand on Friday to talk about what was on their minds, and wages and healthcare were big topics.
“We haven’t had a minimum wage increase in 20 years,” he said.
“You don’t just flip the switch and say now it’s $12.

You have to take a few years to put it in there, because it takes time for people to adapt to that.” “Mental health practitioners around the state are closing their shops, because they can’t make money … because of privatized for-profit companies for Medicaid,” he said.
“They just want to keep all the money and find reasons, excuses to deny claims… .
They’re literally looking for reasons to say ‘no’ to paying so they can keep more money and keep it for longer.

It’s scandalous.” Mason City Globe Gazette: Sand upbeat about his gubernatorial campaign during Mason City stop Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand brought his campaign to the Cerro Gordo County Democratic headquarters in Mason City on Saturday, urging supporters to recognize the importance of the upcoming election and arguing that political conditions have created an opportunity for Democrats to reclaim the governor’s office.
“We’ve got a lot of things that are lining up here,” Sand said, speaking to local Democrats at the event.

“We have an unpopular Republican president, we have an unpopular Republican governor who is retiring, we have a guy who is running on the Republican side who is only a part-time Iowa resident, and we have someone running as the Democratic nominee who has already been elected statewide twice and has the best job approval numbers in the state by 30 points.” “This election, this is the one we are here for right now.
We have three weeks to make sure we can win this thing.

I will say, if Tom Vilsack was here, he would tell you what he’s been saying across the entire state for the last year, which is this is the most important governor’s race in 70 years in Iowa.” “I think it was great to have Rob Sand in Mason City,” Ragan said.
“I see the excitement building for his campaign across both sides of the aisle.
He’s really getting people interested in his message of turning Iowa around.” “I see it when I’m out knocking doors and in his rallies,” Ragan said.
“He’s bringing an approach that speaks to people who want to see Iowa change direction.” ### Become a Sustaining Donor of our campaign We need your help to ensure we have the resources to win.

added: Contribute Home About Roger Issues Newsletter Sign-up DONATE NOW DONATE NOW Roger Hauck Republican for State Senate About Roger State Rep.
Roger Hauck was first elected to the Michigan House in 2016, representing the 99th District which encompasses all of Isabella County and ten townships in Midland County.
As your next state senator he will represent Isabella, Mecosta, Osceola, Clare, Gladwin, and Gratiot counties and portions of Clinton, Saginaw, Midland, Bay and Lake counties.
Hauck serves as chair of the House Regulatory Reform Committee and as a member of Health Policy, Government Operations, and Communications & Technology committees.
At a time when it is imperative that our economy helps our business, and our focus on healthcare must be vigilant, he stands in a position to meet the needs of the 34th district residents.
Roger grew up on a beef and dairy farm and graduated from Beal City High School.
He then attended Central Michigan University before starting a 24 year career at the Delfield Company.
He also co-owns a small building company.
Hauck and his wife, Raschelle, have two adult children.
Hauck enjoys bow hunting and fishing.
He also enjoys riding his Harley Davidson motorcycle.
Prior to serving as state representative, Hauck served as a Union Township trustee.
He is a member of the National Rifle Association, Michigan Farm Bureau, Mt.
Pleasant Sacred Heart, and Eagles Club.

Get Involved Volunteer for the campaign or make a contribution Get Involved Issues Facing Our Great State As State Representative, Roger Hauck has championed common sense reforms affecting the people of the 34th district.
Healthcare Sponsored legislation to prohibit surprise medical billing.
With skyrocketing healthcare costs, patients have a right to know exactly what their healthcare costs will be before they receive treatment.

Infrastructure, Public Safety, and Insurance Reform • Secured $3.1m in funding for the Beal City sewer project. • Secured funding for 9-1-1 services in Isabella County • Supported auto-no-fault-reform to lower Michigan’s highest-in-the-nation auto insurance rates.
As a result, in 2022, families can expect a $400 per vehicle rebate.
Jobs & Economy As a small business owner, Roger knows that small businesses are the backbone of Michigan’s economy.
He also knows that in order for business to thrive, we need less burdensome regulations, a workforce ready for the jobs that are available, and low taxes for both employers and employees.
Taxes & Inflation Inflation is out of control and the cost of living is skyrocketing.
At the grocery store and at the gas station we are feeling it.
That’s why Roger is committed to making sure you keep more of your paycheck.
Government doesn’t know how to spend your money better than you do.
Election Integrity 2020 showed some glaring deficiencies in our elections.

Unsolicited absentee ballot applications, liberal millionaire money fueled into democratic precincts, unclear ballot verification and acceptance processes all deteriorated voters’ faith in our system.
Free and fair elections are the cornerstone of our democracy and every voter deserves to have faith that their ballot counts.
Common sense reforms like requiring photo identification to vote are simple.
Roger will make sure every legitimate vote counts as it should.
Education Kids have gone through the ringer over the last 2 years; in school, out of school, back in school again and so-on.
They have suffered social and emotional set backs and the learning loss has been tragic.
It is imperative that our students are back in the classroom and that they are given the resources they need to get learning back on track.

The New 34th State Senate District The new 34th State Senate district includes all of Osceloa, Clare, Gladwin, Mecosta, Isabella, and Gratiot counties, as well as parts of Lake, Bay, Midland, Saginaw, and Clinton counties.

added: Home Contact Me Donate Meet Jimmy Service over Self Guided by Faith, Family, and Service A Lifetime of Service.
A Steady Hand for Western North Carolina.
Jimmy Rogers has spent his life working, serving, and raising a family right here in Western North Carolina.
A lifelong Haywood County resident, Jimmy believes leadership is not about titles or politics, but about responsibility.

From running a small family business to serving on local boards and more than two decades on the school board, he has learned that good leadership means listening carefully, making thoughtful decisions, and being accountable to the people you serve.
Guided by faith, grounded in family, and deeply connected to his community, Jimmy brings a steady, common-sense approach to public service.
He understands the importance of fiscal responsibility, respect for local institutions, and decisions being made closest to home.
Jimmy is running for the North Carolina House to represent Western North Carolina with integrity, care, and sound judgment — always putting service before self and the needs of the community first.

SENATE Sep 17 Written By Hinson Peed DETROIT, MI – The Detroit Regional Chamber PAC today endorsed Mike Rogers to represent Michigan in the U.S.
Senate.

They cited his plans “to make housing more affordable, grow the economy, and empower employees to create good-paying jobs in Michigan,” calling him “a proven public servant.” They go on to compliment his record of putting “the needs of Michigan and Michiganders above partisan politics and political rhetoric.” “The Detroit Regional Chamber is right: the house is on fire.
And we can’t sit back as it rages on,” said Rogers.
“We need leaders who build our state back, not ones who continue to manage its decline–and I’ll work with anyone to get it done.
We will get kids reading at grade level again.
I have released plans to make housing and healthcare more affordable.
And we’re going to re-attract good-paying jobs in the skilled trades.
I’m grateful for the Detroit Regional Chamber’s support as we fight to Get Michigan Working Again.” Learn more about Mike Rogers and his plan to get to work for Michigan at RogersForSenate.com .

added: 0 Skip to Content MEET MIKE NEWS HOUSING PLAN HEALTHCARE PLAN FAMILY OF SERVICE HOW TO VOTE VOLUNTEER CONTACT MERCH DONATE VIA BITPAY DONATE Open Menu Close Menu MEET MIKE NEWS HOUSING PLAN HEALTHCARE PLAN FAMILY OF SERVICE HOW TO VOTE VOLUNTEER CONTACT MERCH DONATE VIA BITPAY DONATE Open Menu Close Menu MEET MIKE NEWS HOUSING PLAN HEALTHCARE PLAN FAMILY OF SERVICE HOW TO VOTE VOLUNTEER CONTACT MERCH DONATE VIA BITPAY DONATE ROGERS ON FOX: ABDUL EL-SAYED WILL LOOK YOU IN THE EYE AND LIE Oct 14 Written By Hinson Peed DETROIT, MI – Army veteran, former FBI street agent, former House Intelligence Chair, and candidate for U.S.
Senate Mike Rogers today joined Sean Hannity on Fox News’ Hannity to call out Conman Abdul El-Sayed for his repeated lies to Michiganders.
He’ll flip-flop on everything except his support for terrorist organizations.
On Conman Abdul El-Sayed’s Repeated Lies: “This guy is unbelievable.
If [Abdul El-Sayed] has any skill, it’s that he can look you in the eye and lie.
And as a former FBI agent, I can tell you that makes a great conman.
But it doesn't make [him] somebody you ought to trust to have around your family.
He lied about the Muslim Brotherhood, and all of that information is coming out.
He's lied about being a physician.
I mean, the list is going on.
And he lied about his support for law enforcement… Here's the good news: His own words are pretty damning.

He has said, ‘Let's defund the police.’ He said, ‘Let's take guns from police.’ He said, ‘Let's have open borders.’ And by the way, [he said] ‘we owe the world to have open borders and allow illegal immigrants just to flow across and put them on Medicare.’ I mean, these are his own words.
These are not things we're making up and putting on an ad that says this is something that we think he is.

These are his own words.” On Conman Abdul El-Sayed’s Failed Rebranding: “What [Abdul El-Sayed]'s trying to do now is remanufacture who he is in the last 20 days [before the election] to get some votes.
I don't think people are buying it.
I mean, we have coalitions with Jewish Democrats.
We have coalitions with African Americans around the state that should be locked up for Abdul El Sayed.
And if you don't have your base 19 days away from an election, I'm telling you, you're going to have a hard time getting elected.
And that's why you're seeing now he's coming out with: ‘Well, no, really, I'm for law enforcement’ [and] ‘No, really, I'm not for the New Deal.’ Which he lied about; he supports it.

title.after: Artificial Intelligence | Roman Gaskey for State Representative

added: top of page Meet Roman Priorities Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Endorsements Campaign Updates Donate Menu Close Artificial Intelligence We can't fix what we don't measure.
I am a strong proponent of technological innovation, but everything has its limits.
Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing our economy and society.
When a technology is so powerful, unpredictable, and widespread, it is unquestionable that the state has a duty to protect the people.
I have spoken with many state legislators, and I am concerned about their lack of knowledge and initiative on this issue.

When I ask, “What committees are going to regulate AI?” the two most common answers I receive are, “I don’t know,” and, “Maybe Communications and Technology?” For such a transformative technology with serious long-tail risks for our economy, this is completely unacceptable.
Our state can’t mitigate AI’s potential dangers if we’re not monitoring what’s happening and being proactive.
That’s why I propose creating a Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence.
1) Why a Select Committee Which committee in Lansing handles artificial intelligence?
The honest answer: all of them, and none of them.
AI already touches how insurers decide claims, how employers screen applicants, how hospitals schedule care, and how retailers set prices.
Michigan’s committee system divides the world by subject: insurance goes to one committee, labor to another, commerce to a third.

One AI safety bill introduced last session has already moved through three different House committees.¹ The House Communications and Technology Committee handles some AI bills, but its jurisdiction stops where insurance, labor, and commerce begin.
When an issue belongs to every committee, it belongs to none of them.
A select committee solves that problem.
The House creates it for a single purpose, gives it jurisdiction across subject lines, and dissolves it when the work is done.
Michigan has used this tool before, and it works.
In 2019, the House created the Select Committee on Reducing Car Insurance Rates with one job: lower the highest auto insurance premiums in the country.

The Senate’s reform bill went through that committee and became law the same year.² In 2016, a joint select committee of four Republicans and two Democrats took testimony from more than 60 witnesses on the Flint water crisis and produced 36 legislative proposals to prevent another one.³ I propose a bipartisan House Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, with the primary goal of measuring AI’s impact on Michigan.
No committee in Lansing currently has the task of tracking where AI is changing Michigan’s economy, so the select committee would track it on two fronts.
The committee would measure where employers are adopting AI and which jobs it is replacing or reshaping, broken down by industry, region, and age group.
To get reliable numbers, Michigan should require employers that file layoff notices with the state to report whether AI or automation played a role.
The committee would examine how businesses use AI to make decisions about the people they serve: how insurers decide claims, how landlords and lenders screen applicants, and how retailers set prices.

It would draw on the consumer complaints that the Attorney General and the Department of Insurance and Financial Services already receive, and take testimony from businesses, workers, and consumers across the state.
The committee would deliver its findings in a report on AI’s impact on Michigan’s economy by the end of the 2027 session.
If the work remains unfinished, the next Legislature can renew it.
Good policy starts with good information, and right now Lansing is legislating without it.
2) Where the Jobs Go Which Michigan jobs will AI eliminate?
Anyone who claims to know for certain is guessing.
That is why the committee’s first track focuses on workers.
The early national evidence points to white-collar work.
Customer service representatives, bookkeepers, paralegals, translators, and entry-level programmers all perform tasks that AI tools can now complete in seconds.

Researchers at Stanford found that employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations has fallen about 13 percent relative to their less-exposed peers.⁴ The workers losing ground first are the ones just starting their careers.
But national averages don’t tell us where Michigan stands.
Our economy runs on engineering, manufacturing, health care, and professional services in proportions no other state shares.
The committee would find out where the impact actually lands in our state: which industries, which regions, which age groups.
Only then can the Legislature target help where it’s needed instead of spreading it thin based on guesswork.
You cannot retrain a workforce for a disruption you haven’t measured.
AI will reshape Michigan’s economy whether Lansing pays attention or not.
The only question is whether the Legislature sees the change coming or reads about it after the fact.
A select committee gives Michigan the tools to watch, measure, and act before the damage spreads, not after.

title.after: Data Centers | Roman Gaskey for State Representative

added: top of page Meet Roman Priorities Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Endorsements Campaign Updates Donate Menu Close Data Centers A comprehensive plan to protect our energy supply, water, and quality of life, and ensure data centers pay their fair share.
Why are data center developers suddenly knocking on the doors of Michigan townships?
Because a handful of AI companies have promised investors more computing power than anyone has ever built, and they need somewhere to put it.
In November 2025, OpenAI’s chief executive touted roughly $1.4 trillion in infrastructure commitments.
Three months later, the company told investors it now targets about $600 billion in computing spend by 2030, less than half the original figure.
It made $13.1 billion in revenue last year.¹ A company does not cut its plans by more than half when its projections hold up.
Michigan sits downstream of those projections.

OpenAI and Oracle’s planned data center in Saline Township would draw 1.4 gigawatts of power, roughly a quarter of DTE’s current load.² DTE now reports a data center pipeline of more than 8 gigawatts,³ and it has proposed two new natural gas plants costing $6.4 billion.⁴ Recall how utilities earn money: the state guarantees them a return on what they spend.
Every new plant and power line built for a data center grows the base the utility profits from.
DTE has every reason to take the AI industry’s projections at face value.
If those projections fall short, the AI companies will move on.
The power plants, the transmission lines, and the rezoned farmland will stay here.
That is why Michigan needs rules in place before the next contract gets signed, not after.
1) Pay Your Own Way Start with electricity.
A data center that draws as much power as a small city should pay for the power it needs, not hand the bill to everyone else.
Michigan should require every large data center to fund new generation sufficient to cover all of the electricity demand it creates.

Regulators have already shown this can work: the contract they approved this month for Google’s data center in Van Buren Township requires Google to pay for up to 1,600 megawatts of renewable generation and 480 megawatts of battery storage.⁵ What one contract achieved through negotiation, state law should require of all of them.
Then make the utility prove it.
When a data center shuts down early or uses less power than promised, someone has to pay off the plants and power lines built to serve it.
Those are stranded costs, and they land on existing customers unless the contract says otherwise.

In December, regulators approved DTE’s Saline Township contracts on an expedited basis, without the full public review that lets ratepayer advocates test the utility’s claims.⁶ The Attorney General has since appealed, arguing in part that DTE’s own filings admit the deal will raise costs for some customers.⁷ Michigan should end expedited approvals for data center contracts.
Every utility seeking to serve a data center should have to prove, in a full public case, that the agreement protects existing customers from stranded costs.
2) Protect Our Water Data centers generate enormous heat, and many cool their servers by evaporating water.
Michigan’s water belongs to Michiganders, not to the companies that want to boil it off.
The state should prohibit data centers from drawing fresh groundwater or municipal drinking water.
They should use closed-loop cooling systems, which recirculate the same water instead of consuming it, and recycle water wherever possible.
Wastewater should meet strict safeguards before it leaves the site.
And every data center should publicly report how much water it uses, so residents don’t have to take a developer’s word for it.
These requirements should also cover noise.
The low, constant hum of cooling equipment carries for miles in rural areas.
Saline Township secured a 55-decibel limit only by settling a lawsuit.⁸ No community should have to go to court to sleep at night.
Every data center should have to install noise mitigation, and local governments should remain free to set stricter limits.
3) Who Saves Michigan currently exempts large data centers from the state’s 6 percent sales and use tax on construction and equipment purchases, for some projects through 2050 or even 2065.
In exchange, a project needs to invest $250 million and create as few as 30 jobs.⁹ We don’t need to pay companies to come here.
Developers want Michigan for reasons no other state can match: a cool climate that cuts cooling costs, and access to the largest supply of fresh water in the world.
When a company wants something only you can offer, you set the terms.
You don’t pay it to accept them.
You may have seen ads claiming only Sarah Pounds has a plan to protect you from data centers.
The record shows the opposite is true.

Pounds has publicly stated she supports giving data centers tax incentives.¹⁰ In her view, those incentives would come paired with “local” jobs (I don’t know what a non-local job is), labor standards, and water restrictions.
This is a bait and switch: the candidate sold to you as the data center skeptic wants Michigan to pay them to come here.
Michigan jobs, labor standards, and water restrictions should be the bare minimum for any data center that wants to build here, not a bargain we buy with a tax break.
Her approach also gets the logic backwards.
When conditions come attached to an incentive, they bind only the companies that take the incentive.
A developer that skips the tax break skips the standards too.

That is how Michigan’s current exemption already works: its job, wage, and water requirements apply only to projects that claim it.¹¹ Michigan taxpayers shouldn’t hand data centers corporate welfare, and no data center should escape these standards just because it isn’t on the state’s dole.
Write the standards into law for every data center, and repeal the tax breaks.
4) Let Communities Decide As data center fights spread, some will argue the state should take more control of where data centers go.
Local governments exist for a reason.
Michiganders choose their communities because they value their character, whether that means farmland, quiet neighborhoods, or open space.
The people who live with a data center’s traffic, noise, and power lines should decide whether it belongs there.
Developers already push past local decisions.
In September 2025, the Saline Township board voted 4–1 to deny rezoning farmland for the OpenAI and Oracle project.

Two days later, the developer sued the township for “exclusionary zoning.” The township settled within weeks, and the project moved forward.¹² More than 50 Michigan communities have since paused data center approvals so they can write rules before a developer arrives.¹³ Those communities are doing exactly what local government should do.
Lansing’s job is to back them up, not overrule them.

added: top of page Meet Roman Priorities Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Endorsements Campaign Updates Donate Menu Close Energy We need to hold utilities accountable and tie their profits to performance.
If they continue to provide poor service, then they'll have a penalty.
Severe weather is inevitable, and we can all understand occasional outages.
But the sluggish response time to September’s major storm was no anomaly.
In fact, it’s par for the course when it comes to power restoration in Michigan.
Last year, we ranked dead last out of the 50 states and Washington, D.C. in restoration speed.

States with similar climates like Ohio and Indiana resolve their outages in less than half the time we do.¹ When you look at the state of our energy infrastructure, it’s pretty obvious just how far behind we are.
Why do we continue to drape wires through tree canopies on wooden poles, just waiting for the next ice storm?
The excuse that “undergrounding is too expensive” is a result of Michigan-specific policy failures.

Michigan law assesses a utility’s poles, wires, and mains as personal property, taxed by the township where they sit.² When the legislature exempted manufacturers’ equipment from the personal property tax in 2014, it specifically carved out utility property.³ That means every dollar DTE spends burying a line carries a property tax bill on top, and that bill lands on your electric rates.
So, when the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) rejects an undergrounding project as too expensive, the tax is part of why.
We should treat grid hardening the way we already treat new factories.

Extend the manufacturing exemption to new undergrounding and storm-hardened distribution equipment, and reimburse townships for the lost revenue through the same essential-services mechanism the state uses for manufacturers.
Utilities will lose an excuse, and it won’t cost local governments a dime.

2) Hold Them Accountable When discussing the topic of utility companies, I often get asked, “Why don’t we break up the monopolies and let companies compete for distribution?” This is a great question, because this is how other network services like cell service and broadband function.
When it comes to energy, however, scale makes a monopoly model more practical.
Under the current system, there is only one set of the poles, wires, and transformers that physically connect your house to the grid.
"Competition" would mean a second and third set of poles down every street.
This would make any crisis response a nightmare.

When an ice storm knocks out power to 400,000 homes at 2 o’clock in the morning, you want one company with every truck in the state under one dispatcher, not three companies guarding their own trucks and arguing over whose block comes first.
The problem is not the existence of the monopolies themselves—it’s the flawed incentives we’ve set for them.
Michigan’s current model for regulating utility rates is a cost-of-service model.

In this system, the utility spends money on the grid, and the MPSC grants it a fixed return on that spending (i.e., a fixed return on equity).⁴ That means the utility makes the same return regardless of how much time you spend without power.
In a performance-based model, the MPSC sets measurable targets for outcomes such as power restoration times, outages per customer, and cost per customer against peer competitors.
If the utility manages to beat the target, it earns a higher return on equity.
But if it falls short, return on equity is reduced or customers are entitled to refunds.
Michigan took its first step toward this model in 2025, but the MPSC capped the total incentive and penalty at $10 million for 2026.⁵ Against $1.4 billion in profits, that is barely a rounding error.
I propose significantly increasing this cap.
Micromanagement is what we do now: the MPSC spends a rate case litigating whether DTE’s tree-trimming budget is prudent, line by line, for months.
A performance-based approach stops telling DTE how to do its homework and starts grading its test results.
3) Cut Building Costs Changing our regulatory incentives is just one of many tools available to make energy more affordable.
If we want to bring down costs in the long run, the mix of energy sources we decide to use must predominantly be determined by cost and reliability.
Any mandate that portions of the energy supply must come from certain sources prevents utilities from optimizing for cost, forcing them to pass the bill onto ratepayers.
Democrats in Lansing passed one of these mandates in 2023.

Public Act 235 requires 50 percent renewable electricity by 2030, up from about 12 percent when the bill passed, then 60 percent by 2035 and 100 percent “clean” by 2040.⁶ The commission’s own chairman told lawmakers the 60 percent target alone requires roughly 209,000 additional acres of wind and solar.
To find that land, the legislature gave the commission authority to override local zoning.⁷ Washington enacted a mandate of its own last year.
In May 2025, the Department of Energy ordered Consumers Energy to keep the J.H.
Campbell coal plant running past its scheduled retirement, re-extending the order five more times.

Consumers reported a net cost of $259 million⁸ through June of this year—about $615,000 a day—which it now seeks to recover from customers.⁹ When the state or federal government picks the fuel, the utility stops optimizing for price and reliability and starts optimizing for compliance.
An all-of-the-above approach means the MPSC’s resource planning process weighs all sources on the same two criteria, and the cheapest reliable mix wins.

added: top of page Meet Roman Priorities Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Endorsements Campaign Updates Donate Menu Close Healthcare Michigan has some of the highest healthcare inflation in the country, and consolidation is fueling it.
We must crack down on hospital monopolies.
Of all the things in our country that feel broken right now, I’d argue healthcare is at the top of that list.

Just this year, Michigan’s health insurance premiums have increased an average of 20.2% for individual coverage and 11.1% for small-employer coverage.¹ To put that in context, Metro Detroit’s prices have risen 3.7% over the last 12 months.² Our premiums have risen over five times as fast as inflation!
Many Michiganders are considering dropping health insurance altogether, effectively rolling the dice in the hopes that nothing catastrophic happens.
And federal changes are making it worse on two fronts.

Enhanced marketplace subsidies expired at the end of last year, resulting in Michigan marketplace enrollment already falling by 27 percent.³ Further, the One Big Beautiful Bill will cut an estimated $2.5 billion a year in Medicaid funding to Michigan providers.⁴ So, if the state can’t turn up additional revenue, hundreds of thousands of Michiganders will be at risk of being kicked off of Medicaid.
It is a failure of both government policy and market conditions that healthcare is unaffordable for most Michiganders.
We can’t go on like this.
Clearly, Washington is unable or unwilling to fix the problem.
That’s why we need to step up at the state level to address this crisis.
1) How Consolidation Raises Prices Hospital systems do not merge because bigger hospitals deliver better care.
They merge because bigger systems negotiate better prices for themselves.
Every year, each insurer sits down with each health system in the region and negotiates what the system will charge.
When a region has a dozen independent hospitals, the insurer can walk away from any one of them.
When a region has three systems, walking away from one means telling a third of your customers that their hospital is out of network.
No insurer can sell that plan.
So the system names its price, and the insurer passes it on to employers and families in the form of higher premiums.
Southeast Michigan has spent the past four years running this experiment.
A 2022 merger of Beaumont and Spectrum created Corewell, the largest health system in the state.
Then, a 2024 joint venture folded all eight Ascension hospitals (of which, all are in Metro Detroit) into Henry Ford.

Health-market analyst Allan Baumgarten estimated that the second deal would leave the combined system with 43.8 percent of the Detroit-area hospital market.⁵ University of Michigan health economist Thomas Buchmueller summed up the result: “The big problem, in terms of hospital prices, is the lack of competition.”⁶ Insurers are not pocketing the difference.

Michigan’s largest insurer (i.e., Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan) paid out $1.04 in claims for every dollar of premium it collected in 2024, posting a $1.3 billion loss.⁷ Even the health insurance companies can’t afford healthcare.
The money is going to the providers, and the providers with the most market power collect the most.
2) The Contracts Behind the Prices This type of consolidated market power would push prices up on its own.
They write clauses into their insurer contracts that shut down competition before it starts.
Suppose an independent surgical center down the street performs the same procedure for half the price.
Your insurer would like to reward you for choosing it, with a lower copay or a waived deductible.
An anti-tiering clause works the same way: the insurer cannot place the system’s most expensive hospitals in a higher cost-sharing tier, no matter how much more they charge.
The patient never sees a reason to shop, so the system never faces a reason to compete.
Some contracts keep negotiated prices hidden from the very employers paying the bills, and no one can steer patients toward the cheaper provider without knowing which provider is cheaper.
Congress prohibited gag clauses in 2021, but compliance has been uneven.⁸ The most powerful clause is all-or-nothing.
A dominant system owns the region’s top trauma center and its children’s hospital, facilities no insurer can leave out of a network.

So the system bundles them with everything else it owns—every community hospital, every outpatient clinic, every employed physician—and offers the insurer a choice: take all of it at our price, or take none of it.
No one loses more under this arrangement than the independent doctor.
Nearly six in ten physicians nationwide now work for a hospital system.⁹ The ones who remain independent compete against those systems for the same patients.

When an insurer has to take a system’s entire employed physician group, it has little reason to contract with the independent practice across the street, and little reason to pay it fairly when it does.
Ban all-or-nothing clauses, and insurers can build networks around the doctors who offer the best value.
That gives independent practices a way back in.
Texas shows what happens when a state stops halfway.

In 2023, Texas banned anti-steering and anti-tiering clauses but dropped the all-or-nothing ban under pressure from lobbyists.¹⁰ Two years later, insurers there report that dominant systems still demand all-or-nothing terms, and the law’s supporters are working to close the loophole.¹¹ Michigan should ban all four clauses from the start, write the gag-clause ban into state law so state regulators can enforce it, and void any such clause in a contract signed or renewed after the law takes effect.
3) Who Saves This is all a moot point for your bottom line if lower hospital prices don’t ever reach families, with insurers simply keep the savings.
Luckily, the structure of the market solves this question for us.
Most workers with employer coverage are in self-funded plans, where the employer pays claims directly and the insurer only administers the network.
Every dollar the hospital no longer charges goes straight back to the employer and its workers.

For everyone else, federal law already requires insurers to spend at least 80 percent of premiums on care in the individual and small-group markets, and 85 percent in the large-group market, or rebate the difference to customers.¹² Lower prices have to show up somewhere, and the law makes sure they show up on your side of the ledger.
4) Not a Partisan Idea Few reforms draw support from both Texas and Connecticut.
Texas passed its ban with only one dissenting vote in either chamber.

Connecticut passed a broader ban the same year, covering all-or-nothing clauses as well.¹³ In June, the White House Council of Economic Advisers estimated that banning anti-steering, anti-tiering, and all-or-nothing contracts would cut hospital and physician prices by 18 percent and employer premiums by 6.5 percent in affected markets—roughly $1,755 per family per year. ¹⁴ Ohio’s Attorney General joined the Justice Department this year in suing a 16-hospital system over the same contract terms, and the system settled within four months. ¹⁵ 1 Michigan Department of Insurance and Financial Services, "2026 Michigan Health Insurance Approved Rate Changes," October 28, 2025 (individual market average approved increase of 20.2%; small group 11.1%). https://www.michigan.gov/difs/-/media/Project/Websites/difs/OIRF/EHB/PDFs/2026_Approved_Rate_Changes.pdf 2 U.S.

title.after: Housing | Roman Gaskey for State Representative

added: top of page Meet Roman Priorities Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Housing Energy Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Data Centers Endorsements Campaign Updates Donate Menu Close Housing We can address Michigan's housing crisis without eliminating local control, mandating increased density, or radically altering neighborhood character.
1) Protect (Human) Homebuyers The playbook is simple.
A private equity firm arrives with cash and buys homes by the dozen, sometimes an entire subdivision straight from the builder.
A young couple with a pre-approval letter cannot compete with an all-cash offer that closes in two weeks.
Then the firm converts the houses to rentals, and because it now owns a large share of the neighborhood’s rental stock, it sets the price.
The same couple who couldn’t buy the house now pays whatever the landlord asks to rent one just like it.
This does not happen to neighborhoods in isolation.
Institutional landlords now own roughly 72,000 single-family rental homes in metro Atlanta—about 30 percent of that market and ten times the national share.
In Paulding County, corporations own 78 percent of all single-family rentals.
Three companies alone control almost 20,000 houses across the core metro counties.¹ And predictably, in the zip codes where these firms concentrated, homeownership falls and rents rise.
We should act now to prevent this from happening to Metro Detroit.
Once a firm owns a third of a county’s rental stock, no legislature can unwind it.
The cure costs a generation of homeowners.
2) Build More Starter Homes Why do so few builders put up attainable single-family homes nowadays?
It isn’t a conspiracy if you follow the incentives.
Michigan funds local government through property taxes, and property taxes track assessed value.
Every township, city, and village therefore follows the same logic: put the most valuable house possible on every lot.
A $700,000 home on a half-acre generates more revenue than a $300,000 home on the same half-acre, and it demands roughly the same in roads, water, and police.
Nobody at the planning commission has to say this out loud.
The math says it for them.
The fashionable answer embraced by leftists and big developers is “YIMBYism”—stripping local governments of their zoning authority so that developers build whatever the market will bear.
I oppose this policy, and I want to be precise about why.
“Yes in my backyard” policies achieve affordability through density.
They deliver cheaper units by stacking more of them on each parcel: fourplexes on single-family lots, apartment blocks where subdivisions stood.
These types of developments are not what my constituents mean when they can’t afford a house.
Worse, YIMBYism leaves the underlying incentive untouched.
The municipality still wants maximum revenue per parcel; it simply loses the tools to shape what developers build.
Developers gain a free hand to remake community character, and residents who spent decades investing in their neighborhood hear that they should take it up with Lansing.
My approach is different, and to my knowledge no one in Lansing has proposed it.
Instead of overriding local decisions, change the payoff.
Michigan already returns a share of state revenue to municipalities through revenue sharing.
Tie an increased share to attainable housing: when a community approves starter homes, the state makes up the property-tax revenue that community forgoes.
The only thing that changes is that doing the right thing stops costing our communities money.
3) Cut Building Costs Every conversation about housing eventually arrives at the same number.

The Home Builders Association of Michigan estimates that regulation adds roughly $94,000 to the price of a new home in this state.² When John Bitely, a West Michigan builder, first heard that figure, he didn’t believe it.
He told the association the number looked inflated, then spent three days going through his own project costs to prove it wrong.

He came within 1 percent.³ ​ The National Association of Home Builders’ 2026 updated estimate puts the national figure at roughly $132,000, and building code changes over the past decade alone account for about $24,000 of it.⁴ Michigan builds fewer homes as a share of its housing stock than every Great Lakes state except Illinois.⁵ Something stands in the way, and it is not a shortage of dirt. ​ The fix begins with the code.
Not every regulation is red tape.
Fire codes save lives, and nobody proposes to touch them.
But Michigan has layered on requirements over the past decade whose gains in safety and efficiency never matched their cost.

The 2021 energy code, which the state adopted over builders’ objections, adds an estimated $15,000 per home—in exchange for savings so modest that the homebuilders association argues the code violates Michigan’s own seven-year payback law.⁶ We should review the most recently adopted regulations first, with a simple test: did this rule deliver real gains in safety or efficiency, or did it deliver only cost?
Rules that fail the test go. ​ Permitting is the other half.
Permitting decisions belong with local governments, but local control cannot mean unlimited delay.
Today a municipality can require a traffic study, then a wetland study, then a revised traffic study, then a new site plan, with no deadline and no end.
Builders don’t fight this; they leave.
The state’s homebuilders association points to one recent Michigan project that took four years because of the back-and-forth with local government.⁷ ​ The reform is straightforward.
Local governments keep the decision, but they must make it within a required timeline.
They can approve, deny, or request specific, enumerated changes.
They cannot request studies indefinitely until the developer throws up his hands and walks away.

added: Education Property taxes are disastrously up 50% across the state over the last six years.
I support $134 Million in immediate residential homestead property tax relief .

The proposal would move the Education Property Tax Credit to the General Fund, reducing homestead property taxes by up to 20% while continuing to protect Vermonters who qualify for income-based property-tax Vermont now has the highest healthcare costs and healthcare insurance premiums in the nation.
I support more competition in our healthcare system.
Vermont needs more choices when it comes to healthcare coverage.
I support increasing the number of health insurers in Vermont and giving insurers greater flexibility to offer coverage options that meet the needs of individuals, families and employers.
Vermonters' Tax Burden is the 3rd highest in the USA, only behind New York and Hawaii.
I support $250 million in income-tax relief in 2027, with relief targeted toward low- and middle-income Vermonters, Social Security recipients and retired military recipients.

Vermonters must be able to keep more of what they earn Vermont’s Economic Outlook rating is 49 lowest of all states The Vermont State Budget is now $9.4B ($1B more than NH which has twice the population of VT).

Senate to make life more affordable for North Carolina families.

“I have a plan to make stuff cost less, I’m running to put the middle class back within reach for hardworking North Carolinians and I’ll work with anyone I can in the Senate to get it done,” said Roy Cooper .
“Washington DC insider and Big Oil and utility company lobbyist Michael Whatley spent his career enriching himself while working families in Greensboro and around the state paid more.

He’s cheered on policies that have driven up prices and helped double people’s health care premiums – North Carolina can’t afford any more of that.” “Right now, just covering everyday needs can be a struggle,” said Gibsonville native and NC A&T University Senior Breyonne Harper .
“It just shouldn’t be this hard to afford what I need to get by.

While other candidates keep claiming that prices aren’t as high as they actually are, Roy Cooper knows that stuff just costs too much right now and has a track record of delivering results and lowering costs for hardworking people.
Roy truly embodies what it means to be a North Carolinian and he is the leader we need fighting for us in Washington DC.” “My congregation is hurting from rising prices,” said U.S.
Army veteran and Senior Pastor of Mt.
Zion Baptist Church in High Point, Reverend Frank Thomas .
“Pick almost any item these days – it costs more.
Roy Cooper has a plan to make stuff cost less.
Roy is a man of faith who will work with anyone to get stuff done – and he is exactly who we need in the U.S.
Senate.” On the Make Stuff Cost Less tour, Roy released his plans to lower the cost of food and groceries , health care , utilities , child care and housing .
