24 Jul Friday, 3:33 PM · 2026 Brad attends Rochester's 2026 Disability Summit July 24th Today, I had the opportunity to attend Rochester's 2026 Disability Summit at the Heintz Center.
I attended as a parent, caregiver, employment specialist, advocate, and political candidate.
While tremendous progress has been made to support individuals with disabilities and our aging community, there is still much more work to do.

No matter what role I serve in; parent, caregiver, employment specialist, advocate, or State Representative, you can count on me to work tirelessly for individuals with disabilities, our aging community, and their families.
One of the most important lessons I've learned over the past 24 years, since our son Reece was diagnosed with severe autism, is that disability can touch any family at any time.
We are all just one unexpected moment away from needing the same supports and services that so many rely on today.
Until disability affects you or someone you love, it's often difficult to fully understand how complex, challenging, and overwhelming navigating these systems can be.
That's why it's so important that we continue to listen, learn, and advocate for policies and services that help every member of our community live with dignity, opportunity, and support.
21 Jul Tuesday, 12:01 PM · 2026 Brad attends Rochester Area Chamber of Commerce's Linking Leaders & Industry event at Chick-fil-A Miracle Mile.
It was an honor and a privilege, as a candidate for Minnesota House District 25A, to attend the Rochester Area Chamber of Commerce's Linking Leaders & Industry event at Chick-fil-A Miracle Mile.

I want to extend my sincere thanks to Matt and Crystal Stockdale, Owner/Operating Partners, for sharing both their personal journey to becoming Chick-fil-A franchisees and the inspiring story behind the Chick-fil-A brand.
Their presentation highlighted the company's strong values, commitment to servant leadership, and dedication to making a positive impact in our community.
Chick-fil-A employs more than 200 team members across its two Rochester locations, with an annual payroll of approximately $3 million.

Beyond serving great food, they are deeply invested in our community through partnerships with Community Food Response, Channel One Regional Food Bank, and by providing more than 200 meals each month to pediatric patients at Mayo Clinic.
Matt and Crystal also shared valuable insights into the economic challenges facing local businesses with candidates seeking local, county, and state offices.
I appreciated the opportunity to hear firsthand how government policies affect employers and the business community.

Among the topics discussed were: • Rochester's EV charger requirement, which requires one EV charging station for every 50 parking spaces, even when demand is limited. • Extending the allowable work hours for 14- and 15-year-olds from 7:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m., which they described as a significant opportunity to better support their workforce. • The financial impact of implementing Minnesota's Paid Family and Medical Leave program. • The need for a more streamlined and accessible pathway to citizenship for individuals who want to live and work in our communities. • Housing affordability and the rising cost of living, which continue to affect employees and employers alike.
These are important conversations that deserve thoughtful discussion at every level of government.
Working together, we can identify practical solutions that help businesses grow, support employees, and strengthen our local economy.
Thank you again to Matt and Crystal, the entire Chick-fil-A team, and everyone who made this event possible.
Your commitment to your employees, your customers, and the Rochester community is truly inspiring.
Thank you for welcoming us into your story, sharing your experiences as franchise owners, and demonstrating what it means to lead with integrity and service.
Thank you, Rochester Area Chamber of Commerce, for creating this opportunity for us candidates.
It was “my pleasure” to learn more about the Chick-fil-A organization and to express my appreciation for everything Chick-fil-A does to make Rochester a stronger and more caring community.

15 Jun Monday, 3:27 PM · 2026 Vehicle Registraton Costs; Wisconsin vs.
Minnesota This is unacceptable for Minnesotans.
The current formula-based system needs to be re-evaluated.
On top of the base registration tax, drivers are also paying a stack of additional costs, including plate fees, filing fees, technology surcharges, and public safety fees.

While funding roads and bridges is essential, and vehicle registration revenue is directed into the Highway User Tax Distribution Fund (HUTDF), the current structure places an uneven burden on Minnesota drivers.
There was some work done on this this year, but it doesn't take effect until January 2027, with some fees reverting back to 2023.
More work needs to be done, however.

If elected to represent MN House District 25A, I will work across the aisle to reform this system and pursue a more reasonable, transparent flat-fee model, similar to what most other states use for vehicle registration.

added: DONATE Press Releases Tricia Nakamatsu Wins Primary Election for Hawaiʻi State Senate District 13 August 8, 2026 Today, Tricia Nakamatsu released the following statement after election results confirmed her victory in the Democratic primary race for Hawaiʻi State Senate District 13: “I am deeply honored and humbled by the trust the people of our district have placed in me.
Mahalo to every voter, volunteer, supporter, and member of our community who believed in this campaign and made tonight possible.
I also want to thank my family for their unwavering love, encouragement, and dedication throughout this campaign.
Your support has meant everything to me.
“This campaign has always been about the people of our communities and the future we want to build together.

As a fourth-generation member of this community, a working mom, a prosecutor, and a public servant for the past 20 years, I understand the challenges our families face—from the rising cost of living to concerns about public safety, housing, and creating opportunities that allow our children to build their futures here in Hawaiʻi.

“My work experience and life experience have reinforced my belief that lasting progress happens when we listen to one another, work collaboratively, and stay focused on practical solutions instead of politics.

I am grateful for the opportunity to move forward as our party's nominee, and I look forward to continuing to earn the trust and support of community members across District 13 as we head toward the general election.
Mahalo!” Senate District 13 encompasses Dowsett Highlands, Pu‘unui, Nu‘uanu, Pacific Heights, Pauoa, Punchbowl, Pālama, Liliha, Iwilei, Chinatown, and Downtown.
The seat was previously held by Karl Rhoads, who decided not to seek reelection.

Tricia Nakamatsu Officially Enters Race for Senate District 13 May 29, 2026 Yesterday, Tricia Nakamatsu officially filed to run for the Hawai‘i State Senate in District 13, launching a campaign rooted in community, public service, and a commitment to local families.
I am running for State Senate because I believe we deserve government systems that actually work for the people, ” said Tricia.

title.before: Ty for Mississippi

added: top of page DONATE VOLUNTEER HOME ABOUT TY ISSUES FULCRUM PRESS RELEASES VOTE TRANSPARENCY ISSUE Jobs & Economy We need an American economy that works for everyone Raised in the Delta.
Rooted in Mississippi I was raised in the Mississippi Delta, where I learned the value of hard work early in life.
My family depended on farming to get by, and like many kids in our community, I spent my teenage years chopping cotton to help my parents make ends meet.

Mississippi is an agricultural state, and I know firsthand that it’s our family farmers who keep this economy going—not the big corporate monopolies that have spent decades buying up land and shipping profits out of state.
The strength of our farming communities has always come from hardworking families who put in the hours, season after season.
Our family farms aren’t looking for handouts—they just want a fair shot.
A fair shot to earn a living, to turn a profit, and to pass something down to their kids and grandkids.
Senator, I’ll make sure that federal farm bills are written with small family farmers in mind.
For far too long, federal policy has favored big corporations with deep pockets and powerful lobbyists.
I’m not a lobbyist—I’m an advocate for Mississippi’s farmers and farm workers.
I’ll make sure our family farms have a voice at the table and the support they deserve.
Mississippi has some of the most fertile soil in the country—we can grow just about anything here.
That’s why I’ll fight to protect our environment, so future generations of Mississippi farmers can continue working this land and feeding our communities.
Our farmers should be rewarded for their work—not punished by bad trade deals.
I’ll stand against any agreement that undercuts Mississippi farmers, and I’ll fight for trade deals that put our farmers and our economy first.
Mississippi has built a proud reputation in agriculture, growing crops like corn, cotton, soybeans, rice, and more.
I know how critical our family farmers are to this legacy, and I’ll always have their backs.
Building a Better Future for Mississippi Like so many of you, I’m tired of seeing Mississippi ranked last or next-to-last—whether it’s income, health, education, or opportunity.
But here’s what we do have going for us: Mississippi is affordable, and our people know how to work hard.
That’s something we can build on.
We need to attract new industries and businesses to invest in our communities—because their dollars will go further here, and they’ll find a workforce eager to train, grow, and succeed.
When we give people a real chance to improve their lives, they show up and put in the work.
As your next Senator, I’ll focus on bringing good-paying jobs to every corner of Mississippi—especially the areas that have been left behind.
Here’s how I plan to do it: Encourage business investment in Mississippi communities to create stable, good-paying jobs.
Support federal legislation that lowers our unemployment rate and delivers economic opportunities to working families.
Invest in education and skills training , especially in trades and frontline careers that power today’s global economy.
Launch a Year 10 Apprenticeship Program (YTAP) to give high school students the chance to gain practical work experience.
Under this program, 15- and 16-year-olds would work with local businesses in summer apprenticeships—building skills and receiving real feedback that can shape their futures.
We have the talent, the determination, and the heart to build a better Mississippi.
Now we just need leadership that believes in us—and I do.

removed: top of page DONATE VOLUNTEER HOME ABOUT TY ISSUES FULCRUM PRESS RELEASES VOTE TRANSPARENCY All Posts Search Pinkins announces campaign for US Senate Jan 9, 2024 1 min read Pinkins resumes campaign from last year Grant McLaughlin, Mississippi Clarion Ledger Ty Pinkins on Monday announced his campaign to run for the United States Senate and said he hopes to focus on three key issues during his campaign: healthcare, education and the economy.
“I am running because I am concerned about the direction in which our country is going,” Pinkins said during a press conference at the Mississippi State Capitol Building.
“Families are struggling to make ends meet because life is more expensive for Mississippians.

Women’s reproductive rights are under attack by politicians and unelected judges, and our very democracy is being threatened by those who wish to tear down the institutional safeguards provided by our Founding Fathers that have guided us for centuries.” Pinkins previously announced his bid for the Senate in January 2023, but also ran for Secretary of State this past year against Republican incumbent Michael Watson, replacing Democratic candidate Shuwaski Young, who dropped out in August due to health reasons.
Pinkins said if elected to the United States Senate, he hopes to expand Medicaid in Mississippi, which could provide government-funded health insurance for millions of Mississippians.
Pinkins also hopes to one day create more higher-paying jobs for Mississippians, as well as provide more funding for public schools in Mississippi to create a better education for students.

added: October 12, 2026 The Honorable Don Huffines Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts P.O.
Box 13528 Austin, Texas 78711-3528 RE: Investigation of the El Paso Independent School District Under Tex.

Tax Code § 111.003; Request for Selection Criteria, Statutory Basis, and Distribution of the Report Dear Comptroller Huffines: I represent House District 77, home to more than a third of the residents served by the El Paso Independent School District (“EPISD”).
I write about the investigation of EPISD that your office opened at the Governor’s request, and I write now, before your report issues, so the record it will be judged against is complete.
The investigation rests on a statute written for another purpose, a statistic that does not measure what it is said to measure, and a selection that no stated criterion explains.
On each point, the State’s own records answer the question this investigation claims to ask.

THE INVESTIGATION BEGAN ON THE GOVERNOR’S CAMPAIGN CALENDAR On August 19, 2026, the Governor held a campaign event in El Paso1 and criticized EPISD’s spending.2 That same day, invoking Tax Code § 111.003(a)(1) and (2), he asked your office to investigate the spending of up to four independent school districts and to deliver a final report to his office by December 31, 2026.3 Your office announced the review the same day4 and, on October 5, named EPISD, Austin ISD, Prosper ISD and Barbers Hill ISD.5 The Governor supplied one selection standard: “up to four ISDs of varying size and geographic location.”6 Your office’s August 19 announcement also excludes districts “led by state-appointed boards.”7 Neither says anything about spending.
Your office’s announcements add no other criteria, and 1 Daniel Perez, El Paso ISD Among Four Texas School Districts Selected for State Spending Review, El Paso Matters (Oct.
Abbott Blames EPISD’s Financial Woes on “Bloated” Bureaucracy, El Paso Times (Aug.
Greg Abbott to Comptroller Don Huffines (Aug.
Accounts, News Release, Texas Comptroller Don Huffines to Launch Performance Review of School Districts’ Spending (Aug.
Accounts, News Release, Texas Comptroller Huffines Selects School Districts for Performance Review (Oct.
Capital Office: E2.312 | PO Box 2910 | Au stin, TX 78768 District Office: 100 N.

Ocho a | Suite A | El Paso, TX 79901 a Texas Education Agency spokesperson has said the agency will play no role in the reviews.8 The report is due eight weeks after the November 3 general election, and the statute requires that it go to one person: the Governor.9 II.

THE GOVERNOR’S “104 PERCENT” IS A PER-STUDENT FIGURE The Governor has said that EPISD’s administrative costs rose 104 percent from FY2015 to FY2025 while its enrollment fell 21 percent.10 He has identified neither the source nor the measure.

The figure matches TEA’s financial data exactly when measured one way: General Administration spending per student.11 EPISD spent $9,872,122 on General Administration (function 41) in FY2015 and $15,964,257 in FY2025, an increase of 61.7 percent before inflation.
Over the same decade its enrollment fell from 60,556 to 47,994.
Divided among 47,994 students instead of 60,556, the larger total becomes a 104 percent increase per student, from $163 to $333.
More than 40 points of the Governor’s figure measure children who left the district, not dollars it spent.
Declining enrollment is a genuine fiscal problem, and EPISD must solve it.
But the cost of a payroll office, an external audit and state compliance reporting does not fall in proportion to enrollment.
Presenting that result as proof of waste misstates what the number measures.
UNDER THE STANDARD THE STATE BUILT WITH YOUR OFFICE, EPISD EARNS FULL CREDIT Texas already measures a school district’s administrative cost.

The Legislature directed the Commissioner of Education, “in consultation with the comptroller,” to develop the financial accountability rating system for every school district in the State.12 That system, School FIRST, measures administrative cost in indicator 13: Instructional Leadership (function 21) plus General Administration (function 41), divided by total expenditures net of recapture.
For a district of EPISD’s size, full credit is awarded at or below 4.50 percent.13 EPISD’s FY2025 ratio is 4.20 percent.

TEA did not score indicator 13 for any district in the 2025-26 ratings, so this figure is my office’s calculation, applying TEA’s formula to TEA’s own financial data.14 Among the 114 districts in TEA’s largest size class, EPISD ranks 30th lowest; the median is 4.59 percent, and 84 districts spend a larger share on administration.15 Tested against a ratio TEA published for another district, this method produced a figure about 0.4 points higher than TEA’s own.
In that test it erred against the district, not in its favor.
The same system grades financial management as a whole.

For rating year 2025-26, based on FY2025 data, TEA rated EPISD “A = Superior Achievement,” with a score of 92.16 The State graded EPISD’s finances superior for FY2025, the final year of the period the Governor cited.

Ocho a | Suite A | El Paso, TX 79901 District Administrative cost ratio (TEA indicator 13 formula, FY2025) Administrative spending per student TEA FIRST rating, 2025-26 (score) Prosper ISD 3.93% $424 A, Superior (94) El Paso ISD 4.20% $474 A, Superior (92) Barbers Hill ISD 4.27% $635 A, Superior (100) Austin ISD 4.67% $604 B, Above Standard (88) Sources: Texas Education Agency; House District 77 analysis.
Two of your four selections, EPISD and Prosper ISD, rank 30th and 20th lowest among the 114 large districts.
Barbers Hill ISD falls in the next size class, where its 4.27 percent sits well inside the 5.50 percent full-credit line.
NO SPENDING CRITERION EXPLAINS THE SELECTION If administrative cost were the test, EPISD would not have been chosen.
Of the 84 large districts that spend a larger share on administration than EPISD, your office selected one: Austin ISD.

Four of them, Houston ISD, Beaumont ISD, La Joya ISD and Fort Worth ISD, are led by state-appointed boards and fall under your office’s exclusion.17 No announced rule excludes the other 79, including Crowley ISD (7.17 percent), Frenship ISD (6.56 percent), Abilene ISD (6.04 percent), Waco ISD (5.84 percent), Tomball ISD (5.55 percent), Grapevine-Colleyville ISD (5.54 percent), Goose Creek CISD (5.24 percent) and Garland ISD (5.16 percent).

Nine of those 84 districts also hold a lower 2025-26 TEA financial rating than EPISD’s A: they spend more on administration and score lower on the State’s own measure of financial integrity.18 For 46 of the 84, the House member who represents the largest share of the district is a Republican.
Not one of those 46 was selected.
The spending data does not distinguish EPISD from the 79 eligible districts your office passed over.
The calendar does: the Governor campaigned in El Paso on the day he requested this investigation.

SECTION 111.003 IS A REVENUE-LAW STATUTE, AND NO REVENUE LAW HAS BEEN IDENTIFIED Section 111.003 appears in the Tax Code’s chapter on collection procedures, and the Governor invoked two of its subsections.

Subsection (a)(1) authorizes your office, at the Governor’s request, to “investigate the books and accounts of assessing and collecting officers of the state and other officers or persons receiving, disbursing, or possessing public funds.”19 Subsection (a)(2) adds that your office shall “perform other duties and make investigations in relation to public funds as requested by the governor.”20 The Governor did not invoke § 111.003(a)(3), the only provision that reaches an institution’s “policies, management, and operation.”21 Whichever subsection is invoked, the report the statute requires is the same, and it is built around the revenue laws.
For every investigation “requested under Subsection (a),” the report must describe “each 17 Tex.
Agency, Board of Managers, Districts Under an Appointed Board of Managers (accessed Oct.
Capital Office: E2.312 | PO Box 2910 | Au stin, TX 78768 District Office: 100 N.

Ocho a | Suite A | El Paso, TX 79901 violation of the revenue laws” and “the failure, if any, to enforce revenue laws,” and it must include “the name of each person reasonably believed to have committed a violation or to have been guilty of nonfeasance.”22 Any person connected with the public service must submit all books, records and accounts “without delay.”23 And if the report “indicates a violation of revenue laws or neglect of duty, the governor shall notify the attorney general, who shall institute criminal and civil proceedings.”24 Neither the Governor’s request nor your office’s announcements identify a revenue law EPISD is alleged to have violated.

The concern the Governor’s letter describes is whether dollars “directly reach students, classrooms, and teachers, instead of being absorbed by central-office growth, administrative bloat, consultants, and the web of noninstructional bureaucracy.”25 That is a question about how a district allocates its budget, not about the assessment or collection of state revenue.
When a district does not amend its budget as Education Code § 44.006 requires, that is a governance lapse, and EPISD’s is documented below.
I am aware of no authority treating it as a violation of the revenue laws.
Your office’s announcements call this a performance review.
The statute it rests on describes an investigation that ends in the naming of individuals and a mandatory referral for prosecution.
Either your office believes a school district’s budget practices are a matter for criminal prosecution, or it is using a prosecutorial statute to conduct a performance review.
The Legislature has addressed the second case directly.

THE LEGISLATURE HAS ALREADY PRESCRIBED HOW THE STATE REVIEWS A SCHOOL DISTRICT Since January 2004, the Government Code has assigned performance reviews of school districts to the Legislative Budget Board.

Section 322.016 authorizes the Board to “review the effectiveness and efficiency of the operations of school districts,” at its discretion or on the request of the school district, and a district may make that request “only by resolution adopted by a majority of the members of the board of trustees of the district.”26 The Board must file its report with the district, the Governor, the Lieutenant Governor, the Speaker, the Commissioner of Education and the chairs of the House and Senate committees with jurisdiction over public education, and it must make the entire report available to the public on the Internet.27 Section 322.016 gives the Governor no role in initiating a review.
Only the Board or the district’s own trustees may do so.28 None of those protections applies to an investigation under § 111.003, which reports to the Governor alone.

When a general provision conflicts with a special one, the Code Construction Act requires that the two be construed, if possible, so that effect is given to both; if the conflict is irreconcilable, the special provision prevails unless the general provision is the later enactment and the manifest intent is that the general provision prevail.29 Section 322.016 is both the special provision and the later enactment.
Read together, the two statutes divide the work: § 111.003 reaches violations of the revenue laws, and § 322.016 governs reviews of the effectiveness and efficiency of school district operations.
Capital Office: E2.312 | PO Box 2910 | Au stin, TX 78768 District Office: 100 N.
Ocho a | Suite A | El Paso, TX 79901 into whether a district spends too much on administration is the second kind of review, and the Legislature has said who conducts it and who receives the results.
Your office’s own 1999 review of EPISD shows what a school performance review looks like when a district asks for one.
It was conducted at the superintendent’s request, with the endorsement of thenState Senator Eliot Shapleigh.

The review team spent more than seven months on the work, made 142 recommendations, and delivered its report to the Governor, the Lieutenant Governor, the Speaker and every member of the Legislature.30 The present investigation allows less than three months.

The Governor’s own letter says the work must be completed “before the legislative session to provide information necessary to consider appropriate actions and reforms,”31 and on August 19 you said, “We will . . . report our findings to the Legislature and the people of Texas.”32 Nothing in § 111.003 requires it.
The statute directs the report to the Governor alone and says nothing of the Legislature.33 VII.
THE LEGISLATURE HAS BARRED A FIXED CLASSROOM-SPENDING TEST The Governor’s letter frames this investigation around whether dollars reach classrooms instead of administration.
The Legislature has written that test out of the State’s financial accountability system.

The system “may not include an indicator . . . or any other performance measure that” requires a district to spend “at least 65 percent or any other specified percentage of district operating funds for instructional purposes,” or that lowers a district’s rating for failing to do so.34 If your report measures EPISD against a classroom-spending percentage, it will apply a standard the Legislature has barred from the State’s own rating system.
EPISD IDENTIFIED ITS OWN LAPSES BEFORE THE STATE ARRIVED EPISD’s budget problems are already on the public record, because the district’s own oversight put them there.

The district’s FY2025 audit found spending in excess of the board-adopted budget, without the amendments Education Code § 44.006 requires, in eight general-fund functions: instruction; instructional resources and media services; curriculum and instructional staff development; school leadership; guidance, counseling and evaluation services; student transportation; extracurricular activities; and facilities maintenance and operations.35 General administration is not among them, and the general fund as a whole finished the year $5.4 million under budget.36 The district’s outside finance consultants projected a $47.6 million decline in fund balance for FY2026, against the $6.1 million decline in the adopted budget.37 The superintendent has said that the district “was not rightsized to align with enrollment trends” and that “we have taken a close look at every central office position and made significant reductions.”38 Those lapses were identified locally, by the district’s auditors, its consultants and its board, and the corrections began before your office was asked to act.
The board hired a new superintendent on 30 Tex.

Dist., Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, Fiscal Year 2025, at 24.
37 MoakCasey, Presentation to the El Paso ISD Board of Trustees, “Where We Are Now,” at 4 (May 19, 2026).

Ocho a | Suite A | El Paso, TX 79901 December 9, 2025.39 The district reports reductions of 326 central-office and non-campus positions.40 The board president has reported that a projected $37 million shortfall for 2026-27 was reduced to $4.3 million by the time the budget was adopted in June.41 The State did not uncover any of this.
It arrived after the work was underway.

INFORMATION REQUESTED So that the Legislature and the public can evaluate the report on its merits, I request that your office provide the following in writing within fourteen days of the date of this letter: 1.
The criteria and data used to select EPISD, and the basis for passing over the 79 eligible large districts with higher administrative cost ratios.
Each revenue law, by citation, that your office contends EPISD may have violated.
The definitions of “administrative” and “instructional” spending your office is applying, by PEIMS function code, and an explanation of any difference from TEA’s indicator 13.
Whether the report will measure any district against a specified percentage of spending for instructional purposes, notwithstanding Education Code § 39.082(c).

Whether EPISD will receive the draft findings, and whether its written response will be published in the final report, as State Auditor’s Office reports publish the responses of the entities they audit.
Whether the findings will distinguish conditions that predate the superintendent’s appointment on December 9, 2025 from the corrective actions taken since.
Whether any referral to the Attorney General under § 111.003(d) is contemplated.

Whether the complete report, including any names identified under § 111.003(b)(3), will be delivered to the district, the Legislature and the members of the El Paso delegation on the same day it is delivered to the Governor, and posted in full on the Internet.

added: Español ☰ Home Meet Vince The Record Priorities Fair Maps Newsroom Services Contact Donate Press Release · October 12, 2026 Rep.

Perez Challenges State Investigation of El Paso ISD Abbott’s Comptroller passed over 79 districts that spend a larger share on administration; EPISD holds TEA’s top financial rating and ranks 30th lowest of 114 large districts EL PASO, TX — State Representative Vince Perez (D-El Paso) today sent a letter to Texas Comptroller Don Huffines challenging the State’s investigation of the El Paso Independent School District (EPISD).

Using the State’s own records, the letter shows that EPISD’s administrative spending meets the Texas Education Agency’s standard and that the law behind the investigation was written for tax collection.
On August 19, Governor Greg Abbott held a campaign event in El Paso and criticized EPISD’s spending.
That same day, he asked the Comptroller to investigate up to four school districts, and the Comptroller’s office announced the review.
On October 5, the Comptroller named EPISD, Austin ISD, Prosper ISD and Barbers Hill ISD.
The only selection rules announced were districts “of varying size and geographic location,” leaving out those run by state-appointed boards.
The report is due December 31, eight weeks after Election Day, and the only person the law requires it to go to is the Governor.
Accountability only means something if the rules are the same for everyone.
By the State’s own measure, 79 eligible districts spend a larger share on administration than El Paso ISD, and none of them was chosen.
El Paso taxpayers deserve to know why their district was. — Rep.
Vince Perez The letter lays out what the State’s own records show: EPISD is under the State’s own benchmark for administrative costs.
Perez’s office applied the Texas Education Agency’s formula for administrative costs to TEA’s own data.
In 2024-25, 4.20 percent of EPISD’s spending went to administration.
TEA gives large districts full credit at 4.50 percent or less.
EPISD ranks 30th lowest of the 114 largest districts in Texas.
The State rates EPISD’s finances superior.
TEA’s 2025-26 financial rating for EPISD is an A, Superior Achievement, with a score of 92.
Dozens of districts spend more on administration and were not chosen.
Eighty-four large Texas districts spend a larger share on administration than EPISD.
The Comptroller chose one of them, Austin ISD.
Four others are run by state-appointed boards, which the Comptroller excluded.
The remaining 79 were passed over, including eight with a lower TEA financial rating than EPISD.
In 46 of the 84, the state representative for the largest part of the district is a Republican.
The Governor’s “104 percent” counts students who left.
EPISD enrolled 12,562 fewer students in 2024-25 than in 2014-15.
Statewide, Texas public schools lost 76,613 students in a single year, from 2024-25 to 2025-26.
When enrollment drops, the basic work of running a district does not shrink with it: payroll still has to be processed, books audited and state reports filed.
EPISD’s general administration spending rose 62 percent over ten years before inflation.
Divided among fewer students, that became a 104 percent increase per student, from $163 to $333.
More than 40 points of the Governor’s figure are children who left, not dollars spent.
The law being used was written for tax collection.
Tax Code Section 111.003 sits in the Tax Code’s chapter on collection procedures.
A report under it must list violations of the State’s revenue laws and name the people believed responsible.
If the report finds a violation, the Governor must send it to the Attorney General for prosecution.
Neither the Governor nor the Comptroller has named a revenue law EPISD is alleged to have broken.
The Legislature already decided who reviews school districts.
Since 2004, state law has assigned school district performance reviews to the Legislative Budget Board.
The Board can start a review on its own or when a district’s trustees vote to request one, and its reports go to the district, the Governor, legislative leaders and the public.
The Governor has no role in starting one.
The Comptroller’s last review of EPISD, in 1999, was requested by the district’s superintendent, took more than seven months and went to every member of the Legislature.
By the State’s own measures, El Paso ISD spends a smaller share on administration than 84 other large districts, and TEA grades its finances superior.
If spending were the test, El Paso wouldn’t be on this list.
The Comptroller owes El Paso families an explanation of what the test was. — Rep.
Vince Perez EPISD’s own auditors, outside consultants and board identified the district’s budget problems, and general administration was not among the areas its audit found over budget.
The board hired Superintendent Brian Lusk in December 2025.

He has said the district “was not rightsized to align with enrollment trends” and that “we have taken a close look at every central office position and made significant reductions.” The district reports cutting 326 central-office and non-campus positions, and it reduced a projected $37 million shortfall for 2026-27 to $4.3 million.
That work was underway before the Governor asked the Comptroller to act.

The letter asks the Comptroller to answer eight questions in writing within 14 days, including how EPISD was chosen, which revenue law the district is alleged to have broken, whether a referral to the Attorney General is being considered, and whether the full report will go to the Legislature and the public on the same day it goes to the Governor.
In August, Huffines said his office would “report our findings to the Legislature and the people of Texas.” Read the full letter (PDF) ### Media contact: Jose M.
Landeros · info@vinceperez.com Vince Perez is State Representative for House District 77 in El Paso.
He serves on the influential House Ways and Means Committee as well the committees on Higher Education and Local, Consent, and Resolutions Calendars.
He is the former El Paso County Commissioner for Precinct 3 and was named the 2016 County Leader of the Year by American City & County Magazine.

added: Search Menu Skip to content Home Cindy In Indy Donate/Contact/Volunteer Meet Cindy On The Issues:Facts over Politics 2nd Amendment & Gun Violence A Right to Life Agriculture Economic Development/Workforce Education Energy Healthcare On The Issues:Facts over Politics I believe good public policy begins with facts, not politics.
We all have personal beliefs and values that shape our perspectives, and I am no exception.
I am firmly pro-life, support school choice, and believe in protecting our Second Amendment rights.
But having principles does not mean being unwilling to consider other perspectives.
I believe it is my responsibility to examine the facts, listen to all sides, challenge my own assumptions, and understand the potential consequences of every decision.
My goal is not to approach every issue without convictions, but to approach every issue with an open mind, informed judgment, and a commitment to serving the people I represent.

From rising electric bills and utility regulations to consumer choice, renewable energy, and the growing demand from data centers, these are complicated issues that deserve thoughtful discussion.
I’ve created this series of videos to break down these topics, explain how energy policies affect your wallet, and explore potential solutions.
My goal is to provide the facts, examine different perspectives, and give you the information you need to form your own opinions and make your voice heard.
An informed public is an empowered public.

removed: Search Menu Skip to content Home Cindy In Indy Donate/Contact/Volunteer Meet Cindy On The Issues 2nd Amendment & Gun Violence A Right to Life Agriculture Economic Development/Workforce Education Healthcare Mental Health/Substance Abuse Mental Health/Substance Abuse Indiana’s 2022-2023 Budget Addressing Mental Health Needs Restored full funding for mental health programs, including Recovery Works, and appropriates an additional $100M over the biennium to fund mental health initiatives Provided $40M each year in additional funding to increase hourly pay to $15 per hour for Direct Service Providers who serve individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities Increased funding for sexual assault victims’ assistance by 33%, or about $500K per fiscal year Restored the CHOICE In-Home Services appropriation Millions of people in the U.S. are affected by mental illness each year .
Mental illness has wide-reaching effects on people’s education, employment, physical health, and relationships.
Although many effective mental health interventions are available, people often do not seek out the care they need.
It’s important to understand how common mental illness is, so we can understand its physical, social, and financial impact.
21 % of U.S. adults experienced mental illness in 2020 (52.9 million people).
This represents 1 in 5 adults.
1,129,000 adults in Indiana have a mental health condition, which is 4X the population of Fort Wayne.
4.6% of U.S. adults experienced serious mental illness in 2020 (11.4 million people).
This represents 1 in 25 adults.
18 % of U.S. youth aged 6-17 experienced a mental health disorder in 2020 (7.7 million people).
This represents 1 in 6 youth ages 6-17.
90,000 Hoosiers ages 12–17 have depression.

6.7 % of U.S. adults experienced a co-occurring substance use disorder and mental illness in 2020 (17 million people) In 2020 suicide was the second leading cause of death for people ages 10-14 and 25-34 .
Those with mental illness used to be institutionalized and when those institutions started being dismantled, mental health issues became largely criminalized.
It is time to stop using jails and prisons as default mental health facilities.
Instead, we should divert non-violent offenders with mental illness and substance use disorders into treatment instead of incarceration.
This would save lives, foster recovery, and reduce costs.
We should also invest in community-based treatment that keeps people with mental illness out of jail in the first place and ultimately saves taxpayer money.
Addiction Does not Discriminate Addiction is considered a mental health issue, and many times the underlying cause of addiction is a mental health disorder such as anxiety, depression, PTSD or ADHD.

The challenge of addiction affects all of us, from the nearly 700 babies born annually with effects of addiction to the child welfare, criminal justice and healthcare systems that are strained under the burden of the addiction crisis.
There is unprecedented momentum at the state and local levels to make conquering opiate addiction, which includes heroin and prescription painkillers, a top priority.
We also cannot ignore and must address the recent increase in methamphetamine use.
Individuals using methamphetamine have reported this it is cheaper, safer (the risk of overdose is not as high) , and more accessible then heroin.
According to Indiana’s drug intelligence officers local meth labs are no longer common as the Mexican drug cartel is providing a cheaper more potent alternative.
In order to combat substance abuse in Indiana we must first must build awareness while reducing stigma.
Secondly we must increase access to harm reduction services which includes decriminalization.
Decriminalization is not the same as legalization.
We must set into place policy that allows people who are addicted to drugs to get help from the state without entering the penal system.
Finally, Indiana desperately needs more trained professionals equipped to treat substance abuse, including psychiatrists, psychiatric nurse practitioners and primary care providers.
We must make it a priority to increase the number of such providers, as well as create easier access to medication-assisted treatment.

removed: Vote Dave Paul Search for: About Contact Gallery Contribute Events Issues Community Investments Endorsements Home Campaign Educator to run for State House Home Campaign Educator to run for State House Educator to run for State House By district10rep-admin | March 25, 2018 | Campaign | No Comments Dave Paul is a longtime educator and champion for children, public schools, active military and veterans, sustainable economic growth, and the environment FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE CONTACT: Dave Paul (360) 632-2081 OAK HARBOR – Longtime local educator Dave Paul today announced his campaign for Washington State House of Representatives in the 10 th Legislative District.
He is running for the seat currently held by Dave Hayes.
Paul currently is a vice president at Skagit Valley College where he has worked for the last 10 years.
During his tenure, he’s managed a staff of 80 employees, served 5600 students, and managed state, grant and student budgets of $5.5 million.
In the community, he serves on the board of directors for the Oak Harbor Educational Foundation and is currently the President of the organization.
“The engine of our economy starts in our classrooms,” Paul said.

“For a strong economy, our children must have quality public schools, and offer them opportunities for higher education so they can compete for the jobs of tomorrow.” Ensuring that our education system is strong is central to why Paul is running.
Unfortunately, instead of addressing the problem like adults, incumbents in the state legislature used the issue to raise property taxes.
That was a mistake, and it has resulted in even greater funding inequities across our state.
Instead, we should find a more balanced approach.
While at Skagit Valley College, Paul is particularly proud of his work in supporting veterans, active duty military and Department of Defense employees.
He led efforts to expand support for veteran students at the college, including the creation of the Veteran Student Center, the hiring of Vet Corp staffers, and formation of a student Vet Club.
He also implemented the Student Career Experience Program (SCEP) for the Department of Defense to allow current military and DoD employees to earn an Associate Degree or certificate.
“We must honor our military and veterans by helping them transition into high quality jobs when they get home.
There’s no better way to do that by ensuring educational opportunities are available to them,” he said.
Other accomplishments of Paul at Skagit Valley College include making the campus more environmentally sustainable, resulting in lower energy costs and a savings to students and taxpayers.
He also led efforts to expand outreach of financial aid to community groups, resulting in more students being able to attend college who wouldn’t have been able to afford it before.
Raised in rural Washington, Dave graduated from Seattle University, received a masters degree from Miami University (Ohio) and a doctorate from University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

Paul and his wife, Rachel Anderson Paul, live in Oak Harbor with their four children (Jacob, Elizabeth, Eli, and Abigail), where they enjoy kayaking, gardening, hiking, and catching salmon from the beach.

Pinckney Hate Crimes Act This proposed legislation would establish a statewide hate crime law by increasing penalties for certain offenses when they are committed because of bias against a victim’s identity, such as race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, or disability.

Pinckney, who was killed in the Charleston church shooting, the act primarily works through “penalty enhancements,” meaning the punishment for an existing crime, like assault or vandalism, would be more severe if it is proven to be motivated by hate.
Some versions of the bill also include provisions allowing victims to seek civil damages.

South Carolina Medicaid Protection and Expansion Act This bill seeks to fully expand Medicaid eligibility under the Affordable Care Act by allowing low-income adults earning up to about 138% of the federal poverty level to qualify for coverage, significantly increasing access to healthcare for uninsured residents.

It also proposes creating a “Medicaid Stability Fund” to help manage costs and protect the program from potential federal funding changes, while requiring studies on the economic and health impacts of expansion in coordination with hospitals and health systems.
The South Carolina Lactation Support Act This legislation aims to protect and support breastfeeding mothers in the workplace.
The bill would require employers to provide reasonable break time and a private, non-bathroom space for employees to express breast milk during the workday.

It is designed to promote maternal and infant health by making it easier for working mothers to continue breastfeeding after returning to work, while also setting clear expectations for employers to accommodate these needs.
This bill became the foundation for the federal PUMP for Nursing Mothers Act.

We’re excited to announce that applications for the Jennifer Davis for Congress Internship Program are now open!

Jennifer Davis — tech entrepreneur, mom of 10, political outsider, and Republican nominee for Illinois’ 8th Congressional District — is running to bring common-sense business practices, family-first values, and real results to Congress.
We’re done with career politicians, government overreach, crushing costs, and policies that hurt families, limit opportunity, and push out small businesses.
This summer, we’re looking for students ready to gain real-world experience and help deliver meaningful change.

Program Overview Duration: Flexible June–November 3rd 2026 (fulltime or part-time) Location: West Dundee HQ + select hybrid/remote roles Format: Hands-on work with mentorship and weekly team huddles Stipend: Unpaid (college credit eligible); mileage reimbursed Visit for more information: www.votejenniferdavis.com What You’ll Do as an Intern You won’t be fetching coffee — you’ll be helping build a winning movement: Canvass neighborhoods and talk with voters Help run events, town halls, and rallies Create social content, graphics, and videos Research key issues and policy topics Support phone banking and digital outreach Assist with endorsements and volunteers Share ideas to grow our grassroots support How to Apply Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis — apply early for best placement!
2026 Internship Program Overview Committee Overview: We have several committees in our internship program.
Each committee will consist of a team ranging from 3 to 12 members.
Finance Committee - Opportunity to lead fundraising efforts and donor outreach.
Policy Point Committee - Research issues and create messaging that is consistent with the campaign.
Community Events Committee - Plan rallies, township meetings, meet & greets.
Field Team Committee - In charge of canvassing, tracking signs, and voter outreach.
Data and Outreach Committee - Phone banking, Data Organization, Produce Issue Research.
Communications Committee - Tracking and producing messaging for texts and emails.
Digital & Social Media Committee - Reshare content, create dialogue, contribute content.
Volunteer Recruitment Committee - Recruiting and Coordination.
Voter Support Committee - Helping people and listening to what matters most in their communities.
Coalition Building Committee - Coordinate coalition partners' participation in key campaign events.
GOTV Committee - Help voters get to the polls informed and ready to vote, and participate at the polls.
Research & Strategy - Opposition research, support the policy committee with contrast research and factual sourcing.
How to Apply Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis — apply early for best placement!

Volunteer Request a Lawn Sign Subscribe Contact Facebook X-twitter Instagram DONATE Corporate Landlords, California Apartment Association Send Mailers Against Jessie Lopez to AD-68 Residents October 14, 2026 Three weeks before the November 3 election, residents of California Assembly District 68, which includes Santa Ana, Orange, and Anaheim have already received several anti-Jessie Lopez mailers claiming she does not support low-income housing or housing in general.
Upon closer observation, these mailers were sent by corporate landlords from the California Apartment Association, California Association of REALTORS, and California Building Industry Association.
California’s housing debate isn’t just about who can afford a home, it’s also about who has the money and influence to shape housing policy.

Two major players are the California Apartment Association (CAA) and the California Association of REALTORS® (C.A.R.) , powerful real estate industry organizations that spend millions of dollars to influence elections and ballot measures.
Their political activity has been particularly visible in the fight over rent control.
In 2024, CAA sponsored the campaign opposing Proposition 33, which would have expanded local governments’ authority to enact rent control.

C.A.R. also helped fund the opposition, reporting a $22 million contribution from its Issues Mobilization PAC to the campaign opposing the measure. https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2024-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-33-expands-local-governments-authority-enact-rent-control-residential-property-initiative-statute https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/10/california-rent-control-propositions-campaign-money/ Beyond ballot measures, these organizations use political action committees and independent expenditures to support candidates and policies aligned with real estate industry priorities.

CAA’s independent expenditure committee explicitly campaigns for candidates who support the rental housing industry, while C.A.R. funds candidates and political causes that align with its policy goals. https://caanet.org/landing/independent-expenditure-committee/ https://www.car.org/aboutus/ourleadership/ouradvocacy Why does this matter to renters?
Decisions about rent control, eviction protections, and other tenant safeguards directly affect housing stability and affordability.

When well-funded industry groups invest heavily in elections and policy campaigns, voters deserve to know whose interests are being represented—and how campaign spending may shape the choices available to California communities.
Understanding who funds political campaigns is an important step toward holding elected officials accountable and building a housing system that works for the people who call California home.
Jessie Lopez helped champion and pass Santa Ana’s rent control and tenant protection measures, including the use of algorithms to artificially set rent fees.

Opponent David Penaloza voted against Santa Ana’s rent control measures and his State Assembly campaign has received a maximum donation from the California Apartment Association and California Real Estate PAC: Remember to check the bottom of mailers, TV commercials, and digital ads to see exactly who is funding them!

2026 HB76 (Sponsored): Demands transparency from large data centers by requiring strict reporting on high-volume water use.

2025 SB132 (Voted “Yes”): Protects Utah families from rising energy bills by requiring data centers and large energy users to pay for their own power through special utility contracts, third-party generators, or off-grid systems, preventing service costs from being passed on to residents.
2025 HB446 (Sponsored): Strengthens sovereign land leases to regulate mineral extraction and prevent excessive water depletion.
2026 HB348 (Sponsored): Tightens dedicated water right protections and closes regulatory gaps.
2026 HB410 (Sponsored): Establishes targeted programs to fund water leasing and preserve lake levels.
Leading by Example in Public Conservation: Served as floor sponsor on 2026 SB252 , requiring state and local government facilities to conserve outdoor water use and lead the way in water efficiency.

removed: All Articles Search Retirement Should Not Mean Being Priced Out clambton13 Jul 29 2 min read For seniors across Brewster, Dennis, and Yarmouth, affordability is about more than the price of groceries or the number on a property tax bill.
It is about whether someone who has spent decades building a life here can afford to remain here.
Too many older residents are being squeezed from every direction.
Property taxes and insurance costs are increasing.
Utilities, health care, home repairs, licenses, permits, and everyday town expenses continue to add up.
For retirees living on fixed incomes, even relatively small increases can become the difference between remaining independent and being forced to leave the community they call home.

That is why I am honored to have earned the endorsement of Mass Retirees , an organization that has spent decades fighting for the retirement security, health care, and economic dignity of public retirees.

Their work reflects a basic principle: retirement benefits should maintain their value, health care must remain affordable, and people who devoted their careers to public service should not find their security eroded year after year.
Mass Retirees has made improved cost-of-living adjustments and protection from rising health care costs central priorities.
Those fights matter deeply on Cape Cod, where the cost of remaining in the community is especially high.
But supporting seniors also requires action closer to home.
We should also examine the smaller costs that accumulate for older residents.
Towns should have the flexibility and state support to offer sensible senior reductions for appropriate licenses, permits, recreation programs, disposal services, and other municipal charges.
No single fee may appear overwhelming, but together they can place real pressure on someone living on a fixed retirement income.
Existing property tax relief must also be easier to understand and use.
Massachusetts offers a refundable Senior Circuit Breaker Tax Credit for eligible residents age 65 and older based on property taxes or rent paid.
Qualifying seniors may also have access to local exemptions or property tax deferrals, yet many residents do not know these programs exist or struggle to determine whether they qualify.
Reestablishing strong constituent services in this district is part of that work.

A state representative’s office should help seniors and their families navigate state agencies, understand available programs, and connect with local resources that can make later life more secure and sustainable.
State and local government should do more than create programs.
We should make sure eligible residents can actually find and use them.
That means clearer information, coordinated assistance through councils on aging, and simpler application processes.
Our seniors have worked, raised families, volunteered, paid taxes, and sustained these communities for decades.
They should not be treated as an afterthought in debates about housing and affordability.
A strong community allows people to remain connected to their neighbors, families, doctors, and daily routines as they grow older.
Aging in place should not be a privilege reserved for those with substantial financial resources.
It should be an attainable choice.

Learn More Technology should make work easier, not leave Pennsylvania workers behind while big companies pocket the savings.
I’ll fight to hold corporations accountable when they replace workers with AI or automation by requiring them to help fund retraining, job placement, and health coverage.

Workers deserve stronger layoff notice and severance protections, transparency when AI eliminates jobs, and the right to human review when automated systems make decisions affecting their jobs, benefits, or health care.
Progress shouldn’t come at the expense of working families, and companies that profit from replacing workers shouldn’t leave taxpayers to pick up the bill.

added: Make AI Pay Its Way I’m not against technology.
If AI makes your work easier, good for you.
But that’s not what’s happening at a lot of companies.
They’re using it to cut people loose, keep the savings, and hand the bill to the rest of us.
You’ve seen it at the grocery store.
There used to be four cashiers up front.
Now there’s one employee watching six self-checkout machines.
The company’s payroll went down and those workers lost their paychecks.
When they need unemployment, or Medicaid, or help finding something new, taxpayers cover it.
The company doesn’t pay a dime of that.
Here’s what I’ll fight for in Harrisburg.
Big companies that replace Pennsylvania workers with AI or automation should pay into a fund for those workers, based on how many jobs they cut and how much in wages.
That money goes to the people who got hurt: retraining, job placement, and help paying for health insurance so nobody loses coverage for their kids the same week they lose their job.
If a company took Pennsylvania tax breaks or grants to create jobs here and then swaps those workers out for machines, it pays the money back.
Federal law only requires 60 days’ notice for big layoffs, and plenty of layoffs don’t even count.
I want a stronger Pennsylvania law, with longer notice and severance, so nobody finds out they’re done when their badge stops working at the door.
When a company cuts jobs because of AI, it should have to say so publicly.
We deserve to know who’s doing it and how many people it’s hitting.
And a computer shouldn’t get the final say on your life.
Not on whether you’re fired, whether your insurance claim gets denied, or whether you get the state benefits you’re counting on.
You should know when AI made the call, and you should be able to have a real person review it.
Same goes for companies using software to track every bathroom break or quietly set your pay.
If you’re getting rich by replacing working people, you don’t get to stick the bill to them.

added: 0 Skip to Content Home About About CA5 Español Inicio Conoce A Michael Temas Issues Events News Endorsements Donate Open Menu Close Menu Home About About CA5 Español Inicio Conoce A Michael Temas Issues Events News Endorsements Donate Open Menu Close Menu Home Folder: About Back About CA5 Folder: Español Back Inicio Conoce A Michael Temas Issues Events News Endorsements Donate Joint Statement Regarding Incorrect Information in Calaveras County Voter Information Guides Oct 3 Written By Wyatt Nordvik [Modesto, CA] - 10/03/2026 - The Masuda for Congress Campaign issued a joint statement with the Jaron Brandon for State Senate Campaign regarding incorrect information printed and distributed in Calaveras County, California, voter information guides.

The Campaigns demand an immediate reprint of the voter guides, a public statement from the Calaveras County Elections Office, and the establishment of a ballot and voter guide proofing standard, which would allow campaigns to review documents prior to printing.
The Calaveras County Elections Office has not responded to our requests for comment.
“Our campaign is disappointed to find that inaccurate details regarding our platform and candidacy were printed in the voter guides sent to residents,” said Michael Masuda.
“Access to accurate, reliable information is essential for a fair and transparent election.

Voters should have confidence in our elections and we want to reassure voters that these errors do not reflect our official platform, positions, or filing data.” The Jaron Brandon for State Senate Campaign was also impacted.
“Voters deserve clarity and accurate information when they look at their official voter guides,” Jaron Brandon said.

“While administrative errors happen, our priority right now must be ensuring that every resident has the correct details.” The Masuda Campaign encountered similar issues in Calaveras County during the June 2 Primary and is urging the County to establish a process to identify and correct errors before ballots and voter guides are finalized to ensure such issues do not occur.
They are actively contacting local election officials throughout CA-5 to ensure correct materials are issued to the public as quickly as possible.

Voters seeking to verify their ballot details or review the official platforms of each campaign are encouraged to visit their authorized websites at votemasuda.com and votejaron.com or consult updated advisories published directly by the Calaveras County Elections Office.

added: 0 Skip to Content Home About About CA5 Español Inicio Conoce A Michael Temas Issues Events News Endorsements Donate Open Menu Close Menu Home About About CA5 Español Inicio Conoce A Michael Temas Issues Events News Endorsements Donate Open Menu Close Menu Home Folder: About Back About CA5 Folder: Español Back Inicio Conoce A Michael Temas Issues Events News Endorsements Donate Masuda Condemns Surge of ICE Operations in California Oct 9 Written By Wyatt Nordvik “The stories and videos of ICE and immigration enforcement officers that we are seeing across California and the Central Valley are appalling.
Right now, aggressive surges in ICE activity are accomplishing the exact opposite of keeping us safe.
Instead of going after ‘the worst of the worst’, ICE has been directed to target everyone indiscriminately.
They are going after hardworking parents, construction workers, farmworkers, and neighbors who have peacefully lived here for years and are just trying to go to work or school.
Citizens and legal residents, and people going through the legal process are also being detained.
These ICE raids do not make our neighborhoods safer.
They tear families apart, instill fear, and waste taxpayer dollars terrorizing law-abiding people instead of targeting criminals.
When our neighbors are too scared to drop their kids off at school, go to the doctor, or buy groceries, it hurts our entire community.
What’s more, this appears to be part of a broader effort to intimidate our marginalized communities from going to the polls this November.
Tom McClintock, Chair of the House Subcommittee on Immigration, has not only encouraged these brutal tactics, he has actively defended them.
He ignores serious violations of Constitutional rights by federal immigration officers and misleads the public about who is being detained, the vast majority of whom have no criminal record.
His disregard for basic decency and humane immigration enforcement is a cover for his failure to deliver comprehensive, common- sense immigration solutions for his own constituents.

As your representative, I will fight to fix our broken immigration system, hire more judges to clear the administrative backlog, and create fair, trustworthy pathways for people to secure work permits, legal status, and citizenship.

We must hold ICE leadership accountable, halt these destabilizing community sweeps, and ensure federal agencies focus strictly on real safety threats instead of terrorizing families.” Wyatt Nordvik Next Next Joint Statement Regarding Incorrect Information in Calaveras County Voter Information Guides Navigation Media Issues Volunteer California District 05 Endorsements Blog Contact Us Proudly paid for by Masuda for Congress‍ Committee ID #C00905133 Privacy Policy and Terms & Conditions

We fight to defeat politicians who take those rights away.

The Sierra Club Illinois Chapter was formed in 1959 as the Great Lakes Chapter with the mission to explore, enjoy, and protect Illinois.

Through the IFT’s Department of Political Activities, our union supports legislative policy and political objectives at the community, state and national levels.

Original map from Illinois House Dems redistricting site at https://ilhousedems.com/redistricting/ ( map ) Confirm your elected officials and districts at the IL Board of Elections map ( https://votemaura.tiny.us/ILElectedOfficials ) The Hirschauer family voted together for the Primary Election in March 2022.
Vote By Mail / Absentee voting Voting by mail has existed for many years as ‘Absentee’ voting.
It was expanded during the pandemic and Maura was proud to vote to codify this for future voters.
Click here to learn more about Vote by Mail in Illinois.
Learn more vote in-person early You can vote early in-person at a number of locations in each district.
Learn more vote in-person on election day, Nov 3 Election Day is now a holiday in Illinois.
This means that all government offices that are not election offices will be closed unless being used as a polling place.

removed: About Issues Events Vote Donate Contact Back Maura's Story Illinois District 49 Back Contact Maura Volunteer Yard Signs Candidate Endorsement Questionnaire Media Resources About Maura's Story Illinois District 49 Issues Events Vote Donate Contact Contact Maura Volunteer Yard Signs Candidate Endorsement Questionnaire Media Resources Candidate for 2020 Illinois House of Representative District 49 County Clerk Offices in the 49th District: DuPage County Clerk (Wheaton) 630-407-5500 dupagecounty.gov TRACK YOUR DUPAGE BALLOT Kane County Clerk (Geneva) 630-232-3400 clerk.kanecountyil.gov/Elections TRACK YOUR KANE BALLOT Cook County Clerk (Chicago) 312-603-0906 for Elections Department Suburban Cook County 312-603-0944 Vote By Mail: mail.voting@cookcountyil.gov website: cookcountyclerk.com TRACK YOUR COOK BALLOT Illinois State Board of Elections website Vote by Mail info at ISBE results County Election Results 〰️ County Election Results 〰️ County Election Results 〰️ It will be several weeks before results are finalized.
With the record numbers of early and mail-in voters and the mail-in ballots are still being counted, results are not as instantaneous as we'd like.
Local results can be found from each county clerk: DuPage County | Cook County | Kane County A single-date election day is a thing of the past.
Early Voting options are available and, I hope, become a more normalized approach to voting.
Our culture has moved toward on-demand services and utilizing early voting options means that voting can fit into most any schedule!
Applications The Vote by Mail application period for the 2024 General election ends Oct 31.
This is the last day an election authority can receive, by mail, your application for vote by mail.
We recommend doing this much earlier as the time to mail out your ballot to you may mean that you do not receive it in time to vote!
If you apply for Vote by Mail AND If you choose to vote early or on election day, you must bring and surrender your VBM Ballot and Return Envelope or you will be given a provisional ballot.
It's best to avoid this situation.
Ballots Ballots must be completed, SIGNED, and postmarked by or on election day.

Ballots can be refused if the election judges determine the signature does not match that on your registration, so I urge each constituent to send their ballot in EARLY to ensure it is accepted, and if not, that they have the opportunity to vote another way.
FAQ If I request my mail-in ballot, can I still choose to vote in person? or If I don’t get my ballot mailed in, or for whatever reason, can I still vote in person (early or day-of)?
If you received your vote by mail ballot, but want to vote in person, you will need to bring the Mailed ballot to your polling place and hand it in.
You will then be able to vote.
If you were mailed a ballot and you misplaced it, you must go to the polling place and sign an affidavit that says that you did receive it but lost it.
You will be given a provisional ballot.
What if I didn’t get my application?
You can find out how to apply to get a vote by mail ballot at your County Clerk’s website.
(Or Call them) What if I lose my vote by mail ballot?
You should go to vote in person.
You will be given a provisional ballot.
What if I get the ballot but change my mind and want to vote in person?
Bring your vote by mail ballot to the polling place and surrender the ballot to vote in person.
Can I fill out the Vote by Mail ballot and hand deliver it?
Yes.
You can bring it to the polling place on Election Day.
There will also be secure drop boxes provided by election authorities in each county.
What if I applied for a ballot and did not receive it in the mail?
Please contact your county clerk’s office for instructions.
How are we assured against fraud in the vote-by-mail process?
There is no evidence that mail ballots increase electoral fraud.
Several anti-fraud protections are built into the process.
Those who abuse mail ballots can be charged with election fraud and face fines or prison time.
If candidates believe there has been voter fraud, they can present evidence regarding a particular race to the election board or file a lawsuit in a local court.
Authorities review the evidence and decide if there has been actual fraud.
If there is sufficient evidence, local prosecutors can indict the relevant people for mail ballot fraud.
It is a criminal offense to forge a name on a mail ballot, impersonate someone else, steal ballots, or deceive someone about their mail ballot.
For years, military personnel stationed abroad have voted by absentee ballot with virtually no claims of election fraud.
The procedures that already are in use safeguard against abuse and ensure the integrity of the voting process.
The few cases of voter fraud that have been documented tend to be quite localized.
For example, in 2018, North Carolina Republicans were cited for election fraud involving mail ballots.

When you watch videos on our Site, third parties may also place "flash cookies" on your computer.
Deleting or rejecting browser cookies may not remove flash cookies, necessitating a visit to https://www.adobe.com/products/flashplayer/security to disable them.
Refusing cookies could impact certain Site features. ​ Our website utilizes third-party vendors like Google Analytics to analyze user behavior.
Google Analytics uses cookies to collect Internet log data and visitor behavior in an anonymous form.
This information helps us assess website usage and create statistical reports for the Committee to Elect Mike Hoadley.
Google Analytics operates anonymously, never associating your IP address with other data held by Google.
We do not link any data collected from the site with personally identifiable information unless you explicitly submit that information through a form.
This analytics tool reports website trends without identifying individual visitors.

To opt out of Google Analytics tracking across all websites you use, visit this Google page . ​ ​ Disabling Cookies: Your browser's "Help" section typically provides instructions on preventing cookie acceptance, receiving notifications of incoming cookies, and disabling cookies altogether.
Note that rejecting or blocking cookies may affect your ability to fully use our Site.
Web Beacons: Our Site pages and emails may include small electronic files known as web beacons, clear gifs, pixel tags, or single-pixel gifs.

These files allow us to count users who visit these pages, gather statistics about web page popularity, and verify system and server integrity. ​ SMS ​ When you opt-in to our service, we will send you an SMS message to confirm your signup. ​ You can cancel the SMS service anytime by texting "STOP." After you send "STOP," we will confirm your unsubscription.
Subsequently, you will not receive further SMS messages from us.
To rejoin, simply sign up as you did initially, and we will resume sending SMS messages to you.
If you forget the supported keywords, text "HELP," and we will respond with instructions on using our service and how to unsubscribe.
We can deliver messages to major mobile carriers, including AT&T, Verizon Wireless, Sprint, T-Mobile, MetroPCS, U.S.
Cellular, Alltel, Boost Mobile, Nextel, and Virgin Mobile.
Please note that carriers are not responsible for delayed or undelivered messages.
Message and data rates may apply, so it's advisable to contact your wireless provider for details.

For questions regarding this short code's services, you can email us at mikehoadleycampaign@gmail.com . ​ Information Use and Sharing ​ Use of Personal Information: Any personal information we collect is used exclusively for the purposes described during collection or as outlined in this Privacy Policy.

We may share this information with third parties under specific circumstances, such as when you authorize it, when necessary to provide products or services, or as required by law. ​ Use of Non-Personally Identifiable Information: Non-personally identifiable information may be utilized to tailor advertising and content, predict responses to ads, measure ad effectiveness, and provide aggregate reports.

Such information may be shared with third parties for marketing and promotional purposes. ​ We employ web analytics tools and technologies to enhance the Site's usability, identify and correct errors, and provide more relevant content and advertising.

This data is used in accordance with this Privacy Policy. ​ Third Party Use of Cookies: We use cookies to compile aggregate, non-personally identifiable data about Site traffic and interactions to improve user experiences.

We may also share this information with agencies, ad networks, or exchanges to analyze user behavior or customize ads you encounter. ​ Third Party Features ​ ​ Social Media Platforms and Websites: Any information, communications, or material submitted to our Site, such as on social media platforms (e.g., Facebook, Twitter), is done at your own risk without an expectation of privacy.
We cannot control the actions of other users on social media platforms and are not responsible for content or submissions on those platforms.

Be cautious about sharing personal information in public forums, as the information can be collected and used by unknown individuals. ​ If our Site includes interactive features, please be aware that your use of these features may involve publicly posting messages, content, or other information.
While we take precautions, your use of these features is at your own risk. ​ Email Signups ​ E-mail: We appreciate your questions and comments via email.
Messages are shared within our organization with the relevant team.

We may archive or discard messages, but your email address and message are used in line with this Privacy Policy. ​ Submitting Your Email: Providing your email address on the Site may result in its inclusion in the Committee to Elect Mike Hoadley's email list.
You can unsubscribe from our emails at any time by clicking the "unsubscribe" link in each email.

Your email address will be removed from our marketing list, with a reasonable timeframe for processing your request. ​ Suggesting the Site to a Friend: If you use a feature to suggest a page to a friend, we may request your friend's name and email address.
Our Site may automatically send your friend a one-time email inviting them to visit the Site.
We store and use this information in compliance with this Privacy Policy.
Your friend can contact us to remove this information from our databases. ​ Security ​ We employ technology and security measures to protect your personal information.
However, no internet data transmission is 100% secure.

While we strive to protect your data, we cannot guarantee the security of information transmitted to or received from us. ​ Opt Out ​ Overview: We may use non-personally identifiable information to provide more tailored online advertising and content.
If you wish to stop the collection of specific information for tailored online ads and messages, you can opt out here .
Opting out will place a cookie on your browser to indicate that we should not collect data for tailored advertising.
If you delete cookies, use a different browser, or change computers, you may need to revisit the opt-out page.

You can also visit the Digital Advertising Alliance site to opt out of interest-based advertising from other third parties using cookies. ​ Children ​ We strongly urge parents and guardians to monitor their children's online activities.

We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13. ​ Visiting from Outside the United States ​ If you visit our Site from outside the United States, please note that your information may be transferred, stored, or processed in the United States, where our servers are located.
